articles.title: Free corrige un bug qui faisait redémarrer la Freebox Delta en plein téléchargement
articles.text:
Free a déployé lundi une nouvelle mise à jour du Freebox Server, sixième version depuis le 5 novembre. En plus de correctifs de sécurité, elle corrige un problème de stabilité qui pouvait figer, puis faire redémarrer, la Freebox Delta.
C'est une énième mise à jour que l'opérateur Free a décidé de déployer ce lundi 23 novembre 2026. La version 4.13.8 du Freebox Server est disponible depuis midi aujourd'hui, pour les Freebox Revolution, Pop, Delta et Ultra. Free annonce des correctifs de sécurité et la correction d'un « problème de stabilité » propre à la Freebox Delta, à l'origine signalé par un abonné. Comme toujours, il faut redémarrer la box pour l'installer.
Une Freebox Delta qui gelait, puis redémarrait
Il y a quelques jours, un abonné Delta a décrit son problème sur le site de suivi des bugs de Free. Sa box se figeait une à quatre minutes, son interface ne répondait plus, puis redémarrait entièrement, en coupant au passage son réseau câblé pendant une bonne vingtaine de secondes. C'était arrivé cinq fois entre le 11 et le 15 novembre, toujours en soirée, et toujours pendant qu'un ordinateur de la maison, branché en Ethernet, téléchargeait de très gros fichiers depuis Hugging Face, la grande plateforme de modèles d'IA.
Pour l'abonné, le coupable, ce n'est pas la vitesse, mais le nombre de connexions. Comme beaucoup d'outils pensés pour aller vite, son logiciel ouvrait jusqu'à 64 connexions simultanées vers les serveurs, en quelques secondes, pour un débit de 1 à 1,5 Gbit/s. Ses essais vont dans ce sens. 24 minutes de téléchargement à un débit comparable, mais avec seulement un à quatre fichiers récupérés en parallèle, n'ont provoqué aucun plantage. Comme les températures et les ports réseau ne montraient rien d'anormal, il soupçonnait sa Freebox de s'essouffler à suivre autant de connexions ouvertes d'un coup, jusqu'à épuiser ses ressources.
L'autre indique était qu'une fois son logiciel limité à 22 connexions, il a récupéré 55,6 Go à environ 1 Gbit/s sans le moindre gel, lors d'un unique essai. Free l'a remercié le jour même, en reconnaissant ne pas avoir eu le temps de corriger le problème pour la version 4.13.7. L'opérateur a donc résolu le souci, sans en expliquer la cause.
Six versions des Freebox en moins de trois semaines
Décidément, les mises à jour des Freebox s'enchaînent à vitesse grand V. Après les versions estampillées 4.13.3, 4.13.4 et 4.13.5, publiées en 38 heures à partir du 5 novembre, la 4.13.6 avait réparé les enregistrements de chaînes comme TF1 et M6 et la console des machines virtuelles. La 4.13.7 du 16 novembre s'en tenait à la sécurité. La 4.13.8 est arrivée une semaine plus tard.
Pour profiter de la mise à jour, le plus simple reste de passer par l'application Free. Dans « Mes équipements Freebox », touchez « Server internet ». Sur sa fiche, la ligne « Version logicielle » affiche le numéro installé ; en la touchant, l'application indique si une mise à jour est disponible et propose un bouton « Mettre à jour ». La même fiche offre aussi un bouton « Redémarrer », et sans téléphone, le menu « Redémarrage » du boîtier fait l'affaire. Une fois la box relancée, la ligne doit en théorie afficher la version 4.13.8.

articles.title: Black Friday Australia laptop deals for 2026: score up to 52% off Lenovo, Apple, Dell, HP and more
articles.text:
Black Friday Australia laptop deals for 2026: score up to 52% off Lenovo, Apple, Dell, HP and more
I'm tracking the best Australian discounts and you can save a bundle on a new notebook for home, work or gaming
Black Friday falls on 27 November this year, and runs through to Cyber Monday on November 30, but Australian retailers are offering great early discounts on a huge range of laptops.
You can get a Windows machine with 16GB of RAM for under AU$900, and there are also deals on lightweight 2-in-1s through to high-end gaming laptops. Apple deals are also better than usual, with some great prices on refurbished MacBook Neos, or new models from Amazon.
As TechRadar Australia's resident laptop expert, I'm here to help. I've been keeping tabs on price changes across the entire year, so I can confidently tell you what's an actual good buy and filter out all the bad deals. I've been hunting Black Friday deals since the start of the month, as many device-makers started their sales early, and will be here till at least December 3.
If you’re still deciding what to buy, our guides to the best laptops in Australia and the best gaming laptops explain what to look for. It’s also worth checking our HP coupon codes and Lenovo coupon codes if you’re buying direct.
Top retailers for Black Friday laptop deals
- Lenovo: great deals on a wide range of everyday and gaming laptops
- Amazon: sparse but solid laptop deals
- JB Hi-Fi: big discounts on Apple laptops
- HP: take an extra 5% off with code FUTURE5
- Mwave: deals on major PC brands
- The Good Guys: great for MacBooks and Microsoft deals
- Apple: much loved laptops but few discounts when buying direct
After something else entirely? Check out our full coverage of Black Friday deals and get your Christmas shopping done before the rush.
Everyday laptop deals
The Aspire Lite is a budget Windows laptop with a 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 anti-glare screen and a weight of just 1.3kg. The Ryzen 3 and 8GB of RAM are fine for browsing and streaming, and the 256GB SSD is reasonable for the price.
The IdeaPad Slim 3x gives you a roomy 15.3-inch, 1920 x 1200 IPS display and 16GB of RAM at an affordable price. Its eight-core Snapdragon X is well suited to everyday multitasking, though it’s worth checking that any specialist apps or peripherals you rely on support Windows on Arm.
The Dell 15 is well equipped for the money, with a 10-core Intel Core i5-1334U and 16GB of RAM to handle everyday tasks and multitasking. Its 15.6-inch display pairs a 1920 x 1080 resolution with a 120Hz refresh rate for a smooth experience.
The HP OmniBook 3 is an affordable big-screen laptop with a 17.3-inch, 1920 x 1080 IPS display that’s a good fit for watching movies at home. The Intel Core 5 315 and 16GB of RAM can comfortably handle everyday multitasking, and the 512GB SSD gives you room for apps and media.
The OmniBook 5’s 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 OLED display covers the full DCI-P3 colour gamut, so it’s a good pick for editing photos as well as watching movies. At 1.33kg it’s easy to carry, and the Intel Core 5 320 and 16GB of RAM are well suited to everyday use.
MacBook deals
This Apple Certified Refurbished MacBook Neo is an affordable way into macOS and comes with a one-year Apple warranty. The A18 Pro and 8GB of memory suit everyday use, and the 13-inch, 2408 x 1506 display is sharp for a laptop in this price range. Buying refurbished gives a decent discount compared to buying it new for AU$1,049 from Apple.
The MacBook Neo hasn't seen much in the way of discounts yet (in fact, it has had a price rise), so this meagre 5% off is the best we have seen. Still, it's something at least, and it's well worth checking out our MacBook Neo review for the full scoop.
This Apple Certified Refurbished Neo has a 512GB SSD for keeping photos and apps on the laptop, plus Touch ID for signing in and approving purchases. The A18 Pro and 8GB of memory make it a good everyday Mac, and Apple includes a one-year warranty. Buying refurbished gives a decent discount compared to buying it new for AU$1,249 from Apple.
The MacBook Neo hasn't seen much in the way of discounts yet (in fact, it has had a price rise), so this meagre 4% off is not far off the best we have seen for the 512GB model with Touch ID. Still, it's something at least, and it's well worth checking out our MacBook Neo review for a deeper dive.
This is the cheapest option going if you want the M5 Air and with the 512GB SSD. Want to know more? Check out our MacBook Air M5 review.
Apple has raised prices, and we have seen very few discounts so far, making this minor drop worth considering. This is the upgraded Air with the 1TB SSD and M5 CPU with a 10-core GPU (rather than the base spec 8-core) that costs AU$2549 from Apple. Want to know more? Check out our MacBook Air M5 review.
The 16GB MacBook Pro currently has a small discount from Amazon compared to buying it for AU$3,199 from Apple. Read our Apple MacBook Pro M5 review for the full scoop.
Thin and light laptop deals
The Yoga Slim 7 weighs just 1.16kg, yet its 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 OLED display gives movies deep blacks and rich colours. The Core Ultra 5 226V and 16GB of RAM make it a capable everyday laptop for travel.
While we have seen it about AU$200 cheaper, the current discount on the Yoga Slim 7i Aura is not bad. It features the new Series 2 Intel Core Ultra 5 226V CPU, a compact 14-inch 1920 x 1200 OLED display, plus premium features like a facial recognition webcam and Wi-Fi 7. Want to know more? Check out our Lenovo Yoga Slim 7i Aura review.
This Snapdragon-powered laptop has an impressive spec for the price, with an X Elite X1E78100 CPU, 32GB of RAM and a 1TB SSD. It also has a very nice 2944 x 1840 OLED touchscreen display that outputs 100% of the sRGB gamut. We have seen this machine slightly cheaper, but it's still a good deal if its Windows on Arm compatibility suits the apps you use.
MSI packs a 13.3-inch, 2880 x 1800 OLED display into a laptop that weighs under a kilo. The 32GB of RAM and 1TB SSD give you room to tackle bigger projects on the go, such as editing a large photo library.
2-in-1 laptop deals
The 14-inch, 1920 x 1200 touchscreen folds back for tablet use, whether you’re reading or browsing. This HP-refurbished model has a Core i5 and 16GB of RAM that is a good fit for everyday multitasking.
The 14-inch OLED touchscreen folds back for tablet use, and the included pen is handy for handwritten notes or sketches. At 1.38kg it’s light enough to carry to class, and the Core Ultra 5 226V and 16GB of RAM give it the performance to be a capable everyday laptop.
This large-screen 2-in-1 from HP uses the Intel Series 2 Core Ultra 7 258V CPU, giving it a good mix of performance and battery life. The 16-inch laptop also has a 2880 x 1800 OLED touchscreen, 32GB of RAM, 1TB of storage, Wi-Fi 7, Thunderbolt 4 and a facial recognition webcam. We have seen it for slightly less, but this is still a pretty good price if you want a big premium 2-in-1.
Gaming laptop deals
The Victus is an entry-level gaming laptop with an RTX 4050 that’s well matched to its 15.6-inch, 1920 x 1080 display. The 144Hz refresh rate suits competitive games. Use BFDEAL at checkout to get the full discount.
The Cyborg 15 is an affordable option for 1080p gaming, with an RTX 5050 and a 15.6-inch, 144Hz display that suits fast-paced multiplayer games. The 16GB of RAM is a sensible starting point, though a few large game installs can easily fill the 512GB SSD.
The Lenovo LOQ Essential 15 is an affordable way to get RTX 5060 graphics, with a 15.6-inch, 1920 x 1080 display that refreshes at 144Hz for smooth play in fast-paced games. The main trade-off is the GPU’s 65W power limit, so expect lower frame rates in demanding games than you’d get from a higher-powered RTX 5060 laptop.
The Legion 5i gives its RTX 5060 up to 115W, a good match for playing demanding games at the 15.3-inch screen’s native 1920 x 1200 resolution. The 1TB SSD is a welcome inclusion at this price, especially if you keep several big games installed.
The Gaming A16 is a relatively affordable way to get an RTX 5070 and a 16-inch IPS screen in the same laptop. The 165Hz refresh rate suits competitive games, while the 1TB SSD gives you room for a mix of multiplayer favourites and larger single-player titles.
The Legion 5a’s 15.3-inch, 2560 x 1600 OLED display combines deep blacks with a 165Hz refresh rate, so it suits both atmospheric single-player games and fast shooters. The 32GB of RAM also gives you headroom for demanding tasks beyond gaming, such as video editing.
Intel’s 24-core i9-14900HX and 32GB of RAM make this Legion a good fit for heavier workloads beyond gaming, including video editing and 3D rendering. Its RTX 5070 drives a 15.1-inch, 2560 x 1600 OLED display with a 165Hz refresh rate.
The Raider pairs a 140W RTX 5070 Ti with 12GB of video memory with a 16-inch, 2560 x 1600 display that runs at 240Hz. That’s an appealing combination for high-detail gaming, though the 512GB SSD is small for a machine in this class.
The Pro model of one of our favourite Lenovo laptops has a reasonable discount on the RTX 5070 Ti variant. The pre-discount web price is beyond steep, but at this sale price it's decent enough value for a premium gaming machine with an OLED, 2560 x 1600, 165Hz display.
The Legion Pro 7i pairs a 175W RTX 5080 with a 16-inch, 2560 x 1600 OLED display, giving demanding games plenty of graphics power and the deep blacks that make dark scenes stand out. The 240Hz refresh rate also makes good use of the higher frame rates you can reach in competitive games.
The Infinity Y16 pairs a 175W RTX 5090 with a 16-inch, 2560 x 1600 display, making it a good pick for playing demanding games at high settings. The screen’s 300Hz refresh rate is particularly useful for competitive shooters, where the GPU can push much higher frame rates.
For those who want mighty gaming power, the Legion Pro 7i with an Intel Ultra 9 275HX processor and RTX 5090 GPU is one of the better options going, despite the painfully high cost compared to last year. There are very few comparable machines at this price, making it an excellent deal if you are willing to spend big. Read our review to learn more.
Black Friday Australia 2026 laptop deals are here
Morning all, and welcome to our live coverage of Black Friday laptop deals in Australia.
Black Friday officially lands on November 27 this year, but the sales have already started to roll in from the big brands and retailers. Some of them are genuinely great prices on machines I have been watching for months.
Others are... less impressive....
And that's what this live blog is here for. I spent the year tracking laptop prices and promos so I have a clear idea of what a fair street price looks like, and what a real discount is versus an inflated RRP. 
To vet a deal, I check its recent price history and prices during previous sales to see whether it is actually a saving worth caring about.
Laptops are usually at their most competitive around Black Friday and Cyber Monday, but the volume of configurations, coupon codes and, uh, creative pricing strategies from sellers can make it hard to know where to start.
But fear not, as I will highlight the offers that stand out for value, not just the biggest percentage claims, whether you are after an affordable machine for work or study, a creator laptop with a colour accurate screen or a gaming rig from budgets big to small.
Behind the scenes I will be living in the glow of spreadsheets across four displays, and I will keep updating this page right through the Black Friday weekend and into Cyber Monday.
So bookmark this page and check it regularly to see the latest price changes and new deals.

articles.title: Cómo reconocer las trampas de diseño que empujan a comprar y a suscribirse antes del Black Friday
articles.text:
La Comisión Europea propuso el 11 de noviembre una ley que prohibiría los llamados patrones oscuros: diseños de sitios y aplicaciones que presionan o confunden para que el usuario compre o se suscriba. Como todavía es solo un proyecto, antes del Black Friday la defensa depende de reconocer esas trampas.
El texto, llamado Ley de Equidad Digital, es una propuesta que debe negociar el Parlamento Europeo con el Consejo de la Unión Europea antes de convertirse en norma, según el análisis publicado el 16 de noviembre por el estudio jurídico Addleshaw Goddard. Rige, por ahora, únicamente como borrador.
Su lista de prácticas prohibidas sirve igual como inventario de lo que conviene mirar con desconfianza, vengan de donde vengan las ofertas. La propia Comisión, en su documento de preguntas y respuestas, ofrece ejemplos concretos de cada una.
Tres señales de presión para detectar en la pantalla
La primera es la falsa escasez. La Comisión cita avisos como “Solo queda 1” o “¡5 personas más están interesadas!” cuando no son ciertos. Si el aviso no cita una fuente verificable, conviene abrir otra pestaña y comparar el precio y la disponibilidad en otra tienda antes de decidir.
La segunda es la culpa como herramienta. El documento menciona mensajes del tipo “Nos da pena que te vayas” y botones para rechazar una promoción con frases como “No me gustan las buenas ofertas”. Ninguno cambia el precio ni las condiciones: solo buscan que el usuario desista de cancelar o de darse de baja.
La tercera son las casillas ya marcadas. Según la Comisión, las opciones que el usuario debe rechazar, como un seguro o un producto extra añadido automáticamente al carrito, figuran entre las prácticas que la propuesta vetaría en todos los casos. Antes de pagar, revisar el resumen línea por línea evita cobros inesperados.
Un cuarto punto es el precio. La Comisión señala que la ley exigiría mostrar, en las filas virtuales de venta de entradas, el precio actual en tiempo real y el más alto posible. Hasta entonces, quien compra tickets debe confirmar el total final antes de ingresar los datos de pago.
Pruebas gratuitas y renovaciones: cómo no quedar atrapado
El problema que la Comisión describe es conocido: darse de alta es fácil y cancelar es difícil. Algunas pruebas gratuitas pasan a ser de pago sin que el cliente lo acepte, otras se renuevan sin aviso y, a veces, no hay manera de hablar con una persona.
La propuesta obligaría a las empresas a ofrecer una opción de cancelación sencilla y a avisar antes de que termine la prueba o se renueve la suscripción. También exigiría una confirmación activa del usuario para pasar a un contrato pago y garantizaría atención humana cuando otros medios no resuelvan el problema.
Mientras tanto, la guía de aplicación de la Comisión Federal de Comercio de Estados Unidos (FTC) sobre suscripciones plantea un criterio práctico: la cancelación debería ser al menos tan fácil como el alta y estar disponible por el mismo medio, por ejemplo la misma web o aplicación.
Esa agencia también considera inaceptable que se cuelgue el teléfono a quien llama para cancelar o se le dé información falsa sobre cómo hacerlo.
Una regla específica de la FTC que exigía un “clic para cancelar” fue anulada por un tribunal de apelaciones de Estados Unidos en julio de 2025, según el sitio de consumo Checkbook. El criterio general de la agencia sigue vigente como política de aplicación, según el documento oficial de 2021.
Pasos concretos antes de aceptar y para dar de baja
Los sitios de consumo coinciden en lo básico. Antes de dar los datos de la tarjeta, conviene anotar el precio completo, la fecha en que termina la prueba y dónde se cancela. Una captura de pantalla de la oferta y el correo de confirmación sirven como prueba si hay un reclamo posterior.
Para evitar sorpresas, se puede poner un recordatorio en el calendario unos días antes del vencimiento de la prueba. Al cancelar, se recomienda guardar la confirmación. Checkbook sugiere pagar las suscripciones con tarjeta de crédito, porque permite disputar un cobro indebido con el banco, algo que suele ser más difícil con una tarjeta de débito.
La Comisión Europea mantiene en su sitio la propuesta, los anexos y el análisis de impacto de la Ley de Equidad Digital. La propuesta debe ahora pasar por el Parlamento Europeo y el Consejo antes de poder aplicarse en la Unión Europea.

articles.title: ‘It’s time to start running’: Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey says AI-powered cyberattacks are moving faster than outdated defenses
articles.text:
‘It’s time to start running’: Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey says AI-powered cyberattacks are moving faster than outdated defenses
Palmer Luckey says AI attackers are outrunning legacy defenses
- Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey claims AI-built exploits are outpacing legacy defenses
- Luckey predicted AI will favor defenders in the long run, but only if they move much faster now
- US officials say the recent outage wave came from botched updates and rushed patches, not cyberattacks
Palmer Luckey has a blunt message for anyone still running yesterday's infrastructure: "It's time to start running."
Speaking with Andrew Ross Sorkin at the recent The New York Times DealBook Summit, the Anduril co-founder and Oculus founder warned that AI tools are letting attackers build exploits faster than older systems can be defended.
The setting gave Luckey's warning extra weight, as that same morning, Vice President JD Vance pulled out of his own DealBook appearance shortly before he was due on stage, staying in Washington for meetings about a run of outages that had hit Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase, Zelle and the National Security Agency.
An interesting argument at a time when the call was coming from inside the building
Luckey argued that the consequences of advanced AI are already visible, describing what is happening as "the natural effects of a lot of these advanced AI tools" being used to create exploits. When Sorkin asked how worried people should be, he said it "depends on how well prepared you are," then added, without elaborating, that the audience would "find out what's going on soon enough."
The core of his case is a speed mismatch: On one side are attackers he called "very fast-moving," quick to put new technology to work. On the other are "old, outdated systems" that cannot adopt new technology as quickly as it is developed. People who say everything can be hacked, he said, "are right, for now." He also said US adversaries are exploiting that gap for strategic and financial reasons and singled out North Korea, though Luckey offered no specific incidents.
Luckey was not fatalistic about where this ends, however: In the long run, Luckey said, the advantages will "accrue to the side that is most effectively using AI for defense." The danger is the stretch between now and then, and he said, "people are going to have to pick up the pace."
What Luckey did not say, at least in the remarks reported, is that the outages themselves were attacks. That distinction matters here because nearly every official account also says they were not.

"This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation-state," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC. Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio, speaking in Manila, said the country was "not under systemic attack" and that the incidents were not linked, the Associated Press reported.
Microsoft traced its two-day Outlook and Teams collapse to a cascading failure across its servers rather than an intrusion. The FAA's nationwide ground stop was reportedly caused by two newly installed HPE Juniper routers flooding its aging communications network with connection requests. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said there was "zero evidence of anything AI-related," while HPE said the router had behaved as its installer configured it, according to Implicator.
JPMorgan Chase blamed a software bug in on-premises hardware and said there was no evidence it was cyber-related, even as a ransomware group called n0n added the bank and Visa to its leak site, a claim JPMorgan has denied. Apple put its outage down to an internal update.
All roads lead to AI? Not quite
The NSA is where the story turns back toward AI. The agency's classified NSANet network recently went down, and while its own statement cited scheduled maintenance, Clayton said on Fox Business the failure followed a patch for major vulnerabilities disclosed last month, with patched systems failing to come back up as expected.
Those vulnerabilities have a name: PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP runtime, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, rated 9.2 out of 10 and disclosed on October 21. Calif found one of them with help from an OpenAI model, and Wiz independently found both using frontier models from Google and OpenAI.
Wiz argued the episode shows how AI can "change the practical exploitability of longstanding vulnerabilities," and says the bugs reach back to PHP 5.4. PHP powers an estimated 70% of websites, and in October 2026 sites as large as Wikipedia and the Internet Archive briefly went dark to patch.
This is where Luckey's speed argument and the official accounts converge: Attackers did not wait for even a moment. Amazon says it saw a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt four days before public disclosure, and Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince reported thousands of attempts in the 10 hours before the patch, climbing to hundreds of thousands within two hours. Within nine days, researchers had documented Chinese attackers chaining PHP2Shell with a Linux privilege escalation flaw to gain root on 25 servers, some tied to the US government.
Faced with that, defenders did what Luckey prescribes: they ran. Wall Street executives and the NSA told members of Congress that the outages came from rushed attempts to fix AI-identified vulnerabilities, The Washington Sun reported, citing three anonymous sources.
One congressional official said patches were being pushed through all at once, "more than the system was designed for." Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told CNBC that new technology is being layered onto very old systems, and warned that more such disruptions are coming.
Read that way, the outages are not evidence against Luckey's thesis; They are what the gap he described looks like from the defender's side: AI surfaces a decade-old flaw, attackers move within days, and organizations sitting on legacy stacks break their own systems trying to keep up.
The patch-rush explanation should not be stretched over the whole cluster, however: Microsoft's root cause was a latent bug introduced in a July 2026 update, well before PHP2Shell was disclosed. The FAA's trouble began with router work during a copper-to-fiber upgrade, and its administrator explicitly ruled out an AI link. Even the NSA and the DNI did not describe the agency's outage the same way.
Lawmakers have noticed the mixed messaging. Senator Mark Warner, the Intelligence Committee's top Democrat, said the White House had offered no clear explanation and that "people are freaking out," The National News Desk reported. Republican Representative Nick LaLota said he worried the week's events went beyond coincidence. Shoppers cleared Costco shelves of water and batteries, and most of its pricier generators sold out online.
None of this makes Luckey wrong about the threat. AI-driven offense is well documented. In September 2026, Gambit researchers described a likely Chinese, financially motivated operation in which autonomous AI agents stole more than 600,000 payment records, compromising 27 organizations to varying degrees in under a week, with roughly $7,000 in spend over four weeks. CrowdStrike and Censys have tracked ARTEX, an AI agent layer for reconnaissance, being used against South Korean banks, with more than 1,400 exposed consoles found online.
Via TechCrunch
Anduril: Not exactly a neutral party
Luckey is not a neutral commentator: Anduril sells AI-driven defense systems built around its Lattice software, has partnered with Booz Allen to run cyber capabilities on its Menace hardware, and recently landed a Navy deal worth up to $2.9 billion days after Luckey joined a Pentagon weapons initiative. "The side most effectively using AI for defense" is, among other things, a fair description of Anduril's sales pitch, and it echoes his earlier line that there is "no moral high ground in using inferior technology."
That does not make the argument wrong, but it does expose its gap. AI for defense is exactly what found PHP2Shell, and finding bugs faster only helps if organizations can ship fixes without breaking things. On this month's evidence, the bottleneck is less about detection than about legacy stacks, thin testing, and rollouts that cannot absorb emergency change at AI speed. Running requires legs that many institutions do not yet have.
Luckey may well be right that the public will find out what is going on soon enough. If the past week is a preview, though, the next big failure may look less like a hack and more like a fix.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Rahim Amir is a UAE-based tech writer who enjoys building PCs as much as he enjoys writing about them. He has been professionally writing about PC hardware since 2023, focusing on buyer’s guides, hardware reviews, and sponsored content and features related to tech.
Having built hundreds of gaming PCs and being an avid gamer in his spare time, Rahim tends to have stronger opinions about hardware than most. This is particularly on display when he gets his way with powerful, but minimalistic RGB builds even as Small Form Factor (SFF) PCs come a close second.

articles.title: Webworm Suspected of Modifying SoftEther VPN to Evade Detection and Hide Remote Access
articles.text:
The China-aligned threat actor known as Webworm is suspected to be using a custom version of the open-source SoftEther VPN Bridge tool in an attempt to remove recognizable detection fingerprints, while disguising it as network-monitoring software to establish covert remote access to compromised networks.
The modified variant "implements various tricks to hide itself from security tools," Rapid7 said in an analysis, attributing it to the adversarial collective with moderate confidence.
First publicly detailed by Broadcom-owned Symantec in September 2022, Webworm is the name assigned to a China-aligned nation-state group that has targeted government entities, IT services, and electric power companies across Russia, Georgia, Mongolia, and several other Asian nations.
One of the tools used by the threat actor is a legitimate software called SoftEther VPN, with the bridge acting as a pathway connecting the compromised network and the attacker-controlled infrastructure.
The latest findings from Rapid7 revolve around a Windows executable ("netcapa.exe"), which is a modified build of SoftEther VPN Bridge ("vpnbridge_x64.exe") version 4.44, build 9807. The modified version, rebranded as NtMonitor VPN, masquerades itself as Network Monitor Software from a company called Network Systems Solutions Inc. The artifact was uploaded to VirusTotal around mid-January 2026.
"The PDB path included in the executable reads C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\SoftEtherVPN_Stable\src\DebugFiles\pdb\x64_Release\vpnbridge.pdb," the cybersecurity company said. "As such, the tool doesn't hide its identity from reverse engineers, only external interactions."
The renaming is also said to be inconsistent, with many registry key paths still referencing the program as "SoftEther Project," even though a number of other occurrences of "SoftEther VPN" have been replaced by "NtMonitor VPN."
One of the most noticeable changes identified in the altered version is the use of innocuous-looking HTTP endpoints "/update/alive.cgi" and "/update/picture.cgi" to replace "/vpnsvc/vpn.cgi" and "/vpnsvc/connect.cgi," respectively, so that they look like ordinary web application activity.
It also changes the protocol watermark used by SoftEther VPN as part of the handshake process when initiating communication to help the tool distinguish protocol traffic from ordinary HTTP requests. When the connecting client is found to speak the expected protocol, it proceeds with the handshake. If the check fails, the server returns a decoy HTTP response.
The modified version swaps the GIF-based watermark used by the stock SoftEther VPN utility for a PNG-based watermark so as to bypass existing detection signatures based on the GIF watermark.
Some of the other changes introduced to the program are listed below -
- Reducing a resource archive named hamcore.se2 used by SoftEther VPN to its bare minimum, as it's required to be present at runtime, and embedding it directly into the executable, causing the binary's size to increase by about 1.5 MB.
- Changing the name of the configuration file from "vpn_bridge.config" to "setting.conf" and making its contents encrypted with a custom algorithm. The encrypted configuration starts with the magic bytes "RCEN" in ASCII.
What's interesting here is that the attackers have not been found to introduce any new functionality to the tool, indicating the primary focus was on stealth.
"It seems like they methodically analyzed SoftEther's detection surface and implemented counter-measures to all of the easy ways a detection engineer may target it," Rapid7 said, calling the latest evolution a hybrid approach that brings together the attacker's use of custom malware and dual-use tools.
"We are observing a sort of hybrid of the two — stock SoftEther software that is not trojanized, but rebuilt from source in a way that erases much of its detection fingerprint."

Pourquoi choisir l’offre Cloud d’o2switch ?

Du code généré par Claude au site en ligne
Le scénario le plus courant reste le site vitrine ou le blog que Claude vous aide à écrire en HTML ou en PHP, ou sur WordPress, que Softaculous installe en quelques clics. Pour un projet plus ambitieux, comme une petite application Node.js ou Python reliée à une base de données, l’accès SSH permet de lancer vos commandes sur le serveur. Ce même test juge en revanche la configuration un peu juste pour des applications riches : o2switch ne propose pas de VPS, et un projet qui réclame un serveur entièrement à vous ira ailleurs. L’offre convient donc mieux à ceux qui veulent apprendre à déployer qu’à ceux qui cherchent un simple bouton « Publier ».

Pour qui code avec Claude et veut héberger le résultat sur son propre espace plutôt que sur une plateforme à crédits, l’offre Cloud d’o2switch coche les bonnes cases : langages courants, SSH, Git et ressources généreuses. À 11,88 € HT la première année, et un peu plus de 10 € HT avec le code CLUBIC, le ticket d’entrée reste symbolique. La garantie de 30 jours laisse le temps de vérifier que votre projet tourne.

Si votre site n’est qu’un essai, une plateforme gratuite suffira peut-être le temps de valider l’idée. Si vous comptez le faire vivre, notez la date d’échéance dès la commande pour trancher à temps.

articles.title: Truco de GTA 6 para ganar 10.000 dólares cada diez minutos sin completar ninguna misión
articles.text:
Un fallo en el sistema de Grand Theft Auto VI permite a los jugadores acumular grandes sumas de dinero de forma repetida, sin completar misiones ni enfrentarse a las fuerzas de seguridad del juego. El hallazgo se viralizó en redes sociales apenas un día después del lanzamiento del título, cuando distintos creadores de contenido comenzaron a mostrar cómo aprovecharlo.
El mecanismo se basa en un error de programación que impide que ciertos objetos de valor desaparezcan de forma definitiva tras ser recogidos. Esto habilita a los usuarios a repetir una y otra vez la obtención del mismo botín en un lapso breve, algo que en condiciones normales del juego sería imposible.
Dónde está el fallo y qué se puede obtener
El escenario principal del descubrimiento se ubica en Hamlet, una localidad del estado ficticio de Leonida, cerca del refugio inicial del personaje Jason. Allí existe un granero de color rojo con apariencia abandonada que, en su interior, oculta una pequeña oficina con varias bolsas de droga.
Según IGN, los jugadores deben tomar esas bolsas y guardarlas en el escondite secreto de su personaje antes de trasladarlas al maletero de un vehículo. En el mismo granero también hay una furgoneta con una bolsa de dinero en efectivo que puede sumarse al botín.
Se recomienda completar primero el Capítulo 1 de la historia antes de intentar el truco. Quienes lo prueben antes de avanzar al Capítulo 2 deberían gastar el dinero acumulado antes de iniciar la misión conocida como “Trampa para turistas”, dado que esa instancia podría interferir con el procedimiento.
Cómo repetir el botín paso a paso
El proceso para multiplicar las ganancias requiere cargar el vehículo con cuatro bolsas de almacenamiento entre droga y efectivo. Una vez completado ese cupo, el jugador debe guardar la partida y cargarla de inmediato.
Al hacerlo, el personaje reaparece en su vivienda con el auto y los objetos recolectados intactos. Desde ahí, basta con dirigirse a cualquier punto de venta de objetos robados para liquidar el botín por una cifra cercana a los 10.000 dólares.
Lo llamativo del fallo es que, al regresar al granero rojo, las bolsas de droga vuelven a estar disponibles como si nunca hubieran sido tomadas. Esto permite reiniciar el ciclo completo: recolectar, guardar la partida, cargarla y vender nuevamente.
Cada repetición del proceso demora aproximadamente diez minutos, lo que en teoría habilitaría ganancias de unos 60.000 dólares por hora si el jugador domina la mecánica sin interrupciones.
Este no es el único truco para ganar dinero en GTA 6
Un segundo foco del mismo tipo de error fue identificado en las instalaciones de Apollo Aggregates, una fábrica de cemento situada al noreste de Hamlet. Allí también es posible encontrar dinero, drogas y otros objetos de valor, además de una caja fuerte con contenido adicional.
En este caso, una primera visita al lugar permite reunir alrededor de 7.000 dólares. La diferencia respecto al granero rojo es el método para que el botín reaparezca: en lugar de guardar y recargar la partida, basta con subir al vehículo, alejarse cerca de un kilómetro del sitio y regresar.
Los objetos recolectados en Apollo Aggregates pueden venderse en el depósito de un personaje identificado como Brian. Al igual que en el caso del granero, la cantidad final de dinero obtenido depende de lo que el jugador logre recoger y vender en cada ciclo, por lo que no se trata de una fuente de efectivo ilimitado automático, sino de un botín que puede repetirse mientras el fallo permanezca activo.
Rockstar, desarrolladora del título, no confirmó si prepara una corrección para este comportamiento. Debido a que los estudios suelen revisar de forma periódica este tipo de fallos a través de actualizaciones, se desconoce hasta cuándo seguirá siendo posible repetir el procedimiento en cualquiera de los dos escenarios identificados.

articles.title: Timekettle’s LiveTalk AI earbuds are the closest thing to a Babel Fish
articles.text:
Timekettle LiveTalk Black Friday deal: save 20% on the closest thing yet to a real-life Babel Fish
AI-powered summaries help you review important conversations
In The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, Douglas Adams' Babel Fish promised us real-time translation right in our ears. And while TimeKettle's LiveTalk AI translation earbuds aren't quite that quick, they're as close as we've come yet to rapid-fire speech-to-text and speech-to-audio translation.
With Black Friday on the way, TimeKettle's LiveTalk AI Translation earbuds are now $103.20(was $129) at TimeKettle. The offer also includes a free Earbuds Cleaning Pen (worth $9.99) and one year of Extended Care (worth $13).
I'd recommend these buds to international travelers, business professionals, and students who regularly communicate in different languages and want hands-free translation assistance. Chatting in another language can be difficult, especially when you're travelling, attending international meetings, or speaking with clients overseas. The Timekettle LiveTalk AI translation earbuds are designed to help bridge that gap, offering real-time translations for face-to-face conversations, video calls, and presentations.
Timekettle LiveTalk AI earbuds support 54 languages, 108 accents, 25 offline pairs, four translation modes, dual-device connectivity, AI summaries, 200 monthly translation minutes, and four-hour translation battery life per charge.
Why we recommend it
In his four-star review, our expert Alastair said: "The translation quality is excellent and a huge improvement on using Google Translate." Speech-to-text is pretty fast, although speech-to-audio is slower, with a delay of around seven seconds.
He concluded: "When you factor in the different translation approaches and the range of translation options, these small, easy-to-use earphones perform surprisingly well for situations such as watching live presentations, some multimedia content and quick conversations."
Voice Call and Multi-Media modes support translated phone calls, video meetings, and other audio content. You can connect the earbuds to a phone and computer, making them useful for Zoom or Microsoft Teams meetings without installing TimeKettle software on the second device.
Each earbud weighs just 6.9g and uses an open-ear design to leave the ear canal uncovered. Battery life is rated at up to four hours of continuous translation per charge.
Price context & historical value
The Timekettle LiveTalk AI translation earbuds have been reduced from $129 to $103.20 for Black Friday, saving you $25.80. This isn't the cheapest we've seen it - the earbuds have been as low as $97 in the past. The deal also includes a free Earbuds Cleaning Pen (worth $9.99) and one year of Extended Care (worth $13), bringing the total advertised value of the freebies to $22.99.
The Timekettle LiveTalk includes 200 free translation minutes each month, with additional plans costing $5.99 to $9.99 per month. An unlimited translation plan is also available for $14.99 per month.
Should you buy it?
✅ Buy the Timekettle LiveTalk AI translation earbuds if...
You frequently travel internationally or attend multilingual meetings and want translation support for in-person conversations, calls, and presentations.
❌ Skip the Timekettle LiveTalk AI translation earbuds if...
You only occasionally need to translate a phrase while traveling, in which case a free smartphone translation app may be sufficient.
Also consider
The same product is also on sale at Amazon for a slightly higher price, but it comes with a free pair of Polypal P1 AI Translation Earbuds, worth $64.99, which support 43 languages and offer seven translation modes.
These Interpreter Earbuds support real-time translation across more than 50 languages, including two-way conversations, phone calls, and video meetings. They offer Bluetooth connectivity and compatibility with iOS and Android devices for business use.
The deal also includes two free gifts: a protective case worth $29.99 and one year of Extended Care worth $45, with a total value of $74.99.
If you buy this from Amazon, it's priced at $359 with a free pair of Polypal P1 AI Translation Earbuds, worth $64.99.

articles.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: VMware 0-Day, Java4Shell, NGINX2Root, Ruby2Shell, and a Whole Lot of Shell Trouble
articles.text:
A stolen key. A trusted message. A routine update. None of these looks like the start of a major security problem. That's partly why they work. Attackers don't always need to break down a door. Sometimes they just use one that's already open.
This week's stories show how quickly a small opening can turn into a much bigger mess. One breach helps attackers reach another target. Tools people rely on become ways to get inside. Even features built for safety can end up helping the wrong person. And some of the latest research shows just how little effort certain attacks need.
The strange part is how normal it all looks until something goes wrong. A few attacks are clever. Others are almost embarrassingly simple. Both can do real damage. Here's what caught our attention this week.
⚡ Threat of the Week
Threat Actor Exploits VMware vCenter Flaw as a 0-Day — The suspected China-nexus cyber espionage group known as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) has been attributed to the zero-day exploitation of a critical security flaw in VMware vCenter Server in early September 2026. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service that could be exploited to gain unauthorized access to the system. In October, Google described a campaign by Armory Castle to exploit organizations through BeyondTrust's Remote Support tool, using a zero-day to breach the edge appliance and steal secrets useful for network reconnaissance and downstream compromises within organizations. The latest findings show that BeyondTrust was merely an entry point to a deeper and more complex campaign that involved the deployment of backdoors on Linux machines.
Is Your Workforce Secured from AI Threats?
Attackers now weaponize AI to launch personalized phishing attacks faster than employees can react. Fight AI with AI, using realistic simulations to train employees to spot and stop threats. Stop phishing before it becomes a breach.
Book a Demo ➝
🔔 Top News
- Cursor Links Malicious Claude Extension Release to Fireworks AI Incident — Cursor has traced the origins of a security incident involving a malicious version of Anthropic's Claude Code extension in its marketplace to a breach at AI infrastructure provider Fireworks. "An attacker obtained an access key we had issued to Fireworks," Cursor said. "The key was exposed by Fireworks, and the attacker used it to copy data from a read-only storage bucket we used to share data with them." The Cursor incident is another indication of how the rapid adoption of AI-powered development tools and increasingly interconnected software ecosystems has worsened software supply chain risks.
- Cold Relic Exploits Cloud Breaches to Target Organizations — The Russian cyberespionage group known as Cold Relic is turning cloud breaches into a springboard for targeting a victim organization's wider network of trusted relationships. In the first intrusion observed late last year, the attackers gained control of a cloud administrator account and harvested internal communications, employee details, and other organizational records. Cold Relic later used that information to impersonate an employee of the first organization to conduct a social engineering attack on an individual at a second organization. The campaigns "demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse," Google said. "By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners."
- Malicious Web Pages Can Hijack Meta Muse — New research from the NebuSec research team has demonstrated that an attacker-controlled web page can be exploited to gain unauthorized access to user data associated with Meta Muse and compromise the underlying virtual machine (VM) in which it operates. "An attacker could retrieve conversation history and stored memories without triggering Muse's network approval prompts," NebuSec said. "The attack also allowed us to alter stored memories and conversation history, creating risks beyond unauthorized data access. By exploiting a vulnerability in the shared Linux kernel, we escaped the agent's runtime container and obtained root privileges in the underlying user VM." Meta has since addressed the issue.
- New FastUnlock Windows Narrator LockScreen Bypass Detailed — Security researcher Abdelhamid Naceri (aka Chaotic Eclipse) published FastUnlock, a new unpatched Windows 11 zero-day that abuses the Narrator screen reader to get past the lock screen and execute code as the lock screen account "WsiAccount." The attack requires physical access and at least one account linked to an online Microsoft account.
- GL.iNet GoodCloud Exploited to Serve Reverse Shells, Backdoors — Hackers have exploited a vulnerability in GL.iNet's GoodCloud cloud management platform to install malware, backdoors, and remote access tools on customers' routers and KVM devices."An unauthorized party exploited the vulnerability to access and install malicious software on some GL.iNet routers and KVM devices," GL.iNet said. "The attack path has been blocked. We fixed the cloud vulnerability and blocked the access used in this incident. Devices can no longer be newly infected through this attack path. The cloud-side fix alone does not remove malware from devices that were already infected." GL.iNet has not disclosed how the attackers exploited its cloud platform, how many customers were affected, or whether information was stolen as a result of these compromises. RemoteToHome said it examined 183 routers and found suspicious activity on 152, including 24 with root-level reverse shells, 47 with an older persistent backdoor, and 81 showing evidence that attacker-supplied commands had executed. It has also identified a potential command injection vulnerability in the GoodCloud client, although GL.iNet has not confirmed if this is the same vulnerability that was used in the attacks.
️‍🔥 Trending CVEs
Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.
Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-14978, CVE-2026-45110, CVE-2026-49401, CVE-2026-59890 (Unicode Normalization Collision on macOS), CVE-2026-114938 aka Java4Shell (Java 17, 21, 25, and 27), CVE-2026-28400 (Docker Model Runner), CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-113425 aka NGINX2Root (NGINX and NGINX Plus), CVE-2026-120718 (F5 BIG-IP), CVE-2026-126822, CVE-2026-126336, CVE-2026-121812, CVE-2026-123637, CVE-2026-125272 (F5 BIG-IP APM), CVE-2026-120722, CVE-2026-121805, CVE-2026-120285, CVE-2026-120292, CVE-2026-116953 (F5 BIG-IP iRule), CVE-2026-125274 (F5 BIG-IP and BIG-IQ), CVE-2026-114819 (Oracle AI Database), CVE-2026-132825 aka Ruby2Shell (Ruby), CVE-2026-130963, CVE-2026-131031, CVE-2026-131060, CVE-2026-131008, CVE-2026-131054, CVE-2026-130975 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-132165 (Drupal), CVE-2026-123890, CVE-2026-119618 (Broadcom VMware), CVE-2026-114202, CVE-2026-114204, CVE-2026-114205 (ASUS Control Center Express Agent), CVE-2026-126574 (ASUS Control Center), CVE-2026-112115 (ASUS Armoury Crate), CVE-2026-99312, CVE-2026-99362 (Linux kernel), CVE-2026-132798 (Temenos Application Framework Java), CVE-2026-134624 (N-able Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud), CVE-2026-131914 (Idunno.AntiCsrf), CVE-2026-125396 aka Upload2Shell (Ghostscript), CVE-2026-129975 (GPGME), GHSA-qc22-rmgc-vg94 (MONAI Label), CVE-2026-23871 (WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android), and CVE-2026-134814 (binary-parser).
🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars
- 6,000 Social Engineering Attacks Reveal Why MFA Still Fails to Stop Account Takeovers → AI-powered phishing and voice scams are evolving, while attackers exploit weaker authentication and recovery paths to bypass MFA. Join this webinar to uncover real attack techniques and learn how to prevent account takeovers.
- 8 Million Security Events Reveal Why Attackers Can Hide Behind Tools You Already Trust → Attackers abuse legitimate IT tools to evade detection, but only about 12 in a million uses are malicious. Join this webinar to learn how to distinguish real threats from normal activity without drowning in alerts.
- Your GitHub Actions Are SHA-Pinned. But Are They Actually Secure? → SHA pinning locks code to a commit, but doesn't verify its author or origin. Attackers can exploit this trust gap to sneak malicious code past security checks. Join this webinar to learn how impostor commits threaten CI/CD pipelines and how to defend against them.
📰 Around the Cyber World
- Google Cloud-owned VirusTotal has introduced new cipher-agnostic file-encryption verification across Windows and macOS sandboxes to check whether a suspicious file actually encrypts user documents upon execution. This has led to the detection of a .k404 extortion campaign that managed to go undetected by 75 static antivirus engines, while its companion binary ("K404T_Fidye.exe") only had 10 / 75 detections.
- The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned that threat actors can abuse an authenticated WhatsApp Web session to gain unauthorized access to a user's account, allowing them to read messages, send messages while impersonating the user, and misuse the identity of the account holder for fraud, phishing, social engineering, or other malicious activities. Users are advised to log out of sessions when not required and avoid signing in using public computers.
- A large-scale malvertising operation dubbed MoldyRoost that's leveraging advertising infrastructure to deliver iPhone exploit chain kits like Coruna, DarkSword, SilkPath (iOS 17.2.2 to 18.3), and GhostWave (iOS 18.7.3 to 26) with an aim to exfiltrate crypto wallet seed phrases, iCloud Keychain data, messages, and photos. "Just loading the landing page of a MoldyRoost ad on a vulnerable iPhone is enough to get infected," Confidant said. "The exploit runs while the landing page loads, with no decoy download or ClickFix-style command to paste. What MoldyRoost adds is expertise in distributing the exploit kits through malvertising." Only an iOS device running Safari is offered an exploit chain. Other devices are served a working decoy website, an empty frame, or a harmless landing page. More than 480 domains have been linked to the operation between May 12 and November 17, 2026. The activity has targeted over 47 countries, mainly Hong Kong, Japan, Singapore, the U.S., South Korea, the U.K., and India.
- The average time from an infostealer infection to the threat actor logging in via the same credentials is only eight minutes in some cases, according to a report from Elastic Security Labs.
- Unknown threat actors have siphoned an estimated $133 million from Crédit Mutuel Arkéa by using the bank’s own account to wire the funds to other banks, from where it was potentially converted into cryptocurrency. "The attackers used Crédit Mutuel Arkéa's own account to make transactions to other banking institutions, which then potentially allowed them to convert this money into cryptocurrency via specialized platforms," the bank said, adding the attackers did not go through the accounts of customers at its federations or subsidiaries.
- Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's Attorney General puts the number of victims at 149,346. The access data includes images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers.
- Arion Kurtaj, a 21-year-old member of the LAPSUS$ group, pleaded guilty in a U.K. court to hacking Rockstar Games, Uber, BT, and Revolut, after being released from a secure hospital after he was deemed fit to stand trial. He was originally sentenced to an indefinite stay at a hospital due to the severity of his autism.
- Browser extensions associated with Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have been found to be rife with critical vulnerabilities rated 9.6 on the CVSS scoring system. These digital signing extensions are used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals. "All five make the same mistake, they let the website choose which DLL the vendor's native host loads," Bay Area Labs said. "Loading a DLL runs its code and the software built to verify signatures never checked the signature on the code it loaded and on Web PKI and CertiSign WebSigner, a malicious page or iframe, such as an ad, was enough, with no click. On Softplan Web Signer, opening a link was enough. On CertiPlugin and BRy, visiting the page was enough, and the page downloaded the payload automatically." The bug class has been codenamed Sign2Shell. The flaws could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names and potentially breach major organizations. The issues have since been fixed.
- Anthropic has become the latest company to cut its coordinated vulnerability disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity issues, and to 45 days for all other issues, as AI collapses bug discovery timelines. The new deadlines cover reports sent on or after January 1, 2027.
- Recovery from a ransomware attack takes a median time of 20 days, and nearly a third of victims require more than six weeks. "Only 32% were recovered within two weeks and 28% took longer than six weeks," Rubrik said. "The full case, measured until the customer was content to close it, had a median of 26 days and 45% of cases stayed open for more than 30 days."
- Fortra said it's tracking targeted, large-scale "mail bombing" attacks, followed immediately by IT support impersonation on Microsoft Teams. "In the attacks, individual users are being flooded with email, then contacted by the threat actor through Teams as the volume peaks," Fortra said. "In the calls, the threat actors are claiming to be representatives from Internal IT, providing the user both verbal and email instructions they claim will stop the flood, but in reality attempting to compromise the user account, system, or both."
- Tyler Robert Buchanan, 24, of Dundee, Scotland, has been sentenced to six years in prison in the U.S. for his role in conspiring to hack into at least a dozen companies' computer systems via smishing attacks and steal over $11.6 million in virtual currency from individual victims throughout the U.S. A member of the Scattered Spider group, Buchanan pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft in April 2026. He was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the U.S. in April 2025.
- Igor Andreevich D'iu, a 25-year-old Russian national, has been indicted in the U.S. for allegedly acting as a spy of a foreign government to "conduct surveillance and gather information about employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company." Although the name of the company was not disclosed, it's understood to be Palantir Technologies. D'iu was arrested on October 30, 2026. "The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company's assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia," said United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian. He is said to have entered the U.S. illegally through Mexico in June 2026 and was instructed by co-conspirators on Telegram to "identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens while they worked," as well as "include surveillance of company employees and their residences."
- At least $247 million of the stolen funds from the record-breaking Binance hack has now gone into coinjoins coordinated by Kruw to obscure the financial trail, Elliptic has revealed. "Almost all of these coinjoins were coordinated by Kruw, the most widely used coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users," the company said. "A coordinator organizes each coinjoin round, bringing together the users taking part, but never takes custody of their funds." Last week, blockchain investigator ZachXBT accused Kruw of knowingly helping the Lazarus Group launder stolen cryptocurrency assets, calling the threat actor their "largest" user. Arkham Intelligence has also identified 2,173.76 BTC, roughly $154.45 million, flowing into CoinJoin from wallets connected to the $387 million Bitget hack of September 2025, also linked to North Korea. Kruw.io was also the subject of an advisory issued by the U.S. Secret Service in May 2025. "Numerous illicit actors use Kruw.io to launder funds including the Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking collective also known as АPТ38 and TraderTraitor which is subject to U.S. and international sanctions," the advisory said. "The Lazarus Group has previously used Kruw.io to mix approximately $14.3 million in cryptocurrency stolen by the North Korean regime. The Lazarus Group is currently laundering some proceeds of the $1.5 billion Bybit hack through the Kruw.io service."
Conclusion
The tricky part isn't always finding the problem. It's knowing how far it has already spread. A stolen login can lead to another company. A fixed bug can leave infected devices behind. And a tool that worked fine yesterday might be the reason someone gets in tomorrow. There isn't always a clean ending once the damage is done.
That's it for this week's recap. Some of these stories need a closer look. Others are useful reminders to check the things we tend to trust without thinking. Either way, there's plenty here worth keeping an eye on. See you next week, hopefully with fewer surprises.

articles.title: Cómo se está usando la IA para revisar historias clínicas y alertar riesgos con pacientes
articles.text:
Una plataforma colombiana de inteligencia artificial revisa la historia clínica mientras el médico atiende y alerta sobre posibles omisiones, interacciones medicamentosas o riesgos que requieren una segunda mirada. La herramienta, desarrollada por Telepatia, busca apoyar la consulta sin reemplazar la decisión del profesional de la salud.
La propuesta cobra relevancia en un sistema donde los médicos deben escuchar, examinar, decidir y documentar cada consulta en 15 o 20 minutos. Ese ritmo puede dejar antecedentes sin registrar, protocolos incompletos o información clínica con menos detalle del necesario. La IA pretende ayudar a detectar esos vacíos antes de cerrar la nota.
La herramienta escucha y organiza la consulta en tiempo real
Telepatia desarrolla una plataforma que registra la conversación clínica y genera una nota estructurada con el estilo de documentación de cada médico. El sistema busca reducir el tiempo que los profesionales dedican a transcribir síntomas, antecedentes, hallazgos, diagnósticos e indicaciones.
La herramienta también incluye un copiloto de inteligencia artificial que responde dudas en tiempo real a partir de evidencia clínica y del contexto del paciente. Además, cuenta con un sistema de soporte a la decisión clínica que revisa la información consignada y señala elementos que deben ser evaluados por el profesional.
Entre las alertas que puede emitir están antecedentes que no quedaron incluidos, posibles interacciones entre medicamentos, pasos pendientes dentro de un protocolo y hallazgos que podrían requerir una revisión adicional. El objetivo es que el médico tenga esa información disponible mientras toma decisiones, y no al final de la jornada.
Según la empresa, sus soluciones habían contribuido, hasta septiembre de 2026, a evitar más de 200.000 errores médicos. Dentro de esa cifra se encuentran más de 4.000 alertas críticas, identificadas como casos que podían representar un riesgo para la vida del paciente.
La decisión final sigue en manos del médico
La plataforma no prescribe tratamientos ni sustituye la evaluación clínica. El médico revisa cada recomendación, la valida, la corrige o la descarta según el caso. La responsabilidad sobre la historia clínica, el diagnóstico y las decisiones médicas permanece en el profesional que atiende al paciente.
Tomás Giraldo, médico y cofundador de Telepatia, explicó que la consulta exige escuchar, interpretar, analizar, documentar y decidir en un periodo reducido. “Cuando el registro ocupa más tiempo que el propio paciente, sabemos que hay algo que no está funcionando del todo en el sistema de salud”, afirmó.
Giraldo señaló que estas herramientas pueden apoyar varios momentos del trabajo clínico, pero no reemplazan ni el juicio médico ni la relación entre el profesional y el paciente. La firma de la nota y la conducta médica siguen bajo responsabilidad de quien atiende.
Ese límite resulta relevante para la adopción de inteligencia artificial en salud. Los sistemas pueden ordenar datos y detectar patrones, pero no conocen por sí solos el contexto completo de una persona, sus condiciones sociales, su lenguaje corporal o las circunstancias que rodean una consulta.
Las alertas deben ser útiles y no interrumpir la atención
Para funcionar en la práctica, la tecnología debe integrarse con los sistemas que el médico ya utiliza. La plataforma necesita evitar pantallas paralelas, procesos adicionales o avisos constantes que terminen por distraer durante la consulta.
La herramienta no busca imponer un lenguaje uniforme, sino estructurar la información sin perder la manera en que cada médico describe sus hallazgos y razonamientos.
Las alertas también deben mantener un equilibrio. Una advertencia pertinente puede evitar que se pase por alto una interacción farmacológica o un antecedente relevante. Sin embargo, una acumulación de avisos poco útiles puede convertirse en ruido y llevar a que el profesional deje de prestar atención a mensajes importantes.
Por eso, el valor de estas plataformas depende de su precisión, de la calidad de la información disponible y de su capacidad para adaptarse al contexto clínico. Un sistema de apoyo necesita ofrecer datos claros y dejar espacio para que el médico interprete cada situación.
La inteligencia artificial empezó a entrar a las consultas como una herramienta de transcripción y organización. Ahora, plataformas como Telepatia intentan ampliar ese papel mediante la revisión de la historia clínica y el soporte a la decisión.
El avance no se medirá solo por la cantidad de tareas automatizadas. La utilidad dependerá de si la tecnología permite una atención más completa, registros más precisos y decisiones mejor respaldadas. En ese modelo, la IA funciona como apoyo: revisa, advierte y organiza, mientras el médico conserva el criterio final sobre el paciente.

articles.title: La Poste signe son premier accord sur l'IA, et l'algorithme ne pourra pas décider à la place des postiers
articles.text:
La Poste a signé avec la CFDT, la CGT, FO et la CFE-CGC son premier accord encadrant l'usage de l'intelligence artificielle par les postiers. Le texte porte notamment sur les décisions RH, la formation et le droit à la déconnexion.
L'intelligence artificielle a désormais son mode d'emploi à La Poste, négocié avec les syndicats. Conclu le 19 novembre avec la CFDT, la CGT, FO et la CFE-CGC et officialisé ce lundi 23 novembre 2026, ce premier accord sur l'IA encadre jusqu'à fin mars 2029 la façon dont les postiers se servent de La Poste GPT, de Copilot ou du Chat de Mistral. On y découvre par exemple qu'aucun algorithme ne pourra trancher seul une promotion ou une sanction, et que les signataires avouent ne pas savoir chiffrer le temps gagné.
Chez La Poste, l'IA n'aura pas le dernier mot sur les promotions et les sanctions
Dans un groupe comme La Poste qui emploie plus de 170 000 personnes en France, la règle de base autour de l'intelligence artificielle méritait et devait être écrite. Le principe est que l'IA éclaire, et l'humain décide. L'accord dont on a pris connaissance aujourd'hui, qui couvre tous les personnels de La Poste SA, qu'il s'agisse des fonctionnaires ou des salariés, interdit qu'un système d'IA serve de base unique à une décision sur la carrière d'un postier. Que l'on discute de recrutement, d'évaluation, de mobilité, de rémunération ou de sanction, l'accord précise noir sur blanc que rien de tout cela ne sera confié à la seule machine. Si l'outil suggère une option, le manager peut en choisir une autre, et il en reste pleinement responsable.
Certains usages déjà interdits par l'AI Act, le règlement européen appliqué par étapes depuis août 2024, sont purement et simplement bannis, exclus, y compris dans les outils achetés à des fournisseurs. On peut notamment citer la notation sociale, la manipulation des comportements, et la détection des émotions au travail. Un postier qui échange avec un chatbot, ou suit une formation conçue avec l'IA, devra en être clairement averti. Et s'il tombe sur un résultat aberrant, il pourra le signaler à son manager ou au délégué à la protection des données, avec un retour sur les suites données.
Au nom du droit à la déconnexion, les notifications des outils d'IA pourront être coupées hors du temps de travail. La direction et les syndicats décrivent aussi sans se cacher les effets pervers possibles, par exemple une cadence qui s'emballe quand certaines tâches jugées simples disparaissent, une autonomie qui s'étiole, ou des équipes fragilisées. Pour les projets importants soumis au CSE, l'étude d'impact devra scruter le rythme, la charge et le sens du travail. Quant aux gains de temps, tous reconnaissent qu'il est pour l'heure impossible de les mesurer de façon fiable.
La Poste GPT, Copilot, Le Chat : une IA à apprivoiser
Les postiers ne découvrent pas l'intelligence artificielle avec cet accord. Outre La Poste GPT, l'assistant d'IA générative maison, le texte mentionne des licences Copilot de Microsoft et Le Chat du français Mistral AI, rebaptisé Vibe depuis la fin mai. De manière un peu plus discrète pour le grand public, des algorithmes déchiffrent déjà les adresses dans les plateformes de tri, épaulent le service client et les commerciaux, traitent des factures ou rapprochent les compétences des salariés des postes à pourvoir. La Poste dit compter plus de 500 experts de la data et de l'IA aujourd'hui, notamment dans ses filiales Probayes et Openvalue.
Le gros du chantier, sans trop de surprise, reste la formation. Près de 93 000 postiers sont déjà passés par le programme « Objectif IA », et l'accord prévoit des parcours adaptés à chacun, qui concernent des métiers les plus éloignés du numérique jusqu'aux experts techniques. Au programme, on y retrouve de l'aide pour la rédaction de prompts, la sécurité des données, l'éthique, et même deux modules sur l'AI Act (quinze minutes pour tous, 45 pour les plus concernés). Des badges jalonneront la progression, un label certifiant est en préparation et un réseau d'« ambassadeurs IA » pourra épauler les collègues. Le temps dégagé par l'IA est d'ailleurs censé servir en priorité à apprendre.
Pour veiller au grain, l'accord, qui entre en vigueur le 1er décembre, crée un « Comité IA & dialogue social ». Autour de la table, on retrouve des représentants des syndicats signataires, la direction des ressources humaines et les responsables chargés de vérifier que l'IA respecte la loi et que les données sont bien gérées. Leur mission consiste à anticiper les effets de l'IA sur les métiers, à passer en revue les projets les plus importants et à suivre quelques indicateurs, comme la formation ou la prévention des risques. Le rythme reste plutôt modeste, avec trois réunions la première année puis deux en 2028, et la DRH s'engage à répondre sous un mois aux questions écrites de ses membres. Ce comité ne remplace pas pour autant les CSE, les instances élues qui représentent le personnel, qui peuvent toujours être consultées lorsqu'un nouvel outil d'IA change sensiblement le travail des postiers. Une case reste néanmoins vide au bas du document, celle de SUD, qui n'a pas signé.
Sur le papier, La Poste a donc posé ses règles du jeu. C'est maintenant dans les centres de tri, les bureaux et les services clients que l'on saura si l'IA tient sa promesse, à savoir aider les postiers, sans jamais les déposséder de leur métier.

articles.title: Critical binary-parser Flaw Enables JavaScript Injection via Malicious Parser Definitions
articles.text:
A critical security flaw has been disclosed in the popular binary-parser library that could allow an attacker who controls parser definitions to execute arbitrary code.
The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-134814 (CVSS score: 9.2 / 8.1), is a case of code injection impacting binary-parser versions prior to 2.3.1.
"Binary-parser before 2.3.1 contains a code injection vulnerability that allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject JavaScript through string-typed options passed unvalidated by Context.generateOption()," according to a description of the flaw in the NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD).
"Attackers can supply crafted length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, or namely() alias values to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node.js process when the parser is compiled."
According to an advisory released by the project maintainer on November 11, 2026, the problem arose from the fact that some user-controlled string options were inserted directly into the generated JavaScript code without adequate validation.
The parser options include -
- length
- lengthInBytes
- key
- tag
- offset, and
- the alias passed to namely()
"Parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition is not affected," Keichi Takahashi, who maintains the library, said. "These options are now validated as identifier paths (e.g. foo, $parent.len). Expressions such as 'len - 1' are rejected; use a function instead."
CVE-2026-134814 can also be viewed as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-1245 (CVSS score: 6.5), another code injection vulnerability that was fixed back in January 2026 and resulted from insufficient validation of field names and encoding parameters.
"[The flaw] allows attackers controlling parser definitions to inject and execute arbitrary JavaScript within the host Node.js process upon parser compilation," Upwind Security said in an X post. Users are advised to update to the latest version of the library for optimal protection.

Moonlock détecte et élimine les menaces en ligne sur votre Mac
