How to choose the best wireless speaker
It's not easy when the market is awash with wireless, cubes, oblongs, teardrops cylinders and cushions all claiming to be the best, is it? If casting music from your phone or any other Bluetooth device is important to you, a Wi-Fi only connection (even if it uses Apple AirPlay 2) may not be sufficient.
But when it comes to picking a new wireless speaker for your home, room-filling sound is key, so look for models that feature 360-degree grilles and disperse audio at all angles. If it's true audio fidelity you're after, opt for trusted brands such as Sonos, Bowers & Wilkins and KEF – speakers from these companies are always likely to sound brilliant.
If you have an iPhone or an iPad, it might also be worth checking out the best AirPlay speakers, which allow you to stream music, podcasts or audiobooks directly from your devices to your speaker. That means room-filling sound from your phone without the need for a more complex entertainment set-up. With so many fantastic home wireless speakers on the market right now, we’ve selected and ranked only the best ones to include in this buying guide.
Will wireless speakers work with Spotify Lossless?
Spotify Lossless is now finally rolling out to Premium users of the streaming service. It should work with all wireless speakers that already support Spotify Connect, which is Spotify's own way of letting you play music over Wi-Fi, assuming they have a hi-res-capable decoding chip (which basically all will have).
Apps for wireless speakers that have Spotify library support built-in will also be able to access and play Spotify Lossless, but not all offered this at launch – a wait for an update may be necessary in some cases, such as on Sonos.
As you'd expect, a high-end Wi-Fi speaker or multi-room system will get more from the improved sound than a cheaper one with more basic speakers.
Can I turn regular speakers into wireless speakers?
Yes, you can. You don’t necessarily need to replace your old wired speakers to go wireless, but you will need a wireless adapter. These devices can connect to your existing speaker system via an aux or optical input and will then connect to your Wi-Fi or Bluetooth source.
These adapters are essentially a way to upgrade your system, allowing you to stream music from your phone, laptop or smart home devices without having to plug anything in. It’s a good way to make your beloved hi-fi setup more modern, but without spending big on brand new wireless speakers.
How do I control wireless speakers?
Wireless speakers are most really simple to use. Which means you usually have a few options about how you control them.
Some have on-device controls. These are physical buttons that allow you to change volume, play/pause or switch inputs.
You can also control many with apps. Most brands now have a companion app for advanced controls, including EQ, grouping speakers together and streaming.
Many wireless speakers have voice assistants, like Alexa, Google Assistant or Siri built-in, which lets you control them hands-free.
Finally, some speakers support systems like Spotify Connect, Apple AirPlay and Google Cast (AKA Chromecast). These allow you to control playback directly from your streaming app.
The best option will depend on your speaker. You'll tend to find that entry-level Bluetooth models might only offer basic buttons and phone control. But high-end Wi-Fi speakers often become part of a whole home smart system that you can run entirely from your phone or with your voice.
Do wireless speakers offer Hi-Res Audio?
Yes, these days the vast majority of Wi-Fi and multi-room speakers now support Hi-Res Audio.
Hi-Res Audio means the music is streamed at a higher quality than standard CD audio, which captures more detail in the track you're listening to. Some wireless speakers are now certified for this kind of Hi-Res playback, especially models from higher-end brands, such as Bowers & Wilkins and KEF.
Also bear in mind that all of the other devices you're using matter here. For example, the source (like your streaming service or files) must also be Hi-Res, and the connection method has to support it, too.
With Wi-Fi speakers, that's no problem – it's got the bandwidth for Hi-Res Audio and then some, and works across all devices.
Are Sonos wireless speakers still worth buying?
Sonos speakers are still a good choice. However, you should know that Sonos rolled out big changes to its app in 2024. These changes caused frustration among Sonos fans because key features were missing or harder to access, and the rollout felt rushed. Backlash to the changes was loud, which is why Sonos has steadily been issuing updates to restore missing functionality and improve the overall experience.
With all that in mind, we do think the core appeal of Sonos remains intact and the app has been restored to working very well, in our experience. Sonos products deliver strong audio quality, seamless multi-room support, and lots of compatibility with streaming services and smart home systems.
So if you're already in the Sonos ecosystem or considering a Sonos speaker, we still think Sonos devices are absolutely worth buying. However, do keep an eye out for news about ongoing updates – especially if the app experience is a top priority for you.
What are the best wireless speaker brands to look out for?
It really depends on what kind of speaker you're after. If you want multi-room connectivity and excellent sound, look for home speakers from Sonos.
Need a smart speaker? Check out models in the Google Nest and Amazon Echo ranges (and if you're a Siri user, Apple). Bear in mind though, you're not stuck with these brands if you need a voice assistant, as many third-party speakers come with Alexa and Google Assistant compatibility.
If it's pure audio fidelity you're after, brands like KEF, Naim, and Devialet are worth looking into. And, for portability, check out the likes of JBL, Ultimate Ears, Bose, and Urbanista.
What is the difference between these wireless speakers and a Bluetooth speaker?
The key difference about what's in this guide compared to our list of the best Bluetooth speakers lies in Wi-Fi support. Wireless speakers often connect via Wi-Fi, which provides a more stable and high-quality audio stream. That’s because the Wi-Fi connection allows larger data transmissions, which results in better sound quality, especially with high-resolution audio files. Wi-Fi speakers can also connect to multiple devices simultaneously, making them ideal for multi-room setups controlled via apps.
In contrast, Bluetooth speakers connect directly to devices like smartphones, tablets, or laptops using Bluetooth. While convenient and portable, Bluetooth has a shorter range and can be more prone to signal interference and compression, which can affect audio quality.
However, when considering the difference between wireless speakers and Bluetooth speakers, it’s also worth considering that most of the best wireless speakers also have Bluetooth built-in, bringing you both options.
Wi-Fi is relatively uncommon in portable speakers, because it uses a lot more power than Bluetooth, and usually requires a network to connect to. However, there are some portable options in this guide.
What are the disadvantages of wireless speakers?
There’s a lot to love about wireless speakers, but they do have some disadvantages compared to wired speakers. One of the main drawbacks is that they’re dependent on a stable Wi-Fi network. This means that if your Wi-Fi signal is weak or inconsistent, you might experience interruptions or poor sound quality. Setting up wireless speakers can also sometimes be more complex, requiring apps and network configurations.
Another potential downside is latency. Wireless connections can sometimes introduce a slight delay in audio transmission. This could be noticeable when you’re watching videos or playing games. Battery life can also be a concern for portable wireless speakers, as they’d need regular charging.
Can I use a turntable with wireless speakers?
Yes, you can likely use one of the best turntables with wireless speakers, but exactly how will depend on the speakers or the turntable. The simplest option is, of course, if your turntable has wireless capabilities. There are products like the Cambridge Audio Alva TT V2 that can broadcast Bluetooth to headphones or wireless speakers, while some support Wi-Fi to play to certain wireless system, such as the Sonos-friendly Victrola Stream Carbon.
However, a lot of wireless speakers have wired inputs, and they always have their own built-in amplification, so these can be connected to a turntable use RCA wired cabling… as long as either the turntable or wireless speaker has a phono stage pre-amp built in. This is common in turntables, but much less common in speakers, so make sure you've got this somewhere in there.
Finally, there are adapters that you can plug a turntable into to add wireless transmission to them, such as a WiiM Pro Plus or a Sonos Port.
What streaming services do wireless speakers work with?
Most of the best wireless speakers support several different streaming services. Spotify Connect, Tidal Connect, Apple AirPlay and Qobuz Connect are some of the most commonly supported streaming services. Roon is less common, but is often supported by higher-end models.
However, it does depend on the brand of speaker. So, for example, at the time of writing Sonos supports Spotify Connect, Tidal Connect and Apple AirPlay but not Qobuz Connect.
Which is why we always suggest that you check your product's software support before you buy, depending on your music streaming platform of choice. We've listed everything you need to know about support in our reviews, of course, so do click through to those in the guide above.
It's also worth mentioning that if you’re a big podcast or audiobook listener, you'll need to make sure your speaker supports the apps you use most – or that it has Bluetooth as a backup. If you have Bluetooth (or Apple AirPlay and Google Cast, to a degree), you can play basically anything from your phone or other device.
Are wireless speakers' connections reliable?
Generally, yes. However, it does depend on your home Wi-Fi. Wireless speakers rely on a strong, stable signal to deliver quality sound. In most homes with a decent router, you’ll get a smooth experience with little to no dropouts.
But if your Wi-Fi is patchy or overloaded, you might experience some lag or interruptions. Multi-room setups are especially sensitive to network strength, so it might be worth considering a Wi-Fi mesh system or positioning your router centrally for the best possible results; or even using an Ethernet cable to connect directly to your router.
Bluetooth tends to be very stable if you're in the same room, but will drop of quickly when walls get in the way.
What's the best multi-room wireless speaker system?
Sonos is still one of the best choices. Its multi-room setup is intuitive, reliable and it works across a range of speaker types and budgets, which means that you can start with one speaker and expand room by room.
But there are other strong options too. In the guide above, several of the picks have some multi-room functionality, including brands such as JBL, Bowers & Wilkins and Cambridge Audio.
Google Cast and Apple AirPlay can offer multi-room support using speakers from different brands, which is useful for mixing and matching what you need. Google and Amazon also support multi-room setups for their smart speakers.
Will a wireless speaker work if my internet goes down?
This would depend on how your speaker is set up. If you’re streaming directly from the cloud, such as using Spotify Connect or playing music from Apple Music via the Sonos app, then yes. No internet would mean no music.
However, if your speaker also supports Bluetooth, AirPlay/Google Cast, or has an aux input, then you’ve got a backup plan. You would be able to switch to local playback from your phone or laptop until the connection’s back.
Bluetooth and an aux input don't require your network at all. AirPlay and Google Cast both use your home's Wi-Fi network – but this may still be working even if you're internet is down. If it's just the internet that's not working and you have saved music on your phone, you're fine; if your Wi-Fi went down along with the internet, then Bluetooth or aux-in are the only options.
How we test the best wireless speakers
At TechRadar, we get our hands (and ears, of course,) on dozens of wireless speakers every year, so we know exactly which features matter. And we know that the very best models can rival a traditional stereo system when set up properly.
Because manufacturer specs don't always tell the full story, we put every claim to the test in real-world conditions. We pit each speaker directly against its closest rivals to compare audio quality and key features like multi-room compatibility and app support, ensuring that when we call a speaker the best, it has genuinely earned the title.
Our reviewers live with these speakers in their own homes to test day-to-day reliability and consistency, never signing off on a verdict until we're completely confident in the sound. We stream across multiple sources and play a wide mix of genres, from bass-heavy dance tracks to subtle, spoken-word podcasts, to see how well each model adapts.
Backed by years of audio testing and complete editorial independence, our star-rated reviews are strictly earned: if a speaker falls short on sound, design, or usability, it simply won't make this list.

Becky became Audio Editor at TechRadar in 2024, but joined the team in 2022 as Senior Staff Writer, focusing on all things hi-fi. Before this, she spent three years at What Hi-Fi? testing and reviewing everything from wallet-friendly wireless earbuds to huge high-end sound systems. Prior to gaining her MA in Journalism in 2018, Becky freelanced as an arts critic alongside a 22-year career as a professional dancer and aerialist – any love of dance starts with a love of music. Becky has previously contributed to Stuff, FourFourTwo and The Stage. When not writing, she can still be found throwing shapes in a dance studio, these days with varying degrees of success.

articles.title: Wacom Goes Private in $860 Million Buyout Agreement
articles.text:
Monday, November 23rd 2026
Wacom Goes Private in $860 Million Buyout Agreement
Wacom, arguably the industry leader in pen display tech for digital artists, and the maker of the EMR tech inside Samsung's S Pens, has officially declared that it is pursuing a buyout agreement to the tune of $860 million that would see the company return to private ownership. Currently, the Japanese tech maker is listed in the Tokyo Stock Exchange, but this will no longer be the case after the buyout, which will see Korean conglomerate, MBK Partners acquire the company. Wacom will retain its current president, Nobutaka Ide, who is currently facilitating the deal between Wacom and MBK. 
It is theorized that the move to go private was inspired by the accelerating rise of Chinese pen tech makers, like Huion and XP Pen, whose offerings often come dangerously close to Wacom's quality at significantly lower prices. The current buyout offer put forth by MBK Partners is roughly 55% higher than Wacom's per-share closing price as of November 20. The buyout agreement also follows a financial rough patch, during which Wacom failed to turn a profit for three consecutive years until the tide changed during the last fiscal year. The buyout deal is currently pending scrutiny by Japanese regulators and is expected to be completed in mid-February 2027.For the time being, it seems as though not much is changing, and Samsung is even converting its current 6.8% ownership of Wacom into an identical share of the company post-buyout, suggesting that the Korean smartphone maker plans to continue partnering with Wacom on smartphone pen tech.

articles.title: AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates
articles.text:
AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates
Amazon Web Services Inc. is trying to tackle two major headaches for artificial intelligence agents developers with a major update to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers.
Today, the cloud infrastructure giant unveiled a new family of open-weight “decision models” called Strands Decider v2, along with the debut of Box CLI, bringing native sandbox support for popular coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Kiro CLI.
AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025, and recently the project has emerged as the centerpiece of the company’s agentic development strategy. Strands Agents is a software development kit that gives developers a flexible, model-driven foundation for connecting large language models to enterprise data and tools.
After introducing Strands Harness, which allows Strands agents to be deployed in any computing environment, in September, AWS followed up with Strands Decider one month later. Unlike regular LLMs that focus on text outputs, Strands Decider is a category of decision models designed to evaluate scenarios and assign probability scores to a predetermined list of choices. At the time, AWS said decision models can help to improve the efficiency of AI agent workflows, such as routing support tickets or choosing which software tool to invoke to complete a given task.
More decisive agents
With Strands Decider v2, AWS is adding five even more capable decision models to its lineup. The open-weight models are built on Google LLC’s Gemma 4 architecture and they’re available in various sizes, ranging from a lightweight edge version to a beefy 31 billion-parameter variant for complex decision-making. In a blog post, AWS explained that the new models provide greater accuracy across text, image and video tasks, and deliver more optimal confidence scores, so agents can better determine when it’s OK to take an action or escalate to a human decision-maker.
The Strands Decider v2 models have also been given the ability to process longer inputs, including multistep agent execution logs, so they can collaborate with other agents.
So far, AWS has used the Strands Decider v2 agents only internally, but it has seen impressive results. For instance, its engineers were able to replace Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider v2 on the company’s largest internal ticketing system, and in the process they were able to reduce its labelling costs by 98%.
They also cut ticket response times by 78%. But that’s not all they can do – in its experiments, AWS said, the new decider models showed an ability to steer robotic arms, evaluate other AI agents and route routine queries to cheaper models when a more computationally intensive frontier model might be overkill.
The Strands Decider v2 models are available to everyone now under an Apache 2.0 license and can be found on Hugging Face and also the Strands Decider repository on AWS.
Security without sacrifice
Strands Decider is all about enhancing the speed and performance of agents while lowering costs. Meanwhile, Box CLI is all about securing them.
In a second blog post, AWS explained that many developers have taken to running their coding agents in what’s known as “YOLO mode.” That’s where they disable permission and configuration prompts so that those agents can run terminal commands, edit files and call third-party tools as they see fit in order to complete a task. It’s named after the slang phrase “you only live once.”
Agents running in YOLO mode execute much faster, but they do so at the sacrifice of human oversight. And that’s dangerous. An agent without any restrictions can accidentally delete files it really shouldn’t or leak sensitive keys, or it can be manipulated through a malicious prompt to do something else that’s extremely damaging.
AWS’ solution to this is Strands Box, which is an open-source operating system sandbox that enforces strict security policies on every agent action. It launched last month, and with today’s update, it’s getting a new Box CLI that adds support for coding agents including Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and the company’s very own Kiro CLI.
The idea is that developers can wrap their entire workflow within an isolated sandbox to prevent any accidents from occurring. Within the sandbox, the agents will be able to work without restrictions, meaning they won’t have to keep pausing to ask a human developer for permission to do something important.
Instead, the developer simply applies security policies to safeguard the agent’s actions. These policies govern which files, commands and network hosts an agent can access, AWS explained.
The agent’s credentials live outside the sandbox, with application programming interface keys and AWS tokens injected only when a policy-approved request leaves the sandboxed environment. That way, the agent itself never has access to those sensitive keys.
AWS said developers also have the flexibility to switch between task-specific profiles, such as giving a coding agent access to a repository while restricting a troubleshooting agent to read-only diagnostic access.
Like the new decider models, Box CLI in Strands Box is being launched today. It’s a big step forward for autonomous agents, ensuring they can work without constant interruptions while remaining on a very short leash.

articles.title: Black Friday : la Ninja AutoBarista Pro passe à 535,49 € avec le code NUMSN10
articles.text:
Black Friday : la Ninja AutoBarista Pro passe à 535,49 € avec le code NUMSN10
C'est l'une des remises les plus spectaculaires du catalogue Ninja pour ce Black Friday. La machine à café full automatique AutoBarista Pro AE1051EU passe de 899,99 € à 629,99 €. En activant le code promo NUMSN10 au moment de la commande, le prix final tombe à 535,49 €. Soit plus de 360 € d'économie pour s'offrir une machine qui rivalise avec des modèles vendus à plus de 1 500 € .
Le secret de l'AutoBarista Pro : la technologie GrindIQ
La grande force de cette machine, c'est son système GrindIQ. Sur la plupart des automatiques, trouver le bon réglage de mouture relève du casse-tête. Trop fine, le café est amer et l'extraction se bloque. Trop grossière, il est plat. Avec GrindIQ, la machine s'occupe de tout.
Lors de la première utilisation avec un nouveau grain, elle tire un shot, analyse le temps d'extraction via un capteur de pression, ajuste la mouture, et recommence. En deux à trois essais, le réglage est trouvé . Et grâce à la balance intégrée dans le bac à grains, chaque dose est pesée au gramme près. Résultat : une régularité impressionnante, tasse après tasse, sans jamais avoir à toucher aux réglages.
Pendant ce Black Friday, la Ninja AutoBarista Pro AE1051EU est proposée à 629,99 € au lieu de 899,99 €. En activant le code NUMSN10, le prix passe à 535,49 €, soit 364,50 € d'économie (environ 40 %).
Un double bac à grains pour varier les plaisirs
L'une des particularités de l'AE1051EU, c'est son système de double bac à grains interchangeable. Deux trémies de 340 g chacune sont fournies . Vous pouvez y stocker deux cafés différents : un grain corsé pour le matin, un décaféiné pour le soir, ou deux origines pour varier selon l'humeur.
Le mécanisme est bien pensé : le broyeur se vide intégralement après chaque préparation. Quand vous changez de bac, les meules sont propres, et aucun mélange de saveurs ne vient gâcher votre tasse . Un vrai plus pour les foyers où les goûts divergent.
13 programmes et une mousse de lait digne d'un coffee shop
La machine embarque 13 programmes de boissons, de l'expresso au cold brew, en passant par le latte macchiato, le cappuccino, le café filtre et même le café glacé . De quoi couvrir toutes les envies, du petit-déjeuner au goûter.
Le système FrothPerfect gère le moussage du lait avec une buse vapeur automatique. La mousse est fine, onctueuse, et compatible avec les laits animaux comme végétaux . Vous pouvez même lancer le moussage en file d'attente pendant que la machine prépare le café, pour gagner de précieuses secondes le matin.
L'offre Black Friday qui change la donne
À 535,49 € avec le code, l'AutoBarista Pro se place parmi les full automatiques les plus compétitives du marché. Avec son groupe de percolation de 53 mm, son double bac à grains et sa technologie GrindIQ, elle offre un niveau d'équipement qu'on trouve habituellement à des tarifs bien plus élevés . N'oubliez pas de saisir NUMSN10 au moment de la commande pour valider les 364,50 € d'économie.

articles.title: Cómo elegir una lavadora, refrigerador o electrodoméstico antes del precio
articles.text:
Con la llegada del Black Friday, que se realizará la última semana de noviembre, los electrodomésticos vuelven a ocupar un lugar destacado entre las compras de los consumidores. Según Fenalco (Federación Nacional de Comerciantes Empresarios, en Colombia), esta categoría concentró el 24% de las preferencias de compra durante la jornada de 2025.
Sin embargo, elegir una nevera o una lavadora no debería depender solo del descuento disponible en la etiqueta. El tamaño del hogar, la frecuencia de uso y la durabilidad del equipo son factores que inciden tanto como el precio final.
Conocer el hogar antes de mirar el precio
Electrolux identifica cuatro perfiles de consumidores según sus hábitos cotidianos. Para quienes viven solos, una nevera de entre 150 y 250 litros y una lavadora de entre 9,5 y 12 kilogramos suelen ser suficientes.
En hogares de dos integrantes, la recomendación sube a neveras de 200 a 280 litros y lavadoras de alrededor de 12 kilogramos, mientras que para familias de tres o cuatro personas conviene pensar en neveras de 300 a 400 litros y lavadoras de 14 a 18 kilogramos.
Quienes trabajan desde casa deberían priorizar equipos con tecnología Inverter, que reduce el nivel de ruido y mejora la eficiencia energética. Para espacios reducidos o mudanzas frecuentes, una lavadora-secadora de 11 kilogramos integra ambas funciones en un solo equipo y conviene revisar que exista servicio técnico en la ciudad de residencia.
El tipo de carga también importa: la frontal ahorra más agua, maltrata menos la ropa y centrifuga mejor, aunque resulta más costosa. La carga superior, en cambio, es más económica y permite añadir prendas a mitad del ciclo.
En ambos casos conviene priorizar motores Inverter, sin escobillas, que reducen el consumo eléctrico y suelen incluir garantías de entre 10 y 20 años en esa pieza.
Para las neveras, el primer paso es medir el espacio disponible en la cocina y dejar al menos 5 centímetros libres a los lados y atrás para que el motor disipe el calor. La tecnología No Frost evita la formación de escarcha y mantiene una temperatura más uniforme sin necesidad de descongelar manualmente.
Si el uso del refrigerador supera al del congelador, los modelos con congelador inferior resultan más cómodos. En todos los casos, revisar la etiqueta de eficiencia energética y buscar clasificación A o superior ayuda a reducir el gasto eléctrico a largo plazo.
El precio suele ser lo primero que capta la atención al comprar un electrodoméstico, pero una encuesta global de Samsung Electronics muestra que la durabilidad ocupa el segundo lugar entre las prioridades de los consumidores. El 48% la identificó como una consideración central, y el 36% afirmó que su importancia aumentó frente a hace tres años.
Cómo aprovechar ofertas reales durante Black Friday
Para distinguir un descuento genuino de una rebaja inflada, conviene anotar el modelo exacto y su precio normal entre tres y cuatro semanas antes del evento. Esa comparación previa es la forma más confiable de verificar si el precio de Black Friday representa un ahorro real.
También, es útil considerar otras fechas clave, como el Cyber Monday, los días sin IVA o los aniversarios de grandes cadenas, además de los períodos entre enero y marzo, cuando las marcas renuevan catálogo y los modelos del año anterior bajan de precio sin perder funciones.
Revisar alianzas bancarias puede sumar descuentos adicionales de entre el 10% y el 20%, o cuotas sin interés. Por último, conviene calcular el costo total sumando el flete y la instalación, ya que un precio algo mayor que incluya entrega gratuita puede representar un ahorro neto frente a una oferta aparentemente más barata.

articles.title: VMware : une faille critique exploitée depuis septembre, un outil de piratage désormais proposé à 30 000 dollars
articles.text:
Des pirates soupçonnés d'être liés à la Chine ont exploité une vulnérabilité critique de VMware vCenter avant sa correction. Alors que Google révèle les dessous de cette campagne de cyberespionnage, un nouvel outil d'exploitation serait déjà en vente sur un forum clandestin.
Une faille corrigée le 19 novembre, mais exploitée dès le début du mois de septembre. C'est ce qu'ont découvert les équipes de Google Threat Intelligence Group et de Mandiant en enquêtant sur les activités d'ARMORY CASTLE, un groupe de cyberespionnage soupçonné d'entretenir des liens avec la Chine. Identifiée sous la référence CVE-2026-123890 et évaluée à 9,8 sur 10, la vulnérabilité touche VMware vCenter, la console centrale qui permet aux entreprises d'administrer leurs serveurs de virtualisation et les machines virtuelles qu'ils hébergent. Une cible de choix pour les pirates, puisqu'en prendre le contrôle peut leur ouvrir les portes d'une grande partie du réseau informatique de leur victime.
Protégez votre entreprise gratuitement pendant 30 jours
Découvrez Bitdefender Ultimate Small Business Security et protégez votre activité contre les cybermenaces. Aucune coordonnée bancaire requise.
Deux failles zero-day et cinq outils malveillants pour compromettre VMware
D'après les investigations de Google, les hackers ont d'abord exploité une autre faille zero-day (CVE-2026-102764) dans BeyondTrust Remote Support, une solution d'accès à distance utilisée en entreprise. Une fois introduits dans le réseau, ils ont compromis plusieurs équipements Linux avant de rechercher les serveurs vCenter, auxquels ils se sont attaqués à l'aide d'un programme spécialement développé pour l'occasion, baptisé BONESAW.
Cet outil leur a permis de contourner l'authentification de VMware vCenter sans disposer d'identifiants valides, puis de créer un compte administrateur. Les pirates ont ensuite récupéré des informations sensibles, fabriqué des jetons d'authentification pour usurper l'identité d'utilisateurs légitimes et exploré les systèmes de fichiers des serveurs ESXi, qui hébergent les machines virtuelles.
BONESAW faisait partie d'un arsenal de cinq nouveaux programmes malveillants identifiés par les chercheurs, comprenant également des outils de commande à distance et une porte dérobée destinée à conserver l'accès aux systèmes compromis. Son développement pourrait même remonter au mois de juillet, plusieurs semaines avant les premières attaques confirmées en septembre. Le nombre d'organisations touchées n'a pas été communiqué.
La menace pourrait d’ailleurs désormais dépasser le cadre de cette seule campagne de cyberespionnage. Selon Cyber Security News, un individu utilisant le pseudonyme Matilda propose sur un forum clandestin un programme Python à 30 000 dollars, censé exploiter CVE-2026-123890 pour créer un compte administrateur sur les versions 7.0 à 9.1 de vCenter.
Quels correctifs installer pour protéger les serveurs VMware ?
Pour empêcher l'exploitation de cette faille, les entreprises concernées doivent installer sans tarder les correctifs publiés le 19 novembre par Broadcom. Ils sont intégrés aux versions vCenter 8.0 Update 3m, 9.0.2.0200 et 9.1.1.0200. Pour VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x, la procédure est différente : les administrateurs doivent installer vCenter 8.0 Update 3m en suivant les instructions spécifiques de l'éditeur, ainsi que SDDC Manager 5.2.5.
Ces mises à jour laissent toutefois de côté vCenter 7.0, pour lequel aucun correctif public n'est disponible. Les entreprises bénéficiant d'un contrat de support étendu doivent donc contacter directement Broadcom. En l'absence de solution de contournement officielle, restreindre les connexions aux serveurs vCenter aux seules machines autorisées permet néanmoins de limiter leur exposition.
Enfin, puisque la faille a été exploitée bien avant sa divulgation, appliquer le correctif ne suffit pas à écarter toute compromission antérieure. Les administrateurs doivent également examiner les journaux de connexion de vCenter, vérifier qu'aucun compte administrateur suspect n'a été créé et rechercher d'éventuelles traces d'accès non autorisés.

articles.title: 3D printer that promises simultaneous printing from all four heads gets $500,000 in crowdfunding — four-printhead Co Print Quadro MSRP set at just $899, promises reduced waste and faster printing
articles.text:
3D printer that promises simultaneous printing from all four heads gets $500,000 in crowdfunding — four-printhead Co Print Quadro MSRP set at just $899, promises reduced waste and faster printing
The Co Print Quadro is this year's second IQEX 3D printer Kickstarter campaign, and it's much more affordable with an SRP of $899.
The Co Print Quadro is an Independent Quad Extrusion (IQEX) bedslinger 3D printer, carrying four fully functional printheads on one gantry. The 3D printer accessory company’s first 3D printer aims to bring IQEX technology to the masses at a budget price, with an SRP of only $899. It has already raised over $500,000, crushing its goal of only $9,820.
Independent Quad Extrusion, or IQEX, is unlike tool-changer 3D printers. Instead of one print head swapping assemblies, it has four individual print heads. This allows for increased productivity by printing with all four heads at once, or reducing waste by not going through any purging steps.
The Co Print Quadro is a non-enclosed bedslinger, and its design is quite similar to the Bambu Lab A1, albeit much beefier. The four print heads line up on one gantry, with space for three extruders on either side so they can get out of the way while either of the extruders on the edges can print. It has a large build volume of 300mm3, while the unit itself takes up a massive 780 x 620 mm footprint (2.5 x 2 feet).
Co print claims the Quadro can switch colors in one second, beating out tool changers that still need to park, grab, and home each tool, possibly with some priming as well. The Quadro’s demonstration video still used a prime tower, but it’s likely optional, meaning it can achieve zero color-change waste. What’s even more impressive is the copy printing technology, allowing multiple or even all print heads to print the same objects at once, potentially increasing productivity fourfold. Of course, it also has its own slicer for added IQEX functions, and it’s based on OrcaSlicer, so we’ll likely see community mods that make it do even crazier things.
The Co Print Quadro is not without competition, however, as another IQEX printer finished its Kickstarter campaign earlier this year: the LightMake L4, raising $3 million in backing over its $50,000 goal. The L4 is an enclosed Core-XY printer with an even bigger print volume of 354 x 370 x 386mm in a smaller 610 x 620 mm footprint while still able to let each print head reach every corner of the build plate. The L4 has the size and enclosure advantage, but Co Print does plan to sell an enclosure for the Quadro as well for more demanding filaments. The L4 has two gantries and can also print four objects at once, but it has a much higher SRP of $2,400 compared to the Quadro’s $899.
The Quadro is Co Print’s first 3D printer, but the company is no stranger to 3D printing, providing multi-color upgrade kits for Creality, Elegoo, and Flashforge printers, including open-source printer brands like Sovol, Voron, and QIDI. While the products are mostly viewed positively, many forums complain about Co Print’s customer service and support. If Co Print wants to sell a whole 3D printer, it should be prepared to deal with issues and take feedback.
Our customary crowdfunder disclaimer applies. Remember that crowdfunding a project is not a guarantee of receiving a finished product. Backing a crowdfunded project is akin to an investment; you believe in the project and want it to succeed. You are not purchasing a retail product.

articles.title: La última misión del capítulo 1 de 'GTA 6': todo lo que hay que hacer antes del punto de no retorno
articles.text:
Arreglar la casa, explorar el barrio, salir a pescar, entrenar, darle de comer a la serpiente... El principio de 'GTA VI' se presta a la calma total, pero no te confíes porque el juego tiene preparada una trampa que llega cuando menos te lo esperas. Hay un punto en el que la historia avanza de golpe al capítulo 2 y no sólo te saca de 'Leonida Keys', también te deja sin dinero y sin posibilidad de acceder a varias misiones y objetos que ya no volverán a aparecer.
La misión clave. El encargo que activa este punto crítico se llama 'Trampa para turistas' y va justo después de 'Recalibrado', la fiesta nocturna con Cal (si quieres volver a esta zona en algún momento, puedes crear un punto de guardado manual tras esta misión). Una vez aceptes la misión, se activan tres misiones consecutivas que te llevan al capítulo 2. Si quieres hacerte con objetos únicos y completar todas las tramas de esta parte de la historia, deberás hacerlo antes de llegar a este punto.
Pon tu dinero a salvo. El cambio de capítulo te deja con lo puesto. Vas a perder todo tu dinero en efectivo, incluyendo el saldo de la cuenta bancaria. Para no quedarte a cero, ingresa el máximo que te permite la cuenta de ahorros familiares de BuckMe, que son 5.000 dólares. Ese dinero acumulado en la hucha es lo único que sobrevivirá al salto de episodio, así que fúndete el resto. Puedes hacerte tatuajes, comprar ropa, armas o cualquier otra cosa que se te ocurra.
Completa las misiones de Shirley. Shirley es tu vecina y te pide dos favores. El primero es que le compres una botella de ron en una tienda local. Al llegar allí se escuchan ruidos extraños en la trastienda y, si entras, encontrarás un negocio ilegal. Después te pide que le robes el scooter a un vecino. Es una pequeña misión sin mayor importancia, pero si no la completas ahora desaparecerá para siempre.
Meditación con Lucía. Una mañana estás en casa y Lucía te propone meditar con ella. Sal al balcón con ella y acepta la oferta, es tu única oportunidad. Esto abrirá una serie de 18 meditaciones que, si completas, te dan el trofeo "Actitud mental positiva".
Objetos y coleccionables. Hay varios a lo largo del capítulo que no podrás volver a encontrar, como los libros y revistas que hay repartidos por casa de Jason o las gafas de sol que le ofrecen a Lucía en la misión 'Libertad por un día'. Casi al final del capítulo, te encargan limpiar el remolque de Donnie, donde encontrarás un revolver único.

articles.title: The best cordless vacuums 2026 — these are the tried and tested models we'd buy
articles.text:
The best cordless vacuums 2026 — these are the tried and tested models we'd buy
From deep carpet to dog hair, these cordless vacuums can handle it all
Choosing the best cordless vacuum isn’t as simple as comparing suction figures or battery claims on a box. Every manufacturer measures performance differently, and the features that actually matter depend on your home, whether you’re dealing with thick carpets, hard floors, or non-stop pet hair.
That’s why we rely on real-world testing rather than spec sheets. Our reviewers live with and test every cordless vacuum in their own homes, putting each model through its paces on different floor types, stubborn pet hair, and larger debris. We also evaluate everyday comfort, maneuverability, true battery runtime, ease of maintenance, and overall value.
The result is a carefully curated shortlist of the cordless vacuums we genuinely recommend today; whether you’re after a budget-friendly everyday cleaner, a featherweight stick vacuum, or a feature-packed flagship machine.
Score a cut-price cordless vacuum cleaner this Black Friday season
Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
The Black Friday sales are well underway, which means it's now a great time to score a cut-price cordless vacuum cleaner. Our widgets below should flag the best daily prices available from reliable retailers. And while the deal will surely peak with Black Friday itself on November 27, they'll continue into Cyber Monday on November 30, and likely have some discounts still lurking around ahead of the Christmas holiday.
The best cordless vacuum overall

View Original
View Original
View Original
Specifications
Reasons to buy
Reasons to avoid
The Dreame R20 earned the highest overall score in my group test, and was the best all-rounder too – it didn't score below a 3/5 in any category. This vacuum was especially strong on battery life, and comfort and maneuverability. This is all the more impressive given it's the cheapest vacuum in my group test.
The Dreame R20 earned solid cleaning scores across the board, but performed especially well in my deep-pile carpet and pet hair tests. The mini motorized tool was excellent at clearing hair from upholstery. The R20 did a decent job on mid-pile carpet, too, clearing large and small particles well, but required a few passes to get everything completely clean. The slightly lower score on hard floor was due to the floorhead causing debris to pool up when the vacuum was pulled backwards over the spillage.
The R20 is lightweight for a stick vacuum, which means it's relatively comfortable to use, despite a lack of any padding or shaping on the handle. In handheld mode I appreciated that the main body was compact in shape, making it easier to wield, although I did find the finger rest could dig in.
The combination of trigger-operation and a lock button for continual running makes it great for both quick cleanups and longer sessions (surprisingly, it was the only vacuum in my test to offer this user-friendly setup). Although the floorhead pivots extremely well, the connections on my test model were incredibly stiff, making changing attachments a major challenge.
The Dreame R20 uses a flashy-looking screen to convey information, including battery status (shown as a percentage) and any error messages. The modes aren't the most intuitive to understand, but after some use I ascertained that a green fan meant 'regular mode with auto-adjustment based on dirt detected' and a white fan meant 'boost mode'. You get a separate soft head for delicate hard floors, but oddly Dreame hasn't included headlamps here – instead, they're on the general floorhead, and they're not that bright in any case.
Dreame promises a maximum of 90 minutes of cleaning per charge, which is the longest runtime I've heard quoted on the market. However, you'll only achieve this on a relatively clean, hard floor – there's no 'Eco' mode, so the lowest suction option is the auto-adjusting Standard mode. I timed seven minutes of cleaning in Boost mode, which is good but not great.
The best cordless vacuum for pet hair
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Specifications
Reasons to buy
Reasons to avoid
If pet hair is your biggest vacuuming headache, the Shark PowerDetect Cordless is a particularly strong contender. It was the only model in our comparative tests to score 5/5 across every pet-hair challenge. This is a more positive result than our original review, which tested the Pet Multi Tool on human hair on upholstery rather than pet hair across multiple surfaces, might suggest.
Aside from pet hair, it also delivers strong suction across hard floors and carpets. Its redesigned floorhead helps it pick up debris when pulled backwards as well as pushed forwards, and the automatic suction adjustment takes some of the guesswork out of cleaning different surfaces.
The bendable wand is another useful addition, making it easier to reach under furniture without having to crouch down. However, all this comes in a fairly bulky package. At 3.7kg, it's one of the heaviest cordless vacuums we've tested, and isn't as nimble as lighter alternatives.
The Shark PowerDetect came top in every single cleaning test, scoring a perfect 5/5 in every pet hair test and every medium-pile carpet test. In our comparative pet-hair testing, it cleared almost all of the hair from the test surfaces in a single pass. Its excellent performance is down partly to outright power, and partly to a clever floorhead design.
Shark has added a flap that lifts to enable the vacuum to suck up particles when it's pulled backwards over them, rather than causing them to pool up, as is the case with every other vacuum I tested here. This feature is especially useful on hard floors.
Now for the bad news. The Shark PowerDetect is the heaviest vacuum in my group test, and feels noticeably chunkier and less nimble than the rest of the bunch. The weight is more evenly distributed than it is on the Gen5detect – which is heavy and also top-heavy – making it a little easier to use in both handheld and floor-standing modes than that model.
To its credit, Shark has also made a big effort to improve comfort, by shaping the handle ergonomically and adding a rubberized grip and padding. Nothing digs in or sits awkwardly as you clean, which is more than can be said for a number of other models I tried here.
Shark has excelled at the special features, but dropped the ball when it comes to basic usability. The vacuum switches on with a one-press button (good for long sessions but annoying for quick cleanups, because the button isn't reachable from the handle, so you'll need to use your other hand) and it takes a second or so to kick into gear each time, rather than responding immediately, as all the other vacuums did.
When switched on, the screen cycles though various icons representing the suction modes – a leaf for Eco, a boost icon, a target representing the Auto mode, and a water droplet to represent... actually, I have no idea what this is for. I've scoured the product manual for clues, but it's not mentioned anywhere (it's notably absent under "Instructions for use" and "Error codes").
Initially, I couldn't find any way to manually switch between the modes, so I ended up stuck in Auto, which fortunately is the most useful mode. Eventually, I discovered there's a button for mode-switching where the trigger would usually sit – a setup that took some getting used to, and felt especially counter-intuitive as I was moving between the PowerDetect and other vacuums that are trigger-operated. There's a colored ring to indicate how much dirt has been detected, but it's not immediately clear which color means what.
Usability niggles aside, this vacuum has one of the most comprehensive feature lists of any vacuum I reviewed. It can auto-adjust suction based on floor type and dirt levels, but also boost suction on the relevant side of the floorhead when the vacuum approaches the edge of a room, and brighten the headlamps in particularly dark areas. There's also an optional auto-empty dock, complete with odor-neutralizing puck.
My battery-life tests were scuppered somewhat by the fact that I couldn't find any way to manually change to suction mode for this vacuum. However, Shark promises a maximum of 70 minutes cleaning per charge, which is a very solid runtime. The caveat, of course, is that that figure is for relatively clean, hard floors, and runtimes will decrease for anything more challenging.
The best premium cordless vacuum
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Specifications
Reasons to buy
Reasons to avoid
The Gen5detect is the best premium option. It has the best design of all the vacuums I tested, offering advanced features paired with outstanding usability. It managed the joint-longest runtimes, and was a runner-up in all the cleaning tests. However, it's the priciest vacuum of the bunch, and also one of the heaviest.
The Gen5detect was a close second behind the Shark PowerDetect in all my cleaning tests. It suffered from being slightly too powerful in Auto mode on deep-pile carpet, but the suction was strong enough in Eco mode that it cleared spillages very effectively while being much easier to push.
Usefully, Dyson has added an air intake slider to the floorhead to help release some pressure as required (this was missing the Dyson V11 that I also tested, to its detriment). It also proved excellent at handling pet hair, both with its main floorhead and its mini motorized tool.
The Gen5detect is the second-heaviest vacuum I tested, with the heaviest top section. The fact that the weight is concentrated in the top section, which is really rather long, makes it unwieldy to use, with or without the wand attached.
Dyson has added some welcome padding above the handle, but I still found the battery casing could dig into my wrist when I used the vacuum as a handheld. This model switches on and off with a one-press button, which is great for long cleaning sessions but annoying for quick cleanups as it requires both hands to be free (as with the Shark PowerDetect, the button can't be reached from the handle).
The Gen5detect is packed with special features, but unlike with the Shark PowerDetect, Dyson hasn't neglected basic usability factors. A screen near the handle conveys information in an unambiguous way – it'll spell out exactly how long you have left on the battery in your current cleaning mode, as well as flagging any issues and telling you how to fix them. This screen will also tell you, in words, which mode you're using, which after trying to decipher various icons and color-coding systems on other machines, I truly appreciated.
Like a number of vacuums in my group test, the Gen5detect can auto-adjust suction depending on how much dirt it detects on the floor, but this model goes a step further and will report the size and number of particles being sucked up as you clean via a colorful, animated on-screen bar graph. You'll also get a soft floorhead for delicate hard flooring, and it's equipped with a nice, bright laser to illuminate dirt.
You'll get a maximum of 60 minutes of cleaning time in Eco mode, which is not as long as some competitors, but still very decent. (Also factor in that the Eco mode here is powerful enough to still be very useful.) I managed 15 minutes of cleaning in the ultra-powerful Boost mode, which is excellent.
The best budget cordless vacuum
Specifications
Reasons to buy
Reasons to avoid
The Hoover HF3 DynamicClean is proof you don't need to spend Dyson money to get a capable cordless vacuum. It cleans well, weighs very little, and its Anti-Twist brushbar lives up to the hype by preventing hair from wrapping around the roller. The compromises are exactly where you'd expect for the price: battery life, build quality and a little extra noise, but none are deal-breakers if you're shopping on a budget.
The HF3 punches well above its price tag when it comes to cleaning. During testing it picked up everyday dust, crumbs and pet hair with confidence across both carpets and hard floors, only occasionally needing an extra pass on thicker rugs or larger debris. Hoover's Anti-Twist brushbar also deserves a mention, preventing hair from wrapping around the roller and removing one of the more tedious maintenance jobs altogether.
Weighing just 2.54kg, the HF3 is one of the lightest cordless vacuums we've tested, and you notice it straight away. It's easy to carry upstairs, comfortable to push around the house, and the self-standing design is surprisingly handy when you need to stop and move furniture. It isn't quite as nimble around chair legs and awkward corners as pricier Shark or Dyson models, but for everyday cleaning it's an easy vacuum to live with.
Hoover has focused its budget where it matters. You get practical extras including HEPA filtration, LED headlights, a battery display and Anti-Twist technology, rather than flashy features you'll rarely use. The trade-off is that some of the plastics and attachments feel a little flimsy, while the narrow dustbin can be awkward to empty completely, but those feel like reasonable compromises at this price.
The quoted 60-minute runtime comes with a fairly hefty asterisk: it's only achievable in Eco mode. In day-to-day cleaning you'll spend most of your time in Standard mode, where battery life is closer to half that figure, while Turbo empties the battery in around 15 minutes. That's plenty for flats and smaller homes, but larger houses will probably need a mid-clean recharge.
The best lightweight cordless vacuum

Specifications
Reasons to buy
Reasons to avoid
The Detect Pro is perfectly capable of dealing with day-to-day cleaning, but outright suction isn't its biggest strength. It performed particularly well on hard floors, where the automatic Detect mode quietly adjusted power as we moved between surfaces and dirtier patches. The main drawback is the floorhead, which has a habit of pushing debris into small piles when pulled backwards – something Shark later addressed on the PowerDetect.
This is where the Detect Pro earns its place in the lineup. It's the lightest vacuum in our testing, making it effortless to carry upstairs, steer around furniture and convert into a handheld. While the wand can be a little fiddly to remove, it's an exceptionally easy vacuum to live with, particularly if you clean little and often.
Shark packs in plenty of useful technology without overcomplicating things. Detect mode automatically adjusts suction based on floor type and dirt levels, while edge detection boosts power where dust tends to collect. The optional auto-empty dock is another welcome addition. The small dustbin and limited selection of included tools prevent it from matching the Dyson Gen5detect for overall usability.
Battery life is respectable rather than exceptional. While Shark quotes up to 60 minutes in Eco mode (40 minutes in the US), using Detect mode or Boost cuts that figure down considerably. It'll comfortably cope with most small and medium-sized homes, but larger properties may need a recharge before you've finished.
The second-best premium cordless vacuum

The Dyson V11 Advanced may no longer be the newest Dyson in the lineup, but it's still one of the best cordless vacuums we've tested when it comes to outright cleaning performance. It excelled on carpets and pet hair during testing, while its clear LCD screen and excellent battery life make it easy to live with. The main drawback is that it lacks some of the smarter features now found on newer Dyson models, making it harder to justify at full price.
The V11 impressed throughout our cleaning tests, particularly on medium-pile carpet where it cleared both fine dust and larger debris with ease. It was also one of the strongest performers for pet hair, and delivered solid results on hard floors. The only real compromise came on deep-pile carpet, where the lack of an air intake slider made it harder to push despite its powerful suction.
Despite its top-heavy design, the V11 is easy to steer around furniture and lies almost flat for cleaning under sofas and cabinets. It feels noticeably less balanced in handheld mode, however, while the trigger-operated design can become tiring during longer cleaning sessions because there's no lock for continuous running.
The V11's LCD display remains one of the clearest and most intuitive we've used, displaying remaining runtime, cleaning mode and maintenance alerts at a glance. However, newer Dyson models have moved the game on with features like automatic suction adjustment and laser floorheads, leaving the V11 feeling a little dated despite its premium build quality.
Battery life is one of the V11's biggest strengths. It exceeded Dyson's claimed 60-minute Eco runtime during testing, while Medium mode delivered a healthy 33 minutes and Boost lasted around 15 minutes. The removable battery adds some welcome longevity, and the live runtime countdown on the LCD screen takes much of the guesswork out of longer cleaning sessions.
Also tested
Hoover HF3 DynamicClean
The Bissell PowerClean FurFinder remains a strong budget cordless vacuum, particularly for US shoppers who can't yet buy the Hoover HF3 DynamicClean. It offers reliable cleaning performance, a brilliant mini motorized pet tool and excellent value, although its small bin and short battery life make it better suited to smaller homes.
Read our full Hoover HF3 DynamicClean review
Dyson V8 Cyclone
This model is a strong all-rounder, but was just pipped to the post when it came to my top five. The design is basic, and there are no special features to speak of, but this vacuum's cleaning scores were strong, with a 4 or higher on carpet (medium- and deep-pile) and pet hair. At the time of writing, it's not available in the US.
Read my full Dyson V8 Cyclone review
Roborock H60 Hub Ultra
This vacuum earned middling scores in most categories. The cleaning performance was mixed, with a high score for medium-pile carpet, but low scores on deep carpet and hard flooring. 
Read my full Roborock H60 Hub Ultra review
Dyson V16 Piston Animal
The V16 Piston Animal is Dyson's newest vacuum, and big disappointment for me. While the battery life is excellent and I was impressed with many design elements and special features, the cleaning performance was weak across the board, which is inexcusable given the sky-high price. 
Read my full Dyson V16 Piston Animal review
Comparison charts
Testing methodology
Finding the best cordless vacuum isn't all about testing suction power – there are multiple factors that play into how well a vacuum performs. Here's a rundown of the key areas vacuum expert Ruth Hamilton focused on in her group test, why they're important, how TechRadar tests the vacuums, and which models came out on top in each area.
The following was written by Ruth Hamilton.
Carpet cleaning performance
Carpet cleaning ability is of course a key factor in a cordless vacuum cleaner's performance. To efficiently clean carpet, a vacuum needs a good amount of suction, but there's more to it than that. If the suction is too strong a vacuum will be difficult to push, so an air intake slider on the floorhead can help here by reducing the suction pressure. A well-designed beater bar (the roller in the floorhead), with bristles to agitate the carpet fibers and release ground-in dirt, is also a must for efficient carpet cleaning.
How I tested
For the carpet cleaning test, I used dry tea to represent fine particles, and a dry rice and lentil mix to represent chunky particles. I sprinkled a set amount of each on the carpeted floor, then ran over it once with each vacuum on its 'medium' setting, or dropping to its low setting if that proved too difficult to push. I then assessed how much of the spillage had been picked up, and continued cleaning until the spillage was clear. I ran these tests on medium-pile carpet and deep-pile carpet.
I made notes on each vacuum's performance in each test, and gave it a score out of five for its fine particle clearing ability and for its chunky-particle clearing ability. The average score for each floor type is the two scores divided by two.
Highest scorer: Shark PowerDetect
Runner up: Dyson Gen5detect
Hard floor cleaning performance
Cleaning a hard floor requires less suction than tackling carpet, because all the dust and debris is sat on top of the surface. Great hard floor head cleaning performance relies on a floorhead that doesn't cause particles to ping about or pool up. It may also be kitted out with headlamps that illuminate debris that might get missed, and/or a separate soft floorhead designed specifically to buff and clean hard floors without risking scratches.
How I tested
For the hard floor cleaning tests, I used fine particles (dry tea) and chunky particles (a mix of dry rice and lentils). I sprinkled a pile of each on my vinyl floor floor, then approached it forwards with each vacuum in its 'medium' setting to see how efficiently it cleared the mess and if there was any pinging or pooling. I also reversed the vacuum backwards over each spillage to see if it cleared it or simply pushed the particles about. I checked my findings on the studio's own wood laminate flooring.
I made notes on each vacuum's performance and awarded each a score out of 5 for each particle type. The overall score for hard floor cleaning is the two scores divided by two.
Highest scorer: Shark PowerDetect
Runner up: Dyson Gen5detect
Pet hair cleaning performance
Pet hair can be one of the trickiest substances to clean from carpet and upholstery. Great pet hair cleaning relies on strong suction and a floorhead that can effectively lift the hair from carpet fibers so it can be vacuumed up. I also look for a mini motorized tool that can effectively tackle pet hair on furniture.
How I tested
I took bags of dog clippings from a friendly local groomer, and rubbed the hairs into my deep-pile and medium-pile carpet samples. I then passed over it once with each vacuum on its 'medium' mode to see how much hair was removed. I adjusted the setting if required, and continued cleaning until the carpet was clear.
I made notes on performance, and I awarded each vacuum a score out of five for medium-pile carpet and for deep-pile carpet. The overall pet-hair score is an average of these two scores.
To test furniture-cleaning performance, I rubbed hair into a velvet cushion, and used each vacuum's mini motorized tool (if included) to clear it. I made notes on how efficiently it removed the hair, and I've used this information to influence my recommendations. However, I didn't score this element or include it in the overall average for pet hair because not every model I test came with a mini tool included, but most have a compatible tool that's included with some bundles.
Highest scorer: Shark PowerDetect
Runners-up: Dyson Gen5detect and V11 Advanced (tied)
Design and features
In this category I look at the basic design of the vacuum, plus any special features that have been added. I want a vacuum that boasts useful advanced features, but is still user-friendly and doesn't neglect the basics.
For usability, I'm looking at how the machine relays information like remaining battery life and charge level, blockages, which mode is in use, and (if relevant) how much dirt has been detected. I'll also consider the process for emptying the bin and switching attachments.
In terms of special features, I'll look for things like automatic adjustment capabilities (to account for factors like dirt levels, floor type, proximity to room edges, or light levels), a second soft floorhead for delicate hard flooring, a compatible auto-empty dock, and lasers or LED headlamps to light the way or illuminate dust.
How I tested
I scored each vacuum out of five for its interface design, with the highest scores going to machines that present plenty of information nice and clearly, and the lowest going to machines that show minimal information or are confusing in their presentation.
I then scored each vacuum based out of five based on how many special features it offers, and how well those features are executed. The total 'Design and features' score is an average of these two marks.
Highest scorer: Dyson Gen5detect
Runners-up: Dyson V16 Piston Animal, Shark Detect Pro, Shark PowerDetect (tied)
Comfort and maneuverability
One of the big benefits of going for a cordless stick vacuum over a bulky upright is that it's easy to maneuver. That benefit is undermined if the vacuum is too heavy, uncomfortable to hold, or won't maneuver smoothly.
Things that play into this section are the weight of the vacuum and how that weight is distributed, whether the handle is shaped or padded, how ergonomic the design of the handheld section is, and how easily the floorhead pivots. I'll also look at how the machine switches on and off, and if that's conducive to both quick cleanups and longer sessions.
How I tested
I weighed the handheld section of each vacuum (with no wand and no attachments) and then added the wand and primary floorhead to assess the weight in general upright use. I scored each model out of five based directly on these weights, with lower scores going to the heaviest models and higher scores going to lighter ones.
I then gave each vacuum a subjective score out of five for comfort and maneuverability. To gauge this I used each vacuum in floorstanding and handheld mode. The total score for this section is an average of those two marks.
Highest scorer: Shark Detect Pro Cordless
Runner up: Dreame R20
Battery life
The joy of going cable-free can quickly turn sour if your cordless vacuum doesn't have enough battery power for a whole-home clean without you having to stop to recharge. Battery life is a more complicated metric than you might first imagine, though. Many of the models I test these days have an Auto mode, where suction (and thus battery use) increases or decreases based on dirt levels or floor type, making it impossible to give a runtime for this mode.
It's important to consider how much power is tied to that runtime – an Eco mode might last 90 minutes, but if the suction is too weak to pick anything up, that's not useful to anyone. If you're dealing with really ground-in dirt, an ultra-powerful Boost mode that drains the battery quickly is arguably better than one that lasts longer but isn't powerful enough to pull the dirt up.
You'll also want to factor in that a vacuum's runtimes will likely deplete as time goes by. I'd prioritize a removable and swappable battery when choosing a cordless vacuum, as the battery is often the first thing to go – all the vacuums in this group test have a removable battery.
How I tested
I recorded the maximum runtime for each battery (i.e., in its lowest-powered mode). I also recorded how long each model lasted in its highest suction mode. I scored each vacuum out of five in each of those tests based on a set scale – so in Max mode, 3 for 10 mins or less, 4 for 11-15 mins, and 5 for 16+ mins. The overall Battery score is an average of the two scores.
Highest scorers: Dyson Gen5detect, Dyson V16 Piston Animal, Dyson V11 Advanced (tied)
Runners up: Dreame R20, Shark PowerDetect, Roborock H60 Ultra (tied)

articles.title: Echo Studio : l'enceinte connectée Dolby Atmos d'Amazon perd 65 €
articles.text:
Black Friday 2026 - L'enceinte connectée Amazon Echo Studio avec Dolby Atmos est à 174,99 € (-27 %)
Son spatial Dolby Atmos, adaptation automatique à la pièce et hub de maison connectée intégré : l'enceinte Amazon Echo Studio passe à 174,99 € chez Amazon.
Vendue et expédiée par Amazon, l'enceinte connectée Echo Studio en graphite affiche 174,99 € contre 239,99 € pour le prix conseillé, soit une remise de 27 %. Nous lui avons attribué 3,5 étoiles sur 5 lors de notre test.
Un son spatial qui s'adapte à la pièce
L'Echo Studio prend en charge l'audio 3D et le Dolby Atmos, et analyse l'acoustique de la pièce pour ajuster sa restitution en continu, quel que soit son emplacement. Lors de notre test, nous avons apprécié son son agréable et équilibré, la bonne restitution des voix, sa fabrication soignée et son anneau lumineux.
Elle est conçue pour Alexa+, la nouvelle version de l'assistant d'Amazon, et nous avons noté une bonne reconnaissance vocale. L'accès anticipé à Alexa+ est offert, puis le service sera gratuit avec Prime.
Un hub de maison connectée intégré
L'enceinte fait aussi office de hub pour piloter des centaines d'appareils compatibles avec Alexa, comme des ampoules ou des prises, sans boîtier supplémentaire. Elle permet aussi d'étendre la couverture Wi-Fi avec un réseau eero.
Notre test relève toutefois des basses un peu en retrait et un son qui manque de mordant, une puissance limitée, une sensibilité à la réverbération de la pièce, ainsi que l'absence d'entrée filaire et de certification IP.

articles.title: Aevius Labs launches with $22M to bring understandable intelligence to medical data
articles.text:
Aevius Labs launches with $22M to bring understandable intelligence to medical data
Boston-based Aevius Labs Inc., a clinical medical data company, today announced it has raised $22 million in funding led by Insight Partners to build and train artificial intelligence foundation models that can understand and query unstructured medical text, imaging and other data.
A spinout of Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, the company develops AI models that turn information from healthcare, payer, and life sciences organizations into insights other AI tools can act on. The company said it wants to provide a foundational “brain” that can take notes, medical artifacts, clinicians’ transcriptions, lab work, radiology imaging, electronic health record information and other specialty medical data, and make it more accessible to healthcare workers.
The platform can take all this information and use it to represent the whole patient, their medical experience, population studies and actionable insights for clinicians and doctors in the language that they speak. The company said it’s designed to support applications spanning healthcare delivery, operations, and life sciences.
The company was founded by key members of Modella AI Inc., which was acquired by pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca PLC, using the company’s AI model and agent development for oncology research.
“Our mission is to make medicine computable,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rowland Pettit, M.D., Ph.D. “As a physician-scientist, I’ve worked across many types of clinical data, and there is far more knowledge in those records than we’re able to use today.”
The company said its models learn relationships across different forms of medical data and throughout a patient’s history. It does this by building a dynamic, refreshable representation of the patient, essentially a computable picture of the patient and their entire medical clinical state and trajectory that the doctor or clinician can interact with. An organization can use this to build tools to forecast outcomes, identify changes and monitor outcomes over time.
“Most AI agents today piece together their picture of a patient from text, one question at a time,” said co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Ming Yang “Max” Lu, Ph.D. “We’re building a native representation of each patient’s multimodal, longitudinal history that powers prediction and analysis across an entire population.”
Aevius said the capital from the round would support continued research and development of its foundation models and expand the company’s engineering, clinical and commercial teams.
The company is bringing its technology to health systems at large. That means advancing clinical research and reach, anticipating patient needs, and informing care delivery and resource planning.
On the insurance side, catching disease earlier means fewer visits to care providers through preventive care, because catching issues faster means stopping them before they become life-altering, expensive problems to manage. For life sciences, it will help deepen understanding of disease to inform clinical development by using long-term patient histories to study progression and treatment outcomes, identify candidate biomarkers and find patients for clinical studies.
“We’re bringing general medical intelligence to [the] data, so organizations can build on a deeper understanding for their patients,” added Lu.

articles.title: Typing 365 Turns PC Building, Technology and More into Typing Practice
articles.text:
Monday, November 23rd 2026
Typing 365 Turns PC Building, Technology and More into Typing Practice
Typing faster is useful, but what if practice could also teach you something? Typing 365 is a free native Windows app that combines structured typing lessons, educational content, and competitive challenges.
With over 100,000 installs and nearly 4 million typing races completed worldwide, Typing 365 has grown into more than a speed test. Its Albums Store offers themed collections covering technology, science, history, psychology, and more.Build Your PC: A Free Album for First-Time Builders
The new Build Your PC album features 40 free typing exercises about desktop hardware. It covers motherboards, component compatibility, assembly, first boot, operating system installation, and troubleshooting.
Here's the idea in practice: instead of just reading a guide, you type passages such as "Before buying a CPU, check that its socket matches your motherboard and that the board's BIOS supports it." By the end of the album, you've practiced thousands of keystrokes while picking up the fundamentals of building a PC.
You might already know your way around a PC case, but it's an easy recommendation for students, first-time builders, or that friend whose build you always end up helping with.
Why a Native Windows App?
Browser-based typing sites are great for a quick test. Typing 365 is designed for consistent practice, combining a dedicated Windows experience with structured courses, progress tracking, and detailed performance statistics.
Beginners can start with Typing 101, a free course that gradually introduces keys before moving on to complete sentences. Other courses cover keyboard rows, punctuation, and speed development.
During practice, an on-screen keyboard and optional hand guidance support finger placement. The app tracks words per minute (WPM), characters per minute (CPM), accuracy, and mistakes. You can also turn your own notes or technical material into typing exercises.Find Your Weak Spots with PRO Analytics
The free app offers plenty of practice material, while Typing 365 PRO adds detailed analytics for users who want to improve their skills. View speed trends, session history, and keyboard heatmaps, or identify slow words, characters, and letter pairs for targeted practice.
PRO also unlocks exclusive albums, advanced courses such as Typing 102, which focuses on building typing speed, plus additional fonts, keyboard sounds, avatars, and customization options.
PRO is available through a monthly subscription or a one-time lifetime purchase, with US pricing starting at $2.99/month or $29.99 lifetime. Prices may vary by region.
Race Against Other Typists
Prefer competition? Join ranked typing races, compare your results with other players, and climb the global leaderboards. Whether you're chasing a personal best or a higher rank, every race offers a new challenge.
Practice in Five Languages
Typing 365 supports English, German, Spanish, Russian, and Arabic, allowing users to practice across languages and keyboard layouts.
From learning keyboard basics to understanding how a PC comes together, Typing 365 turns everyday practice into something worth your time.
Download Typing 365 for free from the Microsoft Store and start typing.
Typing 365 is available for Windows PCs, with optional premium albums and PRO features.
