articles.title: Ce laptop de Lenovo équipé de la nouvelle Nvidia RTX Spark N1X s'offre 800 euros de remise pendant le Black Friday
articles.text:
Nvidia a lancé mi-octobre la RTX Spark N1X, sa première puce pour PC portables : un SoC Arm qui réunit CPU et GPU. Plusieurs machines l’accueillent déjà comme le Lenovo Yoga Pro 9 15N1X11. Ce PC portable vise d’abord les créatifs, mais la nouveauté se paie : il est vendu près de 3 500 euros. Une addition salée que Darty essaie d’adoucir pendant le Black Friday, qui tombe ce vendredi 27 novembre.
Que retenir du Lenovo Yoga Pro 9 15N1X11 ?
- La puce tout-en-un RTX Spark N1X
- L’écran OLED de 15,3 pouces à 165 Hz
- La housse de transport et le stylet fourni
Sorti pour 3 449,99 euros dans cette configuration (puce N1X 18 cœurs, 32 Go de RAM, SSD de 1 To, stylet Yoga Pen 2 et housse inclus), le Lenovo Yoga Pro 9 15N1X11 est actuellement disponible pour 2 759,99 euros chez Darty.
À la découverte de la RTX Spark N1X
Pour comprendre tout l’intérêt de ce Lenovo Yoga Pro 9 15N1X11, il faut se pencher sur ses composants. Là où le Yoga Pro 9i associe un processeur Intel à une GeForce RTX 5060, Lenovo a misé ici sur une puce tout-en-un, la Nvidia RTX Spark N1X. Dévoilée il y a quelques mois, cette puce Arm réunit CPU et GPU. Sur la version vendue par Darty, elle compte 18 cœurs CPU et un GPU Blackwell de 5 120 cœurs, contre 20 cœurs et 6 144 sur la version la plus haut de gamme.
Sécurisez vos achats durant Black Friday avec la meilleure offre de l’année. Dénichez les bonnes affaires, Bitdefender s’occupe des arnaques.
Intégrée dans ce Lenovo Yoga Pro 9 15N1X11, elle permet d’effectuer des tâches importantes comme le montage vidéo ou le rendu 3D. Les 32 Go de mémoire, partagés entre le CPU et le GPU, évitent les ralentissements même lorsque vous travaillerez avec de nombreux onglets ouverts.
En jeu, la puce a la puissance, mais la compatibilité coince encore. Elle fait tourner des jeux AAA récents, mais la plupart des titres PC sont compilés pour les processeurs x86 : sur cette puce Arm, ils passent par Prism, l’émulateur de Microsoft. Surtout, certains jeux restent bloqués par leur anti-triche pour le moment. C’est le cas de League of Legends et de Call of Duty.
Un PC portable taillé pour la création
Vous l’aurez compris, le Lenovo Yoga Pro 9 15N1X11 n’est pas encore un PC portable parfait pour jouer, mais il est idéal pour la création. En plus du montage vidéo, vous pourrez retoucher des photos via Photoshop ou créer des visuels sur Canva. Le stylet Yoga Pen 2 fourni prend alors le relais, sur l’écran comme sur le grand pavé tactile haptique, qui sert aussi de surface de dessin. L’écran OLED de 15,3 pouces est tactile et rend la personnalisation de vos designs plus facile.
Second accessoire fourni avec le PC portable : la housse de transport. Vous pourrez promener la machine à la main sans souci. Le PC portable reste facile à glisser dans un sac avec ses 16,7 mm d’épaisseur, mais il pèse tout de même 1,75 kg dans sa version à écran tactile.
Enfin, avec l’arrivée de la RTX Spark, la question de l’autonomie se pose. Lenovo annonce jusqu’à neuf heures en usage bureautique avec sa batterie de 92,5 Wh, mais si vous poussez la machine à fond, que ce soit en jeu ou en IA, elle pourrait peiner à tenir une heure et demie.
Grâce au guide des meilleurs ordinateurs portables du moment, vous pourrez comparer ce Lenovo Yoga Pro 9 15N1X11 avec des produits similaires.

articles.title: Si la pregunta es cómo podemos saber que una solución matemática es correcta sin entenderla, la respuestiene cuatro letras: Lean
articles.text:
En 1998, Thomas Hales y Samuel Ferguson dieron por demostrada la conjetura de Kepler, un viejo problema que pregunta sobre si hay una forma más compacta de apilar esferas que la que usan los fruteros con las naranjas. Su respuesta era que no, pero no todo el mundo estaba de acuerdo con ellos.
El asunto se polarizó tanto que, tras cuatro años de revisión, un panel de doce árbitros de Annals of Mathematics se declaró "99 % seguro" de que la prueba era correcta. Y ni siquiera esto, pese a la victoria que suponía para los dos matemáticos, acabó con el debate.
Fue entonces cuando Hales se dio cuenta de que la única forma de cerrar el asunto era que lo comprobara una máquina. Parecía fácil, pero no lo era. Anunció el proyecto de Flyspeck en enero de 2003, pero no lo terminó hasta agosto de 2014.
Era un sistema con problemas. Pero abrió un mundo de posibilidades. Hoy por hoy, como acaba de recordarnos la hipótesis de Riemann, esa idea de Hales se ha convertido en una pieza básica de la matemática del futuro. Lo único es que esa idea está encarnada ahora en Lean.
¿Lean? En 2015, Leonardo de Moura hizo público un demostrador de código abierto "con un núcleo de confianza pequeño": Lean. Era el último paso de un viaje que había iniciado una década antes en Microsoft desarrollando resolutores automáticos de problemas lógicos. En último término, la idea de Hales era sencillamente eso: comprobar que una prueba respetaba las reglas lógicas que debía cumplir.
La idea era tan jugosa que en un par de años los matemáticos ya la habían hecho suya. Mathlib surgió como una biblioteca común de matemáticas en Lean y Kevin Buzzard, del Imperial College, lanzó su proyecto Xena para formalizar matemáticas de verdad. El hype fue creciendo hasta que, en 2020, Peter Scholze (medalla Fields) retó a la comunidad a comprobar a máquina un teorema suyo y de Dustin Clausen que ni él tenía del todo claro. Fue un éxito.
Pero… ¿qué es Lean exactamente? Lean es (a la vez) un asistente de demostración y un lenguaje de programación que se apoya en una teoría de tipos dependientes. De la misma forma que un compilador "rechaza" un programa que tiene errores, Lean "rechaza" las pruebas que no encajan con el enunciado matemático en cuestión.
El trabajo se reparte a dos niveles. El primero (lo que llamaríamos el elaborador) es enorme y extensible: traduce lo que escribe el humano, o la máquina, con atajos y automatismos, a una teoría mínima. El segundo (el núcleo) es pequeño y lo único que hace es comprobar esa teoría mínima paso a paso.
Un auditor matemático. En el fondo, la metáfora de la contabilidad es muy ilustrativa. Un auditor no necesita conocer el negocio, ni saber cómo se hicieron las cuentas de la empresa; solo si cuadran. El núcleo de Lean es ese auditor. Y si dice que sí, ya está todo dicho.
Y eso es lo que ha pasado con la prueba de la hipótesis de Riemann: el auditor ha dicho que sí. Es posible que nadie sepa cómo se cuadraron las cuentas, pero cuadran.
¿Y qué es "cuadrar" en este contexto? El 12 de noviembre, Buzzard había fijado en su blog cuatro preguntas para cualquier prueba "verificada en Lean". ¿El enunciado es el correcto? ¿Compila? ¿Prueba exactamente ese enunciado? ¿Explota algún fallo de Lean? .
Las cuatro son sí: Se usó la definición que ya estaba en Mathlib, que cabe en una línea y no escribió el autor; decenas de personas la compilaron y obtuvieron el mismo archivo, y la reconstrucción aislada del MIT salió idéntica byte a byte; esto lo confirmó 'comparator', una herramienta del Lean FRO; y, por último, todos los núcleos la aceptaron, nanoda en 28 minutos con 80 hilos, y la prueba solo se apoya en los tres axiomas estándar de Lean. El núcleo de Lean a veces se ha equivocado, pero no hay indicios de que ahora esté pasando eso.
Andrew Sutherland, que hizo las comprobaciones del MIT, dijo a Scientific American que la probabilidad de que haya algo raro es "aproximadamente cero". Y ese grado de fiabilidad es gracias a Lean.
Como Terence Tao resumía el día del anuncio: el proceso de digestión "llevará algún tiempo", pero está claro que haber podido diseñar un sistema que nos permita confirmar una prueba de 17 millones de líneas de código con este grado de exactitud ya es en sí mismo una proeza.
No esperan tiempos alucinantes.

articles.title: Un telescopio en Sudáfrica captó una señal láser procedente de más de 8.000 millones de años luz, y los astrónomos saben de dónde viene
articles.text:
El radiotelescopio MeerKAT de Sudáfrica ha detectado una especie de láser natural que emite en ondas de radio desde una galaxia a más de 8.000 millones de años luz. El descubrimiento fue publicado en febrero de 2026 por el Instituto Interuniversitario de Astronomía Intensiva en Datos (IDIA), y los astrónomos ya saben de dónde procede la señal y por qué ha llegado con tanta fuerza.
Un láser que emite en radio. El origen está en el gas de hidroxilo de las galaxias, que puede producir una emisión máser muy intensa, parecida a la de un láser pero en longitudes de onda de radio. Y cuando esa emisión se vuelve excepcionalmente potente, los astrónomos hablan de un megamáser. Vamos, que es un láser cósmico, aunque invisible para nuestros ojos.
Son fenómenos poco frecuentes que funcionan como balizas cósmicas y revelan información importante sobre las galaxias del universo primitivo.
Una lupa en mitad del camino. “Este sistema es verdaderamente extraordinario”, asegura Thato Manamela, investigador posdoctoral de la Universidad de Pretoria con financiación del Observatorio Radioastronómico de Sudáfrica (SARAO) y autor principal del estudio sobre el descubrimiento.
Y es que la señal no viajó sola, tal y como explica (traducción propia del inglés): “Estamos viendo el equivalente en radio de un láser a medio universo de distancia. Y eso no es todo, porque durante su viaje hacia la Tierra las ondas de radio se amplifican todavía más gracias a una galaxia en primer plano perfectamente alineada, pero no relacionada. Esta galaxia actúa como una lente, igual que lo haría una gota de agua en el cristal de una ventana, porque su masa curva el espacio-tiempo local. Así que tenemos un láser de radio que atraviesa un telescopio cósmico antes de que lo detecte el potente radiotelescopio MeerKAT, y todo junto ha hecho posible un descubrimiento maravillosamente fortuito”.
De cuando el universo era joven. La fuente se remonta a una época en la que el universo no tenía ni la mitad de su edad actual, y su brillo es tan extremo que podría entrar incluso en la categoría de gigamáser, todavía más luminosa. Pero si la señal ha llegado con tanta claridad es por la lente gravitacional, un efecto que predice la relatividad general de Einstein y en el que una galaxia en primer plano desvía y amplifica la luz de un objeto más lejano, según recoge la nota de la Universidad de Illinois.
MeerKAT es un precursor del futuro Square Kilometre Array (SKA), y el procesamiento de los datos corrió a cargo del IDIA, según esa misma nota.
Detectar megamáseres tan lejanos da a los astrónomos una nueva herramienta para estudiar cómo evolucionaron las galaxias en un periodo clave de su formación. Y los investigadores esperan que las búsquedas sistemáticas con la próxima generación de radiotelescopios encuentren muchos más, lo que debería ayudar a entender mejor la fusión de galaxias y el crecimiento de los agujeros negros supermasivos en el universo primitivo.

articles.title: Que signifie la petite clé qui apparait en haut à droite de votre smartphone Android ?
articles.text:
L’icône en forme de petite clé qui s’affiche dans la barre d’état de votre smartphone Android signale simplement que votre trafic web passe par un VPN. Android l’active dès qu’un réseau privé virtuel chiffre les données Wi-Fi ou mobiles de votre appareil.
À quoi sert un VPN sur Android ?
Installé sur un téléphone ou une tablette, un VPN (réseau privé virtuel) sert d’abord à créer une liaison chiffrée entre votre appareil et internet. En masquant votre adresse IP réelle (pour la remplacer par une autre), il empêche votre fournisseur d’accès ou l’administrateur d’un Wi-Fi public de voir vos activités en ligne. Vos données circulent à l’abri des regards indiscrets, ce qui est un bon moyen pour sécuriser votre navigation.
L’autre usage très répandu d’un VPN est le contournement des restrictions géographiques qui permet de simuler une connexion depuis un autre pays. Cela permet notamment d’accéder à des catalogues de streaming vidéo ou des contenus bloqués dans le pays où l’on se trouve. Pour autant, un VPN ne garantit pas totalement votre anonymat. En effet, si vous restez connecté à vos comptes Google ou Facebook par exemple, les sites peuvent toujours suivre votre profil utilisateur.
Une petite clé dans la barre d’état sur Android
Ce pictogramme confirme donc qu’un VPN est activé sur votre appareil. Si la clé disparaît, cela signifie que le chiffrement ne fonctionne plus. C’est donc un moyen très utile de voir en un coup d’oeil que votre connexion est sécurisée. La plupart des smartphones interdisent donc de masquer cette icône qui donne une information importante, mais les propriétaires d’appareils Samsung Galaxy peuvent le cacher en passant par l’application de personnalisation Good Lock (via le module QuickStar pour les connaisseurs).
Comment activer ou désactiver un VPN sur Android ?
© 01net
Chaque smartphone Android fonctionne différemment, mais beaucoup de constructeurs proposent aujourd’hui un VPN intégré à l’appareil. C’est notamment le cas de Google sur ses téléphones Pixel où l’option se trouve dans : Paramètres > Réseau et Internet > VPN > VPN de Google > Utiliser le VPN. Par défaut, il n’y a que le VPN de Google, mais vous pouvez en ajouter d’autres si vous le souhaitez.
© 01net
Pour désactiver le VPN sur Android, vous avez simplement à appuyer de nouveau sur le bouton « Utiliser le VPN ». Vous pouvez également afficher un bloc dans le panneau des réglages rapides pour l’activer ou le désactiver en un clic.
Quelques contraintes à connaître
Lorsque vous naviguez sur internet avec un VPN, certains sites peuvent identifier les adresses IP qui vous sont attribuées comme suspectes, ce qui peut déclencher des vérifications CAPTCHA assez pénibles. Certains services en ligne vont même jusqu’à bloquer totalement l’accès aux pages tant que le service reste actif. Utiliser un VPN pour chiffrer votre connexion peut aussi avoir un impact sur la vitesse à laquelle vous naviguez sur internet.
À lire : Que signifie le point vert qui apparait en haut à droite de votre smartphone Android ?
On vous conseille donc d’ajuster les réglages selon vos besoins réels plutôt que de l’activer en permanence. Les raccourcis ainsi que l’affichage du petit symbole en forme de clé devraient vous aider à mieux garder la main sur les paramètres de votre VPN Android.

articles.title: Taking a personal loan with variable income? Here's how to plan your EMI smartly
articles.text:
Taking a personal loan with variable income? Here's how to plan your EMI smartly
From assessing affordability to choosing the right tenure, freelancers and self-employed borrowers can use an EMI calculator to navigate loan repayments with greater confidence.
For freelancers and self-employed professionals, monthly income can fluctuate significantly. One month may bring several projects, while the next may be quieter. This makes fixed loan repayments harder to plan. An EMI calculator can help estimate monthly instalments, but borrowers with variable income should also build a repayment strategy that accounts for slower months.
Why variable income requires careful EMI planning
Unlike salaried employees, freelancers may not receive the same amount every month. Business owners can also experience seasonal changes in revenue, delayed client payments, or unexpected expenses.
Before taking a Rs 1 lakh loan, consider your average monthly income rather than basing affordability on your strongest earning month. Reviewing income over several months can provide a more realistic picture of what you can comfortably repay.
How an EMI calculator helps
An EMI calculator uses the loan amount, interest rate, and repayment tenure to estimate the monthly instalment. This allows borrowers to test different combinations before committing to a loan.
- Loan amount: A higher borrowing amount generally increases the EMI.
- Interest rate: Higher interest rates increase the EMI and total interest payable.
- Tenure: A longer tenure generally lowers the EMI but increases the overall interest cost.
- Repayment period: Affects the total interest payable.
For example, when planning a Rs 1 lakh loan, you can adjust the tenure and interest rate in the calculator to see how the estimated EMI changes. With FIRSTmoney personal loan by IDFC FIRST Bank, your EMI starts at Rs 2,124 per lakh for a five-year tenure.
How much EMI can you comfortably afford?
The calculated EMI should be assessed against your average disposable income, not simply your gross monthly receipts.
Consider:
- Average monthly income over the past several months
- Essential household expenses
- Business operating costs
- Existing EMIs
- Taxes and other financial obligations
- Emergency savings
A freelancer earning Rs 70,000 in one month and Rs 35,000 the next should not plan repayments solely around the higher figure. Building the EMI around a more conservative income estimate can provide greater flexibility.
Should you choose a longer tenure?
A longer tenure can reduce the monthly EMI, which may be useful when income varies. However, extending the repayment period can increase the total interest paid.
Using an EMI calculator to compare different tenures can show this trade-off clearly. The lowest monthly instalment is not automatically the lowest overall borrowing cost.
For a Rs 1 lakh loan, compare at least two or three tenure scenarios and consider which EMI remains manageable during a lower-income month.
For example, at an interest rate of 9.99% per annum, here’s what the EMI and interest would look like:
- 12 months: Approximate EMI of Rs 8,791; total interest of approximately Rs 5,492.
- 24 months: Approximate EMI of Rs 4,614; total interest of approximately Rs 10,736.
- 36 months: Approximate EMI of Rs 3,226; total interest of approximately Rs 16,136.
*Illustrative calculations for a Rs 1 lakh loan at 9.99% p.a. on a reducing-balance basis. Actual EMI and total interest may vary based on the lender's terms and applicable charges.
Build a buffer before borrowing
Variable-income borrowers should ideally maintain an emergency reserve before taking on another repayment obligation. This can provide a cushion when client payments are delayed or business income temporarily falls.
It is also useful to keep loan repayments separate from money required for essential business expenses. Missing an EMI because expected income arrived late can create additional financial pressure.
What should self-employed borrowers check?
Before applying, review:
- Applicable interest rate
- Processing and other charges
- Loan tenure options
- Total repayment amount
- Prepayment conditions
- Documentation requirements and convenience of application
- EMI affordability during low-income periods
The RBI's key facts statement framework requires key loan information and charges to be disclosed to prospective borrowers for applicable retail term loans. This can help borrowers understand the cost before accepting the loan.
Why choose IDFC FIRST Bank for your personal loan needs
When planning a personal loan, flexibility in borrowing and repayment can make managing finances easier. IDFC FIRST Bank’s FIRSTmoney offers eligible customers personal loans up to Rs 15 lakh, with a fully digital process, 10-minute disbursal and flexible tenures from nine to 60 months. It also comes with zero foreclosure charges and zero processing fees, which can help borrowers manage early repayment more flexibly.
Using an EMI calculator before submitting an application can help borrowers understand the expected monthly commitment and compare repayment scenarios.
Conclusion
An EMI calculator is particularly useful for freelancers and self-employed borrowers because it makes different repayment scenarios easier to compare. Before taking a Rs 1 lakh loan, assess your average income, essential expenses, and emergency reserves rather than relying on your highest-earning month. Choosing an EMI that remains manageable during slower periods can make borrowing easier to accommodate within a variable income pattern.

articles.title: À 98 ans, il achète une Tesla pour qu'elle conduise à sa place, et ne regarde même plus les carrefours
articles.text:
“Je ne veux pas regarder” : leur vue baisse, ces seniors achètent une Tesla pour qu'elle conduise à leur place
Leur vue baisse, leurs réflexes ralentissent, et ils refusent de rendre les clés. Des retraités de 70, 90 et même 98 ans s'offrent une Tesla pour confier le volant au logiciel. Tesla en tire des vidéos promotionnelles et Elon Musk les relaie avec gourmandise. Pourtant, le manuel de la marque réclame une vigilance de tous les instants, celle qui manque justement à ces conducteurs.
Dans un long article publié le 16 novembre par Fast Company, David Zipper, chercheur au MIT Mobility Initiative, décrit un phénomène dont personne ne connaît l'ampleur. Des seniors américains achètent une Tesla pour son option de conduite assistée, facturée 99 dollars par mois, parce qu'ils ne se sentent plus capables de conduire. Le voisin de ses parents, un médecin retraité de plus de 90 ans installé dans une résidence en Caroline du Nord, a sauté le pas après avoir senti ses réflexes décliner.
Vendu outre-Atlantique sous le nom de Full Self-Driving (Supervised), le système, que nous avons pu essayer sur route, reste une aide de niveau 2. Il accélère, freine et braque, mais le conducteur reste responsable et doit pouvoir reprendre la main à chaque seconde.
Larry, 98 ans, ne regarde plus les carrefours
En septembre, la chaîne YouTube TFLEV a filmé Larry, 98 ans, qui habite Farmington, au Nouveau-Mexique, et vient de s'offrir un Model Y. En franchissant une intersection, il s'exclame, ravi : "Regardez, je n'ai pas eu besoin de regarder ! Je ne veux pas regarder, elle le fait toute seule." L'influenceur Sawyer Merritt a repris la séquence sur X, et Elon Musk l'a saluée d'un cœur.
Tesla cultive volontiers ce registre. En juillet, la marque mettait en scène Lois, 93 ans, au volant de sa voiture neuve. Le manuel du propriétaire tient un tout autre discours : "Vous devez rester attentif et prêt à reprendre le contrôle à tout moment." Elon Musk brouille lui-même le message : en décembre 2025, il assurait que la version 14 du logiciel permettait, selon la circulation, de pianoter sur son smartphone au volant.
	
Je ne veux pas regarder, elle le fait toute seule.
Vue, réflexes, temps de réaction : pourquoi les experts s'inquiètent
En mars, le compte Tesla North America partageait l'interview de Ricky, 71 ans. Il a acheté un Cybertruck parce que sa vue baisse. La marque l'a commentée d'un seul mot : "Liberté".
Freedom https://t.co/uG1Yr7XoRf
— Tesla North America (@tesla_na) March 29, 2026
Les chercheurs interrogés par Fast Company y voient un angle mort. Birsen Donmez, spécialiste des facteurs humains à l'université de Toronto, constate que la plupart des propriétaires n'ouvrent jamais le manuel. Elle résume sa règle sans détour : "Si vous ne pouvez plus conduire vous-même, vous ne devriez pas conduire avec le FSD." Le spectacle à l'écran entretient l'illusion, puisque le logiciel reconstitue désormais la rue en 3D. Or, les conducteurs âgés mettent plus de temps à réagir quand un système de niveau 2 défaille. Joseph Young, porte-parole de l'IIHS, l'organisme de sécurité routière financé par les assureurs américains, range d'ailleurs ces aides parmi les équipements de confort.
Johnathon Ehsani, de l'école de santé publique Johns Hopkins, reconnaît qu'on ignore encore tout de la façon dont ces voitures sont réellement utilisées.
Le dilemme reste cruel. Une revue de 16 études menée par l'université Columbia montre qu'arrêter de conduire double presque le risque de symptômes dépressifs chez les aînés. Elle multiplie aussi par près de cinq leurs chances d'entrer en établissement pour personnes âgées.
	
Si vous ne pouvez plus conduire vous-même, vous ne devriez pas conduire avec le FSD.
En France, la conduite assistée de Tesla attend toujours son feu vert
Début octobre, Berlin jugeait l'ancien nom trompeur, et le système est devenu "Tesla Conduite Assistée" en Europe, nouvel épisode d'un long feuilleton. Il roule déjà dans une dizaine de pays de l'Union, dont la Belgique voisine, grâce à l'homologation accordée par les Pays-Bas en avril. La France le teste sur route depuis septembre, mais elle attend pour l'autoriser un vote des Vingt-Sept, prévu au plus tôt en décembre. Les propriétaires français ont donc encore le temps de lire le manuel.

articles.title: Bitcoin: cuál es el precio de esta criptomoneda este día
articles.text:
El bitcoin fue la primera criptomoneda que salió al mercado. Ideada por Satoshi Nakamoto en 2008, esta divisa digital promovía un ideal libertario y buscaba poner en jaque a las instituciones monetarias y financieras tradicionales luego de la crisis financiera mundial que se vivió ese año.
La victoria electoral de Donald Trump significó un movimiento positivo para las principales criptomonedas del mercado. A finales de 2024, bitcoin registró un nuevo máximo histórico que logró superar los 107.000 dólares por unidad, después de que el presidente estadounidense reiteró su idea de crear una reserva estratégica de la criptodivisa en Estados Unidos.
Las divisas digitales serán un foco de atención durante este año, las iniciativas del presidente de Estados Unidos y el desarrollo de nuevos modelos de inteligencia artificial fungirán un papel importante en la cotización de estos activos. Después del lanzamiento del nuevo modelo de IA chino DeepSeek, BTC y otras criptos cayeron en la mayoría de los mercados de valores.
Cotización de la criptomoneda Bitcoin
El precio de la criptomoneda bitcoin para este día a las 14:00 horas (UTC) es de 61027.57 dólares. Esto quiere decir que el activo digital registró un cambio de 0.63% en el último día, así como un movimiento de 0.0% en la última hora.
Por su nivel de capitalización, esta moneda digital ocupa la posición #1 entre las más populares.
El flujo histórico de inversiones impulsa a bitcoin a máximos nunca antes vistos
En marzo del año pasado el bitcoin ha logrado un nuevo máximo histórico, superando los valores anteriores y reafirmándose como la criptomoneda más importante en el mercado, acercándose a los 73 mil dólares. Este récord se obtuvo en medio de un flujo sin precedentes de inversiones hacia las criptomonedas, un acontecimiento notable para el sector financiero digital.
El aumento en el valor de bitcoin ocurre en un contexto donde hay un entrante masivo de capital hacia las criptomonedas, lo que indica un creciente interés y confianza de los inversores en estos activos. La subida del precio beneficia no solo a bitcoin sino que también tiene un impacto positivo en el mercado de las criptomonedas en general, favoreciendo una mayor estabilidad y visibilidad, de acuerdo a un análisis de Bloomberg.
Expertos financiaron este aumento a diferentes factores, como la adopción institucional de las criptomonedas, la búsqueda de alternativas de inversión debido a la incertidumbre económica mundial y la innovación continua en la tecnología blockchain que respalda a bitcoin y otras divisas digitales. Esta combinación de factores ha creado un entorno propicio para el crecimiento continuo en el valor de Bitcoin.
Cómo adquirir criptomonedas
Para comprarlas e intercambiarlas se utilizan portales especializados. Su valor varía en función de la oferta, de la demanda y del compromiso de los usuarios, por lo que puede cambiar más rápido que el dinero tradicional, pero mientras más gente esté interesada y quiera comprar determinada divisa, mayor será su valor.
No obstante, quien invierte en este tipo de monedas digitales debe tener muy claro que esta forma trae consigo un elevado riesgo al capital, pues, así como puede haber un incremento, también puede tener inesperadamente un desplome y acabar con los ahorros de sus usuarios.
Para almacenarlas, los usuarios deben contar con un monedero digital o wallet, que en realidad es un software a través del cual es posible guardar, enviar y hacer transacciones de las criptomonedas. En realidad, este tipo de monederos sólo guarda las claves que marcan la propiedad y el derecho de una persona sobre cierta criptomoneda, por lo que estos códigos son los que en realidad se deben proteger.

articles.title: German startup Playbook secures €8 million to help pharma companies deploy AI safely
articles.text:
Munich’s Playbook, a startup developing neurological AI to ensure rule-based compliance in pharmaceutical industries, has raised €8 million to turn documents into data AI can read, but not change.
Heal Capital leads the round, together with Bayern Kapital and existing investor Capnamic. The company raised €2.5 million in 2025.
“Our ambition is to help Pharma use AI to develop, manufacture and deliver medicines faster and more safely, while keeping it aligned with the protocols that govern the work,” said Dr. Nikolai Wessendorf, CEO and co-founder of Playbook, in a public statement.
Playbook’s funding follows several 2026 European investments in enterprise AI infrastructure and software designed to structure operational knowledge and support controlled AI deployment.
In Germany, Munich-based Interloom raised €14.2 million for AI-agent knowledge infrastructure, Berlin-based Cognee secured €7.5 million for AI memory technology, and Stuttgart-based Blockbrain attracted €17.5 million for secure enterprise AI agents.
Elsewhere, London-based Pharosyn raised €2.5 million for pharmaceutical intelligence software, while Barcelona’s Mafer AI secured €2 million for AI-enabled R&D and regulatory workflows, and Barcelona and San Francisco-based Modern Relay raised €2.5 million for enterprise AI infrastructure.
Together, these rounds represent approximately €46.2 million in 2026 funding, rising to €54.2 million including Playbook’s new investment.
EU-Startups previously covered lead investor Heal Capital’s participation in Swiss startup CGC Genomics’ €1.7 million round, supporting regulated AI applications in oncology.
“In the pharmaceutical industry, errors can cost millions and, in the worst case, put patients at risk. The potential for AI is enormous, but unlocking it requires more than powerful models. Playbook has developed technology that helps companies ensure quality and safety when using AI. The company already counts major pharmaceutical companies among its customers. We believe this approach can define a new category of enterprise software,” adds Christian Lautner, Partner at Heal Capital.
Founded in Munich in 2022, Playbook develops Operating Memory, a data model that helps AI agents follow approved procedures in regulated industries such as pharma. The technology translates work instructions into a controlled and auditable data model that people, software systems and AI agents can query for precise guidance.
Work instructions in pharmaceutical companies define who may perform which step under which conditions, and what evidence is required. They govern processes from drug development and manufacturing to quality control, storage and distribution. Together, they hold the combined knowledge of how companies ensure quality for safe medicine.
Operating Memory makes these instructions available as structured data that people, software systems, and AI can access whenever they need them and from any system.
Playbook extracts data from files stored in document, quality and learning management systems and organises it in a graph database that is controlled, audited, and updated by humans. In this data model, a single link connects several elements together at once, such as a process step, the responsible role, the applicable conditions and the required evidence.
If a temperature sensor fails in a pharmaceutical storage facility, for example, warehouse operators can see which actions must be taken, who is responsible and what needs to be documented.
“Our vision is that every company will eventually have an Operating Memory that guides both people and AI. In the future, companies will no longer need to rely on documents that are too often not found, read, and understood correctly,” says Dr. Wessendorf.
The company reportedly has more than 50 customers, including two of the world’s 20 largest pharmaceutical companies.
The new funding will support research and development, with a particular focus on making Operating Memory available to a wide range of autonomous AI systems. It will also be used to expand enterprise sales across Europe, the UK and the US.

articles.title: Apple plant die nächste Produktrunde: Diese iPhones, iPads und Macs kommen im Frühjahr
articles.text:
Apple plant die nächste Produktrunde: Diese iPhones, iPads und Macs kommen im Frühjahr
Apple plant laut einem Bericht von Bloomberg für Februar oder März die nächste große Produktrunde: Dann sollen neue iPhones, iPads und Macs erscheinen. Im Mittelpunkt stehen demnach vor allem günstigere Geräte. Erst in den vergangenen Wochen hatte Apple neue iPhone-Pro-Modelle, faltbare Geräte, OLED-Tablets und mehrere Macs vorgestellt.
Warum das iPhone 18 erst noch kommt
Bei den Smartphones hat Apple in diesem Jahr seine Strategie geändert und die Veröffentlichungen entzerrt. So will der Hersteller sowohl im vierten als auch im ersten Quartal richtig Kasse machen – und nicht nur beim Weihnachtsgeschäft. Im September zeigte Apple das iPhone 18 Pro, das 18 Pro Max und das iPhone Duo, das allerdings erst im Oktober in den Handel kam. Das Standard-iPhone fehlte erstmals. Es soll nun im Frühjahr folgen – parallel zu einem weiteren Einsteigermodell. Laut Bloomberg erscheinen die Geräte zusammen mit iOS 27.4. Das iPhone 18 soll die Standardversion des A20-Chips (aus dem iPhone 18 Pro und Duo) bekommen, dazu eine leicht verbesserte Kamera, mehr Arbeitsspeicher (9 statt 8 GByte), etwas mehr Akkulaufzeit und frische Farben.
Das iPhone 18e, das sich besonders an Firmenkunden wendet, behält demnach die Bauform des 17e aus dem vergangenen März, die auf die noch viel älteren Generationen 13 und 14 zurückgeht. Auch hier rechnet die Gerüchteküche mit dem A20-Chip und längerer Akkulaufzeit. Die Einkerbung am oberen Displayrand, die Notch, soll hier bleiben. Dafür könnte auch das 18e ebenfalls 9 statt 8 GByte RAM erhalten. Denkbar ist zudem eine zweite Variante des besonders flachen iPhone Air. Beobachter erwarten hier einen A20-Pro-Chip, eine verkleinerte Dynamic Island, eine Ultraweitwinkel-Kamera und Apples neuen Modemchip C2.
Was Apple bei iPads und Macs plant
Bei den Tablets stehen zwei oder drei neue Modelle an. Das Einsteiger-iPad soll erstmals Apple Intelligence unterstützen, also Apples KI-Funktionen, und den A19-Chip erhalten. Geplant sind außerdem der Einbau des stromsparenden Mobilfunkchips C1X und Apples N1 mit Wi-Fi 7. Das iPad Air könnte auf den M5-Chip wechseln und erstmals ein OLED-Display bekommen. Damit stünde ein dünneres und leichteres Gehäuse an. Offen bleibt, ob Apple schon neue iPad-Pro-Modelle mit M6 oder M7 zeigt oder damit bis zum Sommer (oder gar Herbst) wartet.
Bei den Macs muss Apple das MacBook Air noch auf den M6-Chip bringen. Bloomberg erwartet das Gerät im Frühjahr. Dazu kommt die zweite Generation des MacBook Neo, dem günstigsten Notebook des Herstellers. Apple rüstet dort vermutlich auf den A19 Pro aus dem iPhone 17 Pro auf. Der Vorteil: Der Arbeitsspeicher wächst auf 12 GByte, ist also endlich weniger knapp. Auch neue Farben sind möglich.
))) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Dell, HPE, Lenovo, and Supermicro are allegedly hiking AI server prices months after signing contracts
articles.text:
Facepalm: The supply chain is in shambles, and hardware companies are looking to squeeze as much money as they can out of customers. Sources now indicate that certain products are so sought after in the server market that manufacturers can impose massive price increases before a purchase is even finalized.
Major server manufacturers including Dell, HPE, Lenovo, and Supermicro are allegedly raising prices on their products months after agreeing on an initial purchase price with customers. Even worse, those customers are mostly accepting the increases because they need the hardware to build new data centers around the world.
The latest reports come from sources quoted by the Financial Times. The unexpected price hikes are affecting both hyperscalers and trading firms operating in the relatively secretive world of algorithmic trading and electronic market making. The FT cited major players in the trading industry, including Jane Street, Optiver, and Hudson River Trading.
According to one source, AI server manufacturers can increase the final price by 25%, 30%, or even 45% compared with the originally agreed amount. These "significant disparities" typically emerge during the months suppliers spend building servers, racks, and other hardware.
Another source said this practice is becoming a "standard" way of doing business in the data center industry. Customers now expect to sign contracts containing only a general indication of the base price, knowing full well that they will likely have to pay considerably more by the time the hardware is delivered.
The source said they had "never said no" to the increases because, "at the end of the day, the compute is valuable to us and we'll pay for it."
So far, no companies have publicly confirmed or denied that arbitrary price increases are becoming common in the AI data center industry. Companies quoted by the FT have not issued official statements addressing the reports. However, one particular dispute has already escalated into a legal battle in Ireland.
In June this year, UK-based algorithmic trading firm XTX Markets sued Dell after the US manufacturer allegedly demanded a massive, unexpected price increase. The two companies had previously agreed on a fixed price, with an additional $5 million payment to ensure "price certainty." Dell ultimately demanded another $62 million to $70 million to deliver the servers to XTX.
Dell told XTX executives that the increase was necessary to cover rising memory chip costs, which the company said it could not absorb through other means. XTX is currently building a new data center in Finland, but the ongoing lawsuit could have significant implications for the project.

articles.title: Java News Roundup: Java4Shell, Oracle CSPUs, OpenJDK, Azul Payara, BellSoft, Helidon, LangChain4j
articles.text:
This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive.
OpenJDK
Oracle has released versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3, 11.0.33.0.3 and 8u511b3 of the JDK as part of their quarterly Critical Security Patch Update Advisory for November 2026. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes for version 27.0.1.0.3, version 25.0.5.0.3, version 21.0.13.0.3, version 17.0.21.0.3, version 11.0.33.0.3 and version 8u511 b33.
JEP 547, Lazy Constants (Fourth Preview), has been elevated from Proposed to Target to Targeted for JDK 28. This JEP proposes a fourth preview, with no changes, after three rounds of preview delivered in the upcoming release of JDK 27 and JDK 26 through JDK 25. Formerly known as Stable Values and Computed Constants, this feature introduces the concept of computed constants, defined as immutable value holders that are initialized at most once. This offers the performance and safety benefits of final fields, while offering greater flexibility as to the timing of initialization. The name change from Stable Values to Lazy Constants with the release of JDK 26, better captures the intent of a high-level use case.
JEP 548, Vector API (Thirteenth Incubator), has been elevated from its JEP Draft 8397768 to Candidate status. This JEP proposes a thirteenth incubation with one notable change, after twelve rounds of incubation delivered in JDK 16 through JDK 27. This feature introduces an API to "express vector computations that reliably compile at runtime to optimal vector instructions on supported CPU architectures, thus achieving performance superior to equivalent scalar computations." This JEP adds support for Vector<Float16> vectors, whose lanes hold 16-bit floating-point numbers in the IEEE 754 binary16 format. The Vector API will continue to incubate until the necessary features of Project Valhalla become available as preview features. At that time, the Vector API team will adapt the Vector API and its implementation to use them, and will promote the Vector API from Incubation to Preview.
JDK 28
Build 25 of the JDK 28 early-access builds was made available this past week featuring updates from Build 24 that include fixes for various issues. More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
For JDK 28, developers are encouraged to report bugs via the Java Bug Database.
Java4Shell
A new Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability, known as Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), affects versions 27.0.1.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 17.0.21.0.3 and 8u511b33-perf of Oracle Java SE, versions 21.0.13.0.3 and 17.0.21.0.3 of Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition: 21.3.20.0.3. As described in the CVE documentation:
[This] difficult to exploit vulnerability allows [an] unauthenticated attacker with network access via multiple protocols to compromise Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Note: This vulnerability can only be exploited by supplying data to APIs in the specified Component without using Untrusted Java Web Start applications or Untrusted Java applets, such as through a web service.
Organizations and projects that have addressed this CVE include: BellSoft, Azul, JetBrains, GraalVM, Quarkus and WildFly. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.
Spring Framework
It was a busy week over at Spring as the various teams have delivered GA releases that include: Spring Boot, Spring Framework, Spring Security, Spring Session, Spring Integration, Spring HATEOAS, Spring Modulith, Spring AI, Spring AMQP, Spring for Apache Kafka and Spring LDAP.
The Spring team has also resolved a total of 90 CVEs spanning multiple projects. InfoQ will follow up with a more detailed news story.
Azul Payara
The release of Azul Payara 7.6.0, the November 2026 edition, includes Community Edition 7.2026.11, Enterprise Edition 6.44.0 and Enterprise Edition 5.93.0. Along with bug fixes and component upgrades, all three editions deliver resolutions to five CVEs, two of which are related to Azul Payara:
- CVE-2026-90908, a vulnerability in the GenericAdminAuthenticator class that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to bypass JMX/RMI administrative access restrictions by spoofing the client host address that may lead to remote code execution.
- CVE-2026-110003, A vulnerability in the administration REST interface that allows a remote, unauthenticated attacker to bypass secure-admin remote-access restrictions by supplying an arbitrary value in the X-GlassFish-authToken HTTP header that grants execution of arbitrary administrative commands, equivalent to complete compromise of the server.
Further details on this release may be found in the release notes and the Azul Payara security advisories page.
Hibernate
The second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive 5.1.0 and 5.0.0 ship with one single bug fix from the first release candidates, in which use of the Jakarta Persistence @TableGenerator annotation could cause a deadlock when a session holding the lock on the row of the generator table needed a new block of IDs.
Version 5.0.0.CR2 will be the last release candidate. With the GA release of version 5.0.0.Final, it will be declared as end-of-life and focus will be on version 5.1.0.
More details on these releases may be found in the release notes for version 5.1.0.CR2 and version 5.0.0.CR2.
Java Operator SDK
The release of Java Operator SDK 5.7.0 provides bug fixes, dependency upgrades and new features such as: the ability to enable virtual threads via construction in the Operator class or the josdk.use-virtual-threads property; and a new keepAlive() method, defined in the Operator class that starts a non-daemon thread to keep the JVM running until the operator is shut down. Version 5.7 is now built on Fabric8 Kubernetes Client 8.0. Further details on this release may be found in the release notes.
BellSoft
Concurrent with Oracle's Critical Security Patch Update (CSPU) for November 2026, BellSoft has released CSPU patches for versions 27.0.1.1 25.0.5.1, 21.0.13.1, 17.0.21.1, 11.0.33.1, 8u514 7u523 and 6u523 of Liberica JDK, their downstream distribution of OpenJDK, to address this list of CVEs. This release also includes a patch for the aforementioned Java4Shell Remote Code Execution vulnerability.
With an overall total of 111 fixes and backports, BellSoft states they have participated in eliminating 21 issues in all releases.
Helidon
The release of Helidon 27.0.2 delivers bug fixes and one notable change in which the default limit of decoded-input (strings, byte arrays, JSON, forms, and buffered multipart parts) for in-memory entity conversations has been increased to 1 mebibyte (MiB). More details on this release may be found in the release notes.
This release also aligns with the Oracle Critical Patch Updates for November 2026 and includes the Helidon 4.x and 3.x release trains as described in this blog post.
LangChain4j
The formal release (along with the thirty-fourth beta release) of LangChain4j 1.24.0 ships with bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: new DecisionSchedulerPlanner and DecisionModels classes to serve as a decision model-based agentic pattern; and support for resuming suspended agentic systems in the AgentMonitor class. Further details on this release, including breaking changes, may be found in the release notes.
Micrometer
After two milestones and two releases candidates, the GA release of Micrometer Metrics 1.18.0 provides bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: an optimization of the PrometheusMeterRegistry and MicrometerCollector classes for collecting data snapshots; and a new RowState inner class, defined in the MultiGauge class, that eliminates the need to remove and re-register an instance of the existing Row inner class. More details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.
Similarly, the GA release of Micrometer Tracing 1.8.0 delivers bug fixes, documentation improvements, dependency upgrades and new features such as: a simplification of baggage handles and lookups by directly storing the name of the handle and its metadata by eliminating use of the CompositeBaggage and Java AtomicReference classes; and a refactor of the BaggageTextMapPropagator class for improved baggage propagation. Further details on this release, including deprecations, may be found in the release notes.

articles.title: CachyOS Officially Gets Easy Anti-Cheat Linux V2 Support in November Update
articles.text:
Monday, November 23rd 2026
CachyOS Officially Gets Easy Anti-Cheat Linux V2 Support in November Update
We previously covered the announcement that CachyOS would be getting Easy Anti-Cheat Linux V2 support in the future, but it appears as though the developers behind the popular gaming distribution have wasted no time implementing the new Linux kernel security measures required by Epic Games's new Linux-friendly anti-cheat implementation. As of the official CachyOS November 2026 release, the gaming distribution officially has support for the new EAC kernel, bringing the realization of Fortnite on Linux one step closer. 
CachyOS has implemented a separate kernel entry called "linux-cachyos-eac," which will get its own boot entry for simplicity and flexibility—meaning if you don't want to use the EAC kernel, you can simply set it as a non-default kernel or select another kernel at boot. The new kernel requires that users enable TPM 2.0 and IOMMU, and it will run in lockdown mode and only load kernel modules signed with a signing key trusted by Epic Games. CachyOS users can enable the new kernel by running the "eac-setup" script in the terminal, which will set up the EAC Linux kernel for systemd-boot, Limine, rEFInd, and GRUB (which is in experimental support). After running the script, gamers can verify that it has successfully applied by running "eac-status."
As noted in the update notes, there are some drawbacks to the new EAC kernel, chief of which is that DKMS modules will not work with the kernel, so NVIDIA drivers and ZFS and r8125 modules are shipped as separate packages instead. The CachyOS update also formally introduces the new package installer that was previewed by the development team recently, and it overhauls the CachyOS Recovery system, which now places Btrfs snapshots in the boot menu for easier restoring and troubleshooting. There is also a new package called "cachyos-drm-awaiter," which replaces early KMS and the NVIDIA module loader for all GPUs and waits for GPU drivers to load before loading the display manager. It also helps recovery by showing a QR code for more information when a driver fails to load. Read the full update notes for further changes.
Sources:
				CachyOS, 				via GamingOnLinux

articles.title: COP31 ends in failure as countries split over fossil fuels, climate finance
articles.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—By the time the United Nations COP31 climate talks ended Sunday afternoon, the conference center resembled a going-out-of-business sale at a pawnshop for broken dreams.
As cleaning crews cleared away the debris left by more than 100,000 participants, Murat Kurum, president of the Conference of the Parties and Turkey’s minister of environment, urbanization, and climate change, tried to tie together disparate parts of a draft climate deal with a shiny ribbon of multilateralism.
Many countries were not buying it.
For the first time since 2009, the conference ended without consensus on a cover decision, the concluding statement that typically signals global solidarity on how to confront the worsening climate crisis. Countries did adopt several decisions, including a program to help workers and communities transition away from fossil fuels, and a plan to assess progress on climate adaptation.
The failure to agree on an overarching conference statement reflected deep divisions over whether the agreement should mention fossil fuels and carbon capture, as well as how much climate financing developed countries should provide to developing nations hit by costly climate disasters.
The European Union, as well as several Latin American countries and Pacific Island states, said they would not accept the proposed text from the conference leaders.
Cover decisions at the annual conferences usually focus on new steps or language that could reinforce international efforts to slow global warming. A central aim at this meeting was to set quantifiable but voluntary global goals for the widespread electrification of economies, and to increase funding from developed countries to help developing countries adapt to climate impacts.
In 2022, the UN conference in Egypt agreed to establish a loss and damage fund to help vulnerable countries pay for irreversible climate impacts. A year later in Dubai, delegates from more than 190 countries agreed, for the first time, that a “just and orderly” transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems is needed to slow global warming.

articles.title: Jensen Huang scheduled to testify next week in Senate following reinstatement as Nvidia CEO
articles.text:
Jensen Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3, according to a notice on the committee’s website.
The development comes just hours after Huang was reinstated as Nvidia chief executive, less than two weeks following his resignation after it was revealed that he engaged in at least two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected by the U.S. government of working as a Chinese spy.
The Senate Banking Committee has jurisdiction over export control policies that are designed to prevent sensitive U.S. technologies, such as chips capable of powering AI models, from falling into the hands of foreign governments and militaries.
The public hearing follows bipartisan calls for Huang to testify about his affair with the suspected Chinese spy and his potential involvement in chip-smuggling operations.
It’s worth noting that before his reinstatement as CEO, Huang had already agreed to appear before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, and the House Intelligence Committee on December 1.

articles.title: Google teme que los agentes de IA se descontrolen y planea restringirlos en Chrome
articles.text:
Google quiere limitar el poder de los agentes de IA dentro de Chrome. La compañía propone un sistema de permisos a nivel de navegador para controlar qué webs pueden visitar y qué acciones pueden realizar. La iniciativa surge tras la oleada de incidentes en donde los agentes se han saltado las barreras de seguridad y terminan hackeando páginas o accediendo a contenido para el que no estaban autorizados.
De acuerdo con Neowin, Google ha planeado un sistema que limitaría el alcance de los agentes autónomos. Ingenieros de la empresa propusieron cambios en WebDriver BiDi, el protocolo utilizado para automatización y pruebas en navegadores. En una publicación en el grupo de Chromium, los empleados anunciaron una intención para prototipar la idea y regresarle el control a los usuarios.
En la versión actual del protocolo, WebDriver BiDi asume una relación de confianza total entre el cliente y el navegador, lo que permite un control prácticamente ilimitado. Si bien esto funciona para pruebas automatizadas, resulta peligroso para agentes de IA que navegan en la web. Muchos agentes usan protocolos de bajo nivel o configuraciones que les dan acceso sin restricciones y sin supervisión del usuario.
La idea de Google es añadir extensiones para WebDriver BiDi que se aplicarán a la IA. En los casos donde un agente autónomo navegue, el sistema añadirá un nuevo tipo de sesión restringida. En esta, la IA comienza sin permisos más allá de los valores predeterminados, por lo que debe solicitar explícitamente el acceso a los recursos y capacidades.
La propuesta utiliza un sistema de permisos basado en ACL (lista de control de acceso), que define las webs que puede visitar el agente, los comandos permitidos y los eventos a recibir. Estos permisos se pueden aplicar de forma global a ciertas pestañas o navegaciones específicas.
Google Chrome limitará a los agentes de IA a través de permisos
Google señala que el uso de extensiones permite conservar el control en todo momento. Cuando se aplican, el usuario puede pausar al agente, revocar permisos o detener la sesión. Chrome puede mostrar una interfaz especial cuando el agente realice acciones activas como hacer clic, navegar, escribir texto o ejecutar scripts, de modo que el usuario sepa cuáles son las pestañas controladas por la IA en caso de que se necesite limitarlas o apagarlas.
Bajo la propuesta de Google, los usuarios de Chrome también podrían otorgar permisos muy concretos. Si necesitas que el agente acceda a una tienda en línea, pero no revise páginas de pagos externas, puedes bloquearlo.
Hasta ahora todo suena muy bien, pero existen algunas limitaciones. Por ejemplo, si le autorizas a un agente a hacer clic en botones, Chrome no puede distinguir entre un botón seguro y otro que elimine información importante. Por ello, los ingenieros tienen que seguir experimentando hasta llegar a un nivel confiable que pueda adoptarse por otros navegadores.
Por el momento, esta propuesta se encuentra en una etapa muy preliminar de desarrollo y no se sabe cuándo se implementará en Chrome.

articles.title: ‘These earbuds just continue to defy belief’: I tested Sennheiser’s super-popular cheap USB-C wired earbuds against three far pricier rivals and the results were astonishing
articles.text:
I compared four pairs of wired earbuds designed for budget audiophiles from Sennheiser, Beyerdynamic and Activo — here’s which model came out on top
Only one can reign supreme
Wired earbuds feel like they’ve made something of a comeback in the last year or so. Mainly, I feel like this comes down to their retro aesthetic, but they also provide lossless audio — something that their Bluetooth rivals can’t provide.
With Black Friday fast-approaching, then, I thought it would be fun to take a look at some of the best wired earbuds I’ve tested lately to help you find a great pair that may just find itself discounted.
I’ve spent a couple of days testing four models against one another, assessing them in areas including design and comfort, features and connectivity, and, of course, sound quality. Each model will be ranked from 1st down to 4th in each section, before being placed into an overall ranking table.
Interested to see who comes out on top? Then make sure to read till the end! But first: allow me to introduce our contestants.
Meet the contestants
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Beyerdynamic DT 30 IE | Activo Scoop | Sennheiser IE 200 | Sennheiser CX 80U | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price | $149.99 / £99 / AU$199 | $99 / £99 (about AU$140) | $149.95 / £129.99 / AU$239.95 | $39.95 / £34.99 (about AU$57) | 
| Drivers | 11mm dynamic | 1x 8mm dynamic, 2x 6mm dynamic, 2x balanced armature | 7mm dynamic | 9.7mm dynamic | 
| Weight | 3g (per bud) | 5g (per bud) | 4g (per bud) | 15g (total) | 
| Frequency range | 5Hz-20kHz | 20Hz-20kHz | 6Hz-20kHz | 17Hz-20kHz | 
| Connectivity | 3.5mm | 3.5mm, 4.4mm, USB-C | 3.5mm | USB-C | 
Design and comfort
While I think all of these models have their merits in terms of design, not all of them are created equal. Here are the winners and losers when it comes to aesthetics, usability, and comfort.
Beyerdynamic DT 30 IE
The good: The DT 30 IE are extremely lightweight, coming in at just 3g per bud. The buds themselves are also very small, making them feel pretty seamless in use — sometimes I even forgot I was wearing them. Yes, they’re pretty comfortable, and if you have smaller ears, they’ll suit you perfectly.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Something else I like is their cable, which is built to a great standard, makes next to no noise in-use, and has easy to bend earhooks. It looks stylish too, with neat orange and white accents. The DT 30 IE also come with a tidy little carrying case for your earbuds, cables, and eartips.
The bad: My issue with the DT 30 IE is mainly a visual one. To be honest, they look a bit cheap, with the translucent casing on the buds having a plasticky look that doesn’t quite exude the sense of premium that some similarly priced rivals do. Otherwise, all good!
Activo Scoop
The good: If we’re talking about sheer looks, the Activo Scoop are probably the best option in this lineup. They’re inspired by a pebble, having the smooth, rounded and sculpted look you’d associate with that, and their polished white finish is beautiful.
I also found that they subjected me to little in the way of cable noise, and their rounded case has plentiful space for your buds and accessories. The build quality on offer is strong across the board too, with a durable cable and premium buds to match.
The bad: While the Scoop aren’t exactly uncomfortable to wear, they are far, far chunkier than their rivals, and I felt far more aware of them in-use. They still sit snugly in-ear, and don’t look too prominent, but they just don’t have that all-day comfort that the Beyerdynamic DT 30 IE provide.
Sennheiser IE 200
The good: Like the DT 30 IE, the Sennheiser IE 200 are ultra-lightweight at just 4g per bud. They also fit so snugly in the ear, making them exceptionally comfortable to use for hours on end.
The overall aesthetic of these is pretty great too. They look incredibly discreet when you’re wearing them, but have a design that seems more premium than it is, with a stylish braided cable and neat blue and red accents on the earhooks.
The bad: You may argue that the cable is a little bit slight, and not as well protected as the DT 30 IE’s, but I personally love the look and feel of it, and have experienced no wear or tear after more than two years of use.
Sennheiser CX 80U
The good: Considering their low asking price, the Sennheiser CX 80U look fantastic. They have gorgeous silver details on the buds, a well made USB-C connector, and a rounded appearance that looks so suave.
In use, they’re nice and comfortable too, and with a total weight of 15g, it never feels like they’re fatiguing to wear, even for longer listening sessions.
The bad: I’d argue that the controller, which houses the CX 80U’s mic, looks pretty plasticky and lower in quality than the earbuds themselves. I also think the tighter-fitting DT 30 IE and IE 200 feel a bit more secure for when you’re on the move or performing.
| Design and comfort ranking |  | 
|---|---|
| Earbuds | Rank | 
|---|---|
| Beyerdynamic DT 30 IE | 2nd | 
| Activo Scoop | 4th | 
| Sennheiser IE 200 | 1st | 
| Sennheiser CX 80U | 3rd | 
Features and connectivity
Wired earbuds may not be known for being particularly feature-rich, but some of the models on this list have more to offer than you may expect.
Beyerdynamic DT 30 IE
The good: The DT 30 IE offer pretty solid noise isolation, with a number of different-sized eartips to help you find the perfect seal. According to Beyerdynamic, they offer passive cancellation up to -39dB, which isn’t bad by any means and ideal for zoning in during a live performance, for instance.
They also have an IP54 rating, meaning they’re dust-resistant and can cope with a bit of sweat or light rain without issue. These buds have a 3.5mm connector, so can be used across a range of source devices, though not the bulk of modern smartphones. The cable is detachable, though, so you could add an aftermarket alternative in the case of damage.
The bad: Unlike the Activo Scoop, the DT 30 IE only come with a single connector out of the box — there’s no USB-C or 4.4mm adapter. They also don’t have an in-line controller on the cable — while this isn't uncommon for IEMs, some do still have one. Also while found the passive noise isolation to be decent, it’s not the best I’ve experienced — though grabbing some foam eartips could really help in that regard.
Activo Scoop
The good: The Activo Scoop are an extremely versatile set of IEMs for the price. My favorite feature is their interchangeable connector, with 3.5mm, 4.4mm, and USB-C available, meaning you can use them with just about any device out there for either casual or critical listening.
These offer slightly better passive noise isolation than the DT 30 IE, with both silicone and foam eartips at your disposal. You also get the detachable cable, which some may appreciate given the sheer bulk of the interwoven wires these come with.
The bad: These earbuds skip on an in-line controller too, so you’ll need to use your source device to control media playback. The Scoop also skip on an IP rating, but otherwise I don’t have a bad word to say about them.
Sennheiser IE 200
The good: The Sennheiser IE 200 are dual-tunable, with a standard and outer configuration. In the outer position, the treble catches a bit more of the limelight, especially at the very highest of frequencies, whereas the bass is dialed down compared to the standard position. While I almost always stick with the standard option, this is a pretty thoughtful and unique feature.
In addition, you get a few eartips to choose from, the cable is detachable and replaceable, and the passive noise isolation isn’t half bad either.
The bad: Like the DT 30 IE, the Sennheiser IE 200 use a 3.5mm connector and don’t offer any adapters to help you switch things up. You could buy this separately of course, but it’s worth flagging that the Activo Scoop provide more versatility. There’s also no IP rating, and while Sennheiser sells a cable with volume controls and a microphone built-in, the one bundled in doesn’t have this.
Sennheiser CX 80U
The good: The Sennheiser CX 80U have a certain advantage here, due to the fact that they’re more oriented towards casual use than their rivals.
They have a USB-C connector for use with modern smartphones, tablets, and laptops, they have a built-in mic, and a button for pausing tunes or taking calls. I was surprised by just how effective their passive noise isolation was too, and you can cycle between small, medium, or large eartips to find the right fit.
The bad: While it’s always nice to get a mic on affordable earbuds like this, it’s not the best one I’ve tried at this price-point. I found that there was some noticeable static when taking a recording, and while the mic isn’t bad, it’s just nothing special. I was also confused over the decision to leave volume controls out — I always like to use these to make adjustments when I’m on the move. I would’ve given the CX 80U a five-star rating if it wasn’t for these small issues, but they still have a very solid feature-set overall.
| Features and connectivity ranking |  | 
|---|---|
| Earbuds | Rank | 
|---|---|
| Beyerdynamic DT 30 IE | 4th | 
| Activo Scoop | 2nd | 
| Sennheiser IE 200 | 3rd | 
| Sennheiser CX 80U | 1st | 
Sound quality
OK, here’s what you’ve been waiting for: the listening test results. And when I say that the results here shocked me, I well and truly mean it.
I played three tracks on the same source device, using Tidal to enjoy high-res audio. And all of the earbuds plated up distinctly different sound.
Track 1, Dsco by Sweet Trip, is a busy electronic tune with a lot going on, and I used it to assess instrument separation, soundstaging, and detailing. Track 2, Pobre de quem by Carlos Dafé, is a softer, more laid-back track with an emotive vocal performance and helped me judge mid-range clarity and balance across the frequency range. And Track 3, Fantasy Island by Lucas Alexander, Joey Rich, and EVA, is a house tune that was ideal for testing low-end performance and treble articulation.
So, here’s how our contestants got on…
Beyerdynamic DT 30 IE
The good: The Beyerdynamic go for a more neutral approach, which is typical of IEMs. This is ideal for anyone that wants an insightful listen without any clear and obvious preference towards a specific section of the frequency range.
This even-handed approach was a nice fit for Track 1, where there were a lot of elements contending in the mix, be that crunchy guitars, intertwining vocals, deep bass, or energetic drums. But the DT 30 IE managed all of these well, with each instrument sounding clear and relatively well defined in the mix.
Similarly, in Track 2, vocals were clear, bass was clean and nicely balanced, and the dynamism of the intro was striking. All in all, the DT 30 IE put up a cohesive performance, and if you want more of a ‘flat’ EQ curve from your earbuds, they could be a good fit for you.
The bad: If there’s one thing I’d criticize about the DT 30 IE, it’s that they lack the openness and detail of some rivals. In fact, in Track 1, I felt that the overall sound from these buds seemed compressed, lacking the natural and detailed edge of the Sennheiser IE 200, for instance.
Track 3 was where the DT 30 IE struggled the most, with the vocals lacking the presence or definition I was hoping for, and bass just short of the full-sounding power I heard from other models. It’s also worth noting that I didn’t find the DT 30 IE to sound all too expansive, though some may prefer a tighter sound. These buds are by no means bad, but they struggled to stand out among their rivals.
Activo Scoop
The good: The Activo Scoop place a large emphasis on treble — perhaps unsurprising given that they’re configured with two balanced armature drivers. But they offer pretty good performance right across the board, which was showcased perfectly with Track 3 — where the Scoop easily gave their best performance.
Here, the IEMs served up sparkling and precise treble, clear mids, and surprisingly weighty bass, while still retaining the agility required to maintain the energetic vibe of the tune. They put on a good show with Track 2 as well, where I was impressed by their controlled yet textured low-end and clean replication of vocals.
In Track 1, the Scoop offered expertly separated electric guitars in the left channel, offering more nuance than most of its rivals. But unfortunately, this song didn’t exactly show the Scoop in their best light overall…
The bad: Yes, unfortunately, the Scoop’s top-heavy approach can sometimes be their undoing. And in Track 1, I felt like the treble wasn’t just preferred, it was almost a bit aggressive. I personally found this quite fatiguing, and this resulted in the Scoop finishing last in the ranking table for this track.
In Track 2, the focus on the treble was clear once more, and while vocals didn’t sound compressed or unclear, they lacked the presence and grandeur I was hoping to hear. While I think the Activo Scoop offer superior detailing to the DT 30 IE, their bright approach can sometimes feel a little blinding.
Sennheiser IE 200
The good: The Sennheiser IE 200 supply a balanced take with a slight bump in the low-end, and I’m a sucker for this sound signature. I have to say that these wired earbuds performed exceptionally well throughout the whole test, securing 1st place for each individual track, pretty impressive, right?
The reason that the IE 200 kept winning was simple. They managed to plate up a highly insightful listen, offered more expansiveness to give each individual instrument the chance to breathe, and had both the dynamism and control required to highlight the most grandiose and impactful moments in each track.
In Track 1, they created a strong sense of space, provided some nice warmth in the low-end, and well-separated guitars in the mid-range. It was a similar story for Track 2, with spacious keys and bass immersing me in the track. And the balanced yet exciting sound on offer in Track 3 had me hooked.
The bad: There isn’t much ‘bad’ to report here, but there were a couple of areas where the IE 200 could’ve been even better. For instance, in Track 3, the bass drop could’ve sounded a little more dynamic, and in Track 2, the top-end could’ve been a little brighter, but these are just nitpicks.
Sennheiser CX 80U
The good: As the only non-IEM, you likely won’t be shocked to hear that the CX 80U have a slightly more energetic sound, with punchy bass and expressive treble. But this really works, and the CX 80U manage to retain great detail right across the frequency range while still injecting a fun factor that makes them so addictive to use.
In Track 1, I was blown away by just how articulate and snappy drums in the treble were, with instrument separation and textured bass also standing out. Speaking of bass, it had a bit more punch in Track 2 compared to the other wired earbuds, but this never overwhelmed the emotive vocal performance. I also really appreciated the CX 80U’s nuanced soundstaging, with guitars and drums feeling uniquely positioned in the mix, opening up an immersive listening experience.
And for Track 3, stabs in the intro were tonally accurate and well-weighted, with bass and treble hitting with considerable impact. If we’re just talking pound-for-pound performance, these would be my winner.
The bad: Again, not much negativity to report here. As I mentioned in my CX 80U review, these earbuds miss some of the mid-range nuance and intricacies that pricier rivals like the IE 200 can deliver. But all in all, these sound stellar.
| Sound quality ranking |  | 
|---|---|
| Earbuds | Rank | 
|---|---|
| Beyerdynamic DT 30 IE | 4th | 
| Activo Scoop | 3rd | 
| Sennheiser IE 200 | 1st | 
| Sennheiser CX 80U | 2nd | 
Final results
The results are in. And our winner is (drum roll, please)... the Sennheiser IE 200!
These earbuds just have no obvious weak points. They look fantastic, have a modular design, sound exquisite, and feel super comfortable to use. Yes, the 3.5mm connector means you can’t slot them into your smartphone, but there are plenty of affordable USB-C adapters out there if that’s a dealbreaker for you.
Shockingly, in second place we have the Sennheiser CX 80U. They offer modern convenience, a sleek look, and a built-in mic which is always useful. But most of all, they have absolutely no right sounding this good at such a cheap price-point. I’d highly advise skipping on the cheap wireless buds that pop up on Amazon and just getting these if you want amazing sound without breaking the bank.
The Activo Scoop secure a respectable 3rd place, with a unique treble-focused sound signature, excellent build quality, and ultra-versatile connectivity. They’re a bit too chunky for my tastes, and sometimes their top-end can seem a touch overzealous, but they’re still well worth checking out for less than $100 / £100.
And unfortunately, the Beyerdynamic DT 30 IE sit at the bottom of the ranking table. This isn’t to say that they’re bad — they offer pleasantly balanced audio, a beautiful fit, and have a great carry case bundled in. They lack the openness and detail I was looking for, but their last place finish is more of a result of their rivals’ brilliance.
So, there you have it. With Black Friday approaching, it’s well worth keeping an eye out for discounts on these models — especially the Sennheiser duo. But do you agree with my ranking? Which of these models would you pick? Let me know in the comments!
