articles.title: Francophone Africa-focused VC Saviu closes 2nd fund at $44m
articles.text:
Paris and Abidjan-based VC firm Saviu has reached the final close of its second fund, Saviu II, at around EUR40 million (US$44 million), and will use it to back around 20 tech startups and tech-enabled SMEs across Francophone Africa.
Founded in 2018, Saviu invested in 12 startups through its first fund between 2018 and 2023, mostly in Ivory Coast and Senegal, and was an early backer of the likes of Lapaire Glasses, Julaya and Paps.
The firm has already notched up several exits, including the sale of ICT4Dev to Push in 2023, Lapaire Glasses to Creadev in 2024, and Rubyx to Cofina last year.
The second fund is four times the size of Saviu’s debut fund, which closed at EUR10 million (US$11 million), with the final close seeing the African Development Bank (AfDB), including via a tranche invested on behalf of the European Commission, and French public investment bank Bpifrance, through its Averroès Africa funds-of-funds, come on board as LPs, along with several corporates and private investors.
They join an existing investor base that includes development finance institutions (DFIs) Proparco and the Dutch Good Growth Fund (DGGF), pan-African group Axian, and more than 60 private investors.
Saviu II will write initial tickets of between EUR0.5 million (US$550,000) and EUR3 million (US$3.3 million), with Saviu leading all its deals as either a reference minority or majority shareholder. The fund is sector-agnostic, but will target digital and tech-enabled business models in sectors such as fintech, healthtech, edtech and climate tech.
Its geographic focus is Francophone Africa, including Ivory Coast, Senegal, Cameroon, Gabon and Morocco, though it will also invest in selected English-speaking markets such as Kenya and South Africa.
The fund has already made 11 investments and recorded one exit. Portfolio companies include Cameroonian telemedicine startup Waspito, Senegal’s Soram, which recycles and leases corporate printers, Gabonese fleet management software provider Pozi, Moroccan tech-enabled real estate agency AgenZ, and South African robotics and coding platform Resolute.
“We are very happy to welcome new institutional and strategic investors within Saviu II,” said Benoit Delestre, managing partner at Saviu. “Their involvement not only validates our investment approach in Francophone Africa but also strengthens our ability to deliver greater value to our portfolio, by fostering impactful connections with corporate partners and international organisations.”
Saviu II follows the firm’s “Seed and Build” model, under which it concentrates on a small portfolio of high-potential businesses rather than spreading capital widely, and works hands-on with founders on business development, recruitment, international expansion and follow-on fundraising.
“The support of long-standing institutional investors such as the African Development Bank and Bpifrance will be a key asset to our renewed investment strategy, providing even greater support to our current and future portfolio companies,” said Samuel Touboul, managing partner at Saviu. “This milestone marks an exciting new chapter in our mission to support talented African founders, building innovative and sustainable companies across the continent.”

articles.title: India ranks sixth globally in GTA VI search volume, says study
articles.text:
India ranks sixth globally in GTA VI search volume, says study
India recorded nearly 9.44 lakh average monthly searches for GTA VI-related terms, ranking sixth globally by search volume. However, it ranked 106th on a per-capita basis, according to a study by The Action Network.
India ranks sixth globally in total search volume for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI), recording approximately 943,900 average monthly searches for the game-related terms, according to a study by The Action Network.
However, when adjusted for population, India ranks 106th globally, with around 66 searches per 100,000 people. This highlights the difference between the scale of interest in a large market such as India and the intensity of interest among smaller populations.
The Netherlands topped the rankings with 2,045 average monthly searches per 100,000 people, followed by France (1,594), Finland (1,514), Switzerland (1,490) and Belgium (1,483). The Netherlands recorded 369,900 monthly searches despite having a population of approximately 18.1 million, compared with France's 1.09 million searches and population of 68.7 million.
Meanwhile, the United States recorded the highest overall search volume, with 3.06 million average monthly searches, followed by other major markets such as Brazil, Germany, France and the United Kingdom. However, the US ranked 22nd on a per-capita basis.
An Action Network spokesperson said: “An analysis of Google search data found the Netherlands to be the world's most GTA VI-obsessed country, with 2,045 average monthly searches per 100,000 people, ahead of France and Finland.”
The study examined average monthly searches over the preceding 12 months for four keywords—GTA VI, GTA 6, Grand Theft Auto VI and Grand Theft Auto 6—across 150 countries and all 50 US states. Search volumes were adjusted for population to determine interest per 100,000 people.
India's growing appetite for GTA VI
The search interest is reflected in GTA VI's launch-day response in India, where gaming cafes, livestreams and social media saw heightened activity.
India has an estimated 550 million gamers, according to Reuters, although most play on mobile devices. This has created an opportunity for gaming cafes to offer access to premium console titles to consumers who may not own expensive gaming hardware.
Gaming cafes charged around Rs 250 per hour to play GTA VI. A Delhi-based cafe received 40-50 enquiries on launch day and was fully booked through the weekend. Reuters also reported crowds at gaming cafes in Delhi, Bengaluru and Srinagar.
The game's popularity has also spilled over into India's creator economy. Popular YouTubers CarryMinati and Mythpat streamed GTA VI for around 10 hours each, with both streams crossing 13 million views by the afternoon of November 19.
A separate analysis by data research platform seodata.dev found that searches for 'GTA 6 price' averaged 49,500 a month in India. It also found that searches for GTA VI's female protagonist, Lucia, were more than nine times those for Jason, at 4,400 and 480 average monthly searches, respectively.
The economics behind the hype
While search rankings indicate growing anticipation for GTA VI, they do not necessarily translate into game sales, pre-orders or active players. This distinction is important in India, where gaming is predominantly mobile-first and premium console gaming remains a smaller market.
Beyond game sales, major releases create opportunities for gaming cafes, content creators, livestreaming platforms, hardware manufacturers and advertisers. The success of GTA V also highlights the commercial potential of long-running gaming franchises that generate revenue through initial sales and recurring online engagement.
Image source: Rockstar Games

articles.title: Ces coins de la carte de GTA VI cachent l’arrivée du futur GTA Online
articles.text:
Des casinos fermés, un zoo fermé, un cimetière et même une petite ville… Plusieurs zones de l’immense carte de GTA VI sont toujours inutilisées dans l’histoire et les missions du jeu. Ce qui laisse à penser que Rockstar Games y prépare son futur GTA Online, voire des extensions narratives.
Pourquoi ces zones de la map de GTA VI restent inutilisées ?
C’est le journaliste de Kotaku Zack Zwiezen qui raconte son aventure sur GTA VI et qui a commencé à émettre des théories, après avoir publié son test comme le reste de la presse. Il explique que plusieurs zones majeures de Leonida ne sont ni visitées par Jason et Lucia, ni exploitées par les missions principales ou secondaires. Zack Zwiezen a pourtant vu deux grands casinos fermés, un zoo particulièrement détaillé (surtout que ce nouvel opus a particulièrement développé la faune), un vaste cimetière et même une petite ville située dans le nord de la carte.
Il a alors interrogé Stephen Donkin, vice-président du design chez Rockstar Games, qui a confirmé que la carte de Leonida avait été pensée « pour le long terme ». Stephen Donkin ajoute que « La carte a été conçue dans une perspective à long terme et en tenant compte de nombreux facteurs. Ainsi, certaines zones de la carte nous offrent des possibilités pour l’avenir, si nous en avons besoin pour le gameplay ou la narration ».
GTA Online, nouvelle histoire… que cachent ces zones de GTA VI ?
Il y a deux lectures possibles face à cette phrase de Rockstar Games. La première : GTA VI pourrait profiter d’une extension narrative dans une future mise à jour. DLC ou mise à jour gratuite ? Impossible de le savoir, mais si cette extension était payante, force est de croire que les joueurs seraient révoltés.
Seconde lecture : ces lieux préparent l’arrivée de GTA Online sur GTA VI. Stephen Donkin a confirmé auprès de Kotaku que les casinos ne feront pas partie de l’expérience avec Jason et Lucia, les deux personnages principaux qu’on peut incarner dans le jeu. D’autant plus que cela pourrait permettre à Jason et à Lucia de gagner facilement de grosses sommes, ce qui déséquilibrerait la progression dans le jeu. Ce qui signifie peut-être qu’avec son propre personnage dans GTA Online, on pourrait jouer au casino. Attention, il ne s’agit que d’une hypothèse, mais une hypothèse plausible.
Avec la taille de Leonida, Rockstar Games a tout l’espace pour développer des activités (notamment économiques), des missions ou même faire évoluer certaines zones, sans devoir retravailler toute la carte. La carte de GTA VI étant environ deux fois plus grande que celle de GTA V, on devrait pouvoir s’y occuper très longtemps et c’est sans doute ce qui est prévu pour GTA Online sur le jeu. cela fait 13 ans que GTA Online est sorti sur GTA V. Lorsqu’il arrivera sur GTA VI, il pourrait occuper les joueurs encore plus longtemps avec encore plus de contenu, surtout avec une carte aussi vaste.

articles.title: Confirmado: la Justicia determina que utilizar la IA en el trabajo sin permiso de la empresa puede ser motivo de despido disciplinario y se apoya en el Estatuto de los Trabajadores
articles.text:
El uso de inteligencia artificial en el trabajo puede entrar en conflicto con las reglas de la empresa. En el caso de un programador informático, ha supuesto, junto con otros incumplimientos, un despido disciplinario (sentencia del Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Castilla y León de 25 de mayo de 2026 que confirma la procedencia del despido).
Para entender la dimensión de la decisión, hay que atender al conjunto de hechos. Aunque se utiliza IA prohibida, la sentencia resalta sobre todo los proyectos para terceros y las compras personales en horario de trabajo. También destaca el incumplimiento sistemático de sus funciones. No se dice qué hubiera pasado si únicamente hubiera incurrido en el uso de IA.
En junio de 2023, la empresa informó a toda la plantilla de que estaba prohibido usar IA. Así estuvo hasta junio de 2025, en el que se permite bajo petición expresa. El trabajador utilizó IA entre enero y mayo de 2025 (en periodo de prohibición).
En España se documentan casos de restricción al uso de ChatGPT por parte de las empresas. Además de esto, en este caso se trata de la utilización del ordenador de la empresa y horas de trabajo para otras actividades.
Motivos que justifican el despido
El informático realizaba proyectos para terceros utilizando los recursos de su empleadora en horario de trabajo. Además de esto, realizaba compras personales. También incumplía las normas de seguridad informática.
En alguna ocasión hubo un retraso y la compañía decidió analizar el histórico del navegador del portátil de la empresa. El empleado alegó que se trataba de una invasión de su intimidad. Sin embargo, el tribunal no aceptó esta pretensión.
El motivo jurídico de despido es el artículo 54.2.d) del Estatuto (incumplimiento de la buena fe contractual/abuso de confianza). Desde la Sala se aprecia la gravedad y continuidad de los incumplimientos. Se desestima el recurso del trabajador y se confirma la decisión de primera instancia.

articles.title: Jensen Huang revient chez Nvidia après onze jours de scandale, d'espionnage présumé et de revirements
articles.text:
Le patron de l'IA mondiale revient : Nvidia réintègre Jensen Huang à l'unanimité
Deux liaisons révélées et une espionne chinoise présumée dans son entourage l'avaient poussé vers la sortie. Six jours après avoir écarté tout retour, le conseil de Nvidia rend les clés à Jensen Huang, à l'unanimité, en assurant que Washington n'y voit aucun danger. Reste une audition au Congrès dans une semaine et une enquête dont personne ne connaît encore l'issue.
Jensen Huang redevient président, directeur général et administrateur de Nvidia avec effet immédiat, a annoncé l'entreprise ce lundi 23 novembre. Le conseil d'administration a voté à l'unanimité après plusieurs entretiens avec lui, et se dit désormais convaincu de sa franchise comme de sa capacité à diriger le groupe.
NVIDIA Board reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO and Board Director.
Read the release: https://t.co/x4bnjiSVil
— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 23, 2026
Le cofondateur de 63 ans avait quitté l'entreprise le 12 novembre, au lendemain des révélations du New York Times sur sa relation avec Kimberly Powell, vice-présidente chargée de la santé. Quelques jours plus tôt, il avait avoué une infidélité alors que les renseignements américains soupçonnaient Alice Huang, une dirigeante de Megaspeed dont il était très proche, de travailler pour Pékin. Espionnage, puces détournées, infidélité : l'affaire a fait tomber en quelques jours le patron le plus puissant de l'industrie des semi-conducteurs.
Dans le communiqué publié par Nvidia, il se dit "honoré de revenir chez Nvidia et de diriger l'une des entreprises technologiques les plus déterminantes au monde, à l'aube d'une nouvelle révolution industrielle". Colette Kress, qui assurait l'intérim, retourne à la direction financière. Harvey C. Jones garde la présidence du conseil.
Six jours pour passer du refus au rappel
Le revirement est spectaculaire. Le 17 novembre, Huang se disait prêt à revenir si le conseil jugeait son retour utile aux actionnaires, aux salariés, à l'entreprise "et à l'Amérique". Le soir même, lors de la présentation des résultats trimestriels, Harvey C. Jones lui fermait la porte : le conseil avait accepté sa démission à l'unanimité et n'avait pas l'intention de le réintégrer.
La pression n'a ensuite cessé de monter. Des salariés réclamaient son retour dès les premiers jours. La pétition "Stand with Jensen" dépassait lundi matin les 206 000 signatures, dont plus de 10 000 de personnes se présentant comme employés du groupe, et Elon Musk l'a signée. Donald Trump a ensuite demandé publiquement au conseil de réembaucher Huang.
Le communiqué invoque surtout l'avis de "hauts responsables du gouvernement des États-Unis", qui suffit au conseil pour affirmer que ce retour ne présente aucun risque pour la sécurité nationale. Aucun nom, aucun service n'est précisé. "Le conseil estime que Jensen est la bonne personne pour diriger Nvidia", résume Harvey C. Jones.
Les investisseurs ont tranché avant même l'ouverture de Wall Street. L'action gagnait plus de 25 % dans les échanges qui précèdent la séance, selon Reuters, après avoir déjà progressé dans la matinée sur un nouveau message de Donald Trump. Entre la veille du départ de Huang et le 18 novembre, le titre avait perdu plus de 13 %. Pour le marché, l'entreprise devenue la première au monde à valoir 5 000 milliards de dollars pesait nettement moins sans son fondateur.
Congrès, enquête interne : le dossier reste ouvert
Le comité d'administrateurs indépendants chargé d'enquêter sur la tentative d'espionnage poursuit son travail avec ses propres avocats, et Huang promet de coopérer. Nvidia crée aussi un comité dédié à la sécurité nationale et au contrôle des exportations, et cherche un responsable de la conformité.
Le 1er décembre, Huang doit répondre à huis clos aux questions de trois commissions de la Chambre des représentants, présidées par Brian Mast, John Moolenaar et Rick Crawford. Le directeur juridique Tim Teter passera le lendemain. Les élus s'intéressent de près aux puces IA détournées vers la Chine, et une enquête pénale vise déjà Megaspeed.
Pour le public français, Nvidia est la marque des cartes GeForce et des puces sur lesquelles tournent ChatGPT ou Le Chat de Mistral. Huang a scellé l'alliance avec OpenAI pour bâtir des centres de données géants et présenté lui-même les nouvelles puces censées multiplier les performances par cinq. Il retrouve son fauteuil, sous l'œil d'une enquête interne, du Congrès et de la justice américaine.

articles.title: Quantum computing: Why African banks and telcos must prepare
articles.text:
Quantum computers could one day break the encryption protecting financial records and sensitive communications across Africa. Machines powerful enough to do that do not exist yet, but attackers need not wait: they could steal encrypted information today and store it until the technology catches up. Security specialists call this “harvest now, decrypt later.”
Quantum computing uses the unusual behaviour of tiny particles to tackle certain problems that would take ordinary computers far longer to solve. If the technology becomes powerful enough, it could break some of the encryption that keeps financial records, private messages and other sensitive information secure. For banks and telecommunications companies, the concern extends beyond when those systems might become vulnerable to whether information stolen now will still need to be confidential when they do.
That mismatch is central to a new report by the Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute, a data-driven, non-profit foundation with an investment arm, produced in collaboration with Accenture, a global professional services and technology consulting company. It argues that emerging economies must begin preparing their digital infrastructure before the threat matures.
Customer records, financial information and sensitive communications may need to remain confidential for years. Replacing the cryptography protecting them can also take years, particularly across complex networks of legacy systems and outside suppliers. For institutions holding long-lived secrets, the deadline to act therefore comes before the technological breakthrough—not after it.
“The key message is that quantum’s commercial impact may still be years away, but its security implications are already here,” Laura Converso, technology research principal director at Accenture, told TechCabal.
Today’s quantum processors can perform specialised calculations, but errors, noise and the difficulty of maintaining stable qubits—their basic units of information—limit what they can reliably accomplish. Developers are working towards fault-tolerant systems that can correct errors and sustain much larger calculations.
IBM aims to make its Starling fault-tolerant quantum computer available to clients in 2029, with more powerful systems planned for 2033 and beyond. Even a functioning fault-tolerant system would not necessarily be powerful enough to break widely used encryption, leaving African institutions without a firm date against which to plan their security upgrades.
NVIDIA is also working to connect quantum processors more closely with existing supercomputers. Its newly unveiled native QPU scheduling in Slurm 26.11, alongside GPU-accelerated qubit-control and error-correction tools in CUDA-Q, is designed to integrate quantum hardware into mainstream computing workflows. Support from hardware makers including IBM, Quantinuum and Pasqal points towards an increasingly connected classical–quantum computing ecosystem, rather than an immediate breakthrough in code-breaking capability.
For African institutions, the FII Institute report argues, preparation need not mean building quantum computers or betting on a particular developer’s timetable. The immediate priorities are to identify information that requires lasting protection, locate vulnerable cryptography and plan its replacement. Alongside that security work, countries can develop specialised capabilities and partnerships that give them a role in the wider quantum economy.
“Sensitive information stolen today could be decrypted in the future, while large-scale cryptographic migrations can take more than a decade to complete,” the report noted.
Existing security threat
Banks, telecoms companies and other organisations rely on encryption methods that sufficiently powerful quantum computers could eventually break. Although computers powerful enough to do this do not yet exist, the threat has already begun through a method known as “harvest now, decrypt later.” Attackers can steal encrypted data today and keep it until future quantum computers become powerful enough to unlock it.
This could put bank customers’ personal details, financial records and transaction information at risk. Telecoms companies also hold sensitive customer communications and operate networks that other essential services depend on. Government agencies, energy companies and hospitals face similar risks because they store information that must remain private for many years.
The report warns that sectors holding valuable information and running important infrastructure could be at risk.
“Banks managing decades of customer records, governments holding classified communications and energy and telecom operators running critical national infrastructure all face the same reality: The cost of acting now is far lower than the cost of being caught unprepared,” the report said.
Africa risks lagging
The need to prepare is even greater because investment in quantum technology is not spread evenly around the world.
The report estimates that more than 35 countries have funded national plans for quantum technology, with governments committing nearly $66 billion in total. The United States, Europe and China account for about $43.4 billion, or 65.8% of that funding.
A group of 11 developing economies accounts for about $1.6 billion, or 2.4% of global funding. These countries include India, Brazil, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Malaysia, Thailand, the Philippines, Pakistan, South Africa and Türkiye. This figure does not represent Africa’s share of global funding. The report does not give a separate figure for the continent.
South Africa is the only African country included in this comparison. Its South African Quantum Technology Initiative, supported by the Department of Science, Technology and Innovation, builds on years of research in optics, photonics and laser science.
The country is also exploring ways to use quantum technology to improve measurement and secure communication, including tests of quantum key distribution, a method of sharing digital security keys that can reveal when someone tries to intercept them.
Across much of the rest of Africa, governments have yet to develop clear national plans for quantum technology because it is a nascent technology. Without these plans, African countries risk relying heavily on foreign technology and falling behind as other countries adopt stronger security systems.
Getting prepared
For African organisations, quantum readiness starts not with buying quantum computers or replacing every system, but with identifying vulnerable cryptography and data that needs long-term protection.
“The priority is to gain visibility into what information needs protection, for how long, and where vulnerable cryptography sits across the organisation and its supplier ecosystem,” Converso said.
For banks and telecom companies, the next 12 to 24 months are less about predicting when a powerful quantum computer will arrive than understanding what it could put at risk. That work needs someone in charge. She said senior executives must assign responsibility and funding, making quantum preparedness an institutional priority rather than leaving it solely to technical teams.
The first challenge is knowing what needs protecting. Organisations must identify the sensitive information they hold, trace how it is secured and determine which systems would cause the greatest harm if their protections failed. That assessment must extend to suppliers, whose software, equipment and services form part of the same security chain.
What they find should guide the transition. Rather than attempting to replace everything at once, banks and telecom operators need a plan for moving away from vulnerable cryptography. They also need “crypto-agility”: the ability to change cryptographic protections without rebuilding entire systems. New technology purchases are an opportunity to build in that flexibility, provided buyers check that products can support quantum-safe security.
Much of the transition will depend on companies outside their control. Preparing early means asking suppliers how their products will adapt and testing new protections together before deploying them widely. A bank’s migration plan will be of limited use if the systems it depends on cannot make the transition alongside it.
The difficulty will vary sharply. An institution with ageing systems, a complex technology estate and numerous suppliers will face a different task from one with fewer dependencies. For banks reliant on legacy platforms and operators managing large industrial networks, the upgrade could be particularly demanding, making an early understanding of those dependencies essential to planning the work.
The report argues that African countries can benefit from the growing quantum industry without trying to build their own expensive quantum computers or compete directly with global technology powers.
“The opportunity is to identify where national strengths can create lasting strategic value, rather than replicating the capabilities of the quantum leaders,” it said.

articles.title: En 2019 tomamos la primera foto de un agujero negro, en 2026 hemos confirmado que Einstein siempre tuvo razón
articles.text:
En 2019 se produjo uno de los hitos científicos más importantes de los últimos tiempos. Por primera vez, un equipo internacional de científicos logró fotografiar un agujero negro. Bueno, el agujero negro en sí no. Eso sería imposible. Básicamente, obtuvieron una imagen de su silueta, pero eso es lo máximo que se podría obtener, así que fue todo un logro. Sin embargo, como cualquier otro logro científico, requería una revisión por parte de un grupo independiente de científicos para que pudiésemos estar seguros de que no se trata de un error o una casualidad. Dicha revisión se ha hecho esperar, pero por fin la tenemos. Y no solo demuestra que la foto es buena, sino que le da de nuevo la razón a Albert Einstein.
Posibles errores. Hay dos razones por las que esta famosa foto sería candidata a albergar errores. Por un lado, el agujero negro M87* está muy lejos de la Tierra, a 55 millones de años luz. Por otro, la imagen se obtuvo gracias a una red de muchos telescopios, conocida como Telescopio del Horizonte de Sucesos (EHT por sus siglas en inglés). Estos están ubicados a lo ancho de todo el planeta y unen fuerzas para actuar como un único gran telescopio llamado interferómetro. Todos los telescopios estaban en la parte interna de nuestra atmósfera, por lo que las señales captadas por cada uno de ellos podrían estar distorsionadas por dicha atmósfera. Además, el conjunto ofreció una gran cantidad de señales que se procesaron para dar lugar a una sola imagen. En ese procesamiento también se podría haber producido algún error.
En palabras del autor principal del estudio que se acaba de publicar, Samuel Lai, “es tan difícil como hacer una foto de un donut posicionado sobre la Luna desde el jardín de tu casa”.
Todo está bien. Para comprobar si la imagen del agujero negro es correcta, Lai y su equipo desarrollaron una técnica de aprendizaje automático llamada GenDIReCT. Su objetivo era reconstruir la imagen desde cero, filtrando las interferencias de la atmósfera terrestre y los sesgos que podrían surgir al combinar telescopios de todo el planeta en un único interferómetro del tamaño de la Tierra. Al introducir los datos públicos del EHT, sin usar el método de reconstrucción original, se obtuvo una imagen prácticamente idéntica a la que se publicó en 2019. El modelo no tenía información sobre cómo es un agujero negro, de hecho se había calibrado con imágenes no astronómicas. Por eso, la coincidencia es aún más poderosa.
Einstein tenía razón. Con su Teoría de la Relatividad General, Albert Einstein explicó que la gravedad no es exactamente una fuerza que “tira” de las cosas, sino un efecto por el cual la masa de los objetos provoca la curvatura del espacio tiempo. Ocurre de un modo parecido a cuando se deposita un balón sobre una cama elástica. Cuanto más pesa el balón, más se hunde la cama elástica. Según esta teoría, si algo concentrase muchísima masa, el espacio tiempo se curvaría tanto que nada, ni siquiera la luz podría escapar de él. Se generaría un hoyo profundísimo en la cama elástica, si seguimos con esta metáfora. Los agujeros negros cumplen con esa previsión, aunque el propio Einstein no estaba seguro de que existiesen.
Con la foto de 2019 se sugirió que Einstein tenía razón, ya que en ella se veía justo lo que cabía esperar: un anillo brillante con el centro oscuro, y con un tamaño muy cercano al que predecía la relatividad general. Aquello ya fue un respaldo importante a la teoría. También se apoyó con fotos posteriores. Sin embargo, en el caso de la imagen inicial, si estaba alterada todo podría haber sido una simple casualidad. Al demostrar que no hay errores, se apoya aún más fuertemente la teoría de Einstein.
Otras aplicaciones. Lo mejor de todo es que la técnica que han desarrollado estos científicos podría tener aplicaciones muy beneficiosas también aquí en la Tierra. Por ejemplo, al reducir los errores cuando se combinan datos de varios sensores para mapear estructuras desconocidas, podría ser útil para mapear terremotos. Incluso se cree que podría tener potencial para mejorar las imágenes médicas.
Esto es algo bastante común en el estudio del espacio. Muchas herramientas que nacieron para comprender el cosmos luego han tenido multitud de aplicaciones sin salir de nuestro planeta. Es una forma muy útil de recuperar la inversión que se hace en estudiar el espacio.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI earns $US3.8bn on its first day to make it the biggest entertainment release of all time
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI is officially the biggest entertainment release of all time after racking up $US3.8bn at the end of its first full day.
That’s $5.74bn in Australian dollars.
The game is projected to earn more than $US5bn
Rockstar Games pre-sold 32.5 million copies of the game ahead of its official launch last week which easily eclipsed the previous chapter, Grand Theft Auto V which earned $US1.5bn in its first 5 days of release.
The Grand Theft Auto VI haul in a single day is almost $US1bn more than the most successful movies of all time including Avengers: Endgame which has made $US2.943bn since it was released in 2019.
James Cameron’s Avatar released in 2009 has made $US2.924bn.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day, released earlier in 2026, has racked up $US2.524bn.
International sales data shows 75 per cent of GTA VI sales were for the PlayStation 5 with 25 per cent for Xbox.
Rockstar Games is reportedly developing a multiplayer expansion for Grand Theft Auto VI one with a PC version of the smash-hit game.

articles.title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
articles.text:
AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
- Date:
  November 21, 2026
- Source:
  York University
- Summary:
  AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.
- Share:
Artificial intelligence may be much less like the human brain than scientists have long assumed. A new study from York University has uncovered a surprising weakness in AI models that are widely used to understand how the brain processes visual information.
For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks (ANNs), computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system. Their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience.
But the new findings raise an important question: Just because AI can successfully imitate certain responses in the brain, does that mean it actually processes visual information in the same way?
"Artificial intelligence systems are often described as 'brain-like' because they can predict activity in parts of the brain that help us recognize objects," says York University Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, senior author of a new study. "Until now, scientists mostly tested this in one direction. They asked whether AI models can predict brain activity."
A New Test Reveals a Hidden Problem With Brain-Like AI
The York University team decided to approach this question from the opposite direction. Rather than simply measuring how well AI could predict the activity of brain cells, they investigated whether recorded brain activity could also predict what was happening inside the AI models.
If these systems truly operate like the brain, the researchers reasoned, the relationship should work in both directions. To investigate, they developed a method called reverse predictivity testing, which allowed them to evaluate similarities that conventional tests could overlook.
"Ultimately, we need computational models to truly understand the underlying neural mechanisms of how we recognize objects. How do we see objects move? While it's a very easy task that we do every day, computationally, though, it's a very challenging problem," says Kar, the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience.
The research team, which included York Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec, a trainee with the university's Connected Minds program, examined responses to a wide variety of visual images.
Their tests included 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. These objects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations.
AI Can Predict Brain Activity, but the Reverse Tells a Different Story
The results revealed a significant disconnect between artificial intelligence and biological vision.
AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, which are the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. However, when the researchers reversed the process, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.
This difference was particularly revealing because the researchers did not observe the same problem when comparing neuronal activity across different brains.
"The results were striking. While AI models can predict the neurons we recorded in the brain fairly well, the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. Interestingly, this is not the case when neurons from one brain is compared against ones from another brain," says Kar.
The findings suggest that an AI system can produce results that closely resemble those of the brain while relying on very different internal mechanisms. In other words, matching the brain's responses does not necessarily mean that the underlying processes are the same.
Kar warns that this distinction could become increasingly important as artificial intelligence advances. If researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences between those models and actual primate brains could accumulate over time.
That would undermine one of the main reasons neuroscientists use these systems in the first place: to develop realistic explanations of how the brain works.
"The findings suggest that today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. Importantly, the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior," says Kar.
Why the Discovery Matters for Neuroscience and Human Behavior
The implications extend well beyond computer vision. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to help researchers design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Many of these applications depend on the assumption that AI models process information in ways that resemble the human brain.
If that assumption is incorrect, researchers could draw misleading conclusions from models that appear accurate on the surface but operate differently underneath.
"Our findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. We show that models that were previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use. We provide a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field," says Muzellec.
Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism. For now, however, the newly identified differences highlight the need for caution when using existing models to investigate human behavior or guide clinical research.
The concern may also apply to other areas of neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. If those systems also rely on internal processes that differ from biological ones, researchers may need to reconsider how much they can reveal about the nervous system.
Building AI That More Closely Matches the Human Brain
Rather than suggesting that artificial neural networks should be abandoned, the findings provide a way to make them more useful and scientifically reliable.
By identifying which features of an AI model correspond to real neural activity, researchers can focus on developing systems that more accurately reflect the biological mechanisms behind perception.
"Our approach helps identify which parts of an ANN truly match brain activity, allowing us to build more reliable models for understanding how people see and interpret the world," says Kar. "This is especially important for our autism research program, which builds on models of the neurotypical brain as a baseline."
A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical. Establishing accurate models of these patterns is important for researchers investigating how perception and information processing may differ in conditions such as autism.
To help other scientists put their findings into practice, the team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement.
Published in Nature Machine Intelligence, the study introduces a new approach to evaluating artificial intelligence that goes beyond measuring how well a system performs a task. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important.
The discovery could help guide the development of a new generation of AI models that not only recognize the world with impressive accuracy, but also offer a more faithful picture of how the human brain makes sense of what it sees.
Story Source:
Materials provided by York University. Original written by Sandra McLean. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Sabine Muzellec, Kohitij Kar. Reverse predictivity for bidirectional comparison of neural networks and biological brains. Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; 8 (3): 474 DOI: 10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0

articles.title: Plex and TheTVDB failed to reach a deal, and carefully sorted libraries are the collateral
articles.text:
What we know so far: Plex will stop using TheTVDB as a TV show metadata source early next month after the media server company and the database's owner failed to reach a new agreement. Plex is directing users to The Movie Database (TMDB) as the replacement source for episode titles, descriptions, and artwork. However, Plex's TMDB integration can't yet handle several episode-ordering formats that many users rely on, meaning some carefully organized libraries may soon display episodes in the wrong order.
Metadata support is a big part of what makes Plex feel like a streaming service rather than just a folder of video files. When Plex matches a show with an external database, it automatically fills in episode titles, plot summaries, posters, and other details, saving users from having to enter them manually.
TheTVDB, a community-maintained database, has become one of the most popular metadata sources among Plex users because it offers detailed show information and multiple episode-ordering options.
Plex announced the change in a post on its forums but has not explained why the negotiations fell through. The company said metadata already in users' libraries will remain intact, meaning existing collections won't be wiped or reorganized. However, libraries that continue using TheTVDB will stop receiving metadata for new episodes and seasons after the cutoff.
Plex said it will attempt to match new episodes using other metadata sources, but given the sheer number of TV shows available, those alternatives may not work equally well for every series.
The main technical sticking point is episode ordering. TheTVDB supports arrangements that Plex's TMDB integration does not, and two options are particularly important to users. DVD ordering follows the episode sequence used in physical releases, while absolute ordering numbers every episode in a continuous sequence rather than dividing them into seasons. Both are useful for shows whose original episode numbering differs from their broadcast order, a common source of confusion when media software tries to match video files with database listings.
Plex Announcement - Upcoming Change: TheTVDB Metadata Support Ending on December 3rd
by u/samwiseg0 in PleX
Anime fans may be hit hardest. Long-running anime series often use episode numbering that doesn't fit neatly into Western-style seasons, and TMDB's grouping system can differ significantly from TheTVDB's. In a Reddit thread discussing the announcement, commenters criticized both companies for failing to reach an agreement. Many also argued that TMDB alone doesn't offer the flexibility they need to keep their libraries organized.
Plex has acknowledged these limitations. The company said it plans to add support for TMDB episode groups, allowing users to select alternative episode arrangements through TMDB. However, Plex has not provided a release date, meaning the feature may not be ready before TheTVDB support ends.
Until then, Plex is advising users who rely on alternative episode ordering to continue using TheTVDB. This means keeping their existing library structure while giving up metadata updates for new episodes, at least until support for TMDB episode groups arrives.
The announcement comes at a difficult time for Plex. It follows reports of malicious cryptominers causing Plex to run slowly and generate excessive heat on some systems, as well as criticism surrounding the company's collection of user data. Both issues have fueled complaints from a user base that tends to be technically savvy and protective of its self-hosted setups.

articles.title: Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture
articles.text:
Agoda has introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce code coupling and enforce domain boundaries without rewriting the existing service. The approach combines component-based code organization, automated architecture checks, and incremental migration. The team reported 64% shorter median code review time and 34% shorter time to initial substantive feedback for framework-backed changes compared with legacy code.
The change addresses growing maintenance challenges in BAPI, which coordinates cancellations, booking amendments, refunds, and customer communications. Agoda extracted the API from its aging core monolith in 2019 through a largely line-by-line migration. As development increased, merge requests more than quadrupled between 2022 and 2025, while some files exceeded 4,000 lines.
The team characterized the migration as a tactical design trade-off, drawing on John K. Ousterhout's A Philosophy of Software Design,
We had deliberately traded a strategic design approach for a tactical one to prioritize speed to market. This tactical mindset was exactly what the business needed at the time.
Rather than undertake a complete rewrite, the team introduced architectural boundaries incrementally.
The framework, called Platform, organizes code around business domains such as cancellations, rebooking, and payments rather than technical layers. Each component encapsulates its business logic and data access behind defined interfaces, with application, service, repository, and model layers contained within the component. This package-by-component approach aims to localize changes and reduce dependencies between business domains.
Platform framework boundaries inside a domain module (Source: Agoda Blog Post)
Agoda uses the Data Mapper pattern to keep repository-specific models, including database entities and API payloads, out of business logic. Typed builders centralize object creation and transformations, making it easier for developers to find where domain objects and service inputs are constructed.
The team also uses ArchUnit to encode architectural constraints as automated tests in continuous integration. For example, repository-specific models can only be accessed by their respective repositories. Violations fail the build rather than relying on code reviewers to identify unauthorized dependencies manually.
The team described these constraints as architectural fitness functions, a concept discussed by Neal Ford and Mark Richards in Software Architecture: The Hard Parts. One engineer explained:
By codifying our layer boundaries into an ArchUnit test suite, our CI pipeline serves as an automated guardrail, catching structural drift on every pull request before a human reviewer ever sees it.
Platform is now the default for new modules, while existing functionality is migrated incrementally when feature development provides an opportunity.
Agoda compared framework-backed and legacy merge requests in Q2 2026. Median review completion time was 1.08 hours for framework-backed changes, compared with 3.02 hours for legacy changes. Time to first substantive feedback was 10.34 hours versus 15.77 hours. Between June and August, framework-backed changes also used 29% fewer AI prompts per 100 changed lines, although median prompts per merge request were similar (20 vs. 22). Agoda cautioned that the AI findings were directional due to the short observation period. A related approach is Spring Modulith, which provides module verification and dependency-cycle checks for Spring Boot applications.
