articles.title: Tri-screen portable monitors aren’t for the faint of heart
articles.text:
Living in New York City means making the most of limited space. As a result, I’m always interested in tools that can boost my productivity at a small desk, in a cramped office, or working on the go.
I’ve experimented with dual-screen laptops in multiple form factors and numerous portable monitors, including ones with projection capabilities. I’ve had particularly good results with dual-screen portable monitors.
Naturally, a portable monitor with three full-size screens was the next logical step.
To get a four-screen (including my laptop’s screen) experience, I tested KYY’s X90G ($360 as of this writing). It’s a portable monitor with three 15.6-inch IPS screens. Each screen has 1920×1080 resolution, its own control buttons, and is specced for up to 400 nits of brightness.
The X90G isn’t the only tri-screen monitor available, but it stood out to me because of its design. Some of the X90G’s rivals place the three displays above the laptop screen, which would require you to look away from the laptop screen repeatedly.
Instead, the X90G places one screen on the left and right sides of the laptop screen and one above the laptop display for a more cohesive—but not completely unified—visual workspace.
The X90G also has better compatibility than its rivals by supporting Linux and Android in addition to Windows and macOS (on systems using an M1 processor or better).
Most laptops should fit in the X90G’s designated area, but many workstations and gaming laptops won’t, since it doesn’t support laptops larger than 17.3 inches.
A bevy of bezels
Let’s get something out of the way: If you hate bezels, a triple-portable-monitor isn’t for you.

articles.title: El exceso de stock bajará los precios de la memoria RAM para PC y SSD en 2027
articles.text:
Los precios de la memoria RAM para PC y las unidades SSD caerán de forma significativa desde la segunda mitad de 2027, cuando empresas y distribuidores reduzcan el exceso de inventario o stock acumulado durante la escasez de componentes.
La demanda de memoria alcanzó su punto más alto en el segundo trimestre de este año, concretamente en marzo, pero las compañías siguieron comprando existencias para asegurarse suministro ante la expectativa de que la escasez persistiera durante el próximo año. Esa acumulación dejó reservas superiores a la demanda real del mercado.
La previsión corresponde a Lee Min-hee, analista de la firma financiera surcoreana BNK Investment & Securities, y fue recogida por The Korean Economic Daily.
El desequilibrio se observa en la diferencia entre consumo y producción: la demanda de memoria DRAM, un tipo de memoria dinámica de acceso aleatorio, crecería 24% interanual este año, mientras que los envíos de los fabricantes superarían 38%. Para Lee, ese volumen será “el nivel más alto desde 2016”.
Por qué bajarán los precios de las memorias en 2027
Los clientes y distribuidores comenzarían a utilizar sus existencias entre el segundo y el tercer trimestre de 2027. El proceso, denominado “ajuste de inventario en el canal”, reducirá los pedidos nuevos a los fabricantes y presionará los precios a la baja.
La caída afectaría principalmente a la memoria RAM destinada a computadoras personales y a la memoria flash NAND utilizada en las unidades de almacenamiento SSD. El pronóstico llega después de un período en el que la escasez de memoria encareció productos tecnológicos para los consumidores.
Asimismo, la demanda de inteligencia artificial (IA) impulsó esa falta de componentes, porque los fabricantes priorizaron la producción y el suministro de memorias de alto rendimiento para centros de datos.
Quiénes son los principales fabricantes de memoria en el mundo
Samsung, Micron y SK Hynix concentran cerca del 90% de la producción global y orientaron sus inversiones hacia nuevas plantas de fabricación.
SK Hynix fue la única compañía que aumentó su producción este año, tras poner en funcionamiento en febrero de 2026 una fábrica en Corea del Sur dedicada a memoria de alto ancho de banda, conocida como HBM.
Este tipo de componente está dirigido a aplicaciones que requieren gran capacidad de procesamiento, como la infraestructura de inteligencia artificial.
Por qué la demanda de memoria para inteligencia artificial caerá
El consumo de memoria para inteligencia artificial podría moderarse por los cambios en el desarrollo de modelos lingüísticos de gran tamaño, o LLM. Lee sostuvo que “la creciente competencia está provocando que los modelos ligeros, que utilizan menos memoria y recursos computacionales, se conviertan en la norma”.
El analista anticipó “una desaceleración significativa en el ciclo de inversión en infraestructura relacionada el próximo año”. Entre los factores mencionados figuran retrasos en la construcción de centros de datos en Estados Unidos y la crisis de Nvidia tras la salida de quien era su director ejecutivo, Jensen Huang, una situación que afecta el papel de la empresa como proveedora de inteligencia artificial.
No obstante, la competencia entre los fabricantes para ampliar su capacidad continuaría. Lee prevé que la producción global de DRAM aumentará 50% en tres años y se duplicará en cinco años frente a los niveles de finales del año pasado, mientras muchas fábricas de memoria NAND comenzarán a operar el próximo año.
Cómo impactará esta caída de precios a los consumidores finales
La corrección en los valores de las memorias RAM y las unidades SSD será un alivio directo para quienes buscan armar o actualizar sus computadoras personales. Tras meses de sobrecostos impulsados por la prioridad dada a los centros de datos, el mercado volverá a favorecer al comprador minorista.
Esta reducción abaratará el costo de fabricación de laptops, consolas y teléfonos inteligentes. Como resultado, los fabricantes podrán ofrecer aparatos con mayor capacidad de almacenamiento y rendimiento sin trasladar incrementos al precio final.

articles.title: UK-based Agon raises €63.98 million at €411.3 million valuation to build Europe’s sovereign defence AI infrastructure
articles.text:
Agon, a London-based defence AI startup building sovereign infrastructure for autonomous military systems, has raised a €63.87 million ($70 million) Series A round at a valuation of €411.3 million ($450 million).
The round was led by Northzone with participation from returning investors Lakestar, XYZ, Lux Capital, and Global Founders Capital. The UK Government’s Sovereign AI Fund and the National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF) also joined the round, marking their first joint investment. Roelof Botha, the former head of Sequoia Capital, has come on board as a personal investor.
“AI is rapidly transforming how wars are fought, from the use of drones through to how rapidly soldiers can interpret battlefield information. The UK needs sovereign defence AI capabilities to bolster our national security in this new era,” said Kanishka Narayan, UK Minister for AI.
The investment from the UK Government’s Sovereign AI Fund forms part of the government’s broader Sovereign AI agenda. At the Budget, the Chancellor announced an additional £140 million for the Sovereign AI Fund, which will back promising early-stage AI companies with a meaningful UK presence. The funding for Agon marks the fund’s expansion into a new focus area: Physical and Industrial AI, covering robotics, autonomous systems, and advanced manufacturing.
Founded by former British Army officer and Anduril and Applied Intuition alumnus, Tristan Constant, alongside Junaid Hussain, co-founder of Cambridge Aerospace and Iconic, Agon wants to become Europe’s sovereign defence AI lab. Its primary product is a synthetic virtual lab, a virtual training environment where AI models for autonomous defence systems can be tested rapidly and affordably against realistic battlefield simulations.
The company, which has a second office in Berlin, has assembled talent from Anduril, Applied Intuition, Google, Helsing, Palantir, Amazon, and Havok, and is chaired by David Helgason, founder of gaming engine company Unity. The raise brings Agon’s total raised to date to €94.1 million ($100 million), following its emergence from stealth earlier this year with €28 million in Seed capital.
“Agon was born out of a project to bring together a coalition of European founders, operators, researchers, veterans, investors, and governments to build what we collectively believe to be urgently needed for our sovereignty and safety. Europe cannot afford to outsource the foundational AI capabilities on which its future security will depend. We founded Agon to build that capability here, giving European defence the infrastructure and models it needs to retain technological advantage,” said Hussain, co-founder of Agon.
The bulk of the fresh capital will go towards recruiting world-class AI researchers and funding the significant compute infrastructure requirement to run a full-scale AI lab.
“Europe is in an AI arms race as we enter the era of agentic warfare: intelligent agents and machines that will need to understand their environment, make decisions and adapt at a speed and scale that humans alone cannot match,” said Constant, co-founder and CEO of Agon.
Agon wants to become the foundational AI platform for European autonomous defence, developing and training the foundation models that the continent’s military system will rely on. “We exist to build the sovereign infrastructure and AI foundation models to allow us to train, test, and evolve autonomous defence systems – in Europe, for Europe – to outperform adversary capabilities,” added Constant.

articles.title: Microsoft admite: alguns e-mails não foram entregues no apagão do Outlook
articles.text:
Microsoft admite: alguns e-mails não foram entregues no apagão do Outlook
Usuários do Outlook ficaram horas sem acesso ao serviço em razão de uma falha nos sistemas da Microsoft.
Tal como prometido, a Microsoft divulgou um relatório sobre o “apagão” que afetou o Outlook e outros serviços em 12 de novembro. Além de explicar a causa do problema, o documento também revela algumas consequências, entre elas, o fato de que alguns e-mails não foram entregues quando o problema ainda se manifestava.
A razão disso é que, durante a falha, o Exchange Online (do qual o Outlook depende) estava instável a ponto de ter dificuldades tanto para processar o recebimento quanto o envio de mensagens. Isso levou a uma espécie de fila de espera de e-mails a serem entregues.
Em uma tentativa de evitar que os envios falhassem de modo massivo, a Microsoft estendeu o prazo de novas tentativas de entrega de e-mails cujo envio falha de 24 para 48 horas. Funcionou, mas parcialmente, como observa o Neowin.
Os e-mails associados a contas do Microsoft 365 para organizações foram todos entregues, mesmo que com atraso. Já algumas mensagens que tinham como destino endereços de usuários domésticos do Outlook inativos há mais de 30 dias expiraram e, com isso, retornaram ao remetente.
Uma conta de e-mail inativa não está, necessariamente, desativada. Para ser considerada como tal, presumivelmente, ela deve ficar sem acesso após determinado período de tempo (aqui, 30 dias). Isso sugere que o problema das mensagens não entregues não gerou um grande impacto, embora a Microsoft não tenha revelado o número de contas ou de mensagens afetadas.
Apesar disso, o “apagão” foi considerado grave porque também derrubou alguns mecanismos de segurança importantes, a exemplo do Zero-hour Auto Purge (ZAP), que identifica mensagens maliciosas já entregues e tenta removê-las automaticamente das caixas postais.
O Safe Links, que verifica a segurança de endereços em mensagens do Outlook, também falhou, o mesmo ocorrendo com o sistema de gerenciamento de e-mails em quarentena acessado por administradores de TI.
Mas, claro, a principal consequência foi a dificuldade de acesso aos serviços da Microsoft. O próprio Outlook só voltou à normalidade no dia seguinte ao incidente.
Tal como a Microsoft havia adiantado, a causa do problema estava em uma atualização de software nos gateways de rede do Microsoft 365, que são servidores responsáveis por receber e distribuir as conexões dos usuários entre os serviços da empresa.
Para evitar novas interrupções, a companhia revelou uma série de medidas. Por exemplo: a Microsoft planeja redistribuir, até o primeiro trimestre de 2027, as capacidades de gateway de modo que um servidor com sobrecarga não prejudique outros, causando uma reação em cadeia similar à que deu origem ao recente problema.
Os detalhes estão no relatório final da Microsoft.

articles.title: Meta throws out its net-zero goal — its competitors should be furious
articles.text:
Meta’s new sustainability report buries the lead: The company is almost certain to miss its own goal to reach net zero by 2030, and it’s refusing to commit to a new timeline.
“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones — including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets — so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” wrote Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net-zero and sustainability at Meta, in the introduction to the company’s 2026 sustainability report.
That’s a lot of words to say that Meta will continue to pollute if that means it can continue its AI rollout.
Such is the risk of voluntary targets. Companies can make and break them with little to lose, betting — often rightly — that they can ignore them with just a small hit to public opinion, which is fickle anyway. (Remember the Cambridge Analytica scandal? Most people don’t.) There’s almost no risk to the bottom line.
“We remain committed to net zero, but are re-evaluating the 2030 timeline and interim milestone. We’ll continue investing in emissions reductions and reporting our progress annually,” a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch.
A few years ago, Meta was arguably one of the better corporate stewards of the climate. The company has been one of the largest purchasers of clean power, and it set ambitious goals for water conservation.
More recently, though, its multibillion-dollar bet on natural gas at its Hyperion data center in Louisiana has undone much of that progress. Natural gas may burn cleaner and more efficiently than coal, but its impact on global warming can be just as bad when the leaky infrastructure needed to burn it is factored in.
Despite years of clean power procurement, Meta’s greenhouse gas emissions have more than doubled in the last four years. Between 2024 and 2025, its data center emissions increased more than 12 times, and Hyperion isn’t online yet.
That commitment to natural gas led to the company’s departure from RE100, a corporate renewable energy initiative, in July. The company had been part of the group for a decade, though the two split after RE100 started requiring more rigorous reporting toward renewable energy targets.
“When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned,” they added. “The reality has been far more complex. Demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected, arriving on a timeline measured in quarters rather than decades, and meeting it has meant building at a pace and scale the industry has never attempted.”
That’s all true, but when put that way, it sounds like Meta has little agency in the matter. But the company’s decision to chase AI was a conscious one.
You could argue that Meta has a fiduciary duty to chase after its peers, which have also dived headfirst into AI. But there’s precious little data to support the idea that AI will be a profit driver for a company like Meta, which is almost entirely consumer-focused.
CEO Mark Zuckerberg is optimistic that improving Muse’s energy efficiency will turn that around, but how much will everyday people be willing to pay for software that translates your offhand thoughts into surreal memes? Or monitors your emails so you won’t forget to reply to your mom? Meta is betting that it’ll be enough to support a $200 billion-plus data center, and probably more.
The choice of the fuel to power those AI ambitions was also a conscious one. Natural gas power plants, besides being able to run 24/7, are actually not a great fit for AI data centers. Turbines like to run at constant speeds, while AI data centers’ energy requirements surge and sag depending on the load. They need batteries as a buffer, which begs the question: Why not just connect to the grid and use batteries to bridge any gaps during times of peak demand? That’s what one expert recommends.
Meta’s bet on natural gas appears mistimed. Long-duration energy storage is coming into its own — and geothermal energy appears poised to become the next major power source on the grid in the U.S. Companies like Fervo, Mazama, and Quaise have been logging milestones at a rapid clip, potentially unlocking tens of gigawatts of capacity. The technology isn’t competitive with natural gas today, but it very well could be in the mid-2030s, just a few years after Meta completes Hyperion. Geothermal is also not vulnerable to supply chain shocks, like what happened with natural gas and the Iran War.
Beyond that, the company’s decision to abandon its 2030 net-zero goal risks fomenting the sort of backlash that leads to regulations with real teeth. Such regulations won’t just apply to Meta, and the broader industry would be justified in their frustration.
In that light, Meta’s timing couldn’t be worse. Surveys show the general public doesn’t hold AI or data centers in high esteem, rightly sensing that the infrastructure development is driving a rapid and often-unchecked expansion of polluting infrastructure.
The tech industry has spent over a decade trying to prove that it would be different from previous industrial juggernauts like oil and gas or automobile manufacturing. In a single PDF, Meta might have undone much of that goodwill. After this, who will trust another tech company’s voluntary net-zero goals?

articles.title: Anthropic lança IA que revisa, corrige e aprova alterações em códigos
articles.text:
A Anthropic anunciou, nesta segunda-feira (23), o Claude Ship, ferramenta que utiliza agentes de inteligência artificial (IA) para revisar, corrigir e aprovar alterações em códigos de programação. A novidade busca automatizar etapas do desenvolvimento de softwares e reduzir a necessidade de intervenção humana em tarefas rotineiras.
O sistema foi desenvolvido para trabalhar com repositórios do GitHub e está disponível para assinantes dos planos Claude Team e Enterprise. A novidade reúne três componentes: Code Review, que já estava disponível, e dois novos agentes em fase beta, chamados PR Steward e Claude Approvals.
A proposta é permitir que desenvolvedores deleguem tarefas posteriores à criação de um código. Assim, em vez de interromper o trabalho para corrigir problemas identificados durante uma revisão ou aguardar a aprovação de outro profissional, os agentes podem assumir parte desse processo.
Como funciona o Claude Ship?
O Claude Ship combina três ferramentas com funções diferentes:
- Code Review: analisa alterações propostas no código e identifica possíveis problemas antes que sejam incorporadas ao projeto. O recurso já está disponível de forma geral;
- PR Steward: trabalha na correção de problemas identificados durante a revisão, além de lidar com verificações automatizadas que falharam, conflitos entre alterações e comentários de outros desenvolvedores;
- Claude Approvals: avalia se uma alteração pode ser aprovada automaticamente, seguindo as regras estabelecidas pela equipe responsável pelo projeto.
O PR Steward também registra comentários explicando o que foi modificado e como desfazer as alterações, caso necessário. Entretanto, esse agente não tem autorização para aprovar ou incorporar mudanças ao código por conta própria.
Essa responsabilidade fica com o Claude Approvals, que utiliza políticas definidas pela equipe para determinar quais alterações podem avançar sem uma aprovação humana.
Leia mais:
- Claude teria ajudado a resolver um dos maiores enigmas da matemática
- Anthropic e o paradoxo do IPO bilionário
- Como os irmãos Amodei moldaram a cultura excêntrica da Anthropic
- Anthropic e SpaceX impuseram regras incomuns e irritaram bancos no IPO
IA também poderá aprovar mudanças em softwares
A possibilidade de delegar aprovações a uma IA é um dos principais diferenciais do Claude Ship. As equipes podem estabelecer regras em arquivos dentro dos próprios repositórios, determinando quais alterações são consideradas rotineiras e quais exigem avaliação humana mais aprofundada.
O sistema também pode considerar informações produzidas pelo Code Review e classificadores personalizados para tomar decisões.
A Anthropic recomenda que empresas comecem utilizando o recurso em modo de observação. Nesse formato, o Claude avalia as alterações e indica quais aprovaria, mas não executa a aprovação automaticamente.
Dessa maneira, as equipes podem avaliar o comportamento do agente antes de permitir que suas decisões sejam utilizadas como requisito para incorporar mudanças aos projetos.
Ferramenta busca acompanhar avanço dos agentes de programação
O lançamento acontece em momento no qual ferramentas de IA estão assumindo uma parcela cada vez maior da produção de códigos. Com isso, a revisão e a aprovação das alterações podem se transformar em obstáculos para equipes que utilizam agentes para acelerar o desenvolvimento.
A própria Anthropic afirma que o Claude escreve a maior parte do código produzido pela equipe responsável pelo Claude Code. A empresa desenvolveu o Ship justamente para acelerar as etapas posteriores à criação das alterações.
O recurso também oferece controles para administradores, que podem escolher quais repositórios serão atendidos, definir a profundidade das revisões e estabelecer limites mensais de gastos.
O Claude Ship está disponível para organizações que utilizam os planos Team e Enterprise e trabalham com projetos hospedados no GitHub. O Code Review já está disponível de forma geral, enquanto PR Steward e Claude Approvals permanecem em fase beta.
A Anthropic ressalta que a ferramenta utiliza tokens e pode gerar custos adicionais conforme a quantidade e o tamanho das alterações analisadas, além da frequência das revisões. A empresa também alerta que o Claude Ship pode deixar passar erros, vulnerabilidades de segurança e outros problemas.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: GTA 6 para PC podría llegar antes de lo esperado por culpa de una filtración
articles.text:
Grand Theft Auto VI tendrá una versión para PC hasta la primavera de 2027, pero eso no significa que habrá ports no oficiales. Una filtración de la versión de Xbox ha abierto la puerta para desarrollar recompilaciones del juego de Rockstar Games, las cuales se podrían ejecutar en PC. Un grupo de hackers compartió la pieza que hacía falta, por lo que ahora la pelota está en la cancha de los desarrolladores independientes.
De acuerdo con Videocardz, Cyberleek publicó el ejecutable de GTA 6 para Xbox, el único componente que hacía falta para completar la filtración de todo el juego. Este archivo permitiría a los desarrolladores descifrar cómo es el proceso de arranque o cómo interactúan los distintos sistemas que componen el juego. Sin el ejecutable, los proyectos solo podían analizar los recursos extraídos, como los gráficos, shaders o archivos de datos, pero trabajaban a ciegas.
Uno de los primeros proyectos que intenta llevar GTA 6 al PC es Leonida. Según el repositorio de GitHub, esta recompilación tiene como objetivo ejecutar el código del juego de forma nativa en Windows. Aunque la Xbox Series X|S y el PC comparten la arquitectura del CPU, el juego depende del hardware específico de la consola, por lo que estos juegos necesitan resolver estas dependencias.
Leonida se encuentra en una fase muy temprana de desarrollo y el juego todavía no arranca. Los desarrolladores han conseguido implementar muchas de las herramientas que se necesitan para analizar archivos, exportar recursos y preparar la infraestructura. El repositorio menciona que han conseguido exportar los modelos 3D, texturas, audio y shaders, pero todavía faltan las piezas más importantes, como la capa que traduce Direct3D 12 de Xbox a Vulkan, el soporte de ray tracing y más.
La IA ayudará a que GTA 6 llegue a PC antes de tiempo
Una de las características de estas recompilaciones es el uso de la inteligencia artificial para ayudar en el desarrollo. A diferencia de los proyectos de recompilaciones que veíamos hace tres o cuatro años, la IA ha avanzado tanto que ya permite acelerar la traducción de shaders, depuración de errores o asistir en las tareas de ingeniería inversa. El lanzamiento de GPT-6 Astra y Claude Opus 5.5 hace unos meses dio pie a una oleada de recompilaciones de juegos que hasta ahora se mantenían exclusivos de consola.
El siguiente reto será llevar GTA 6 a PC antes de que salga la versión oficial durante el primer trimestre de 2027. Con el acceso al ejecutable filtrado, los desarrolladores podrán acelerar el desarrollo apoyándose en la IA, aunque tendrán que resolver todos los inconvenientes que conlleva una recompilación, como reimplementar partes del sistema de la consola y asegurarse de que el rendimiento es estable.
Antes de emocionarse, hay que entender que una recompilación de GTA 6 no llegará de inmediato y, de hacerlo, no ofrecería todas las ventajas de la versión oficial. A diferencia de la recompilación, que intenta adaptar el código original de consola, la versión nativa de PC llegaría con soporte completo para el hardware, incluida una configuración avanzada para las tarjetas gráficas o el soporte para mods.
Otro detalle es que Take-Two no se va a quedar de brazos cruzados y es probable que los abogados de la compañía se encarguen de matar cualquier intento de llevar GTA 6 al PC antes que ellos.

articles.title: 'Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk' — Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang without answering any of the lingering questions about him, Alice Huang, and Megaspeed
articles.text:
Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO, and we guess all other questions will be dealt with later — if ever
Nvidia's board just reversed course
- Jensen Huang has been reinstated as Nvidia CEO
- He resigned a week and a half ago
- Nvidia's board claims Huang poses "no national security risk"
In a stunning turnaround, Nvidia's board has officially reinstated momentarily disgraced Jensen Huang as CEO.
"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," wrote the board in an official statement.
The news comes after US President Donald Trump supported Huang's return, and US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent used some crafty wordplay to reverse his earlier comments that Nvidia needed to look "outside" for a new CEO. As he told CBS's Face the Nation on Sunday, "I said they need to go outside; Jensen is on the outside."
Now that's some verbal jiu-jitsu.
Perhaps you've been fixated on tech outages (see Outlook, banks, FAA) or just preparing for and then playing GTA 6 for the last two weeks, and have no idea why Jensen Huang resigned from the chip company he co-founded 33 years ago. If so, here's the abridged version. 
Whispers about Jensen Huang's possible relationship with a Megapseed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), leaked a few weeks ago. The Singapore-based company is a big Nvidia customer. It may also allegedly be funneling Nvidia chips to China. With the exception of certain lower-powered chips, exporting US chips to China is against US policy.
The FBI has been investigating whether Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy. As all this was coming to light, there were fresh allegations of Jensen Huang having affairs with multiple co-workers.
Jensen Huang admitted in a memo to an infidelity and apologized, but with the new relationship revelations, he resigned.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Almost as soon as Huang stepped down, there were calls for his return. He's been depicted as a unicorn founder and CEO: basically one of a kind and irreplaceable.
Social media was split, or at least platforms were split. On Threads, the sentiment was generally anti-return, especially with a lack of clarity on what Huang and even the US government knew and didn't know about Alice Huang and Megaspeed.
On X, there was a more full-throated call for his return.
During Nvidia's November 17 earnings call, which was run by interim CEO Colette Kress, the board made it crystal clear that it was moving on, stating it "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
A shifting of opinion
When it comes to business, the weight of opinion on social media carried about as much weight as a tinfoil feather.
Pressure, though, from shareholders, and especially the White House, may have swayed the board. "In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government," revealed the board in its official statement.
Jensen Huang does his best to sound contrite in the same Nvidia release: "I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. "
Trump has been unwavering in his support for Jensen Huang, and it's clear the President believes an Nvidia with Jensen Huang is more knowable than one with a new, potentially untested CEO. The President also quickly cheered Huang's return on Truth Social.
What does this mean?
Initially, it's business as usual for the world's most important AI company, but questions swirling around Jensen Huang, Alice Huang, Megaspeed, China, and the US officials will linger.
To its credit, Nvidia is being somewhat transparent about this new reality, admitting that "Mr. Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," and its investigation of those events continues: "The Board reiterated that the committee’s investigation will proceed to conclusion. Mr. Huang fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it."
Still, this now seems like a largely toothless effort. As the board noted in its statement: "The Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk."
That rapid reinstatement of Huang proves that whatever Huang did or didn't know, and what his interactions with Alice Huang may have enabled, doesn't really matter. Huang is back in the driver's seat without any answers.
As these answers arrive, which might at least prove Alice Huang is a spy and that, thanks to her alleged efforts, China got Nvidia chips it should not have had access to, it's unlikely that the board will take any action.
Jensen Huang's role as not only the leader of Nvidia, but now one of the world's most important and now untouchable AI executives, is likely cemented not just for the immediate future, but at least through the Trump administration's end.
Two years from now, the world will have moved on; we'll have more agentic AI thanks to Nvidia's latest chips, maybe making decisions for us we no longer want to or feel qualified to handle. For example, getting to the root of what happened with Jensen Huang, Alice Huang, Megapseed, China, and the Trump Administration.
It's also worth noting that, while the reinstatement of Jensen Huang may have helped Nvidia stock and the tech stock market at large, it will have zero impact on the price of technology running Nvidia GPUs. It's not like this choice was made to help consumers. This is a move intended to raise the fortunes of AI tech companies and AI development.
Nvidia's old GPU/gaming business is likely immaterial, as is any whiff of clarity — and maybe justice — surrounding whatever did or did not happen with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

articles.title: Canadian scalper places 40+ Nvidia RTX 5090s on Facebook Marketplace for over $6,600 apiece — ironically still cheaper than Memory Express's 10,000 CAD retail price, purportedly selling every unit quite quickly
articles.text:
Canadian scalper places 40+ Nvidia RTX 5090s on Facebook Marketplace for over $6,600 apiece — ironically still cheaper than Memory Express's 10,000 CAD retail price, purportedly selling every unit quite quickly
Retail pricing situation makes the entire situation quite the tragicomedy.
The lowest rungs of hell may be reserved for politicians, yes, but scalpers have a gated community somewhere in the same area code. The latest emotion-inducing story on this topic comes from Ontario, Canada, wherein a person from Oakville had an ad listing what appear to be over forty RTX 5090s for sale, priced at 9,500 CAD (over $6,600 USD) for the cheapest, and also having the gall to demand an extra 500 CAD (about $350 USD) for one with a sealed box.
The magnanimous magnate wanted to perform the transactions at his nearby police station, and claimed that "testing is available." Some Canadian police stations do open their lobbies for this purpose for added public safety. The scalper said in his ad that he had models from most every manufacturer, including Nvidia's Founders Edition and even Dell.
Should the statements by commenter "goudacheeseguy" be true, the person selling the card is their business partner. The cards purportedly came from their small neocloud outfit and are being sold as they eventually got their hands on Nvidia B300, B200, and Pro 6000 servers "with the money [they] made shorting AI funnily enough." It's possible they're telling the truth, as the presence of the Dell and Nvidia FE cards, plus the fact they're apparently mostly open-box units, would fit with that story.
Nevertheless, the response from commenters was swift and harsh. Some pointed out that the photograph depicting windows of a street-level basement, coupled with the fact that Oakville isn't that huge, could have a master geo-guesser like Rainbolt pinpointed where the scalper was.
In a similar vein, other people remarked on the danger of the seller being followed home for discussing a five-finger discount. His laissez-faire attitude infuriated some commenters, as he stated that "[he has] other models too probably missed some, too lazy to check which ones."
There's some irony in this story, however. It's safe to say that scalpers don't garner the same amount of love as puppies, and yet the 9,500 CAD he was asking for the cards is actually on par with or lower than commercial offerings. A commenter pointed out a Canadian Customs auction of an RTX 5090 that seemingly ended up selling for 8,300 CAD.
As of right now, an RTX 5090 at Memory Express will set you back around 10,000 CAD, and even the cheapest card at Newegg Canada is going for 9,300 CAD, though it's a pretty sweet combo deal (for these times), as you do get a motherboard, a case, and a power supply included in that price.

articles.title: Her Startup selects 12 women-led startups for 2nd accelerator cohort
articles.text:
Women-focused accelerator Her Startup has selected 12 tech startups from seven African countries for its second cohort.
Her Startup is backed by KSH Foundation, Tomorrow Foundation and EHA Impact Ventures, and is this year running the programme with Founder Institute Morocco.
After receiving 468 applications from 33 countries, more than double the number for its first edition, 20 founders were shortlisted, and the accelerator increased its intake from 10 to 12. The selected startups get Founder Institute training, startup capital through convertible revenue-based financing, and six months of mentorship.
Half the cohort comes from Nigeria, namely Kadosh Mechatronics, which makes solar-powered greenhouse sensors; FriendnPal, an AI-powered mental health platform; Glorious Farmgate, a poultry automation startup; Fuse Varsity, an ed-tech company; Odnaworld, an agrifood firm; and TESA Global Solutions, a media-tech company.
The other six startups are SAB Biomanufactures (Tanzania), which turns brown seaweed into products for agriculture and food preservation; Uptech Africa (Malawi), an agri-tech marketplace; AEN Holdings (Uganda), which repurposes used batteries; EON (Ethiopia), a plastics recycler; Dosy (Egypt), a micromobility platform for women; and UNTUM Recycling (South Africa).
“The selected founders can look forward to an intensive and transformative journey combining mentorship, practical insights, expert guidance and access to a valuable entrepreneurial network,” said Youssef Koun and Hicham Sentissi, who lead the Founder Institute Morocco chapter.

articles.title: Jensen Huang isn't out of the woods yet
articles.text:
It’s safe to say no one expected this.
Monday morning, Jensen Huang returned as CEO of Nvidia, after resigning the position following news of multiple affairs, including one with a subordinate and one with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence services. With so much of the AI industry built on top of Nvidia’s AI infrastructure, Huang’s departure looked like an imminent threat to the business — and the mood on his return has been ecstatic. Share prices are rocketing back up, particularly for neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius, and the Nasdaq rose 7% on the news.
Still, tech leaders should be clear-eyed about all the problems likely to come with Huang’s reinstatement. President Trump is already telling reporters that the U.S. government found no national security concerns resulting from the affair, but the broader national security concerns aren’t so easy to dismiss, and Trump’s involvement may do more harm than good for Nvidia and its partners. This isn’t the end of the problems caused by Huang’s affairs; it’s likely just the beginning.
Most importantly, serious questions remain about how Nvidia chips were smuggled into China, and how much Nvidia knew about it. Among Jensen Huang’s defenders, it’s become common to question whether Alice Huang was really a spy, but it’s clear that a lot of restricted chips were flowing into China through her company. Just this weekend, The New York Times reported sustained contact between Alice Huang and a member of China’s Ministry of State Security during the same period she was having an affair with Jensen Huang.
With Democrats in control of Congress, including investigative bodies like the House Oversight Committee, there are plenty of ways to force the issue. Nvidia’s role in violating U.S. export controls would likely have been the subject of prolonged uncomfortable investigation, whether Huang returned or not. But with him back in the CEO’s seat, there will be a lot more riding on any revelations that come up — and any new revelations will damage Nvidia as a company alongside Huang himself.
Then there are the questions raised by Trump’s intervention. It’s unprecedented in American history for a sitting president to intervene to clear a CEO accused of being a national security risk. Simply pressing the Department of Justice to exonerate Huang would have been a scandal, but calling the Nvidia board goes significantly further. Huang has already donated $25 million to Trump’s ballroom project, so it’s easy to make the case that Trump was intervening on behalf of a donor, setting national security risks aside for his personal benefit.
All of this is happening just as Democrats retake Congress, with all of its associated investigative powers. Even if they can’t fire Huang or remove Trump, there are lots of uncomfortable questions that are still unanswered. Was there any Department of Justice inquiry into whether Huang had committed a crime, or did Trump make the call on his own? Did the intelligence services make any official assessment that could be subpoenaed into the congressional record? Investigating Democrats will be particularly interested in Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who oversees export controls and retains significant financial ties to the industry through his firm, Cantor Fitzgerald.
If all of this sounds exhausting, you’re getting a sense of what the next year will be like for anyone following national news. Congress will keep a steady drip of embarrassing revelations, milking as much political juice as possible out of Huang and everyone associated with him. Trump will keep lashing out, often making things worse for everyone involved. (Trump’s statement to CBS, which defends Huang in racist terms while also accusing him of treason, is an early taste.) It’s going to be ugly and sad, and the most successful tech company of the last decade will be right at the center of it.
I have to assume that this was the scenario the board was concerned about when it decided to remove Huang two weeks ago. Since then, the cost of removing him has gone up: an open letter from Nvidia’s employees and partners, a tanking stock market, and, ultimately, direct intervention from the president of the United States.
But nothing has lowered the cost of keeping Huang, and the ugly scenario the board foresaw earlier this month is still very much in place. We’re about to see it come to life.

articles.title: Anthropic researcher tunes chess software to turn a 200 MHz Pentium Pro into a behemoth that would handily defeat Kasparov and Carlsen — 1995 PC with 64 MB of RAM would crush Kasparov 9 times out of 10
articles.text:
Anthropic researcher tunes chess software to turn a 200 MHz Pentium Pro into a behemoth that would handily defeat Kasparov and Carlsen — 1995 PC with 64 MB of RAM would crush Kasparov 9 times out of 10
A mere 200 MHz chip with hyper-optimized software is enough to destroy all humans.
Readers with back pain probably recall the much-discussed 1996 chess challenge, wherein the world champion Gerry Kasparov faced off against IBM's Deep Blue chess-optimized computer. The nascent clanker lost the match with a 4-2 total, but still stunned the world by being the first piece of electric sand to win a single game against a grandmaster. Modern chess engines will utterly destroy any human, but Anthropic engineer Nicholas Carlini wondered if granting old hardware new bytes would give the machine a better chance. Spoiler: yes, indeed it would.
To understand the task, here's a quick primer on chess scoreboards. A player is rated worldwide with an Elo system (first devised for chess), wherein they lose or gain points in proportion to the difference to their opponent's rating — meaning that winning a match against Magnus Carlsen would net you a lot of points versus defeating me, who only learned about the en passant rule a handful of years ago.
At his prime, Kasparov ranked about 2800 points. Given that Deep Blue eventually barely won against him in a subsequent rematch, that is a good starting point for any. Contemporary chess engines like Stockfish have an estimated Elo of about 3,300, far higher than any human — guaranteeing it'll win most matches against a human.
Nicholas Carlini got hold of a 1995-era machine, packing a Pentium Pro CPU with all of its 200 MHz of clock speed, and 64 MB of RAM. For his first experiment, he grabbed Crafty, a 1996 chess engine, and measured how well it would do. It came in at 2,000 Elo with 1 second allotted, and 2,400 @ 10s. Running that software on a Ryzen 7 resulted in a 2,600 rating — good, but not enough.
Since Crafty's source code is available, he got Claude to mod it with modern features, and eventually reached a ceiling of 3,000 Elo @ 10s per move. That's quite an impressive feat already, especially considering that the lone Pentium Pro represented but a small fraction of the hardware that Deep Blue had. An Elo delta of +200 means this iteration would defeat Kasparov three out of every four games, while a +400 delta means a victory nine out of ten times.
Carlini then pulled out the big gun: Stockfish. He had to ask Claude to modify it to use only 32-bit arithmetic instead of 64-bit, and limit its workspace to the measly 64 MB of RAM, minus whatever the system harness took. Right off the bat, the figures were revealing: 2,500 @ 1s, and 3000 @ 10s.
The engineer performed a few optimization passes, and eventually got 2,850 @ 1s; 3,100 @ 10s; and almost 3,200 @ 30s — enough to put every human in their place, especially in a grandmaster tournament setting where there's no fixed time per move. You can play the bot using the link on the respective blog post. We'd wish you the best of luck, but there's no such concept in chess.

articles.title: Sarvam clarifies AI strategy amid debate over hosting Chinese models
articles.text:
Sarvam clarifies AI strategy amid debate over hosting Chinese models
Co-founder Pratyush Kumar contends that a model’s country of origin and the location of the infrastructure on which it runs are two different matters. Building inference infrastructure does not take away from Sarvam’s core focus on its own models, he says.
After Sarvam AI’s Token Factory attracted both support and criticism, particularly over its inclusion of Chinese-developed AI models, co-founder Pratyush Kumar has sought to address the questions surrounding the platform’s funding, use of computing resources, and its relevance to Sarvam’s indigenous AI ambitions.
Kumar said the IndiaAI Mission offered around 20 startups access to graphics processing units (GPUs) at a 40% discount. Sarvam used this support to train its 105-billion-parameter model from scratch. He noted that the government did not fund Sarvam directly, with the subsidy instead going to GPU cloud providers.
Launched on November 16, Token Factory allows developers and businesses to access multiple AI models through a single application programming interface (API), with charges based on the number of tokens processed. Tokens are small units of text that an AI model reads or generates, while inference is the process of generating responses using a trained model.
The platform’s catalogue includes Sarvam’s own model alongside open-weight systems such as DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Google’s Gemma. Open-weight models make their trained parameters available for others to download and run.
Kumar emphasised that this business operates independently of the government-supported training effort. “We serve multiple open-weight models on GPUs we have privately procured, without any government support,” he said. Sarvam has also said that its subsidised compute allocation ended in March 2026.
The inclusion of Chinese-developed models has fuelled the debate over technological sovereignty. Sarvam’s position is that a model’s country of origin and the location of the infrastructure on which it runs are two different matters. Hosting open-weight models on Indian GPUs means prompts need not be sent to overseas model providers.
However, domestic hosting does not make a foreign-developed model Indian or transfer its intellectual property. Nor does it, by itself, resolve concerns about software supply chains and model behaviour.
Sarvam says zero data retention, under which prompts and responses are not stored, is available on request, while operational logs are governed separately. Data residency alone is not a complete privacy guarantee.
Kumar maintained that building inference infrastructure does not take away from Sarvam’s core focus of developing its own models. On November 22, the company announced Sarvam-105B-1711, an updated open-weight version of its 105B model, claiming improvements in reasoning, tool use, and Indian-language performance.
Sarvam noted that the model’s average score across eight benchmarks for conversational agents had risen from 42.6 to 73.9. Kumar also indicated further releases across vision, speech and edge AI, alongside efforts to secure more advanced computing infrastructure for training larger models.
The commercial opportunity highlights a wider industry shift. As AI becomes part of everyday applications, the cost of running models repeatedly can matter as much as the cost of developing them. Sarvam is not alone in pursuing this market.
Other Indian players, including L&T, Jarvislabs, Utho Labs and Mirror Security, are also developing similar offerings, competing with established global providers such as Together AI and Fireworks AI.
This activity is unfolding alongside government efforts to strengthen domestic AI capabilities. The IndiaAI Mission, approved in 2024 with a five-year outlay of about Rs 10,372 crore, supports foundation-model development and shared computing infrastructure. A July government update said 20 indigenous model proposals had been identified and 93 lakh GPU hours sanctioned across 237 projects.
Edited by Swetha Kannan

articles.title: Ericsson sees mining and utilities powering SA's 5G growth
articles.text:
Ericsson, a global telecoms network equipment giant, has spent decades building South Africa’s telecommunications infrastructure. Now, as operators prepare another phase of investment, the question is whether they can make money from 5G.
South Africa’s mobile operators are now under pressure to turn years of 5G investment into sustainable returns. With consumer data revenue facing pricing pressure from fibre competition, the next growth opportunity lies in enterprise connectivity, private networks and artificial intelligence (AI)-powered services that businesses are willing to pay a premium for.
Siseko Ngxola, head of Ericsson South Africa, believes operators must move beyond connectivity as a commodity and develop services businesses will pay a premium for.
“Safe to say the full benefit of 5G has not been fully realised. The networks today, as they are, are still sitting on 5G non-standalone,” Ngxola told TechCabal on the sidelines of the Africa Tech Festival in Cape Town on Thursday.
South Africa’s operators have largely deployed 5G non-standalone networks, which use 5G radio technology alongside existing 4G core infrastructure. Moving to 5G standalone will introduce dedicated 5G core networks, enabling capabilities such as network slicing, lower latency and more reliable connectivity for enterprise applications.
The opportunity, according to Ngxola, lies in serving industries where network reliability, security and predictable performance are critical. Mining companies, ports and utilities are among the sectors Ericsson sees as potential customers for private 5G networks, which can support connected machinery and industrial automation.
“5G will also unlock the journey for AI for enterprise customers,” Ngxola said. “They’ll be able then to have an offering that can be targeted to the likes of your mines, your ports, your utilities, where you can provide these predictable and guaranteed services over secure networks.”
Ericsson is pursuing this opportunity with systems integrator ComSol, which is helping develop private 5G deployments. Ngxola said the partnership would take Ericsson beyond equipment supply into deploying, operating and managing industrial networks.
Ngxola said power utility Eskom had also started formal tender processes to engage the market on adopting 5G in its power plants. He said businesses will need evidence that private 5G can improve productivity, reduce downtime or deliver operational efficiencies.
Ericsson expects monthly mobile data traffic to rise from 5.3GB per user in 2025 to 12GB by 2031. Ngxola also pointed to growing uplink traffic as AI-driven services generate more activity across networks.
He cited Ericsson’s work with Verizon, a United States telecommunications network operator, where AI-powered network optimisation delivered reported spectral efficiency improvements of 8.9% in the downlink and 8% in the uplink.
“Technology should not be adopted for the sake of adopting technology,” Ngxola said. “It must be to address certain challenges.”
In South Africa, mobile operators face growing competition from fibre providers such as Vumatel, Openserve, MetroFibre and Frogfoot. Telkom’s home fibre catalogue lists 30Mbps packages from R495 ($28.32) a month on Vumatel and R499 ($28.55) on Openserve, offering households an alternative to mobile data for everyday internet use.
Ngxola said fibre providers had created pricing pressures that mobile operators could struggle to match because of limits on radio capacity and the economics of running mobile networks. Differentiated connectivity could help them compete on services rather than data prices.
Advanced connectivity also requires investment in the infrastructure supporting mobile services. In November, MTN South Africa, the country’s second-largest mobile operator, selected Ericsson to modernise its voice core network using its cloud-native internet protocol (IP) multimedia subsystem (IMS), with deployment expected across 2026 and 2027.
The upgrade will support higher-quality voice, prepare the network for voice over 5G and introduce AI-powered features such as spam protection and branded calling.
Branded calling could allow businesses, including banks, to identify themselves and the purpose of calls on customers’ phones, improving answer rates and creating a new revenue stream for MTN, according to Ngxola.
Yet spectrum costs, infrastructure investment and energy constraints compete for operators’ capital. Ngxola believes the investment cycle is an opportunity to rethink how networks generate value as AI and enterprise digitalisation create demand for more sophisticated connectivity.

articles.title: Elijah Wood: el regreso al papel de Frodo tras 27 años
articles.text:
Elijah Wood ha vuelto a calzarse los pies de hobbit de Frodo Bolsón más de dos décadas después de rodar la trilogía de Peter Jackson, en este caso para ‘El Señor de los Anillos: La caza de Gollum’, la nueva película ambientada en la Tierra Media. Y, en unas declaraciones a Deadline que recoge el portal neozelandés Rova, lo ha resumido así: “Fue precioso y surrealista, y parecía que no hubiera pasado el tiempo”.
Un viaje atrás en el tiempo. Según cuenta el actor, volver al plató fue como regresar al pasado, y le bastó con mirar hacia abajo para que el cuerpo recordara lo que ya había vivido: “Ya he visto estos pies así, conozco este vestuario”. Vamos, que tiró de memoria muscular. Y es que, como explica él mismo, la sensación lo transportó de golpe: “Es como si de repente se esfumaran 27 años y estuvieras otra vez ahí dentro”.
Las ganas venían de antes. No es la primera vez que Wood habla de esta película con entusiasmo. En enero de 2026, antes de que empezara la producción, ya le decía a Screen Rant en la Fan Expo de Nueva Orleans que el proyecto era como “volver a reunir a la banda” en lo creativo, con “ese núcleo original del grupo que vuelve a juntarse para contar esta historia, que será como una exploración muy divertida de este personaje al que todos queremos tanto”.
Fin del rodaje. Pero Wood no es el único que ha dado novedades. Andy Serkis, que además de dirigir la película vuelve a interpretar a Gollum, confirmó en noviembre de 2026 en el programa ‘The Morning Mosh Pit’ que el rodaje principal había terminado, según recoge GeekTyrant en su crónica del fin de rodaje.
Caras conocidas y nuevas. La película recupera a varios personajes de la Tierra Media con sus intérpretes de siempre: Ian McKellen vuelve a ser Gandalf, Wood repite como Frodo y Lee Pace hace lo propio con Thranduil. Al reparto se suman además Anya Taylor-Joy, Kate Winslet, Jamie Dornan y Leo Woodall, según el anuncio del inicio del rodaje que recogió Hypebeast.
Una misión contrarreloj. La historia sigue la peligrosa misión de Aragorn para atrapar a Gollum antes de que este le revele a Sauron dónde está el Anillo Único. Se sitúa entre los acontecimientos de ‘El Hobbit’ y los de ‘La Comunidad del Anillo’, y se apoya en buena parte en lo que J. R. R. Tolkien dejó escrito en los apéndices de ‘El Señor de los Anillos’, tal y como explica la guía de GamesRadar sobre la película.
Eso sí, habrá que esperar para verla en pantalla, porque la película tiene previsto su estreno en cines el 17 de diciembre de 2027.

articles.title: Claude Code Adds Experimental Code Mode to Orchestrate Tool Calls with JavaScript
articles.text:
Anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code, an experimental feature in which the model writes JavaScript to drive its tools instead of requesting each Bash, Read, or Edit call separately. Code Mode is off by default, requires Claude Code v2.1.323 or later, and is enabled with the CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 environment variable. Anthropic warns it may change or be removed in any release.
In a normal session, Claude asks for one tool call, reads the full result, and decides the next step. In Code Mode, one script can run commands in parallel, pass one result into the next call, and return only the output the model needs. The documentation's example finds a file with rg, raises a retry limit, runs the tests, and returns just the path and test output. The conversation still shows each tool call and diff, while the generated code sits in the transcript viewer. Anthropic recommends it for edits repeated across many files, searches that need filtering, and independent commands. Code that Claude waits on stops after ten minutes; sessions started in auto or bypassPermissions mode can push it to the background for up to two hours while the conversation continues.
The permission model is the part architects should read first. Each call inside a script still goes through deny and ask rules and PreToolUse hooks, but in auto mode the classifier reviews the script before it runs, not each call, and cannot see values computed at run time. A git push can now reach a hook as cd 'app' && git push, so hooks must check every part of a command; a hook matching the REPL tool can read the JavaScript from tool_input.code. Project settings cannot enable Code Mode, so a cloned repository cannot switch it on, and administrators can block it through managed settings.
Code Mode runs only in interactive terminal sessions of the native build, on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, or Fable 5.2, through a Claude subscription or Console account. It does not work with -p, the Agent SDK, the VS Code panel, the Desktop app, Amazon Bedrock, gateways, or zero-data-retention organizations. Agent teams need v2.1.326. Anthropic has published no token or latency figures for it.
George (@bolyki) compared Code Mode with normal mode across eight interactive Sonnet 5.5 runs and posted:
Same results every time. Context 20-25% smaller. On the bigger task: 37% fewer tokens, 19% lower cost. But it is not faster, and on a tiny task it cost more.
Ravi Madabhushi, who builds agent auth infrastructure, pushed back on claims that the feature makes MCP obsolete:
It doesn't materially change anything wrt authentication, authorization and audit policy layers; Your agent still makes those same MCP calls, with the same auth tokens and context and what materially changes is how much context gets into the model window and how much can be discarded.
The idea, and the name, predate Anthropic's release. Cloudflare introduced Code Mode for MCP converting MCP tools into a TypeScript API that models code against inside sandboxed Workers, where bindings keep API keys away from generated code. Anthropic's own post on code execution with MCP described one workflow dropping from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens, and the Claude API offers programmatic tool calling in a remote code execution container. Code Mode instead runs the script in the developer's local session, against Claude Code's built-in tools and permission system.
Code Mode remains opt-in and experimental, and Anthropic collects feedback through /feedback. Setup steps and troubleshooting are in the Claude Code documentation

articles.title: Review: The Asus ProArt P16 offers a glimpse of a future powered by local AI
articles.text:
Buying a new computer in the last few years has meant wading through all manner of AI branding nonsense. Most of the AI pitches for laptops are little more than marketing hype, but the launch of Nvidia RTX Spark could bring a meaningful improvement in AI capabilities to the device you use every day. Asus has adopted Nvidia’s new chip in its latest ProArt lineup, offering a staggering amount of memory to run local AI models.
While it doesn’t have a traditional GPU, the Asus ProArt P16, with up to 128GB of memory, can also be your primary gaming and productivity machine, but this unified experience comes at a high price. If you want to run a small army of agents on your laptop, you’re looking at $7,000 for the top-end ProArt P16, and despite being more approachable on Windows, local AI still requires a lot of trial and error.
The PC stuff
Before we dive into the AI agents, let’s talk about the ProArt P16 as a laptop. Nvidia’s pitch is that the RTX Spark can be your one true machine for AI, productivity, and gaming. And it doesn’t skimp on the specs.
| Specs at a glance: Asus ProArt P16 (2026) |  |  | 
|  | Base config | As reviewed | 
| Screen | ASUS Lumina OLED, 16.0-inch, 3K (2880 x 1800) 16:10 touch screen, 120Hz, 1100 nits peak brightness | ASUS Lumina Pro OLED, 16.0-inch 4K (3840 x 2400) 16:10 touch screen, 120Hz, 1600 nits peak brightness | 
| OS | Windows 11 Home | Windows 11 Pro | 
| CPU | Nvidia RTX Spark N1X (5120-core GPU, 18-core CPU) | Nvidia RTX Spark N1X (6144-core GPU, 20-core CPU) (4.00 GHz) | 
| RAM | 64GB LPDDR5x unified memory | 128GB LPDDR5x unified memory | 
| GPU | Blackwell RTX GPU | Blackwell RTX GPU | 
| Storage | 1TB SSD | 2TB SSD | 
| Networking | Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4 | Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.4 | 
| Ports | 3x USB 4.0 Gen 3 Type-C with support for display / power delivery (data speed up to 40Gbps) 1x USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A, 1x 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack | 3x USB 4.0 Gen 3 Type-C with support for display / power delivery (data speed up to 40Gbps) 1x USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A, 1x 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack | 
| Size | 13.94 x 9.57 x 0.51 ~ 0.63 inches | 13.94 x 9.57 x 0.51 ~ 0.63 inches | 
| Weight | 3.90 lbs (1.77 kg) | 3.90 lbs (1.77 kg) | 
| MSRP | $4,399.99 | $6,999.99 | 
| Battery and charging | 99.9WHrs, 140W USB-C adapter | 99.9WHrs, 140W USB-C adapter | 
Asus has released numerous ProArt laptops, but this one is notable for including the new Nvidia Spark RTX chip in its most powerful configuration. The Spark N1X has a 20-core Grace CPU, divided between 10 high-performance Arm Cortex-X925 cores and 10 power-efficient Arm Cortex-A725 cores. The performance cluster reaches boost speeds between 4.0 and 4.1 GHz, while the efficiency cores peak at 2.8 GHz. Memory caching on the processor totals 49MB, split between 24MB of shared L3 cache and 25MB of L2 cache.
Graphics and AI are the purview of the Nvidia GB20B Blackwell GPU. It packs 6,144 cores in this configuration across 48 streaming multiprocessors, backed by its own 24MB L2 cache. These 5th-generation Tensor Cores support the full suite of Nvidia technologies, including DLSS, Reflex, ACE, G-Sync, CUDA, and NVFP4. In all, you’re looking at up to 31 TFLOPS of FP32 graphical performance and about 1,000 TOPS of FP4 AI compute.
