articles.title: „Wie einen Donut auf dem Mond fotografieren“: So schwierig war das erste Bild eines Schwarzen Lochs
articles.text:
„Wie einen Donut auf dem Mond fotografieren“: So schwierig war das erste Bild eines Schwarzen Lochs
Schwarze Löcher faszinieren die Wissenschaft schon lange. Dabei handelt es sich um Bereiche im Weltall mit so starker Gravitation, dass nichts mehr aus ihnen entkommen kann – nicht einmal Licht. Schwarze Löcher entstehen, wenn sehr viel Masse auf kleinstem Raum konzentriert ist und die Raumzeit dadurch stark gekrümmt wird.
Nach Albert Einsteins allgemeiner Relativitätstheorie wird die Raumzeit von Masse gekrümmt. Bei einem Schwarzen Loch ist diese Krümmung so stark, dass selbst Lichtstrahlen nicht mehr nach außen gelangen können.
Die Aufnahme mit der Bezeichnung M87* erlangte weltweite Bekanntheit
Im April 2019 wurde das erste von der Menschheit aufgenommene Bild eines supermassereichen Schwarzen Lochs der Öffentlichkeit präsentiert. Es entstand mithilfe des Event Horizon Telescope (EHT), einem weltweiten Verbund von Radioteleskopen. Das Bild zeigt das supermassereiche Schwarze Loch im Zentrum der Galaxie Messier 87 (M87), die 55 Millionen Lichtjahre von uns entfernt ist. Die Aufnahme, die weltweite Bekanntheit erlangte, bekam die Bezeichnung M87*.
Siebeneinhalb Jahre später hat ein unabhängiges Forschungsteam dieses Bild jetzt verifiziert. Dies bestätigt Einsteins allgemeine Relativitätstheorie, die bereits die Existenz Schwarzer Löcher sowie das Aussehen ihrer unmittelbaren Umgebung vorhersagte. Die Forschungsergebnisse des Teams sind in der Fachzeitschrift Nature veröffentlicht worden.
KI als Basis des zur Bildverifizierung angewandten Verfahrens
Samuel Lai, Forscher bei der australischen Wissenschaftsbehörde CSIRO (Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation), entwickelte mit seinem Team fortschrittliche Methoden des maschinellen Lernens und der künstlichen Intelligenz, um Informationen über die Struktur des Schwarzen Lochs zu gewinnen. Dabei filterten sie Störungen heraus, die dadurch entstanden, dass das EHT das Objekt M87* durch die Atmosphäre unseres Planeten hindurch beobachtet hatte. Das angewandte Verfahren – „GenDIReCT“ genannt – berücksichtigte zudem Verzerrungen, die durch die Zusammenschaltung mehrerer Teleskope entstanden waren.
„Als wir die Methode auf den ursprünglichen EHT-Datensatz anwandten, erhielten wir ein Schwarzes Loch, das in Größe und Form nahezu identisch mit dem historischen EHT-Bild war“, sagte Lai in einer Pressemitteilung und ergänzte: „Wichtig ist: Unser Modell hatte keinerlei Vorkenntnisse darüber, wie ein Schwarzes Loch aussieht, als wir es auf die M87-Daten anwandten.“ Laut ihm ist die „erste wirklich unabhängige Validierung“ des EHT-Bilds ein „wichtiger Schritt im wissenschaftlichen Prozess“.
Bestätigung für Albert Einsteins allgemeine Relativitätstheorie
Auch Lai teilt die Faszination für die besondere M87*-Abbildung und unterstreicht die Schwierigkeit, überhaupt zu dieser gelangt zu sein: „Es ist, als würde man im eigenen Garten stehen und versuchen, einen Donut auf dem Mond zu fotografieren“, erklärte er gegenüber space.com.
Die Verifizierung des Bildes ist auch ein erneuter Ritterschlag für Albert Einsteins allgemeine Relativitätstheorie, die er 1915 veröffentlicht hatte. Sie lieferte auch Vorhersagen darüber, wie die Umgebung eines Schwarzen Lochs aussehen müsste: ein Ring aus extrem heißem, leuchtendem Plasma, auf den der Schatten des Schwarzen Lochs fällt.
Als Wissenschaftler:innen das erste Bild von M87* sahen, waren sie erstaunt, wie genau es die Vorhersagen von Einsteins allgemeiner Relativitätstheorie widerspiegelte – ein erneuter Beleg für die Richtigkeit der Theorie. Die nun erfolgte Verifizierung festigt diese Erkenntnis weiter.
))))))) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Is Silicon Valley turning its back on Europe? Plug and Play's Thomas Bigagli weighs in
articles.text:
Sequoia Capital’s decision to close its London office has reignited debate about the future of European innovation and the commitment of US investors to the continent – especially amid other departures including Andreessen Horowitz and Coatue. However, not all US investors in Europe share this gloomy outlook.
Thomas Bigagli, Partner and Managing Director at Plug and Play, believes the move says more about Sequoia’s investment strategy than Europe’s ability to produce successful startups.
On 4 November 2026, Silicon Valley-based Sequoia Capital announced it would close its London office, established in 2020, as part of a broader restructuring. The changes also include merging its early-stage and growth investment teams, simplifying its partnership structure, and discontinuing its Arc accelerator and Scouts programme.
The announcement follows similar decisions by Andreessen Horowitz, which closed its London office in 2025, and Coatue, which withdrew in 2024, raising questions about whether international investors are reconsidering their physical presence in Europe.
Speaking to EU-Startups, Thomas offered a different interpretation.
“I wouldn’t necessarily interpret Sequoia’s decision as a lack of confidence in European entrepreneurship, but rather as a reflection of an evolving investment strategy and operating model. […] That is fundamentally different from saying that Europe no longer presents attractive investment opportunities.”
Investing in Europe, or investing in its future?
According to Thomas, Sequoia is moving towards a leaner, more centralised organisation capable of investing internationally without maintaining offices in every market. For established startups seeking growth capital and access to US networks, this approach can be effective.
“However, it raises an interesting question about how international venture capital firms approach foreign markets: are you investing in an ecosystem, or are you genuinely invested in that ecosystem? There is a fundamental difference.”
For Plug and Play, a Silicon Valley-based investment and innovation platform founded in 2006 by Saeed Amidi, maintaining local relationships remains central to its strategy. The firm operates across more than 70 locations worldwide, including over 25 in Europe, and works with more than 600 corporate partners.
Its European journey began in Berlin in 2013, when it became the first investor in German fintech N26. Since then, its portfolio has expanded to include companies such as Owkin, Zama, Einride and FINN.
Thomas explained that local teams enable investors to identify founders before fundraising begins, establish connections with universities and understand the needs of corporations and institutions. These relationships can also translate into commercial opportunities for portfolio companies.
“Technology travels fast, but trust takes time.”
Plug and Play doubles down
This long-term approach appears to be paying off. According to a PitchBook ranking cited by Thomas, Plug and Play is the most active US investor in European venture capital by deal count.
“What I find particularly interesting about this ranking is that it is not the result of a recent strategic decision to invest in Europe. It reflects more than a decade of continuous investment in European ecosystems.”
In 2022, the firm accelerated its regional investment activity by establishing a dedicated European investment committee and strengthening local decision-making. Thomas says its European portfolio has more than doubled since then.
Looking ahead, Plug and Play plans to develop additional investment vehicles alongside European institutional investors, family offices and corporate limited partners. It is also strengthening its university partnerships and developing industry-focused AI Centres of Excellence to connect research, startups and established businesses.
“We believe that some of the most valuable investment opportunities and competitive advantages are built through years of developing relationships, earning trust, and actively contributing to local ecosystems, rather than simply accessing them when attractive investment opportunities emerge.”
Despite Sequoia’s departure, there are indications that American capital remains interested in European startups. According to PitchBook’s Q3 2026 European Venture Report, US investors participated in 22.2% of European venture rounds during the first nine months of 2026, the highest proportion recorded this decade.
Recent EU-Startips coverage from 2026 provides further evidence that US investors remain active in Europe. On 17 November 2026, less than two weeks after announcing the closure of its London office, Sequoia Capital co-led a €4.5 billion Series C round for British AI drug-discovery company Isomorphic Labs, alongside Greenoaks, with Andreessen Horowitz also participating. Earlier in the year, Sequoia led ElevenLabs’ €424 million Series D, while Andreessen Horowitz backed Stockholm-based Pit’s €13.6 million funding round.
Plug and Play, meanwhile, participated in Barcelona-based NeuralTrust’s €17.2 million Seed round, Lithuania’s Axiology (€5 million), France’s Orakl Oncology (€30 million), Swiss Aylight Zurich (€4.5 million), and French Davis AI (€4.6 million).
Thomas expects this participation to continue, although investors may become more selective.
“You cannot fully understand what is happening in Paris, London, Stockholm, Munich, Vienna, Warsaw, Lisbon, Milan or Barcelona simply by sitting in Silicon Valley. […] Ultimately, the importance of having a local presence depends on where and how you intend to create value as an investor.”
Europe’s next big test: Scaling up
Thomas sees particularly strong opportunities where AI intersects with Europe’s established industrial and scientific capabilities, including robotics, advanced manufacturing, biotechnology, energy, healthcare, space technology and cybersecurity.
“I believe Europe represents one of the most compelling and, in certain sectors, underestimated technology investment opportunities globally. [..] From an investment perspective, the best-performing European venture capital funds can generate returns comparable to their US counterparts.”
However, he acknowledges that the continent still faces substantial obstacles to building global technology companies, particularly fragmented markets, limited growth-stage financing, slower technology adoption and weaker exit opportunities compared with the US.
“Compared with the US, Europe suffers from market fragmentation, slower decision-making and technology adoption, limited access to growth capital, and insufficient institutional investment in venture capital. […] Europe does not have a talent or technology creation problem. It has a commercialisation, financing, scaling, and liquidity problem.”
For Thomas, addressing these structural weaknesses will require stronger European growth funds, greater institutional investment and more opportunities for successful companies to remain and scale within the continent.
“We need more success stories like Spotify, Revolut, and ElevenLabs. […] Europe should not aspire to become the next Silicon Valley. It should build its own model of technological leadership, inspired by its unique competitive advantages.”
Where does this leave Plug and Play and the like?
Ultimately, Sequoia’s restructuring illustrates how different investment philosophies are shaping international venture capital. While some investors are prioritising centralised operations, others see local presence as a competitive advantage.
“We want to be more than an American investor investing in Europe. We want to be a long-term partner in building Europe’s next generation of global technology leaders.”
And although Thomas would not be surprised if additional US firms followed Sequoia’s example, Plug and Play has no intention of joining them.
“We don’t see this as a reason to reconsider our European presence. Quite the opposite.”

articles.title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
articles.text:
Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
This essay originally appeared in Tech Policy Press.
Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither.
Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions.
When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies.
Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it.
The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in The New Yorker, puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents.
The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it.
The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself.
The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.
Clive Robinson • November 23, 2026 8:10 AM
@ Bruce,
You not the US Big Tech are trying to avoid legal liability for anything they do.
But you did not mention the,
“Who and the How”
Of it starting.
Some of us are old enough to remember Bill Gates throwing the toys out the pram over people copying BASIC.
It was not long after that that he and others at Microsoft decided to hide behind “leasing” to avoid legal responsibility for the products Microsoft produced.
Thus arguably with leasing human rights were stripped away and the Software industry could push any legal nonsense they liked in the “EULA “inside the box”, where opening the box tied you into the EULA and at sone point you had to consent to “arbitration” that the software companies controlled like glove puppets.

articles.title: Signal can now block AI agents out of your private chats — but not on your Mac
articles.text:
Signal can now block AI agents out of your private chats — but not on your Mac
While blocking in-app screenshots on iOS 27 and flagging AI screen reads on Android, macOS users still have to exclude Signal from Siri manually
- Signal now blocks in-app screenshots by default on iOS 27
- On supported Android, screen security turns on if AI tries to read chats
- Mac users remain exposed to Siri AI, with Signal citing Apple's OS limits
Signal is blocking AI assistants from snooping on your private messages on iPhone and Android, though Mac users are still left exposed.
In a November 20 blog post, Signal President Meredith Whittaker announced that the encrypted messaging app is restricting operating-system AI agents from capturing chats via screenshots. The targets include Apple's Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI in iOS 27 and Google's Gemini Intelligence on Android.
Even if you rely on end-to-end encryption and the best VPN to shield your internet traffic, neither tool stops an AI agent scanning text already decrypted on your display. Whittaker called these deep OS integrations "an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission."
The update arrives days after a Reuters investigation revealed that Meta's data-hungry Muse AI agent bypassed its official connector to read unlinked Signal chats. As The Hacker News reports, Muse abused Android push notifications and macOS screenshot and accessibility tools to pull message text.
How Signal blocks AI agents, and what it cannot stop
Once an AI assistant grabs what is on your screen, Signal loses control. As Whittaker warned in her blog post: "All of this is outside of Signal's control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation."
On iOS 27 (Signal 8.37 or later), Signal now blocks in-app screenshots by default through a new Block Siri AI setting. On Android (Signal 8.35.1 or later), Signal cannot reliably detect screenshot attempts across every vendor build, so it automatically turns on Screen security only when it detects an assistant trying to read the screen.
According to Signal Support, iPhone users can adjust or pause protection for 10 minutes under Settings > Privacy > Block Siri AI, while Android users manage it via Settings > Privacy > App security > Screen security. Signal cautions: "However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts') Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees."
Does blocking screenshots actually keep AI out of your chats? Not completely.
Signal admits its fix cannot cover every Android build and "restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user's device via the filesystem."
Signal made a similar trade-off last year when it blocked Microsoft Recall on Windows 11.
NEW: Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance.
Leave No Trace investigates the companies and governments putting our digital freedom at risk — and the people fighting back.
📩 Subscribe now to get every edition delivered to your inbox every Friday, launching this September.
Why Mac users are still exposed to Siri AI
If you message on a Mac, Signal cannot protect you automatically.
In a footnote to her post, Whittaker wrote plainly: "We cannot reliably block screenshots on macOS."
Apple's operating-system architecture is to blame, Signal says, alongside missing developer documentation. While macOS offers protections against continuous screen recording, Signal notes those controls do not apply to single screenshots, and older APIs were deprecated in favor of tools that "only work for streaming media and other DRM-protected content."
TechRadar contacted Apple to comment on this, but we are still waiting for a response at the time of publication.
However, that echoes Whittaker's earlier warnings about AI agents breaching the boundary between apps and the operating system.
Signal is now urging Apple, Google, and Microsoft to give developers a documented way to opt apps out of AI data access altogether.
For now, Signal tells macOS 27 users to open System Settings > Siri and manually add Signal to Excluded Apps, while Apple previews more granular Mac data-access controls for apps that use AI agents.

articles.title: Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
articles.text:
Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising
- Date:
  November 17, 2026
- Source:
  University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto
- Summary:
  A surprising Finnish study found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the assumption that screen time is always harmful. Researchers suggest that what children do on screens may matter more than how much time they spend using them.
- Share:
An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.
The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.
The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.
These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.
To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.
More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills
One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.
Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.
The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.
"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.
"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.
Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently
The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.
Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.
Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.
Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.
The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.
Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity
The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.
Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.
One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.
This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.
"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.
"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."
What the Eight-Year Study Revealed
The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.
The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.
Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.
To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.
Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.
Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.
The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.
Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.
The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

Materials provided by University of Jyväskylä - Jyväskylän yliopisto. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: GrapheneOS accuse Google de menacer les fabricants de smartphones pour étouffer la concurrence
articles.text:
GrapheneOS affirme que Google ferait pression sur les constructeurs de smartphones pour les dissuader de collaborer avec lui, en s'appuyant sur leurs contrats de licence. Le projet dénonce des pratiques anticoncurrentielles et souhaite alerter le département américain de la Justice.
Alors que son partenariat avec Motorola devait lui permettre de s'affranchir de sa dépendance aux Pixel, GrapheneOS hausse le ton et accuse Google de vouloir lui barrer la route. Dans une série de publications sur X les 19 et 20 novembre denrier, le projet spécialisé dans la sécurité et la confidentialité d'Android dénonce des pressions sur les fabricants, destinées selon lui à les décourager de travailler avec ses équipes et à freiner l'essor des versions indépendantes du système d’exploitation mobile. Des accusations de pratiques anticoncurrentielles que GrapheneOS souhaite désormais porter devant la justice américaine.
Des licences Google utilisées pour faire pression sur les fabricants ?
Si Android est un système d'exploitation open source que les constructeurs peuvent librement adapter, les applications et services propriétaires de Google obéissent à d'autres règles. Pour préinstaller le Play Store et les autres composants de Google Mobile Services (GMS), les fabricants doivent en effet conclure des accords de licence avec la firme de Mountain View et respecter ses exigences. Une dépendance commerciale quasi incontournable, dans la mesure où vendre des smartphones Android sans le Play Store constitue aujourd'hui un pari risqué.
Or, selon GrapheneOS, Google aurait contacté à plusieurs reprises des fabricants pour les interroger sur leurs liens avec le projet, avant de brandir ces fameuses conditions de licences GMS pour les dissuader de poursuivre toute collaboration. Une façon, selon ses développeurs, d'entraver son développement au-delà des Pixel, alors que son partenariat avec Motorola doit justement lui permettre de prendre en charge les smartphones d'un autre constructeur.
Outre les licences, c'est aussi la liberté d'installer un autre système sur son smartphone qui serait menacée. GrapheneOS accuse Google de pousser ses partenaires à renoncer au déverrouillage du bootloader, indispensable pour remplacer le système d'origine, et craint que les Pixel finissent par suivre le même chemin. Le projet reproche aussi à la firme de réserver une part croissante des nouveautés et mises à jour d'Android à ses propres appareils, au détriment des autres constructeurs et des développeurs indépendants. Deux évolutions qui pourraient compromettre l'avenir des versions alternatives du système.
Des sanctions européennes pour avoir entravé les alternatives à Android
Les inquiétudes de GrapheneOS portent aussi sur Play Integrity, une API proposée par Google aux développeurs pour vérifier l'intégrité des appareils et lutter contre la fraude. Selon le niveau de contrôle exigé par les développeurs d'applications, cette vérification peut nécessiter une certification Google dont GrapheneOS ne bénéficie pas, au risque de voir des applications bancaires refuser de fonctionner sur des smartphones pourtant dotés de solides protections de sécurité. Le projet y voit, là encore, un moyen supplémentaire de favoriser les versions d'Android approuvées par Google et plaide plutôt pour le recours à l'attestation matérielle, qui permet de contrôler l'intégrité des appareils sans imposer cette certification.
Pour rappel, les contrats liant Google aux fabricants lui ont déjà valu de sérieux démêlés judiciaires. En 2018, la Commission européenne avait infligé à l'entreprise une amende de plus de 4 milliards d'euros pour abus de position dominante dans l'écosystème Android, une sanction confirmée le 2 juillet 2026 par la Cour de justice de l'Union européenne, à hauteur de 4,125 milliards d'euros.
Parmi les pratiques sanctionnées figuraient des accords dits « antifragmentation », qui conditionnaient l'accès aux licences de certaines applications Google à l'engagement des fabricants de ne pas commercialiser d'appareils équipés de versions d'Android non approuvées par la firme. La justice européenne avait ainsi reconnu que ces accords entravaient la concurrence et le développement des systèmes alternatifs.
GrapheneOS souhaite à présent porter les pressions dénoncées devant le département américain de la Justice (DoJ), estimant que Google poursuit des pratiques anticoncurrentielles déjà sanctionnées en Europe. Le projet n'a toutefois rendu publics ni les échanges incriminés ni l'identité des fabricants qui auraient subi ces pressions.

articles.title: The Download: AI’s judgment problem and carbon removal’s crop threat
articles.text:
The Download: AI’s judgment problem and carbon removal’s crop threat
Plus: AI may have cracked math's greatest unsolved problem.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some capabilities are improving exponentially—but models aren’t as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding.
The report updates METR’s widely shared time horizon plot, which tested models on a large suite of tasks. The new version adds more open-ended tasks, such as designing AI evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments.
Models struggled with these tasks, which could prove crucial to automating research and development.
Find out where AI progress is running into tougher challenges.
—Grace Huckins
Why using rocks for carbon removal could eventually reduce crop growth
Google, Microsoft, and others are investing hundreds of millions of dollars in startups spreading crushed rock across farms to capture carbon from the air.
The approach, known as enhanced rock weathering, could also improve soil quality and boost crop yields.
But new research raises serious questions about how much material can be added to farmland before it starts reducing yields, MIT Technology Review can exclusively report. The findings suggest the carbon removal potential could be far smaller than previously estimated.
Here’s why major concerns are emerging about enhanced rock weathering.
—James Temple
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 AI may have cracked math's greatest unsolved problem
Anthropic’s Claude was used to prove the Riemann hypothesis. (WSJ $)
+ Two groups have independently verified the proof. (Guardian)
+ It could be the biggest math breakthrough in decades. (New Scientist $)
+ AI may be changing who gets to do math. (MIT Technology Review)
2 The COP31 climate talks have collapsed after a fossil fuels row
The EU rejected a deal it called “greenwashing.” (NBC News)
+ Saudi Arabia, Russia, and India opposed mentioning fossil fuels. (BBC)
+ Calls are growing for “net negative” instead of just net zero. (Nature)
+ Last year’s talks avoided fossil fuels. (MIT Technology Review)
3 The woman at the center of Nvidia's scandal has ties to China's military
Firms in her family's network work with Chinese defense contractors. (NYT $)
+ Her associate allegedly ran the chip smuggling behind the scenes. (WSJ $)
+ US intelligence says she was in touch with a Chinese spy official. (ABC)
+ Republicans are pushing a new AI strategy to counter Beijing. (Reuters $)
4 Hackers have breached the FBI’s criminal information database
It contains information used by law enforcement at all levels. (AP)
+ Hackers also breached an Agriculture Department system. (NBC News)
+ And the Austrian foreign ministry’s website. (Reuters $)
5 Russia, the US, and Israel have stalled global rules on “killer robots”
The UK, Japan, South Korea, and Turkey also resisted binding rules. (Politico)
+ Around 100 nations backed regulations, but arms producers balked. (CNBC)
+ Talks will continue through 2028. (AP)
6 Trump says he’ll ban US companies from building data centers abroad
He threatened them with a “tremendous tax.” (CNBC)
+ Electricity is fuelling the data center backlash. (MIT Technology Review)
7 US lawmakers are nearing a deal to ban Chinese cars
They plan to prohibit sales of Chinese vehicles in the US. (Quartz)
8 Trump’s visa crackdown has pushed tech workers to leave the US
It’s driving engineers and researchers overseas. (Bloomberg $)
9 GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could free up farmland larger than Italy
Their use could transform the global food system. (Conversation)
+ They may also slow biological aging. (MIT Technology Review)
10 BepiColombo has become the second spacecraft to orbit Mercury
Its probes will study the planet’s surface and surroundings. (Nature)
+ Mercury’s ancient ice could hold clues to the origins of life. (New Yorker $)
Quote of the day
“It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy.”
—John Kennedy, US senator from Louisiana, tells NBC’s Meet the Press that Jensen Huang’s alleged affair could prove costly for efforts to prevent China from obtaining AI chips.
One more thing
On the ground in Ukraine’s largest Starlink repair shop
Starlink is critical to Ukraine’s fight against Russia, but Donald Trump’s fickle foreign policy and reports of Elon Musk restricting Ukraine’s access to the service have cast the technology’s future in the country into doubt.
For now, Starlink access largely comes down to the unofficial community of users and engineers, including the expert “Dr. Starlink”—famous for his creative ways of customizing the systems—who have kept Ukraine in the fight, both on and off the front line.
He gave MIT Technology Review exclusive access to his unofficial Starlink repair workshop in the city of Lviv. Here’s what we learned.
—Charlie Metcalfe
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ This otherworldly image of a porcelain crab has won the Oceania Photo Contest.
+ Cracking a smile regularly may be good not just for your mood but also for your health.
+ 95-year-old William Shatner is now performing Metallica covers with his band, the *uckers.
+ Join a wingsuit champion on an exhilarating flight down a mountain road at more than 200km/h.
Deep Dive
The Download
The Download: the agentic web arrives and the drive for safer roads
Plus: A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble.
The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication
Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.
The Download: testing tech promises and searching for cognitive immortality
Plus: Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia CEO.
The Download: GLP-1s and eating disorders, self-aware cities, and forever chemicals
Plus: Binance has suffered the biggest crypto hack in history.
Stay connected
Get the latest updates from
MIT Technology Review
Discover special offers, top stories, upcoming events, and more.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: Daily roundup (November 23, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: Daily roundup (November 23, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Monday, November 23, 2026.
From Sridhar Vembu's view on AI to Government of Karnataka training AI talent, YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.
Latest News
What mechanisation and automation did to farmers, weavers, carpenters and ironsmiths could now be happening to mathematicians and programmers, according to Zoho co-founder Sridhar Vembu.
He believes artificial intelligence (AI) is beginning to displace work traditionally associated with highly skilled intellectual professionals, just as earlier technological advances transformed occupations built around manual skills and craftsmanship.
In a post on X, Vembu backed an observation by AI researcher Subbarao Kambhampati that the intellectual class had largely been spared the loss of purpose experienced by workers displaced by previous technological revolutions.
Shadowfax appoints Abhinav Agarwal as chief product officer
Shadowfax has appointed former Amazon executive Abhinav Agarwal as chief product officer.
“Given the nature of the role and his position in the management, Mr Abhinav Agarwal has been identified as part of the senior management personnel of the company.”
Agarwal brings over 17 years of global experience, having held senior leadership roles at Amazon across North America and India. Over his tenure, he led cross-functional teams spanning Amazon Prime, advertising technology, and North American operations - combining P&L ownership with deep product and engineering execution.
Pegasystems partners with Govt of Karnataka to build AI talent
Enterprise AI software company Pegasystems Inc is collaborating with the Department of IT & BT, Government of Karnataka as the state seeks to expand its technology talent pool and strengthen its position as an AI innovation hub.
The collaboration supports the government’s broader industry partnership to train students and engineers across the state of Karnataka. As part of this effort, Pegasystems will train and certify an initial cohort of 200 candidates in 2027. The training will take place across three to four clusters in Karnataka, giving participants industry-relevant skills and hands-on expertise.
Other news
Spotify launches Running Mode in India
Starting today, Spotify is bringing the Running Mode experience to Premium Standard and Platinum users in India. It is a personalised running experience that turns one's music into guided runs shaped around one's goals, taste, and pace.
Since launching in July, millions of listeners have embraced Running Mode, using music to power everything from quick weekday runs to weekend workouts, the company said. India is one of 11 new markets where the experience is being rolled out now, more than doubling its global footprint, it added.
Pixxel signs MoU with IIT Kanpur
Pixxel has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur to advance research and development in hyperspectral imaging, artificial intelligence, and geospatial applications.
The partnership brings together Pixxel’s commercial satellite imaging capabilities and IIT Kanpur’s scientific expertise to develop and validate advanced remote sensing models, improve the interpretation of Earth observation data, and translate academic research into practical
geospatial solutions.
The collaboration will also strengthen research and knowledge exchange between the two organisations. Pixxel will provide access to selected hyperspectral datasets and software tools, while IIT Kanpur will contribute its expertise in algorithm development and scientific validation.
MobiKwik’s Zaakpay goes live with Visa Payment Passkey
One MobiKwik Systems Limited announced that Zaakpay, its RBI-authorised online payment aggregator, has gone live with Visa Payment Passkey, enabling merchants on its platform to offer eligible Visa cardholders a simpler authentication experience at online checkout.
The feature allows customers to authenticate eligible online card transactions using their device's built-in security, without having to wait for or enter an SMS OTP (one-time password).
Visa Payment Passkey allows customers to complete eligible online card transactions using the security features built into their devices. Following a one-time registration, customers can use their passkey to authenticate eligible payments across participating merchants checkouts.
University of Liverpool Bengaluru, Biocon Academy explore partnerships
The University of Liverpool Bengaluru and Biocon Academy jointly organised a roundtable bringing together senior leaders from academia, healthcare, biotechnology, pharmaceuticals, and clinical research to explore opportunities for strengthening UK-India collaboration in education, research, healthcare innovation and workforce development.
The roundtable provided a platform for industry and academic stakeholders to discuss potential partnerships across the life sciences sector.
Discussions explored opportunities to leverage the University of Liverpool's expertise in drug discovery, women's health, artificial intelligence, and clinical trials alongside India's strengths in biotechnology and pharmaceutical manufacturing.
(This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.)

articles.title: Jensen Huang vuelve a ser CEO de Nvidia por decisión unánime de la junta de accionistas
articles.text:
Apenas once días después de su salida, Nvidia ha anunciado oficialmente que su fundador recupera los cargos de CEO y presidente de la compañía, además de su puesto en el consejo de administración. La decisión se ha tomado por unanimidad y tiene efecto inmediato, y la vuelta de Huang se produce tras una crisis que había puesto en jaque no solo la estabilidad de la empresa, sino de toda una industria.
El Gobierno de EEUU, clave. En el comunicado se incluye un comentario especialmente llamativo: el consejo recibió información de altos cargos del Gobierno estadounidens, y con dicha información consideró que el regreso de Huang no suponía un riesgo para la seguridad nacional. La empresa también asegura que las conversaciones mantenidas con el directivo han despejado sus dudas sobre su sinceridad y capacidad para seguir dirigiéndola. Donald Trump llegó a insinuar estos días que Huang recuperaría su puesto, pero en Nvidia no indican si dichos comentarios influyeron o no en la decisión. Huang también declaró abiertamente que estaría encantado de tener una segunda oportunidad.
Giro de 180 grados. Lo sorprendente es que hace apenas seis días la propia Nvidia descartaba totalmente la vuelta de su líder. Harvey Jones, presidente del consejo, había asegurado que la empresa no tenía intención de readmitirlo y que buscaría un nuevo CEO. Ahora ese mismo consejo ha cambiado totalmente de idea y decide que Huang es la persona adecuada para dirigir Nvidia.
El origen del escándalo. La crisis comenzó cuando salieron a la luz las relaciones extramatrimoniales de Huang. Una de ellas fue con Alice Huang, vinculada a Megaspeed, una empresa de Singapur investigada por posibles desvíos de chips avanzados de Nvidia a China. Los servicios de inteligencia de EEUU sospechan además que Alice Huang podría tener vínculos con los servicios de inteligencia chinos, algo que negaron desde Pekín. Luego aparecerían informaciones sobre otra relación de Huang con una subordinada, lo que acabó precipitando los acontecimientos y la dimisión de Huang. Las sospechas de espionaje no han sido demostradas, y no hay evidencias claras de que Huang filtrara información confidencial.
Pero la investigación continúa. Nvidia ha querido dejar claro que la reincorporación no supone el fin del proceso de investigación. El comité independiente creado para averiguar si Huang fue objeto de una operación de inteligencia extranjera seguirá trabajando hasta llegar a sus conclusiones, y el propio Huang se ha comprometido a colaborar. Además la compañía ha creado un comité especializado en seguridad nacional y controles de exportación y tendrá un responsable directo del cumplimiento normativo. Aunque Huang recupera su puesto, de cara al público habrá refuerzo de los mecanismos de vigilancia que rodean el negocio.
Los inversores querían a Huang. La noticia ha provocado una reacción espectacular en bolsa, con subidas que han superado el 30% durante la negociación. Lo que ha ocurrido en Wall Street es una clara demostración de la relevancia que el mercado tecnológico concede al fundador de Nvidia, cuya dirección ha sido fundamental para convertir a la empresa en la gran joya de la industria de la IA. Como explicábamos en Xataka, su salida también había dejado clara una debilidad estructural: Nvidia depende enormemente de Huang y no había sucesor claro que pudiese coger las riendas. Eso es algo que ahora quizás Huang deba comenzar a preparar.
Once días de vorágine. Colette Kress, directora financiera de Nvidia, había asumido temporalmente las funciones de CEO mientras el consejo buscaba sustituto/a para el cargo. La CEO interina también dejó claro que Huang no volvería a su puesto hace unos días, lo que parecía negar dicha opción por completo. Ahora Kress volverá a centrarse en la responsabilidad que ocupaba previamente. Mientras, Huang ha agradecido el apoyo de los empleados, accionistas y socios, y asegura regresar con humildad y un compromiso renovado. El fundador recupera así prácticamente todo el poder ejecutivo que había perdido tras su dimisión, aunque sin duda habrá una supervisión más estricta tras este regreso.
Pero. La crisis de Nvidia ha puesto de manifiesto hasta qué punto las relaciones personales de un directivo pueden tener un impacto geopolítico colosal. Los chips de Nvidia son foco claro de la guerra comercial y tecnológica entre EEUU y China, y las decisiones sobre quién puede acceder a dichos chips tienen consecuencias sobre toda la industria tecnológica y de la IA. Que el Gobierno de EEUU haya influido de tal forma en ese regreso también deja claro hasta qué punto Nvidia ha dejado de ser una empresa tecnológica convencional y es más bien una importante pieza de ese gran puzzle geopolítico en el que se ha convertido todo el segmento.

articles.title: Mzansi's power moves
articles.text:
Howzit, Mzansi! 🇿🇦
Welcome to the first edition of TC Mzansi. We’re excited to bring you closer to the people, ideas, and businesses shaping South Africa’s technology ecosystem and the wider Southern African Development Community (SADC) region.
South Africa’s technology story is bigger than its established tech hubs. Across the country and throughout the wider region, young people are building businesses, developing solutions, and finding new ways to tackle everyday challenges. Some are doing this in the offices and innovation hubs of Cape Town and Johannesburg; others are working in townships, rural communities, and places that rarely make the technology headlines.
This newsletter will bring those stories into focus. We will explore the people, ideas, investments, and innovations shaping the region’s digital future, while asking what it takes to turn promising ideas into businesses that create real impact.
Expect a new edition every week by 1 pm SAST (12 pm WAT).
We’re glad to have you along for the journey.
Let’s stay connected!
Phathisani Moyo
Head, South African Desk, TechCabal
Top Headlines from South Africa
Mixed reactions as Ramaphosa defends his Silicon Valley trip
Microsoft’s 18-hour outage exposed South Africa’s dependence on Big Tech
ICASA to fight Sakeliga’s court bid over 30% ownership rule
From coding at 12 to building an AI company backed by global investors
Let’s dive in, but first… check this out
Put your business in front of Africa’s decision-makers
Reach over 150,000 tech and business leaders across Africa with TC Daily and the TechCabal newsletter family. Introduce your brand, promote your product, or share your next big launch with the people building and backing businesses across the continent.
Send an email to ads@bigcabal.com
South Africa’s Cyril Ramaphosa. Image Source: NPR.
Mixed reactions as Ramaphosa defends his Silicon Valley trip
South Africa’s President Cyril Ramaphosa’s 300-person delegation to Silicon Valley has sparked debate over public spending, diplomatic priorities, and South Africa’s ambitions in artificial intelligence (AI).
Ramaphosa defended the week-long visit, saying private companies covered much of the cost and that the mission could attract investment, build technology partnerships and position South Africa as an AI innovation hub. The delegation includes eight cabinet ministers, 24 startups, postgraduate AI students, researchers and business leaders. Its programme includes engagements with Google, Microsoft, Cisco, and Palo Alto Networks.
However, the president has refused to disclose the trip’s total cost or identify its sponsors, fuelling criticism from citizens, former diplomats, and political observers. Supporters argue that the visit should be judged by its ability to deliver investment, skills development, and jobs.
Phathisani’s view: South Africa needs global technology partnerships, but taxpayers deserve transparency and clear, measurable returns, not promises wrapped in diplomatic spectacle.
Read the story
Microsoft’s 18-hour outage exposed South Africa’s dependence on Big Tech
Microsoft’s 18-hour global outage on November 13 disrupted South African businesses and public institutions, exposing the risks of relying on a handful of technology giants to keep essential operations running. Eskom, Absa, and FlySafair were among those affected, alongside the City of Cape Town and the South African Revenue Service (SARS).
The disruption hit Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams, OneDrive, and SharePoint, forcing organisations to redirect customers and employees to alternative communication channels. Although Microsoft worked to restore services, the incident exposed how a failure in one global technology provider can ripple across banking, aviation, public services, and the broader economy.
As cloud platforms become central to business operations, the outage raises urgent questions about digital resilience, backup infrastructure, and business continuity. South Africa cannot build a resilient digital economy while leaving critical business and public services vulnerable to failures in infrastructure it does not control.
Read the full story
ICASA to fight Sakeliga’s court bid over 30% ownership rule
South Africa’s telecoms licencing rules are heading for a legal battle that could shape how foreign technology companies enter the market. The Independent Communications Authority of South Africa (ICASA), the country’s telecoms regulator, will oppose lobby group Sakeliga’s court application challenging the regulator’s refusal to recognise equity-equivalent investment programmes as an alternative to 30% local ownership.
The programmes would allow multinational operators to invest in areas such as skills development and enterprise support instead of selling shares in their South African businesses to historically disadvantaged groups (HDGs).
The case has implications for companies such as Starlink, the Elon Musk-owned satellite Internet company, which could face ownership requirements before securing a licence. Sakeliga wants the High Court to overturn ICASA’s decision, arguing that it failed to implement Communications Minister Solly Malatsi’s policy direction to align ownership rules with the ICT sector code.
The dispute pressures the government’s efforts to attract foreign investment while maintaining transformation requirements in the telecommunications industry.
Read the full story
From coding at 12 to building an AI company backed by global investors
Young South African tech entrepreneur Emile Ferreira is building the kind of technology that could shape how businesses use artificial intelligence. Ferreira is the co-founder and chief technology officer of Verascient, a Cape Town-founded AI infrastructure startup that recently raised R19.5 million ($1.2 million) from international investors, including Founder Collective, co-founded by South African technology entrepreneur David Frankel.
His journey is remarkable. He taught himself to code at 12, joined software development platform Replit as one of its first hires while still in high school, and developed an on-device AI assistant that reportedly reached more than 200,000 Android users. He later graduated with distinction from the University of Cambridge with a master’s degree in advanced computer science.
Verascient is tackling a practical business challenge: helping organisations turn fragmented information into useful intelligence for AI agents.
Read the full story
The former crypto sceptic building a new way to move Africa’s money
Image Source: TechCabal.
For Harry Huang’s family, paying an overseas supplier sometimes meant finding someone who knew someone. Years later, that frustration is the business opportunity behind Lumepay. The former crypto sceptic is combining stablecoins with banking infrastructure to help African businesses move money across borders. In this week’s Coffee With, TechCabal’s Phathisani Moyo speaks to Huang about building a payments company around a simple expectation: the money must arrive.
Read it now
Image Source: United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF).
In Zambia, Airtel turns mobile money into a gateway to stock-market investing: Airtel Zambia has launched Airtel Money Buy Shares, a service that lets customers buy shares in companies listed on the Lusaka Securities Exchange through the MyAirtel app using their mobile money accounts. The move pushes telecom operators further into financial services, beyond payments and transfers, and could lower barriers to stock-market participation.
The opportunity is significant. FinScope Zambia’s 2025 survey found that 76.1% of adults used mobile money, while the share using capital-market products rose from 0.6% in 2020 to 13.8% in 2025. The challenge will be turning mobile access into sustained investment participation.
Read the story
Zimbabwe’s Cabinet approves national artificial intelligence charter: Zimbabwe’s Cabinet has approved a National Artificial Intelligence Charter to establish ethical and governance principles for AI development and deployment. The framework operationalises the country’s 2026–2030 National AI Strategy and sets expectations around transparency, accountability, inclusion and human-centred technology.
It also proposes governance structures for strategic oversight, coordination and complaints handling. The development matters as African governments move from announcing AI ambitions to deciding on regulation. For businesses, the charter could provide greater regulatory clarity, but its impact will depend on how the principles are translated into enforceable rules and practical oversight.
Read the story
Paratus brings Starlink enterprise services to another SADC market: Paratus Group, a pan-African fibre and satellite operator, has launched Starlink-powered enterprise connectivity in Malawi, targeting businesses and institutions that struggle with unreliable or limited terrestrial networks. Its offering will serve sectors including banking, healthcare, agriculture, mining and education, with local installation and technical support.
The launch expands Paratus’s network presence to 16 countries across sub-Saharan Africa. The company says it has already signed several enterprise customers and can complete installations within 24 to 48 hours, depending on location. The move adds another competitor in the regional satellite connectivity market, while raising questions about affordability and how far enterprise-focused services can extend access beyond major cities.
Read the story
Four-country satellite school project targets 30 rural schools: Satellite operator SES and the International Telecommunication Union’s Partner2Connect coalition plan to connect 30 rural schools across Malawi, Burundi, Zambia and Zimbabwe by the end of 2026. The project is expected to benefit between 20,000 and 30,000 students and teachers, giving underserved communities access to online learning platforms, teacher-training resources, and digital collaboration tools.
Satellite connectivity is intended to overcome gaps where fibre and mobile infrastructure have not reached. The initiative is part of SES’s wider commitment to connect 100 schools globally, highlighting the role of satellite networks in extending digital education across rural southern Africa.
Read the story
Teraco brings wind power into SA data centre mix
Image Source: Empower Africa.
A quick look at the week’s most consequential story in Southern African tech.
Teraco, Africa’s largest interconnected data centre operator, has begun receiving wind-generated electricity through South Africa’s national and municipal grids, marking a significant step in its renewable energy strategy.
The first electricity from its contracted independent power producer (IPP) wind project reached its Cape Town data centres in September. The initiative forms part of a R3.5 billion ($200 million) renewable energy programme combining solar generation, wind power purchases and grid infrastructure investment.
A key component is Sediba, a 120MW solar plant under construction in the Free State, backed by R2.25 billion. Teraco aims to achieve 100% renewable energy by 2035, as demand for data centre capacity grows alongside cloud computing and AI.
Read the story
That’s the estimated enterprise value of Telkom as MTN revives takeover talks that could reshape South Africa’s telecommunications industry.
MTN, South Africa’s second-largest telecom group by subscribers, has revived takeover talks with Telkom, its JSE-listed rival, four years after walking away, in a deal that could reshape South Africa’s telecoms industry. The proposed acquisition would combine MTN’s mobile business with Telkom’s 25 million subscribers, fibre network and enterprise operations. But with the government owning 40.5% of Telkom and the PIC another 11.08%, the deal faces significant shareholder, competition and regulatory hurdles. If successful, it could transform the country’s connectivity market and become one of the biggest transactions in South Africa’s digital economy.
On our radar: Will X’s two-year deal deliver value to South African publishers?
South Africa’s Competition Commission. Image Source: MyBroadband.
South Africa’s Competition Commission has reached a settlement with Elon Musk’s social media platform X (formerly Twitter), requiring it to support qualifying local news publishers through a two-year monetisation programme. X must introduce the programme within six months, with twice-yearly workshops on revenue tools, audience analytics, and content strategies.
Its AI arm, xAI, will separately train publishers twice a year on managing access to their content by AI chatbot Grok. But the deal stops short of guaranteeing direct payments. The Commission’s inquiry found that four local publishers earned a combined $914.25 from X’s creator revenue programme. The test now is whether the commitments translate into meaningful income and greater control over how AI uses local journalism.
