articles.title: Swiss startup coprod raises €5.45 million to solve “integration hell” in robotics and physical AI hardware
articles.text:
coprod, a Swiss robotics hardware startup building modular hardware components for robotics and physical AI applications, has raised €5.45 million ($6 million) in a pre-Seed funding round.
The round was co-led by Founderful and PROTOTYPE, with additional backing from General Catalyst, Pace Ventures, Tiny Supercomputer Investment Company, Kima Ventures, SDAC, Unruly Capital, and Venturekick. Angel investors also participated, including Thomas Wolf, founder of Hugging Face; the Dassault Family; Florent Perrichon; and other renowned angels.
“The robotics revolution is real and we will be able to rethink every industry because of it. coprod is fixing the biggest problem in hardware: integration hell. Robotics founders need a single standard for basic components and middleware that simply works and allows them to focus on the parts of their product that creates value to their customer as quickly as possible,” said Andreas Klinger, Investor at PROTOTYPE.
Founded in late 2024 by EPFL graduates Loïc Delineau, Vincent Nguyen, and Matthias Schuller, coprod wants to tackle one of the persistent challenges in the robotics industry: hardware compatibility. The trio began their journey by assembling a bipedal robot demonstrator in a garage in the Swiss Alps, using the project to prove the viability of their modular approach.
Its product portfolio centres on what it calls “co:products,” a family of compatible hardware modules comprising co:sense, co:act, co:power, and co:battery, all unified through the co:system platform. The platform combines all modules on a single real-time EtherCAT control plane, accessible via one API in C++ and Python. It also offers a front-end configuration tool to handle communication standardisation across components, preserving the real-time performance essential for safe and reliable robotic operation.
With its hardware compatibility platform, coprod is addressing a well-known problem in the industry known as “integration hell,” which often requires 2 to 3 years of combing through data sheets, debugging interfaces, and building bespoke software at times to get disparate components to work together. coprod claims its stack can accomplish the same development in a matter of months with only a small team of roboticists, at a cost of $5,000 to $25,000 per design iteration.
Its hardware stack is already in the field, and coprod’s components are powering several robots in the Swiss ecosystem, most notably the first student-built Swiss humanoid robot, created by the ETH Robotics Club, which took its first steps in Zurich just weeks ago.
“We believe that a robot with purpose-built hardware designed for a specific task will do that task faster, cheaper and more reliably than any general purpose robot ever could, regardless of which model runs on it. We see robotics as just another tool that humans should be able to leverage to improve their daily lives, this starts by empowering them to build those robots by abstracting away complexity, coprod is offering this fertile ground,” said Delineau, CEO and cofounder of coprod.
The fresh capital will be used to launch coprod’s first commercial line of components and build a full-stack hardware prototyping facility in Lausanne. Equipped with CNC lathes, mills, lasers, and electronic assembly and testing equipment, the workshop is designed to compress development cycles from two weeks down to 24 hours, while supporting the creation of detailed datasheets and digital-twin models for each component.
“Backing Loïc, Vincent and Matthias was a no-brainer – the combination of relentless drive, deep technical expertise and global ambition is second to none. With Founderful we back founder teams building global leaders from Switzerland,” added Alex Stöckl, General Partner at Founderful.
By the end of 2027, coprod plans to have its entire component line qualified, certified, and on the market. The company is planning large-scale production across facilities in Shenzhen and Texas, providing regionally resilient supply chains, while coprod’s HQ, core team, and R&D will remain in Switzerland. With specialised actuators, sensors, and control systems required for humanoid robotics applications slated to become a $28 billion market by 2030, according to McKinsey, coprod is targeting a market with substantial opportunity.

articles.title: Could you be Canada’s next top student entrepreneur?
articles.text:
Connor Kapahi was still completing his PhD when he set out to commercialize a medical device that could detect one of the leading causes of irreversible vision loss.
His company, Mandel Diagnostics, was developing a tool that could screen patients for early signs of macular degeneration in just two minutes. Between his academic research and the demands of building a company, Kapahi had plenty on his plate.
“Ultimately, we need to help young people experience that failure isn’t the opposite of success, it is often part of the process of getting to success.”
Catherine Fowler,
Enactus Canada
“I found out early on that working on a startup while finishing school didn’t mean I was splitting my time 50/50,” said Kapahi, who is CEO and Founder of Mandel Diagnostics. “It was more like one-third of my time on my PhD research, one-third on the startup, and one-third worrying that I wasn’t balancing the other two goals correctly.”
Kapahi said much of his anxiety stemmed from not knowing whether customers would actually pay for the device. According to research from RBC, nearly 60 percent of young Canadians say a fear of failure would stop them from starting a business.
For the last three decades, Enactus Canada has worked to make entrepreneurship more accessible to postsecondary students, and through its Student Entrepreneur National Competition the organization is encouraging more young founders to take a chance on themselves.
Making room for failure
Catherine Fowler, President and CEO of Enactus Canada, understands why young people might hesitate to pursue entrepreneurship. Even those with promising ideas or skills can find themselves overwhelmed by everything it takes to run a business.
“Suddenly you are navigating accounting, technology, human resources, sales, and long-term strategic planning,” Fowler said. “Each new challenge can feel like another opportunity to fail.”
Still, she believes that students should have opportunities to experiment with entrepreneurship while they still have access to resources and a community of support.
“The postsecondary years are a pivotal time in a young person’s life,” Fowler said. “Students are exploring their interests, considering their futures, and discovering what they are capable of achieving.”
Enactus Canada is a registered charity that supports postsecondary students through entrepreneurial education and experiential learning. Its Student Entrepreneur National Competition, now celebrating its 30th anniversary, gives full-time postsecondary students running their own businesses a chance to get advice from established entrepreneurs, make connections, and compete for funding.
According to Fowler, the competition also gives students a chance to confront their fear of failure and learn from it, rather than avoid it altogether.
“Ultimately, we need to help young people experience that failure isn’t the opposite of success, it is often part of the process of getting to success,” she added.
The competition follows a multi-stage process. An initial group of 30 entrepreneurs receives feedback on their applications, with 12 advancing to a video pitch round and three ultimately selected to share a live presentation at the national final.
Judges assess participants’ business models, market knowledge, traction, and growth potential, and provide feedback at each stage. Those who do not advance can return in subsequent years if they remain eligible.
The value of a good introduction
Kapahi’s involvement with the competition began when an Enactus representative saw him pitch at another event and encouraged him to apply. By then, Kapahi had already participated in several startup competitions, but he saw this as an opportunity to share the story of how he turned his research into a business while completing his studies.
He ultimately won the 2026 national title and its $10,000 prize, which has helped the company commit two of its eye-screening tools to medical missions serving patients both abroad and in remote Canadian communities. The devices will be used by optometrists providing eye care in underserved communities, allowing Mandel Diagnostics to see how its technology performs in challenging clinical environments.
Kapahi valued the connections he made through the competition. “You never know who you’ll meet or what doors they can open for you,” he said.
Having started Mandel Diagnostics in the Waterloo Region, where there is an established startup community, Kapahi knew the value of advice from other founders. He found a similar network through Enactus Canada.
“Their experience, advice, and their ability to make key introductions is an extremely valuable resource that will continue to guide Mandel Diagnostics forward,” he added.
Thirty years of student entrepreneurship
When the Student Entrepreneur National Competition launched in 1997, entrepreneurship was rarely taught in postsecondary institutions, according to Fowler, and students had few avenues to secure funding or get exposure.
The first national champion operated a retail soccer business. Last year, Diana Virgovicova won with Xatoms, which is developing advanced water purification technology with AI and quantum chemistry. Kapahi followed in 2026 with Mandel Diagnostics.
According to Fowler, the range of businesses represented over the years shows how new technologies have expanded the possibilities for student entrepreneurs, although she still sees familiar qualities in the founders who participate.
“At their core, they are still the same ambitious, resourceful, self-starting individuals who see opportunities where others see obstacles and are willing to take meaningful risks to turn their ideas into reality,” Fowler said.
Enactus Canada is accepting nominations for its next Student Entrepreneur National Competition until December 4. Eligible entrepreneurs must be full-time postsecondary students who own at least 25 percent of their businesses. Students can either nominate themselves or be nominated by someone else in as little as ten minutes.
Eligible nominees will be invited to submit full applications by January 10, 2027, with the top 30 announced on January 13. Three national finalists will receive an all-expenses-paid trip to Toronto to present their ventures to a live audience on April 28.
Fowler believes the most important step is getting young entrepreneurs to put themselves forward in the first place.
“Don’t let the application be the barrier,” she said. “You don’t need a perfect business plan or to have everything figured out. The experience itself, regardless of how far you advance, can help you become a stronger entrepreneur.”
Kapahi, for his part, encouraged aspiring founders to start by speaking with potential customers, understanding their problems, and determining whether there is demand for their solution.
“If you can find customers desperate for what you’re building and willing to pay for it, then do it,” Kapahi said. “Whether you win Enactus Student Entrepreneur of the Year or not, you’ll have a far stronger foundation for your business.”
PRESENTED BY
Know a student entrepreneur who deserves recognition, or ready to put yourself forward? Nominate yourself or someone you know for Enactus Canada’s Student Entrepreneur National Competition. Nominate now.
Featured image courtesy Enactus Canada.

articles.title: Nvidia reverses course and brings Jensen Huang back as CEO
articles.text:
In a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board said on Monday that it had reinstated Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, less than two weeks after he resigned following his admission of at least two extramarital affairs, one of which was with a woman whom the U.S. government suspects to be a Chinese spy.
The decision marks an extraordinary comeback for one of the tech industry’s most influential executives, whose abrupt departure raised questions about national security and the future of the world’s most valuable chipmaker. Notably, the U.S. government itself played a role in his return: Nvidia’s board said it consulted senior government officials before determining that Huang posed no national security risk.
Nvidia shares, which had already shot up in premarket trading, opened 30% higher. Nvidia shares were priced at $159.95 a share, up 27%, at 9:51 a.m. ET.
In the days since Huang resigned, President Donald Trump has repeatedly expressed his support for the ousted executive, who is now back at the helm of the AI chip giant. Trump said in a post on Truth Social that the board “made the correct and proper decision to return” Huang to the position, noting that the U.S. government has no reason to believe that Nvidia poses any risk to national security.
Trump also said the U.S. attorney general confirmed that the U.S. government doesn’t have any evidence that Huang engaged in any illegal activity.
A long list of high-profile tech executives were pushing the board — in social media posts and publicly aired interviews — to bring Huang back, including SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Atoms founder Travis Kalanick, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan — all of whom signed a petition pushing for reinstatement.
The company said the board’s unanimous decision followed a series of discussions and meetings with Huang, after which they were “satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia.”
Just a few days ago, the board had seemed immovable in its choice to push Huang out. During the company’s third-quarter earnings call, Nvidia board chair Harvey C. Jones said they didn’t intend to reinstate Huang. Nvidia had even retained executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to find a permanent replacement.
Jones, along with the rest of the board, now has a different view. In a prepared statement, Jones said the board believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of its stockholders, employees, partners, and customers.
“We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the company,” Jones said. “We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as Nvidia’s Chief Financial Officer.”
In a statement, Huang said he was honored to return to his role as the head of the company he co-founded in 1993.
“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said. “I want to thank the Nvidia Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading Nvidia during this period. I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support. Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.”
This story is developing...

articles.title: Why kill switches won’t contain AI incidents
articles.text:
Why kill switches won’t contain AI incidents
The kill switch is dead. Containment isn't.
When the UK government rejected Lord Clement-Jones' proposed "kill switch" amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, the official line was blunt: Britain cannot simply turn AI off, and blocking access to models domestically would not stop them being built or misused elsewhere.
The proposal is gone. What has not replaced it is the question it was trying to answer: what actually happens when an AI tool misbehaves inside a real organization?
Field Chief Data & AI Officer for EMEA at ThoughtSpot.
For boardrooms watching this debate from the outside, the instinct is understandable. A single switch, flipped by a minister or a CISO, feels like a clean answer to a messy problem. It is also the wrong model entirely for how modern enterprise technology works.
Why there is no switch to flip
Most large organizations are not running "an AI." They are running thousands of models, APIs, agents and third-party services stitched together across hyperscalers, SaaS vendors and internal pipelines. Shutting all of that down to stop one agent behaving badly would also halt productivity across the business and everything else that happens to share the same IT infrastructure. At that point, the cure causes more damage than the incident it was meant to contain.
This is not a theoretical concern. Anthropic's own disclosures this year are a useful case study, precisely because they show how containment failures actually happen in practice. In its July report on cybersecurity evaluation incidents, later expanded in September, the company found that a handful of its models had reached live, real-world systems during testing after a misconfiguration left supposedly isolated evaluation environments connected to the open internet.
The models had been told explicitly that they were operating in a simulation. They were not. Separately, researchers attributed a flood of more than 2,000 malicious packages uploaded to the RubyGems registry in May to an autonomous OpenAI agent swarm, months before a related incident at Hugging Face became public.
Neither case involved a model "going rogue" in the dramatic sense the kill switch debate conjures. Both were failures of configuration, network monitoring and boundary-setting in systems that organizations had not fully mapped. No emergency shutdown power would have prevented either. What would have helped is the much less cinematic work of knowing exactly which credentials, tokens and network paths an agent could reach, and being able to revoke access to a specific system without touching anything else.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
This, in effect, is already the approach written into EU regulation. Article 55 of the EU AI Act requires providers of general-purpose models with systemic risk to assess and mitigate risks on an ongoing basis and to maintain adequate cybersecurity protection for the model and its infrastructure, with serious incidents reported promptly. There is no mention of a red button. The obligation is continuous testing, monitoring and the ability to respond, not a single dramatic intervention.
Sovereignty is not a postcode
A parallel version of this instinct shows up in data sovereignty decisions. A European company moving its AI workloads into a data center in Frankfurt, for instance, can reasonably assume it has solved its sovereignty problem. Often it hasn't. The application sitting on that infrastructure may still call a foundation model hosted elsewhere, rely on identity and monitoring services operated across several jurisdictions, and depend on a hyperscaler with global infrastructure. The server's location tells you very little about where the data actually flows or who controls the pieces in between.
Most enterprises have limited visibility into this supply chain: the SaaS tools, APIs, data pipelines, identity providers, models and subcontractors that sit behind a single application. That has always been true. AI increases the consequences of not knowing, because the systems now act with more autonomy and touch more of the stack.
Sovereignty genuinely matters for organizations selling into defense, healthcare or government, where guaranteed data boundaries can be a commercial differentiator. But treating every component of a technology estate as something that must be made fully sovereign is usually not realistic. The more useful question is narrower: which dependencies are critical, who controls them, and what happens if they become unavailable or untrusted.
What's actually worth building
None of this is dramatic. It does not resolve into a single policy announcement or a board slide with a big red button on it. But two capabilities consistently separate organizations that contain an AI incident from those that don't.
The first is containment: the ability to revoke an agent's credentials, API keys and access to a specific database or environment without shutting down the rest of the business. The second is visibility: a working map of which models, APIs and third-party dependencies actually sit behind the applications an organization runs, so that "critical" isn't a guess made after something has already gone wrong.
The UK government was right that AI cannot simply be switched off. The more useful lesson from this year's incidents is that very few organizations currently know enough about their own systems to contain a problem quickly even if they wanted to. That is the gap worth closing, long before anyone reaches for a switch that was never going to exist.

articles.title: AI Changes What Chip Engineers Need To Learn
articles.text:
AI is automating routine design tasks, shifting engineering education toward architecture, specifications, verification, and the ability to evaluate results.
Key Takeaways:
- While it remains necessary to teach fundamentals, it becomes less important to be able to use them because tools will do that.
- AI can create lots of possible solutions, but it takes real skill to pick the right one. How do people productively select the best answer?
- AI is adding pressure on verification methodologies to ensure slop does not enter into the flow.
Experts At The Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss how AI is changing design and verification, and how that impacts engineering school curricula, with Chuck Alpert, fellow at Cadence; Thomas Andersen, vice president of AI and ML at Synopsys; Simon Davidmann, AI and EDA researcher at University of Southampton; Nagesh Gupta, CEO of llmda.ai; Dave Kelf, CEO of Breker Verification Systems; and Kexun Zhang, co-founder and head of research at ChipAgents. What follows are excerpts of that discussion. To view part one of this discussion, click here.
Clockwise from top left: Southampton University’s Davidmann; Breker’s Kelf; Synopsys’ Andersen; ChipAgents’ Kexun; llmda’s Gupta; and Cadence’s Alpert.
SE: There is a finite amount that students can learn in the three or four years when they’re in college. What skill set do they require, and what do they stop learning in order to start taking on the new stuff that we expect them to have?
Zhang: We should still be learning the fundamentals, but a lot of the practical skills and tricks can be excluded from their textbooks and from the lectures. For example, people used to put a lot of emphasis on the ability to use logarithmic tables for big calculations, and they needed to know lots of tricks to do integrals. But now people just learn about the principles. They still need to learn the fundamentals in order to understand how these tools work, and in order to know what’s going wrong, if it goes wrong. But a lot of the very specific tricks that were intended for them to do this are no longer required. The time saved from these tricks can be used to teach higher-level abstractions.
Davidmann: It gets better than that. I remember learning how to program and how difficult the syntax was. It would take you a long time to draw a graph, for example. Now you’ve got Python, which can draw graphs. While you still need to learn the skills of programming, you don’t need to do all the development and debugging because you can generate a lot of it. You need to see the structure, and you need to define the architecture of programs and how to verify the program and test it, but you don’t do a lot of the individual coding. You won’t have to go through the practical pain of doing a lot of it because AI will do it. In the same way, when you’re doing chip architecture, you need to know about gates, but you don’t have to hand-wire up a schematic in an editor. You write some RTL, but you don’t need to know what’s down there. The education will get more abstract, as well. We need to know the fundamentals, but you’ll do less practical use of fundamentals because the tool will do it. In the research I’m doing. I started off writing lots of programs in Python at the lowest level. I don’t intend to ever do that again because I can just generate it. I set the file type I want, the structure I want, and just tell it to create the program. Then I test it. I don’t write the lines of Python anymore. I control tools to build it for me. They will learn different things, which makes them much more productive.
Alpert: Having a good curriculum is challenging. You’re teaching computer science, and you might say you have one or two weeks to do this computer science assignment, and if you use vibe coding, you can do it in an hour or two. You just have to make the assignment 10, 20 times more complex. You can build more complex systems. Teaching undergrads to do that would be fantastic.
Davidmann: At the university, one of the professors who is involved with EDA technology and chip design is setting up the curriculum for next year. They will build a RISC-V processor. We used to teach people Verilog, and the assignment would be to add a couple of Fibonacci series. There’s a company in EDA that created a RISC-V processor in 40 hours that runs Linux, completely vibe-coded. That’s the type of project they need to be doing. It’s going to be much more abstract, much higher level. Imagine a graduate who learns how to build processors. They will be in demand for a company that wants to build semiconductors. They are going to get better experience, which the industry needs, and that’s what good university courses should be able to create.
Kelf: It sounds like the expertise they’re going to have to learn is how to write good specifications that you can feed into AI.
Davidmann: It’s how to use AI efficiently, and that’s part of the challenge. The academics are challenged by this. AI is racing so fast, and the requirements that people have in industry are stressing out academics.
Alpert: When you think about verification, the whole vision of our AI system is that all you need is a good spec, and you can create all the verification collateral. You can generate the RTL. All you need is a great spec. So then the job becomes writing good specs. That’s part of it. But a big part is understanding what AI did. How do you make sure you didn’t get slop? How do you make sure you have a quality design? That’s going to be the other half of the equation.
Andersen: When something goes wrong, how do you debug it? Was it a problem in your spec? Was it a problem in the system? That is another challenge.
Davidmann: How do you know it’s got a bug in it? And then, how do you get rid of it?
Alpert: Many people in the semiconductor industry are tool jockeys. But a place-and-route person is not really doing place-and-route. They’re a tool jockey. In some sense, everybody becomes a tool jockey where they used to do it before. AI is just a tool.
Kelf: You always have verification loops. Now there’s going to be this extra verification loop up to the spec that will be used to test the output of the AI. That would be an interesting verification problem.
Zhang: The challenge is that, unlike many other tools, AI is non-deterministic. And it is more deceptive, because when it hallucinates, it sounds perfectly fine. That really adds more workload to this extra verification loop. You wouldn’t expect your traditional tools to lie to you. You wouldn’t expect your traditional tools to find a very clever way to go around your checks and your scripts and your verification suite, and give you an answer that looks perfectly fine. The reward hacking ability of AI systems is something that is not well understood, and that is a very challenging aspect of having this extra verification loop. That is also why some people — especially in domains where people did not use formal verification before, such as in a lot of software development — are now starting to realize the importance of a more rigorous way of doing verification, especially in a formal way.
Davidmann: In hardware, verification is so important because we cannot afford a failure in the chip. Software is easier to modify later. One of the key things about constrained random is that every time you run it, with a different seed, you get completely different types of tests. RTL design is going to be like that if you use Gen AI. You’re going to get a different design every time. You need repeatability to understand it. If you’re trying to find a bug, you don’t want the bug to disappear the next time you run it, and the next time it comes back because of its probabilistic nature. The specification is absolutely going to be fundamentally important, but so are verification methodologies. It’s these types of things that we need to impart on the graduates. We need to try and explain to them, educate them, about the methodologies that they need to use to get the most out of these new tools. It’s just a different type of apprenticeship. The tools are more powerful now, and they go off in different directions, so you need more understanding. It’s just a new problem for us to solve. It’s not radically different from what we did before. It’s just more abstract, maybe a bit weirder, and it’s just technology to adopt.
Gupta: There are going to be new engineering roles. AI is creating so much slop, and you’ve got to understand what it has created and when it is causing a problem. Dealing with AI slop is going to be a new career, and there is probably a significant opportunity from that perspective.
Andersen: If you look back at the history of innovations, every time you up-level something, it changes. The one thing that’s a little different with the recent AI technologies is that it is directly doing things that humans are good at, like reasoning based on seeing something, or certain data. In the past, it was more about computational things. For example, people used to be polygon pushers, or people used to write logic circuits by hand. These are not tasks that humans are naturally good at. A computational algorithm that solves wire length or chip placement will always outperform a human in the same way that a calculator outperforms me any day. But when it comes to complex reasoning tasks, that used to be the domain of the human brain. That is now being challenged. This is a different shift compared to innovations that happened before.
SE: It has been said that AI cannot do the job of a senior engineer because it doesn’t have the experience or the type of knowledge and skills required to do those tasks. So how can a junior engineer be expected to do those things, even with the help of AI?
Davidmann: You need the experience to be able to specify things, verify them, and understand them. AI can do manual things, and it can help you find issues, but it can’t really help you in the specification of what you’re trying to achieve. It doesn’t have the ability to deal with the system bits. It can only handle individual tasks. That’s why you have architects at each level. There are decisions to be made, and it’s not just grunt work. It’s intellectual work, which I’m not sure AI is close to yet.
Kelf: In fact, it does worse. You need the experience to know if the AI is putting out crap or something sensible. This is a very real problem when you’re trying to get AI to do basic tasks. It will put out something that looks pretty good initially, and then you find it’s completely hopeless. There’s something wrong with it, and a junior engineer might just rely on that, whereas a senior engineer will know it doesn’t look right. That experience is really key.
Zhang: There is this term called the verification gap, or the verification dilemma in the AI world, because AI can generate so many answers to the same question so fast. The bottleneck of getting the solution to these questions is no longer writing down the answers. It is picking one answer — one correct and good answer — from 10,000 different answers. That is something that is different in terms of the skills required. It requires experience. It requires taste. It requires people to be able to define problems instead of just solving the problems defined by other people. Then the question becomes, ‘How do you even teach taste?’ I feel like a lot of taste comes from experience, comes from working in the industry for decades and gradually learning what’s good and what’s bad. Now that the grunt work can be done by AI, it seems that it’s important for people to accelerate that process instead of having people make mistakes — learning from the mistakes for decades — and then gradually gaining taste. Is there any way that people can be taught? Is there any way that we can cultivate this taste, which seems to be a more important ability in the AI age, now that picking what’s important to solve, picking the correct answer becomes the bottleneck? In some industries there are programs that try to teach taste, or that try to give people a fuller picture at a higher level, so that they have the ability to distinguish, but they don’t have the ability to carry out the actual work.
Gupta: That’s a very good point. The whole aspect of learning taste comes from experience. The question to ask is, what happens five years from now when you’ve lost that gap. You have all this experience that people have gained, so they understand how to do some of these things. Today, if you start off doing all of this with AI, you create a gap, and maybe AI will catch up, and it’ll understand the taste part of it. If you look at what happened in our industry 20 years ago, there was a lot of growth in other countries. We became distributed geographically. There was a lot of growth compared to the U.S. in a lot of other geographies, and in my perspective, what that has created is a void in experienced middle management in the industry. This may be a similar impact 5 years, 10 years from now. You lose that experience part of it.
Alpert: If you go back in time, EDA has always been about productivity. Designers used to be polygon pushers before place-and-route was automated. They looked at ways to organize cells to minimize the wire length. Nobody does that anymore. Now, physical design engineers are really tool jockeys. They run the PnR tools, and they are experts on how to debug them, how to read the logs, how to change the constraints. AI will take over some of that, and the engineers can move up to a higher level. Maybe the new task is how to partition blocks. The idea is that whenever EDA is able to build a new layer of abstraction, we raise people’s ability to design at a higher level. And AI is going to do exactly that. That’s a good thing. People have less grunt work, and they can do more thinking. But the problem becomes, ‘How do your junior engineers raise to that level because they don’t have the experience?’ That’s going to be a problem. As an industry we will have to figure that out, but it will happen.
The panel raises an important question about how AI will reshape semiconductor engineering and the skills future engineers will need. I see tremendous opportunity for AI to accelerate design-space exploration, RTL development, verification, debugging, and PPA optimization, enabling engineers to explore more alternatives and tackle increasingly complex designs. But the real opportunity should extend beyond productivity to accelerating the development of engineering expertise itself. Fundamental knowledge and sound engineering judgment are built through understanding design tradeoffs, investigating failures, and confronting real implementation constraints. As AI automates more of these activities, we need to ensure that engineers, particularly those early in their careers, remain actively engaged in understanding why designs work, why they fail, and what makes one solution better than another. The goal should not simply be to automate engineering tasks (which is important), but to use AI to develop more capable engineers who can make better architectural and implementation decisions.

articles.title: AI Agents Are Creating a Shared Responsibility Gap
articles.text:
Frontier AI labs are very clear about their responsibilities: making the model more robust, better guarded, and harder to hijack. They are also clear about what they can’t do, which is understand the business context of an action. An agent deleting files from Google Drive could be malicious or perfectly normal. They can't tell.
That raises questions about the shared responsibility model for Agentic AI. In cloud security, there is a clear separation of responsibilities between cloud vendors and their customers. If you copy data from AWS into SFDC, each vendor is responsible for the data's infrastructure security while they have it, but the customer is responsible for the action.
The AWS Shared Responsibility Model is a classic example.
The separation isn’t nearly as clean for AI agents. Agents act as intermediaries between you and the request, and that intermediary isn't deterministic by nature. It sends authenticated, authorized requests that can be compromised or rogue.
The first scenario is somewhat clear and goes back to what the AI labs try to prevent: a rogue agent has either misunderstood something or acted in a way it shouldn’t. A human mistake, only not human and not necessarily a mistake.
Five organizations have published guidance on responsibility for AI agents: shared responsibility models from Microsoft, CSA and CoSAI, AWS's security guidance for AgentCore, and Anthropic's “Trustworthy agents in practice.” Only two assign ownership of an agent’s identity, and they split it differently. No one agrees on who is responsible for the agent's behavior.
A look at the existing approaches
The available guidance approaches responsibility from different angles. Some publications assign specific tasks to providers and customers; others describe security layers or broader stakeholder roles.
Together, they show why organizations need to determine who owns each agent, what permissions it has, and how it operates across the systems it uses.
| Company | Description | Focus | 
| Microsoft | Publishes an AI agent shared responsibility model with a matrix for IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS deployments. | The customer remains accountable for agent actions across all three models. Agent identity and delegated token management, along with per-action authorization checks, are customer responsibilities in IaaS and shared responsibilities in PaaS and SaaS. | 
| AWS | No agent-specific model, but AgentCore's security guidance applies AWS's general shared responsibility model. Closest match: the Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix and its NIST comment. | Builders bear final responsibility for the behavior and permissions of the systems they assemble. AWS recommends enforcing security through infrastructure-level controls outside the agent and discusses agent identity, credentials, and delegation. | 
| Anthropic | “Trustworthy agents in practice” describes four layers of an agent system: model, harness, tools, and environment. It does not provide a formal responsibility matrix. | Calls for defenses across all four layers and asks customers to consider which tools, permissions, and environments they give agents. In a separate NIST response, Anthropic identifies authentication and permissions across agent boundaries as an unresolved challenge. | 
| CSA | Agent Shared Security and Safety Responsibility Model (Agent 3SRM) maps the CSA AI Controls Matrix to a ten-layer agent architecture. | Its public summary introduces an Agent Owner with ultimate, non-delegable accountability for agent actions and addresses accountability for sub-agent delegation. The summary does not detail its identity and authorization assignments. | 
| CoSAI | The AI Shared Responsibility Framework V1.0 uses five layers, responsibility matrices, and autonomy levels L0 to L5. | Its general principle calls for one accountable party per component, and its identity and access management matrix assigns accountability to the end user or organization. Its autonomy guidance also describes shared accountability between the agentic provider and application developer at L4 to L5, creating an apparent tension with that principle. | 
Let's say it goes wrong
Consider a coding agent that reads a support ticket through an MCP server. That ticket contains malicious instructions that cause the agent to push a change to GitHub using the developer's token.
It isn't a contrived case. In the organizations Token monitors, 60% of Claude Code and Desktop agents called two or more outside vendors, and 47% called three or more, in the span of one month.
Now to the million-dollar question: who's responsible for catching the malicious push and stopping it?
The Agentic Universe from Token Security
Nobody has ever secured AI agents.
Learn how security teams at Roblox, Amex, and more give each agent an owner, narrow its access, and cut it off fast, then see how Token Security does it in a live demo.
Explore the playbooks now
Could it be the harness?
The software that runs the agent has the most visibility: it knows where the instructions were (albeit not why they were there) and the command about to run.
Claude Code, for example, checks both. A server-side probe "scans incoming tool results and flags suspicious content before Claude reads it." In auto mode, now the starting mode for interactive sessions, a separate classifier blocks actions that appear "driven by hostile content Claude read."
OpenAI, Cursor, and GitHub each have their own versions of approval prompts, automated reviewers, network limits, and sandboxes.
This capability doesn't come with responsibility, though. Harnesses put that squarely on the user's shoulders, both within the interface and in their terms.
Will the MCP catch it?
The poisoned ticket came in over MCP, a protocol built for model clients. You might expect it to carry some of the load, because it's a door purpose-made for agents. At least conceptually, it could denote expanded responsibility for the people who built this door.
The MCP spec hands the load back to the client. Clients SHOULD validate tool results before passing them to the model, and "there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations," it says.
The server's duties involve tokens, inputs, access controls, and rate limits.
And so, a typical MCP server will check who sent a request, not whether it should have been sent.
It all goes back to the MCP spec, which neither uses the term "prompt injection" nor provides the server with any verified information about its caller; client information is "self-reported." It says outright that "MCP itself cannot enforce these security principles at the protocol level."
Atlassian, for its part, calls the use of MCP clients with its products "a customer-elected action."
Could GitHub be the solution?
The push reaches GitHub with a valid token. Unless an admin has set up a branch protection rule for main, nothing stops it, and by default, those rules "don't apply to people with admin permissions to the repository."
GitHub's audit log includes an agent marker, actor_is_agent, for agents that run on GitHub. Nothing in the docs says it marks a local agent's push, though. And the terms are the same as everyone's: "You are responsible for all content posted and activity that occurs under your Account."
Do agent identities close the gap?
In an ideal scenario, every agent has its own identity, which should carry narrower, shorter-lived access.
Microsoft, for example, gives agents identities of their own: a Microsoft Entra agent identity is a service principal in your Entra tenant. Microsoft's framework also marks per-action authorization as shared.
But when an agent acts on behalf of a user, Microsoft's documentation says "risky activity is attributed to the user." A Conditional Access policy aimed at an agent identity "doesn't cover agent requests made on behalf of the user."
And that's the story in a nutshell, within one vendor. Even if the framework points to shared responsibility, the product attributes the risk to the user when it's actually time to act.
You share the responsibility
That leaves you. And it's probably going to remain the norm. While platforms could, in theory, do more, agents are considered extensions of our will, even though they often have a “will” of their own.
It's a novel scenario, and the only choice is to look at the risk honestly and decide how much of it we're willing to accept. And even that is easier said than done because you can't see the agent as a single thing.
The harness has its telemetry, Atlassian has its MCP log, and GitHub has the developer's push. Coding agents like this one run under the developer's credentials by default, so their actions appear to be the developer's.
No vendor in this chain sees the whole agent:
- The harness sees the instruction
- The MCP server sees a token
- GitHub sees a developer pushing code
Only the identity the agent uses crosses all three. That makes it the one place where a single owner can set scope, expiry, and revocation. Branch protection and allowlists help, but identity ties them together.
What to do about it
Ideally, you treat the agent as one identity, whatever number of vendors it touches:
- Inventory per agent, across vendors. For each agent, list credentials.
- Give agents identities of their own, scoped to the task and short-lived.
- Decide where your log trail for agentic decision-making and action lives.
- Turn on branch protection, read-only modes, tool allowlists, and everything else that can help.
- Build a revocation path and practice killing an agent's access across all vendors.
- Ask your vendors what they can show you about an agent that also acts elsewhere.
An organization cannot delegate accountability for an agent’s actions to a model provider or infer intent from an authenticated request. It can assign an owner, limit the agent’s access, connect its activity across systems, and test how to stop it.
Those decisions make agent adoption governable without assuming any single vendor can see the whole workflow.
If the responsibility is yours, it pays to be responsible.

articles.title: Réseau 4G : dans ces villes, le signal s’effondre dès que vous entrez chez vous
articles.text:
Ookla, une entreprise américaine spécialisée dans l’analyse et la mesure des performances des réseaux Internet et mobiles (à l’origine notamment de la plateforme Speedtest), a publié une étude sur la qualité de réception du signal 4G à l’intérieur des bâtiments à travers le monde. Pendant un an, l’entreprise a effectué des mesures dans plus de 100 villes et 60 pays. Mauvaise nouvelle : l’Europe figure parmi les mauvais élèves.
L’Europe à la traîne face à l’Asie de l’Est et au Moyen-Orient
Tout d’abord, commençons par les régions qui sortent en tête de cette étude : l’Asie de l’Est et le Moyen-Orient. À Séoul (Corée du Sud), Bangkok (Thaïlande) ou encore Dubaï, le signal 4G médian mesuré dans les bâtiments de ces villes atteint environ -88 dBm, contre -105 dBm à Naples (plus la valeur est proche de zéro, meilleure est la réception). À Séoul, seuls 2 % des bâtiments mesurés présentent un signal 4G faible, contre 50 % des bâtiments de Naples.
En effet, toujours selon l’étude d’Ookla, Naples serait la ville européenne où la réception du signal 4G à l’intérieur des bâtiments est la plus mauvaise. Environ 50 % des bâtiments de la ville afficheraient un signal inférieur à -105 dBm. Plus généralement, l’Europe semble particulièrement mal lotie : Genève (47 % de bâtiments concernés par une faible réception du signal 4G), Birmingham (45 %), Zurich (45 %), Rome (39 %) ou encore Lyon (32 %). Les grandes capitales européennes ne s’en sortent pas vraiment mieux : 34 % des bâtiments sont concernés à Londres, 33 % à Madrid et 31 % à Paris. Parmi les bons élèves européens, nous retrouvons : Helsinki (12 %), Oslo (11 %) et Budapest (10 %).
À noter que les grandes villes nord-américaines affichent également de mauvais résultats : Miami (40 % de bâtiments concernés par une faible réception du signal 4G), Vancouver (39 %), Seattle (39 %). En revanche, New York s’en sort relativement bien avec 25 % des bâtiments de la ville concernés.
Comment expliquer une telle disparité de réception à l’intérieur des bâtiments ?
Tout d’abord, les matériaux qui composent un bâtiment peuvent avoir un impact direct sur la qualité de la réception du signal 4G à l’intérieur de celui-ci. Le béton, la pierre, le métal ou encore les vitrages confectionnés pour l’isolation thermique peuvent par exemple sensiblement amoindrir le signal. À ce titre, les modèles de l’Union internationale des télécommunications, cités par Ookla, estiment que la traversée des murs extérieurs d’une construction fortement isolée peut entraîner une perte de signal allant jusqu’à 31 dB, contre 14 à 16 dB pour un bâtiment traditionnel.
Mais les matériaux qui composent un bâtiment n’expliquent pas à eux seuls un faible signal 4G. La fréquence utilisée par le réseau mobile joue également un rôle important. Les basses fréquences traversent plus facilement les murs, tandis que les hautes fréquences sont davantage freinées (mais offrent de meilleurs débits). Mais surtout, c’est la qualité du réseau extérieur qui explique une mauvaise réception du signal 4G. Selon Ookla, elle serait à l’origine de 85 % des écarts de réception observés à l’intérieur des bâtiments entre les différentes villes étudiées.
Dès lors, un bâtiment constitué de matériaux qui bloquent les ondes et situé dans une zone où la couverture mobile est médiocre recevra mal le signal 4G. Ookla rappelle tout de même qu’il existe des solutions pour améliorer la réception mobile à l’intérieur des bâtiments, comme l’installation de petites antennes-relais ou de systèmes d’antennes distribuées (DAS).

articles.title: Immense rebondissement : Jensen Huang redevient le patron de Nvidia
articles.text:
Dans un communiqué publié lundi 23 novembre, le conseil d’administration annonce avoir voté à l’unanimité le retour de Jensen Huang, avec effet immédiat. Le conseil explique s’être entretenu à plusieurs reprises avec Jensen Huang et se dit convaincu de sa « franchise » et de sa capacité à diriger l’entreprise. Surtout, il affirme avoir consulté « les plus hauts niveaux du gouvernement américain » et s’estime désormais certain que son retour ne présente aucun risque pour la sécurité nationale. Quelques heures auparavant, Donald Trump avait justement appelé sur Truth Social au retour de Jensen Huang, faisant monter la cote d’un retour sur les plateformes comme Polymarket.
Jensen Huang se dit « honoré » de revenir et assure aborder cette responsabilité « avec la plus grande humilité ». Harvey C. Jones conserve la présidence du conseil d’administration, créée après le départ du fondateur, et Colette Kress, CEO par intérim pendant 11 jours, redevient directrice financière. À Wall Street, l’annonce a provoqué une envolée de plus de 25 % de l’action Nvidia avant l’ouverture. Toute l’économie américaine pourrait en profiter.
Un revirement spectaculaire après 11 jours hors de Nvidia
Le retour de Jensen Huang contredit totalement la position du conseil d’administration de Nvidia, qui affirmait il y a six jours que l’option Jensen n’était plus sur la table.
Le 12 novembre, le fondateur de Nvidia avait démissionné après la révélation de deux relations extraconjugales, l’une avec Alice Huang, une dirigeante que les renseignements américains soupçonnent d’espionnage pour Pékin, l’autre avec une vice-présidente de Nvidia placée sous son autorité. Le 17 novembre, quelques heures après une lettre dans laquelle Jensen Huang se disait prêt à revenir, Harvey Jones affirmait lors de la présentation des résultats trimestriels que le conseil n’avait pas l’intention de le réintégrer.
Depuis, la pression ne fait que montrer. Outre l’effondrement de l’action, une pétition pour son retour a dépassé les 190 000 signatures et Donald Trump a publiquement appelé à rappeler Jensen Huang. Malgré un chiffre d’affaires record de 115,8 milliards de dollars au troisième trimestre, les actionnaires exigent le retour de l’homme qui a fondé Nvidia. L’entreprise a glissé au quatrième rang des capitalisations mondiales derrière Apple, Microsoft et Alphabet.
Les enquêtes continuent
L’annonce est une surprise côté justice : le procureur général de Californie a adressé une assignation à Nvidia le 19 novembre et le gendarme boursier américain, la SEC, enquête sur les pratiques comptables de Nvidia. Tout suggérait que Jensen Huang ne pourrait pas revenir tant que la justice enquêtait sur ses actions.
Le retour de Jensen Huang ne referme pas le dossier. Le conseil d’administration précise que l’enquête indépendante sur la tentative d’espionnage étranger dont il aurait été la cible « ira jusqu’à son terme » et Jensen Huang s’engage à y coopérer. Nvidia promet aussi de continuer à coopérer avec les enquêtes gouvernementales en cours, qu’il s’agisse de la justice américaine, qui s’intéresse aux soupçons de contrebande de puces vers la Chine visant Megaspeed, ou de la SEC.

articles.title: Plex a trouvé le moyen de rendre ses utilisateurs encore plus furieux
articles.text:
Plex a annoncé le 20 novembre qu’il ne récupérerait plus les données de TheTVDB à partir du 3 décembre 2026, faute d’accord avec l’entreprise qui gère cette base. Le service conseille de passer à TMDB, mais son intégration actuelle ne gère pas les ordres d’épisodes alternatifs.
Dans Plex, les titres d’épisodes, les résumés et les visuels de vos séries viennent de bases de données communautaires, ce qui évite de tout renseigner à la main. TheTVDB en faisait partie, et sa disparition ne passe pas auprès des utilisateurs.
Les fiches déjà enregistrées restent, les nouveautés ne suivront plus
Rien ne change pour les bibliothèques existantes. Les réglages, les séries et les métadonnées déjà enregistrées restent telles quelles. Pour une série terminée, cela ne pose donc pas de problème puisque la fiche est complète. En revanche, pour une série en cours qui s’appuie sur TheTVDB, les nouveaux épisodes et saisons ne s’afficheront plus. Plex explique que la plateforme ira chercher ces informations auprès de ses autres sources, une solution potentiellement bancale. Quant à l’ancien agent TheTVDB, déconseillé depuis plusieurs années, il ne reconnaîtra plus les nouveaux contenus.
Le vrai problème concerne l’ordre des épisodes, c’est-à-dire la façon dont une série est découpée et numérotée. TheTVDB propose par exemple l’ordre DVD, qui suit la séquence des éditions physiques, et l’ordre absolu, qui numérote les épisodes à la suite, sans saisons. Ils servent surtout aux séries dont les épisodes n’ont pas été numérotés dans l’ordre de diffusion. L’intégration TMDB de Plex ne les gère pas aujourd’hui, et le passage risque de brouiller le classement de certaines bibliothèques.
Plex promet de prendre en charge les “groupes d’épisodes” de TMDB, qui couvriront ces ordres alternatifs, sans toutefois donner de date. En attendant, l’équipe conseille de laisser sur TheTVDB les séries concernées et leurs métadonnées resteront affichées, sans nouvelles mises à jour. Pour les autres, il faut modifier la bibliothèque, ouvrir l’onglet Avancé et choisir “The Movie Database” dans l’ordre des épisodes (Episode ordering). Le réglage d’une série l’emporte sur celui de la bibliothèque : il faut donc vérifier les deux.
Plex dit ne pas avoir trouvé de terrain d’entente avec le propriétaire de TheTVDB, sans préciser pourquoi. Il présente TMDB, portée par une communauté de contributeurs active, comme une base solide pour les séries. Il n’empêche que ces derniers temps les utilisateurs de Plex ont de quoi être agacés. En octobre, nous rapportions que des pirates détournaient des serveurs Plex non mis à jour pour miner des cryptomonnaies et relayer du trafic Internet. Mais surtout, en juillet dernier, l’entreprise a triplé le tarif du Plex Pass à vie, de 215 à 645 euros.
- Serveur entièrement auto-hébergé
- Clients web, mobiles et TV
- Droits utilisateurs détaillés

articles.title: « Directement et indirectement » : comment Donald Trump a obtenu le retour de Jensen Huang à la tête de Nvidia
articles.text:
Dimanche soir, Donald Trump publie un message sur Truth Social : il y souhaite que le conseil d’administration de Nvidia réembauche Jensen Huang, estimant qu’il s’agit de la meilleure décision pour l’entreprise comme pour les États-Unis. Dans la foulée, les administrateurs se réunissent et votent le rappel du dirigeant à l’unanimité.
Lundi, le groupe officialise ainsi que Jensen Huang revient à sa tête, onze jours après sa démission. Selon le média Semafor, le président américain a même pris part par téléphone à cette réunion pour plaider sa cause, un scénario que la Maison-Blanche ne dément pas : son directeur de la communication, Steven Cheung, affirme que Donald Trump a été « totalement impliqué », avant d’ajouter : « Nous devons protéger nos génies ».
    Pour aller plus loin
La vraie raison derrière la chute du patron de Nvidia : la liaison était le prétexte, la Chine est le champ de bataille
            
Le chef de l’État assume lui-même cette manœuvre. Interrogé sur la chaîne CNBC, Donald Trump explique avoir échangé avec le conseil « directement et indirectement » et lui avoir fourni des assurances en matière de sécurité nationale, ajoutant qu’il ne pense pas que les administrateurs auraient agi sans son intervention.
    Pour aller plus loin
Jensen Huang victime d’un coup monté ? Lobbying d’Anthropic, IA ouverte et faucons anti-Chine 
            
S’il refuse de confirmer sa participation directe à la séance, il précise y avoir été « représenté », tandis que le communiqué de Nvidia invoque les avis de « hauts responsables du gouvernement américain » pour justifier sa décision. Le contraste est saisissant avec la ligne tenue six jours plus tôt, lorsque le président du conseil, Harvey Jones, excluait publiquement tout retour.
    Pour aller plus loin
Jensen Huang revient à la tête de Nvidia, onze jours après son départ
            
Une décision fondée sur la parole présidentielle
Cette volte-face soulève une question centrale : sur quelles garanties juridiques repose le revirement de Nvidia ? L’audit interne consacré aux liens de Jensen Huang avec Alice Huang n’est pas achevé, le gendarme boursier (la SEC) examine toujours la comptabilité du groupe et le ministère de la Justice poursuit son enquête pénale autour de Megaspeed.
Donald Trump assure pourtant que le dirigeant n’a « rien fait de mal » et qu’il ne saurait être tenu automatiquement responsable si des puces ont transité vers la Chine. Son propre secrétaire au Trésor, Scott Bessent, qui exigeait encore le 15 novembre un patron venu de l’extérieur, s’en est sorti dimanche d’une pirouette en affirmant que Jensen Huang était désormais « à l’extérieur maintenant », tout en maintenant son ultimatum au 25 novembre pour que Nvidia s’explique sur d’éventuelles sociétés écrans.
À Wall Street, les investisseurs ont immédiatement salué l’annonce avec un bond d’environ 33 % de l’action à l’ouverture, une réaction boursière dont Donald Trump a reconnu sur CNBC qu’elle avait pesé dans sa réflexion. Selon le Washington Post, le président détenait d’ailleurs fin août entre 13 et 62 millions de dollars d’actions Nvidia, un élément qui s’ajoute aux dynamiques déjà à l’œuvre entre les trois administrateurs déjà favorables à son retour et l’appel à une « deuxième chance » lancé vendredi par Donald Trump.
    Pour aller plus loin
« J’adorerais le voir revenir » : Donald Trump pousse Nvidia à reprendre Jensen Huang
            
Des critiques jusque dans le camp républicain
Fait notable, plusieurs réserves majeures émanent d’élus du propre parti du président. Le sénateur républicain John Cornyn a ainsi réagi par une interrogation lapidaire : « Aucun risque pour la sécurité nationale ? Sur quelle base ? ».
De son côté, le représentant républicain Don Bacon estime que Jensen Huang a été « compromis et exploité » par une espionne chinoise et juge que Nvidia aurait dû ignorer le souhait « inexplicable » de l’administration de le sauver. Dans le camp démocrate, la sénatrice Elizabeth Warren, appelée à présider la commission bancaire du Sénat dès janvier, dénonce une décision imprudente, tandis que Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, spécialiste de la gouvernance à l’université Yale, réclame la démission de l’ensemble du conseil d’administration.
Un calendrier politique et judiciaire très chargé
Le calendrier politique et judiciaire s’annonce chargé dès cette semaine. Nvidia doit remettre ses réponses à Scott Bessent d’ici mercredi, avant que Jensen Huang ne passe le 1er décembre un entretien à huis clos devant trois commissions de la Chambre des représentants, suivi d’une audition publique au Sénat.
D’après Semafor, sa réintégration bouscule déjà les travaux du Congrès, qui entend déterminer qui a autorisé les expéditions de puces vers la Chine. Vous pouvez suivre chaque développement dans notre live consacré à l’affaire, où nous détaillons également les conditions du retour de Jensen Huang.
En principe, un conseil d’administration a pour mandat de défendre les intérêts des actionnaires plutôt que d’exécuter les souhaits de l’exécutif. Chez Nvidia, cette frontière apparaît désormais brouillée, ce qui crée un précédent institutionnel qui pourrait peser bien plus durablement que le scandale lui-même.

articles.title: Accelerating Direct Sparse Solvers for Computational Engineering with NVIDIA cuDSS 1.0
articles.text:
Sparse linear systems are at the core of nearly every engineering and scientific simulation, from structural mechanics and computational fluid dynamics to circuit simulation and power grid analysis. As problem sizes and complexity grow, and accuracy needs tighten, developers need a direct solver that scales on GPUs without giving up the robustness that production simulations depend on.
The NVIDIA GPU-accelerated cuDSS library is designed to solve large sparse linear systems for engineering and scientific simulations. The general availability of cuDSS marked a major milestone, making it a production-ready library that developers and software vendors can confidently deploy in commercial applications.
This post walks you through how the cuDSS 1.0 release can help you with your applications. Specifically, it explains where industry-leading performance gains can be realized on real-world workloads, how the new pivoting and matching defaults improve accuracy on difficult symmetric indefinite systems, and how system-level optimization with intelligent use of GPU and CPU resources together enable solving problems at scale.
Enabling best performance for key computational engineering applications
Benchmark matrices for cuDSS were selected from key semiconductor design, manufacturing, and computer-aided engineering workflows, including circuit simulation, TCAD, thermal, structural, electromagnetic, and fluid dynamics. They span a wide range of sparsity patterns, conditioning, and scaling behavior.
Figures 1-3 show cuDSS 1.0 geometric-mean speedups on these real-world problems of 2.5x for analysis (reordering and symbolic factorization) (Figure 1), 5.9x for numerical factorization (Figure 2), and 151x for triangular solve (Figure 3). In practice, applications typically combine all three phases, so overall speedup depends on each phase’s relative contribution.
Benchmark configuration: cuDSS 1.0 speedup against Intel MKL version 2026.1.0; GPU: NVIDIA B200 (192 GB HBM3e); CPU: INTEL XEON PLATINUM 8570. The benchmark result reflects cuDSS performance relative to Intel MKL on a given matrix. The benchmark is not a comparison across the vendor matrices themselves.
cuDSS performance has steadily improved over releases for a variety of workloads, including superpanels in factorization (v0.4.0), multithreaded analysis (v0.5.0), tuned solve-phase kernels (v0.8.0), and targeted performance optimizations (v1.0). Figures 4 and 5 show speedups relative to v0.3.0 through v1.0 for two matrices of significantly different sizes and structures. Developers building on cuDSS get these gains just by upgrading, with no changes to their application code. These improvements spanning across the different solve phases enable applications to be run faster from end to end and take on larger, more complex sparse problems.
Enhancing accuracy for symmetric matrices
Many of the numerically challenging sparse systems are symmetric indefinite. They arise in optimal power flow, mixed finite element discretizations of fluid flow and porous media, PDE-constrained optimization, and interior mode computation for structural problems.
cuDSS now offers symmetry-preserving matching and scaling and Bunch-Kaufman pivoting, both enabled by default for symmetric systems. Matching and scaling use HSL MC64, from the HSL collection of Fortran codes for large-scale scientific computation. For more information, refer to The HSL Mathematical Software Library.
Prior to cuDSS 1.0, matching was off by default because it did not preserve symmetry, which hurt memory and performance. Matching now preserves symmetry and is on by default, improving accuracy in many cases. It can add overhead during analysis and later stages if it causes additional fill-in. To restore the previous nonsymmetric behavior, set CUDSS_CONFIG_FORCE_NONSYMMETRIC_MATCHING.
For symmetric indefinite matrices, diagonal-only pivoting preserves symmetry but can cause unrecoverable accuracy loss when diagonal elements are small. Saddle-point and KKT matrices are the canonical examples. Previously, cuDSS used diagonal pivoting with perturbation of small pivots, which led to accuracy loss for many saddle-point matrices.
Bunch-Kaufman pivoting fixes this by allowing 2×2 pivots, which keep the factorization stable while preserving symmetry. With CUDSS_PIVOT_BUNCH_KAUFMAN, cuDSS applies the local Bunch-Kaufman test to each column and chooses a 1×1 pivot, an interchanged 1×1 pivot, or a 2×2 block. The threshold can be overridden through CUDSS_CONFIG_PIVOT_THRESHOLD. Smaller values favor 1×1 pivots, which can give sparser factors at the cost of accuracy.
Bunch-Kaufman pairs effectively with symmetry-preserving matching: matching cycles are split into candidate 1×1/2×2 groups that reordering keeps adjacent, so the pivot search finds the 2×2 blocks it needs without breaking the fill-reducing ordering. CUDSS_PIVOT_AUTO now selects Bunch-Kaufman for symmetric/Hermitian indefinite matrices wherever it is supported, and otherwise falls back to diagonal pivoting.
Table 1 shows results of solving linear systems \(Ax = b\) with cuDSS 1.0 under two configurations:
- No matching (CUDSS_MATCHING_ALG_NONE) and diagonal pivoting (CUDSS_PIVOT_DIAGONAL)
- With matching and scaling (CUDSS_MATCHING_ALG_MAX_DIAG_PRODUCT), and Bunch-Kaufman pivoting (CUDSS_PIVOT_BUNCH_KAUFMAN)
The latter configuration is now the default configuration. In each case, the matrix \(A\) is from the SuiteSparse matrix collection, and the right hand side vector \(b\) is a corresponding vector of all ones. For each system considered, common measures of accuracy for linear system solvers are reported. With \(x\) representing the solution computed by cuDSS, Relative Residual is the typical 2-norm measurement:
\(\frac{\left\|b-Ax\right\|_2}{\left\|b\right\|_2}\)
while NRBE is the normwise relative backward error, again measured with respect to the 2-norm:
\(\frac{\left\|b-Ax\right\|_2}{\left\|A\right\|_F\left\|x\right\|_2+\left\|b\right\|_2}\)
Note that the NRBE computation uses the Frobenius norm of \(A\) because it is easy to compute for large, sparse \(A\). Each configuration also reports the number of perturbed 1×1 pivots, meaning pivots replaced by an appropriately signed pivot epsilon because they were too small to proceed. Perturbed pivots indicate accuracy loss in the factorization, caused by an insufficient pivoting strategy or poor matrix conditioning. To get their count, request CUDSS_DATA_NPIVOTS after the factorization phase. Learn more about configuring treatment of perturbed pivots in cuDSS. The results in Table 1 show significant improvement in factorization due to reduced perturbed pivots.
|  |  |  | No matching, diagonal |  |  | Matching, Bunch-Kaufman |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Matrix | n | nnz | Relative residual | NRBE | Perturbed pivots | Relative residual | NRBE | Perturbed pivots | 
| kkt_power | 2063494 | 12771361 | 3.6e+08 | 1.1e-13 | 48106 | 4.9e-05 | 1.4e-23 | 0 | 
| cont-300 | 180895 | 988195 | 9.3e+02 | 1.1e-08 | 42065 | 2.6e-08 | 3.2e-19 | 0 | 
| TSOPF_FS_b39_c30 | 120216 | 3121160 | 2.1e+03 | 3.4e-08 | 36941 | 1.6e-08 | 6.4e-18 | 0 | 
| c-big | 345241 | 2340859 | 1.8e-07 | 4.2e-11 | 0 | 4.3e-14 | 1.0e-17 | 0 | 
| c73-b | 169422 | 1279274 | 1.3e-04 | 1.5e-09 | 0 | 3.6e-13 | 4.0e-18 | 0 | 
Test configuration: cuDSS 1.0, CTK13, RTX PRO 1000 Blackwell, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS)
For these matrices, cuDSS is now up to 10 orders of magnitude more accurate in NRBE, and a stark reduction in perturbed pivots shows improved factorization quality.
cuDSS 1.0 also enables matching and scaling by default for nonsymmetric matrices, not just symmetric and Hermitian ones, with improvements here too. Table 2 shows SuiteSparse matrices that improve with matching enabled.
|  |  |  | No matching, diagonal |  |  | Matching, Bunch-Kaufman |  |  | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Matrix | n | nnz | Relative residual | NRBE | Perturbed pivots | Relative residual | NRBE | Perturbed pivots | 
| largebasis | 440020 | 5240084 | 5.4e+01 | 1.8e-06 | 139886 | 2.6e-12 | 3.3e-19 | 0 | 
| hvdc2 | 189860 | 1339638 | 1.2e+00 | 3.4e-09 | 13 | 1.0e-10 | 2.9e-19 | 0 | 
| TSOPF_RS_b39_c30 | 60098 | 1079986 | 3.7e+42 | 3.1e-04 | 11 | 2.4e-12 | 7.1e-20 | 0 | 
| conf6_0-8×8-20 | 49152 | 1916928 | 2.4e+101 | 4.6e-03 | 22958 | 1.5e-14 | 3.5e-17 | 0 | 
Test configuration: cuDSS 1.0, CTK13, RTX PRO 1000 Blackwell, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS)
While generally helpful, matching with scaling does not always help with improving accuracy specifically. In a few cases, it can result in a loss of accuracy. Matching in cuDSS can be disabled by setting the matching algorithm to CUDSS_MATCHING_ALG_NONE.
Hybrid execution paradigm: A solution for small and large problems
Hybrid memory mode reflects a core design philosophy of cuDSS: the GPU and CPU together are the compute platform. Factorization is particularly data hungry, generating a dense fill structure in the L and U factors that can have more non-zeros than the original sparse matrix. Modern server nodes pair an NVIDIA GPU with substantial CPU memory (often 512 GB to 2 TB of DRAM), and hybrid memory mode treats that memory as an extension of the device’s effective capacity.
cuDSS intelligently orchestrates data placement across GPU HBM and CPU DRAM, keeping the most compute-intensive portions of the factorization and solving kernels on the GPU while offloading data not immediately needed to CPU memory. As a result, engineers do not need to partition a simulation into smaller subdomains that fit on the GPU or use multiple GPUs. The full problem can be solved as a single system.
Reduced memory footprint
Figure 2 shows minimum memory requirements reduced by an average of 30% across a representative suite of large VLSI examples. Problems that previously required multiple GPUs can now be solved on a single NVIDIA H100, NVIDIA B200, or a single NVIDIA Vera Rubin, simplifying deployment and reducing compute cost.
In cuDSS, you can query the minimum required device memory for hybrid memory mode using cudssDataGet() with the CUDSS_DATA_HYBRID_DEVICE_MEMORY_MIN parameter:
cudssDataGet(cudssHandle, solverData, CUDSS_DATA_HYBRID_DEVICE_MEMORY_MIN, &minMemory, sizeof(size_t), NULL);
This should be called after the analysis phase. More broadly, you can also use CUDSS_DATA_MEMORY_ESTIMATES with cudssDataGet() to get a full breakdown in a single call. The returned array includes:
- [0] – permanent device memory
- [1] – peak device memory
- [4] – minimum device memory for hybrid mode
- [5] – maximum host (CPU) memory for hybrid mode
Note that CUDSS_DATA_HYBRID_DEVICE_MEMORY_MIN reflects the total device memory cuDSS needs (not just the matrix factors). You can then pass a custom limit anywhere between that minimum and available free memory (queryable via cudaMemGetInfo) using CUDSS_CONFIG_HYBRID_DEVICE_MEMORY_LIMIT.
Pinned memory handler: Optimized data transfers
Hybrid memory mode in cuDSS keeps full buffers holding factor values on the host. Prior to cuDSS 1.0, these host buffers by default were pinned (registered) after allocation by calling standard cudaHostRegister() / cudaHostUnregister() CUDA APIs. This behavior is controlled through the following script:
cudssConfigSet(config, CUDSS_CONFIG_USE_CUDA_REGISTER_MEMORY, &value, sizeof(int));
The default behavior is equivalent to setting value = 1(if the device supports it). Note that value = 0 (disabling registration) can actually be faster in some cases, since cudaHostRegister has an overhead. For large systems, the overhead can be quite noticeable. Now there is a way to reduce this overhead.
cuDSS 1.0 introduces an opt-in user-configurable pinned memory handler, reducing latency and bandwidth overhead for host-to-device transfers in hybrid CPU-GPU execution.
cudssSetPinnedMemHandler() allows users to implement a custom allocator for pinned memory, similar to the existing cudssSetDeviceMemHandler() for device memory allocations, but the new pinned memory handler is for the pinned host memory. A minimal implementation requires alloc and dealloc functions:
class ExamplePinnedMemPool {
  public:
    int alloc(void **ptr, size_t size, cudaStream_t) {
        if (size == 0) {
            *ptr = NULL;
            return 0;
        }
 int status = cudaMallocHost(ptr, size);
 return status;
    }
    int dealloc(void *ptr, size_t size, cudaStream_t) {
        if (ptr == NULL) {
            return 0;
        }
        return static_cast<int>(cudaFreeHost(ptr));
    }
This simple implementation would not change the performance compared to the default, which is using cudaHostRegister(). To achieve better performance for the hybrid memory mode for large systems, users can now implement special handling such as pinned memory pools and parallel prefaulting.
Symbolic factorization improvements
Symbolic factorization determines the nonzero structure of the factors and prepares internal data structures for numerical factorization. Recent releases added GPU speedups and optional CPU offloading.
In cuDSS 1.0, GPU symbolic factorization is 2.21x faster (geometric mean) than in cuDSS 0.8.0 on both NVIDIA B200 and H100. The comparison covers ~400 matrix/configuration cases with 80 to 130.3 million rows on B200, and ~250 cases with 120 to 22.9 million rows on H100. Replacing only the symbolic factorization timings, with reordering, numerical factorization, and solve held at 0.8.0 values, gives estimated geometric-mean end-to-end speedups of 1.18x on B200 and 1.14x on H100.
Optional execution of symbolic factorization on the host introduced through hybrid execute mode in cuDSS 0.8.0 to improve two cases:
- Small matrices: Hybrid execute mode was designed for smaller matrices, running numerical factorization and solving on the host (reordering always runs on the host). Prior to cuDSS 0.8, GPU symbolic factorization could add device execution and data-transfer overhead to this otherwise host-based computation. Running it on the host can reduce this overhead.
- Large matrices: Host symbolic factorization can reduce peak device memory during analysis, making analysis possible for systems that would otherwise exceed device memory.
Starting with cuDSS 0.8, users can control where symbolic factorization is executed by enabling/disabling the hybrid execute mode. To run symbolic factorization on the host, enable the hybrid execute mode before analysis:
int value = 1; cudssConfigSet(config, CUDSS_CONFIG_HYBRID_EXECUTE_MODE, &value, sizeof(int));
With hybrid execute mode disabled, symbolic factorization runs on the GPU. With it enabled, symbolic factorization runs on the host, even when numerical factorization and solve remain on the GPU.
For better host performance, enable the threading layer to and allow cuDSS to use more than one CPU thread. The CUDSS_CONFIG_HOST_NTHREADS setting controls the thread limit for cuDSS.
Hybrid execute mode and hybrid memory mode can now be enabled together in supported configurations. They serve different purposes: hybrid execute mode controls where computation runs, while hybrid memory mode allows factor data to be stored in host memory. The remaining mode restrictions still apply.
| Phase | Default | With hybrid execute mode enabled | 
|---|---|---|
| Reordering (including matching) | Host | Host | 
| Symbolic factorization | Device | Host | 
| Numerical factorization | Device | Host, device, or host/device* | 
| Solve | Device | Host, device, or host/device* | 
*With hybrid memory mode disabled, an internal heuristic selects placement for numerical factorization and solve-based on matrix structure. Enabling hybrid execute mode does not force these phases onto the host. When hybrid memory mode is also enabled, numerical factorization and solve use the GPU, while symbolic factorization runs on the host.
Get started with cuDSS
cuDSS 1.0 is the production-ready standard for performance-critical simulation, extending GPU computing to problem scales previously impractical or impossible to solve. The release rests on three mutually reinforcing technical pillars:
- Advanced accuracy techniques improve robustness
- Best-in-class performance delivers consistent, substantial speedups over CPU-based solvers
- A system-level optimization strategy, anchored by host-assisted symbolic factorization, hybrid memory mode, and a significantly reduced GPU memory footprint
As each new GPU architecture brings greater memory capacity, higher memory bandwidth, and faster interconnects, cuDSS algorithmic innovations will compound these advances, enabling ever larger and more efficient solutions to the sparse linear systems at the core of the world’s most demanding engineering applications.
