articles.title: Get Started with GPU-Accelerated DuckDB Analytics Using the Sirius Core Extension
articles.text:
As datasets grow, analytical queries can take longer to run, slowing down data exploration, pipelines, and applications. For developers using DuckDB, reducing query times helps keep analytics responsive and can lower compute costs.
NVIDIA and DuckLabs collaborated to release Sirius as a DuckDB core extension, bringing GPU acceleration to DuckDB’s analytical query engine. With two SQL commands, you can install and load Sirius to accelerate supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs without rewriting your SQL or changing database schemas.
Sirius, developed through a collaboration between the University of Wisconsin–Madison and NVIDIA, is an open-source, GPU-native SQL engine.
This post introduces the core extension, shows you how to run your first GPU query, and explains how Sirius integrates with DuckDB.
Accelerate DuckDB queries without rewriting SQL
Sirius accelerates supported queries as a whole. DuckDB handles SQL parsing and optimization, while Sirius executes the resulting query plans on the GPU. The core extension brings this capability into DuckDB’s standard workflow: install Sirius, load it, and run your queries.
With this release, you can:
- Install directly from DuckDB. Use INSTALL sirius; and LOAD sirius; to download and activate the extension.
- Retain familiar SQL. Execute supported analytical queries on NVIDIA GPUs without translating them into a separate GPU programming API.
- Use CPU fallback. Queries with unsupported features fall back to DuckDB’s CPU engine.
Start with a small example, then apply the same workflow to your own analytical queries.
Run your first GPU query
You’ll need DuckDB 2.0 and an NVIDIA GPU with a compatible driver.
Create a sample dataset
Open DuckDB with a file-backed database.
duckdb getting_started.duckdb
Use DuckDB’s TPC-H extension to generate a small analytical dataset for this example.
INSTALL tpch;
LOAD tpch;
CALL dbgen(sf=0.01);
CHECKPOINT;
The TPC-H extension creates the example tables, including lineitem, which contains order line items. It supplies sample data for this walkthrough and is separate from the Sirius extension.
The CHECKPOINT statement persists the generated data so Sirius can read the native DuckDB tables.
Install and load Sirius
In the same DuckDB session, install and load Sirius.
-- Sirius is approximately 700 MB; download time depends on your connection.
INSTALL sirius;
LOAD sirius;
The core extension automatically selects the CUDA backend for your driver. INSTALL downloads the extension, and LOAD activates it in the current connection.
Run an analytical query
With Sirius loaded, run the following SQL query.
SELECT
    l_returnflag,
    SUM(l_quantity) AS total_quantity
FROM lineitem
GROUP BY l_returnflag
ORDER BY l_returnflag;
This query groups line items by return flag and calculates the total quantity for each group. Supported queries execute on the GPU while retaining the same SQL syntax used with DuckDB.
The query returns:
l_returnflag  total_quantity
A                 380456.00
N                 774222.00
R                 381449.00
You now have a complete workflow: create data, load the extension, and execute an analytical query. The small dataset keeps setup quick and illustrates how to use Sirius; it is not intended to demonstrate a performance advantage.
Use the same approach with your own DuckDB tables or supported Parquet workflows. Queries with unsupported features automatically fall back to DuckDB’s CPU engine.
Understand how Sirius executes queries
Sirius integrates GPU execution into DuckDB’s query-processing workflow. DuckDB remains the application’s SQL interface and handles query parsing and optimization. Sirius executes supported queries on the GPU and returns results through the same connection.
This integration lets developers continue expressing analytical operations in SQL while using GPU parallelism for supported workloads. The application receives query results through DuckDB, preserving the interface used by existing scripts and applications.
Compare Sirius GPU and DuckDB CPU benchmark results
We evaluated Sirius against CPU-based DuckDB using cold runs of queries derived from the TPC-H benchmark, with data stored in Amazon S3. Tests covered scale factors 100 (100 GB), 1,000 (1 TB), 3,000 (3 TB), and 10,000 (10 TB), measuring total query runtime and query-time compute cost under default and tuned settings. These tests used pinned development builds. Sirius timings exclude result fetch/export, while DuckDB timings include CSV output. Query-time compute costs cover measured instance runtime and exclude startup, validation, storage, S3, and idle time.
With tuned settings, Sirius running on AWS instances with two NVIDIA GPUs delivered 3.25x to 5.50x speedups over the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configurations. At SF1K, total query runtime fell from 347.3 seconds to 63.2 seconds. At SF3K, runtime dropped from 752.4 seconds to 160.6 seconds, delivering a 4.69x speedup. Query-time compute cost at SF3K also decreased by approximately 71%.
The largest cost advantage appeared at SF10K. The tuned two-GPU configuration completed the workload in 729.9 seconds compared with 2,369.4 seconds for the best tested CPU-based DuckDB configuration. This represents a 3.25x speedup and approximately 79% lower query-time compute cost.
The results also show how workload size affects configuration choices. At SF100, one GPU offered the lowest cost, while two GPUs delivered the shortest runtime. At SF10K, the tuned two-GPU configuration outperformed the tuned single-GPU configuration in both runtime and cost. Tuning was particularly important at this scale: at SF10K, the default configuration with two GPUs was marked “did not finish,” while the tuned configuration completed the workload in 729.9 seconds.
The Sirius repository provides a benchmark runner, query definitions, configuration details, and setup instructions for reviewing the test setup and evaluating performance on your own hardware. Results will vary with query structure, dataset size, hardware, and cache conditions.
Get started with Sirius
The Sirius core extension brings GPU-accelerated analytics into DuckDB’s familiar SQL workflow. Install the extension, run the example, and explore how GPU execution applies to your data.
As your data grows, use Sirius to accelerate supported queries while keeping your SQL, tools, and workflow in DuckDB. Share your results and feedback with the Sirius community.

articles.title: Voyager 1: NASA-Sonde erreicht historische 24-Stunden-Lichtgrenze
articles.text:
49 Jahre im All: Voyager 1 knackt Rekord-Distanz von 26 Milliarden Kilometern
Seit 49 Jahren schwebt die Raumsonde Voyager 1 durchs Weltall. Trotz ihrer alten Tage ist die Sonde noch teilweise funktionsfähig. Und schon bald wird sie einen Meilenstein erreichen, den zuvor noch kein anderes menschengemachtes Objekt im Weltall erreichen konnte.
Voyager 1 erreicht historische Lichttag-Distanz
Die Raumsonde wird als erstes einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein. Dies entspricht etwa 25,9 Milliarden Kilometern. Wie das Wort „Lichttag“ schon sagt: Das Licht, das von einem Objekt in dieser Distanz ausgestrahlt wird, benötigt 24 Stunden, um die Erde zu erreichen. Die Nasa hat den Moment, an dem Voyager 1 einen Lichttag von der Erde entfernt sein wird, schon exakt berechnet. Demnach ist es am 18. November um 5:16 Uhr US-Ostküstenzeit so weit. Zu diesem Zeitpunkt wird die Distanz der Sonde zur Erde exakt 25.902.068.356 Kilometer betragen.
Ein Radiosignal, das die Kontrollstation auf der Erde in Richtung Voyager abschickt, ist dann ebenfalls einen ganzen Tag unterwegs. Das sorgt für massive Delays in der Kommunikation. „Wenn man ‚Voyager ‚Hallo‘ sagen will, schickt man seine Nachricht ab, geht nach Hause und wartet zwei Tage, bis man endlich eine Antwort bekommt“, sagte Suzanne Dodd vom Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) der Nasa in der Mitteilung.
Voyager 1 reagierte zweimal nicht auf Kontaktversuche
Erst kürzlich kam es zu einem Zwischenfall, der den Meilenstein fast verhindert hätte. Das Funk- und Kommunikationsnetzwerk der Nasa hatte am 18. und 19. Oktober Voyager 1 kontaktiert. Doch die Raumsonde blieb bei beiden Kontaktversuchen stumm. Wie die US-Raumfahrtbehörde kürzlich bekannt gab, löste sich das Problem aber von selbst. Am 20. Oktober meldete sich Voyager zurück. Seitdem ist die Kommunikation stabil.
Mittlerweile haben Nasa-Ingenieur:innen auch die Ursache herausgefunden. Eine Gruppe von Triebwerken der Voyager 1 ging unerwartet offline. Das System schaltete dann automatisch eine Backup-Gruppe hinzu. Um diesen Wechsel fehlerfrei durchzuführen, begibt sich das System in eine Art abgesicherten Modus und pausiert bis zur Umsetzung alle anderen Funktionen.
Fast 50 Jahre im All: Voyager 1 trotzt dem Zahn der Zeit
Voyager 1 startete am 5. September 1977 von Cape Canaveral aus. Seitdem bewegt sie sich mit einer Geschwindigkeit von über 60.000 Kilometern pro Stunde durchs All. Die Nasa-Sonde erforschte zunächst Jupiter und Saturn. Im Sommer 2012 trat sie als erstes von Menschen geschaffenes Objekt in den interstellaren Raum ein.
Doch ein Jahr vor ihrem 50. Geburtstag nagt der Zahn der Zeit an der Sonde. Deswegen musste die Nasa im Frühjahr 2026 ein weiteres Instrument abschalten, den Teilchenmesser LECP. (Low-energy Charged Particles). Die Abschaltung spart Energie, die der Sonde ein Jahr weiterer Lebensdauer verschaffen soll. Von ursprünglich elf Instrumenten an Bord der Voyager 1 sind damit nur noch zwei aktiv.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 05.11.2026 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.
Interessant! Aber… die NASA Kontaktiert am 18.10. und die Sonde blieb still…
2 Tage auf eine Antwort warten, dann am 20.10. eine Antwort.
also, nicht still geblieben, oder? Aber genug für einen spannenden Artikel… denke ich!
;) Heiße Mädchen warten auf dich — Miss4.fun

articles.title: Hackers infectaron con malware routers de la marca GL.iNet y dispositivos de control remoto a través de su nube
articles.text:
GL.iNet, fabricante de routers domésticos y de viaje, confirmó que hackers aprovecharon una falla en sus servicios de administración remota en la nube para instalar software malicioso en routers y en dispositivos KVM, equipos que permiten controlar una computadora a distancia.
“Corregimos la vulnerabilidad en la nube y bloqueamos el acceso usado en este incidente”, afirmó GL.iNet en su aviso. La compañía precisó que los equipos ya no pueden infectarse por esa vía, pero esas medidas no eliminan el malware de los que ya fueron infectados.
GL.iNet no informó cuántos clientes resultaron afectados, cómo entraron los atacantes ni si se robó información. Tampoco ha publicado un identificador oficial de la falla. Según BleepingComputer, la empresa investiga si las computadoras conectadas a los KVM infectados también quedaron comprometidas.
Cómo comprobar si un equipo está infectado
La señal que dio GL.iNet es un proceso en ejecución con el texto exacto crond -i /tmp/.log. En un router se busca desde el panel de administración, en la sección de procesos del menú LuCI, o por SSH con el comando ps | grep tmp. En un KVM se usa la terminal del propio dispositivo, no la de la computadora conectada.
Si aparece, la empresa pide tratar el equipo como infectado. En un KVM recomienda instalar la versión beta de seguridad o restablecer los valores de fábrica, lo que borra la configuración. Si no aparece y no hay otra sospecha, no hace falta limpiar nada, pero sí instalar la actualización estable.
Esa actualización estaba prevista para el 22 de noviembre de 2026, para routers y KVM. Para los KVM, BleepingComputer indica las versiones 1.10.3 o posteriores en los modelos RM10, RM1, RM1V2, RM1PE y RM4PE, y 1.8.7 o posteriores en el RMQ1.
Privacy Affairs informó que, a las 15:15 UTC del 22 de noviembre, el servidor de GL.iNet no listaba ningún firmware estable nuevo para diez modelos de router.
Qué encontraron usuarios e investigadores
Tras el aviso, clientes e investigadores difundieron pruebas de malware hecho para equipos GL.iNet y de accesos remotos con permisos de administrador que conectaban los routers con la dirección 170.39.226[.]219. BleepingComputer analizó un script malicioso que reconoce varios modelos de GL.iNet, se disfraza con el nombre del proceso del aviso y reemplaza una herramienta de red para ocultar sus conexiones.
El script incluye comentarios escritos en chino por su programador, según el medio citado. La nota no atribuye el ataque a ningún grupo ni país.
La consultora RemoteToHome Consulting, que administra routers GL.iNet, analizó 183 equipos y halló actividad sospechosa en 152. Entre ellos, 24 tenían accesos remotos de administrador, 47 una puerta trasera más antigua y 81 mostraban comandos ejecutados por los atacantes. Los investigadores aclararon que esos hallazgos pueden no coincidir con los de otros clientes.
Los mismos investigadores identificaron una posible falla en el cliente de GoodCloud, la plataforma de gestión remota de GL.iNet: un componente pasaría valores enviados desde la nube a comandos del sistema sin validarlos. GL.iNet no confirmó que esa falla se usara en los ataques.
Privacy Affairs reportó que algunos archivos de esa puerta trasera antigua tienen fechas de septiembre de 2025 y que la revisión de GL.iNet no la detecta. Un integrante de GL.iNet la mencionó en el foro entre los casos que la empresa examina.
Los desarrolladores de una herramienta comunitaria de limpieza advierten, según el medio citado, que puede ser necesario reinstalar el firmware sin conservar la configuración, porque los archivos maliciosos pueden sobrevivir a una actualización común. GL.iNet avisará por correo a los clientes que identifique como afectados.
El incidente confirma que cerrar una vulnerabilidad no elimina por sí solo las consecuencias de un acceso previo. Los usuarios deben comprobar sus equipos, actualizar el firmware y, ante señales de infección, restablecer la configuración o reinstalar el sistema para recuperar condiciones seguras.

articles.title: Palo Alto and Elastic snap up AI startups. The prize? Enterprise trust and control.
articles.text:
Palo Alto and Elastic snap up AI startups. The prize? Enterprise trust and control.
They say that to understand where an industry is heading, you have to follow the money. And two acquisitions announced this past week suggest that established infrastructure vendors see a big opportunity in helping enterprises take greater control of the AI systems they deploy — and ensuring those systems are secure, reliable and trustworthy.
In early November, Applied Compute, a startup specializing in post-training and inference for open-weight AI models, announced it had raised $350 million at a $3.25 billion valuation, less than 18 months after its founding. Then last Wednesday, cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks swooped in with a $4.5 billion bid to buy the startup outright.
The following day, search and observability giant Elastic announced plans to acquire HoneyHive, a four-year-old startup specializing in AI agent observability and evaluation.
While the deals target different parts of the enterprise AI stack, both point to a growing push by established vendors to bring more of the AI development and operations toolchain in-house.
An acquisition spree
A quick peek at the wider acquisitive landscape suggests a broader trend at play. Last month, observability giant Dynatrace completed its $915 million acquisition of Arize, an AI observability and evaluation platform. And back in July, SAP acquired Prior Labs, a specialist in AI models for structured data, while more recently, payments giant Stripe acquired AI model routing platform OpenRouter.
Palo Alto Networks and Elastic themselves have been on something of a buying spree, the former in particular.
Palo Alto Networks kicked off the year by completing its $3.35 billion acquisition of observability company Chronosphere in January, saying this was about “unifying observability and security for the AI era.” This was followed by its $21.1 billion purchase of identity security giant CyberArk. Since then, it has acquired endpoint security startup Koi, AI gateway provider Portkey, mobile observability specialist Embrace, and AI-native enterprise automation startup Console.
Elastic, meanwhile, acquired Deductive AI in August, bringing AI-powered incident investigation into its observability platform.
For Jason Andersen, an analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, such deals reflect several pressures facing established software vendors. Some need specialized AI technology better suited to their existing customers, while others see acquisitions as a way to accelerate their AI strategies and expand into new markets.
“There are many cases where an incumbent feels that general purpose AI tools do not fit their value proposition, and they need something more tailored to their customer bases.”
“There are many cases where an incumbent feels that general purpose AI tools do not fit their value proposition, and they need something more tailored to their customer bases,” Andersen tells The New Stack. “I also am seeing all sorts of companies using the acquisitions to jumpstart their own repositioning.”
Palo Alto Networks is a case in point. A veteran of the cybersecurity industry, it started out as a firewall specialist before expanding into cloud security, threat detection and security operations. And as with just about every major technology company today, AI is driving much of its strategy.
On the company’s earnings call last week, Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, suggested that Applied Compute could create an opportunity larger than the company’s core cybersecurity operations.
“If it works, I think this will dwarf the abilities that we have in cybersecurity,” Arora said. “This could be bigger than what we do today.”
“If it works, I think this will dwarf the abilities that we have in cybersecurity. This could be bigger than what we do today.”
Applied Compute specializes in post-training and inference, helping enterprises customize open-weight models for their own needs and run them in production. Its slogan itself sums up its core raison d’être: “The best AI is built, not bought” — a somewhat ironic message, now that Palo Alto Networks is buying the company for $4.5 billion.
Applied Compute has worked with companies including Microsoft and Nvidia, while Palo Alto Networks itself said it had been a “prospective customer.” Arora sees securing an increasingly diverse mix of enterprise AI models as a big business opportunity.
“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured.”
“Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured,” Arora said in a press release announcing the deal.
In a separate LinkedIn post, Applied Compute CEO Yash Patil, who worked on post-training infrastructure and Codex at OpenAI before co-founding the company in May 2025, said that he and his two co-founders had built Applied Compute on the belief that “every company should own its intelligence,” arguing that businesses will increasingly need to develop and control their own AI models.
“We think training, serving, and improving proprietary models will become a normal part of running a company.”
“We think training, serving, and improving proprietary models will become a normal part of running a company,” he writes. “To do useful work, a model needs to access sensitive data and systems, comply with policies, and remain explainable, verifiable, and auditable. This is the reason we’ve always prioritized security, and why joining Palo Alto Networks will help us go further faster.”
Evaluating the AI opportunity
Elastic’s acquisition of HoneyHive, meanwhile, targets a different part of enterprise AI: understanding how agents behave, and whether they’re doing what they’re supposed to. HoneyHive, which claims big-name customers such as Nvidia and MongoDB, brings tracing, evaluation and testing capabilities that Elastic plans to integrate into its existing observability platform.
In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Elastic explicitly describes the HoneyHive acquisition as a move to help its customers “observe, evaluate, and trust the agents they run in production.”
In a separate blog post announcing the deal last Thursday, Santosh Krishnan, senior vice president of observability and security at Elastic, argues that the rise of autonomous agents creates a new challenge for developers: understanding whether their AI systems are making sound decisions, even when the underlying software is functioning as expected.
“Reliable agents need more than traditional application monitoring,” Krishnan writes. “AI observability provides visibility into agent behavior and the ability to evaluate the quality of its decisions and outcomes.”
By combining HoneyHive’s agent-specific capabilities with Elastic’s existing monitoring tools, the company hopes to give developers a clearer picture of how their agents interact with the applications and infrastructure supporting them.
“This combination could also enable teams to evaluate production telemetry more broadly, helping them understand not only how their AI applications are performing, but whether their agents are achieving the intended outcomes,” Krishnan adds.
But what does the acquisition mean for developers already using HoneyHive who don’t want to adopt the broader Elastic platform? Krishnan tells The New Stack that existing customers will continue to be supported during the integration, with HoneyHive’s capabilities eventually expected to become native Elastic offerings.
“Customers will retain the flexibility to adopt use-cases of interest, without committing to use all the capabilities of the platform,” Krishnan says, adding that more details on the combined product roadmap will be shared in the coming months.
One stack to rule them all?
While both deals reflect growing demand for greater control over enterprise AI, Andersen cautions against assuming that model training, evaluation and observability are all converging into a single stack.
“Training is very distinct and most organizations will likely never need to do training on a model at least until the skills become more commonplace and costs go down,” Andersen says.
Most agent platforms already include some observability capabilities, Andersen notes, but evaluation is a different story. Enterprises have several ways to assess model outputs, including using other AI models, and the right approach depends on what an agent is designed to do.
“I think that over time evaluations could become a major embedded component of agentic platforms, but right now they are distinct,” Andersen says.
Beyond questions around convergence, there are perhaps more immediate reasons for established vendors to acquire AI startups, including access to specialist talent and the potential to reduce costs.
“Aside from strengthening their customer position, a lot of these startups have really smart people to inject some new minds into a company,” Andersen says. “And / or it could be a way to save the incumbent money by bringing a technology in house, versus having to pay OpenAI or some other company.”
Palo Alto Networks’ deal, in particular, fits that mold: it brings Applied Compute’s research team in-house, giving the company additional expertise in developing and adapting AI models, with Patil set to become co-chief AI officer once the transaction closes.
And Andersen expects more deals to come, with buyers driven as much by necessity as by opportunity.
“The issue right now is that valuations are sky-high, as is the cost of money vis-à-vis interest rates,” he says. “So, while I can’t speculate on a specific name, I would say that these purchases are increasingly going to happen with buyers that are under some pressure to deliver better results.”

articles.title: Microsoft confirms Windows printing issues affecting Forcepoint users
articles.text:
Microsoft confirmed that some Forcepoint users may experience printing issues after installing the November 2026 Windows 11 hotpatch.
In a Friday service alert seen by BleepingComputer, Microsoft said this known issue affects only systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later.
According to Microsoft, the printing problems stem from a compatibility issue between the KB5132043 Windows hotpatch update and the Forcepoint DLP Endpoint Agent endpoint data loss prevention solution.
"After installing the November 2026 Windows hotpatch update (the Originating KBs listed above), devices running Forcepoint DLP Endpoint Agent might experience printing issues," Microsoft said. "Affected users might find that the print option is greyed out or encounter errors when selecting a printer. This issue occurs because the Print Spooler service fails to start."
While a fix is not yet available, Forcepoint has shared a temporary workaround for its customers in this support document, which can be accessed after signing in to the Forcepoint support portal.
Last week, Microsoft also warned that the KB5132043 hotpatch is causing installation and launch issues affecting Office and third-party applications on Windows 11 systems.
These two known issues should not affect systems with the standard November 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates, only those that have installed the hotpatch updates pushed through Microsoft's Windows Autopatch, a cloud-based enterprise service designed to automate Windows and Microsoft 365 updates.
However, as the company confirmed two weeks ago, the November 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates may also break printing for users trying to print documents with complex formatting on server (Windows Server 2016 or later) and client (Windows 10 or later) devices.
Microsoft unveiled Windows Autopatch in April 2022, saying it would be available for free to customers with a Windows 10/11 Enterprise E3 license or greater starting in July 2022. Windows Autopatch was made available in public preview in early June 2022 and reached general availability in July 2022.
In March, it announced that it would turn on hotpatch security updates by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through Microsoft Intune and the Graph API on systems with the May 2026 Windows security updates installed.
One month later, Microsoft fixed a Windows Autopatch bug that deployed driver updates restricted by administrative policies on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices belonging to customers across the European Union.

articles.title: 367 ch et une carrosserie bodybuildée : Volkswagen signe une bombe électrique, mais il y a un gros hic
articles.text:
Trop sages, les voitures électriques ? Volkswagen a déjà tenté de démontrer l’inverse avec sa défunte gamme GTX, sans grand succès. Résultat, c’est au tour du blason GTI de faire son apparition sur les véhicules à batterie, histoire de dresser un parallèle subtil avec les modèles thermiques. Au cas où la mayonnaise ne prenait toujours pas, le constructeur allemand déballe une version encore plus radicale de ses GTI électriques, la Clubsport.
Ce label bien connu déjà appliqué aux sportives à essence prend donc place sur les modèles électriques. Voici l’ID. Polo GTI Clubsport, qui fête au passage les 50 ans de la première Golf GTI. Et quelle manière de le faire ! La citadine est littéralement transformée avec une carrosserie élargie de 100 mm grâce à des passages de roues gonflés de 50 mm de chaque côté. Les conséquences de ce changement sont immédiates.
Ailes élargies de 10 cm et deux portes en moins : le retour d’un détail oublié sur la Polo
Il a fallu supprimer les portières arrière de l’auto, ce qui la transforme en deux portes, une configuration qui n’a pas été vue depuis la Polo de cinquième génération. Les jantes ont naturellement été revues, avec un kit BBS de 19 pouces noir aux bordures rouges. La face avant gagne pour sa part une lèvre plus proéminente optimisant l’appui aérodynamique. Le capot accueille de son côté deux grandes ouïes posées aux extrémités.
La poupe suit cette tendance radicale, avec un immense aileron en fibre de carbone flottant bien au-delà de la lunette arrière avec deux bras prenant prise au centre du toit. De par sa taille XXL, le diffuseur est immanquable. À bord, c’est un déluge d’Alcantara qui attend les occupants. Ces derniers prendront place dans deux sièges baquets Recaro équipés de harnais rouges à cinq points avec des surpiqûres assorties.
Arceau rouge à la place de la banquette et baquets Recaro : ambiance pistarde assumée
Mauvaise nouvelle pour la praticité, la banquette arrière a été remplacée par un arceau de sécurité couleur Rouge Tornado. Plus sympa pour la course, mais moins commode au quotidien. Volant et écrans sont en revanche identiques à ceux de l’ID. Polo GTI. Le châssis a été revu avec une hauteur de caisse abaissée de 15 mm alors que les suspensions pilotées ont été recalibrées.
Côté mécanique, l’ID. Polo GTI Clubsport reprend le moteur APP550 de l’ID.7 avec ce coup-ci 367 ch et 550 Nm de couple. L’auto demeure une stricte traction, ce qui a nécessité l’installation d’un différentiel autobloquant pour limiter le patinage des roues. Le 0 à 100 km/h est en effet abattu en 4,7 s, contre 6,8 s pour l’ID. Polo GTI. Excitant, sauf que le véhicule n’est encore qu’un concept dont la commercialisation demeure incertaine.

articles.title: Jensen is BACK at NVIDIA
articles.text:
What an odd few weeks. The big news today, of course, is that Jensen Huang has been reinstated as NVIDIA’s CEO. The markets immediately responded by adding roughly 30% or about $1T in market cap. I think folks realized this was the right option.
Jensen is BACK at NVIDIA
One of the big catalysts to this was that the U.S. government came out and said that they do not believe that having Jensen as the CEO of NVIDIA is a national security risk.
“In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.” (Source: NVIDIA)
It seems the government sign-off gave the board air cover on one major risk factor: that the Megaspeed issue would turn into a major national security investigation. With that off the table, then there was the challenge of alleged workplace conduct.
Workplace conduct is always a challenge because it opens NVIDIA up to claims from current and former employees. There was an early 2010’s case in California (note I have a 2007 JD from California’s largest law school, but never practiced, so this is not legal advice) for workplace sexual harassment in the $168M range, that was then significantly reduced to under $100M, then settled. What I have been telling folks for the past week and a half is that for the company to lose $1T in shareholder value, even $1B in a legal fund pays a lot of attorneys to cover other claims. It felt like Jensen’s value was wildly out of line with what it would cost to settle the cases. Again, I am not condoning the allegations, but at some point, I would have a hard time believing NVIDIA’s board did not have a team developing a range of exposure if they were to settle claims that could then be weighed against the cost of not having Jensen on the team. When it was comparing those two numbers plus potential government action, I can see how a board would have been more conservative.
Perhaps the other big one is that NVIDIA’s team accepted the news publicly, but what is hard to quantify is that folks who have been at NVIDIA for many years and built this enormous business are very loyal to Jensen. It has been really strange reading mainstream media reports about how Jensen can get passionate in meetings as if that were a major issue. Every CEO, especially founders, gets passionate because the business is personal. I would venture to guess that any of Jensen’s direct reports who have been there for a few years have earned enough to walk away if they wanted to, and they truly did not like working for Jensen. Maybe to put it another way, in the week and a half since Jensen resigned, I never heard an NVIDIA employee say “good riddance” or anything like that. Folks supported the board, but only spoke positively about Jensen’s leadership. It turns out when you create a market segment big enough to be measured in percentage of US GDP, it creates wealth for your employees, suppliers, customers, and partners that makes them loyal. Installing someone from the outside as CEO just does not replace that.
Final Words
More than a few executives were probably hoping to land the role and are disappointed, but realistically, those are hard shoes to fill. Jensen’s focus on the AI supply chain, sales to big customers, and loyalty among employees who have done well under his watch are exceptionally hard for anyone to replicate. Moreover, executives might be able to rise to the job, but NVIDIA added over $55B in revenue last quarter versus the year-ago quarter. Revenue-wise, that is roughly in the ballpark of adding an American Airlines annual revenue to NVIDIA on a quarterly basis. Moving that fast, it is hard for someone to grow in place in that role.
Perhaps the most fascinating part is what this means for executive compensation. The market saw what it meant to have Jensen out as NVIDIA’s CEO not just for NVIDIA, but for others in the ecosystem. Delaware’s compensation cases with Elon Musk now have a new data point showing this class of CEO can have an outsized impact on shareholder value. Not all CEOs are the same, and an individual can be uniquely valuable to an organization. Is Lisa Su the same at AMD? What about Mark Zuckerberg at Meta? Hock Tan at Broadcom? Michael Dell and Jeff Clarke? Or someone like Matt Murphy, who took Marvell from a very rough company a decade ago to a company zipping along today? The other side of this is figuring out the set of circumstances and formula for when a high-flying CEO can be ousted.
Personally, I think the board made the right decision in bringing Jensen back to NVIDIA, even if it means some clean-up needs to happen.
> Personally, I think the board made the right decision in bringing Jensen back to NVIDIA, even if it means some clean-up needs to happen.
What a pathetic comment. Only spineless cowards would say that.
What the board actually said is “it’s ok for our CEO to have multiple relationships with subordinates, even though it is company policy for that to be a firing offence for any employee.”

articles.title: Jusqu’à 72 % d’économies sur la recharge : l’offre choc d’Auchan pour les voitures électriques, mais sous conditions
articles.text:
Auchan baisse le prix de la recharge électrique à 0,09 €/kWh : dates, bornes et conditions
Du 24 novembre 2026 au 13 janvier 2027, Auchan propose la recharge électrique dès 0,09 €/kWh. Une opération agressive face à la concurrence, mais soumise à plusieurs conditions.
Sur les bornes publiques françaises, le prix du kilowattheure varie fortement selon les réseaux et la puissance, faisant vite grimper la facture. À l’approche des fêtes de fin d’année, Auchan a décidé de frapper un grand coup avec l’opérateur français Le Plein afin de séduire les automobilistes. Du 24 novembre 2026 au 13 janvier 2027, l’opération abaisse le coût net de la recharge jusqu’à 0,09 €/kWh sur 394 points de charge installés sur les parkings participants, mais pas sans contrepartie.
Des économies sur la recharge, mais reversées sur la cagnotte
Dans les stations Le Plein participantes, la réduction se décline selon trois paliers de puissance. Sur les bornes Éco (11 kW), le coût net chute de 0,32 à 0,09 €/kWh grâce à un remboursement de 0,23 €/kWh, soit jusqu’à 72 % d’économies. Les bornes rapides passent de 0,42 à 0,19 €/kWh (-55 %) avec ce même remboursement de 0,23 €/kWh. Enfin, sur les bornes ultra-rapides, le tarif glisse de 0,58 à 0,39 €/kWh (-33 %), avec 0,19 €/kWh reversés.
Concrètement, pour une session de 25 kWh sur une borne lente Éco, l’automobiliste règle d’abord 8 € avant de récupérer 5,75 €, ce qui ramène sa dépense nette à 2,25 €. Une opération qui s’avère attractive sur le papier, à condition de ne pas être pressé sur cette puissance limitée à 11 kW.
À noter que la remise n’est pas déduite directement au moment du paiement. Les clients doivent en effet régler leur recharge au tarif habituel, avant de recevoir le montant remboursé sous 1 à 3 jours sur leur cagnotte Waaoh!, le programme de fidélité d’Auchan. Pour en bénéficier, il faut donc détenir une carte Waaoh!, l’associer à son compte Le Plein et payer depuis l’application de l’opérateur. Les sommes cumulées servent ensuite à régler des achats chez Auchan.
Avec cette remise différée, Auchan espère surtout attirer de nouveaux conducteurs de voitures électriques dans ses magasins pendant les fêtes.
Ce que vaut l’offre d’Auchan face à Lidl, E.Leclerc et Carrefour
Sur le coût net, Auchan et Le Plein prennent l’avantage avec 0,09 €/kWh en charge lente et 0,19 €/kWh en rapide. Chez la concurrence, la mécanique diffère : E.Leclerc mise sur un tarif direct via Charge E-Lec dès 0,17 €/kWh en 22 kW (0,45 €/kWh maximum en rapide) sur plus de 3 000 bornes, avec cumul de Tickets E.Leclerc (variable selon les magasins) et 50 % reversés sur la première recharge jusqu’au 31 décembre 2026.
Lidl privilégie aussi la remise immédiate, sans cagnotte. Via Lidl Plus, la recharge revient à 0,18 €/kWh en 22 kW et 0,29 €/kWh en rapide (DC). Carrefour Énergies propose quant à lui des tarifs plus élevés (0,39 à 0,54 €/kWh), compensés par 10 à 15 % de remise sur la carte fidélité et une première heure en 22 kW 100 % cagnottée grâce à la carte payante PASS.
Imbattable en prix net jusqu’au 13 janvier 2027, Auchan reste cependant limité à 394 points de charge (carte ici). Lidl, Carrefour et E.Leclerc dominent par leur simplicité d’accès grâce à un réseau plus étendu, même si leurs prix restent supérieurs durant cette période promotionnelle.

articles.title: Neuralink patient plays GTA VI using only his mind, shows how the controls work
articles.text:
In context: Another game has joined the list of titles that Neuralink patients have played using their minds. The company posted a video on X of an unnamed trial participant using the brain-computer interface to control the action in Rockstar's blockbuster Grand Theft Auto VI, which is a big step up from using a mouth stick and iPad – previously his only way to play games.
Neuralink shared the two-minute clip on November 20, just one day after GTA VI landed on consoles. It shows the player taking Jason under a bridge in a speedboat and steering into a narrow channel to collect a package. He also gets into a fistfight and a shootout, but the part where he flies a seaplane gives us a better idea of how the controls work.
Alongside the gameplay is a graphic of a PlayStation 5 controller that lights up as he plays. To pull the nose of the plane up, he imagines sliding his right hand forward. Thinking about tapping his ring finger registers a press of the square button. He mentions having a control mapped to his foot, too.
 – Neuralink (@neuralink) November 20, 2026
Before the surgery, the mouth stick limited him to a handful of games, and playing them left him with a sore jaw. "I was essentially like a bird just pecking at an iPad," he says. Being able to control a computer again meant that "you just immediately get your portal to the world back."
Back in March 2024, Neuralink's first implant recipient, Noland Arbaugh, showed how he could play chess just by thinking about where he wanted the cursor to go. He'd also managed to stay up until 6 am playing Civilization VI, something plenty of Civ fans can relate to.
A few months later, a second participant, Alex, paired his implant with a mouth-operated QuadStick to play Counter-Strike 2. Using the joystick alone had forced him to choose between moving and aiming. With the implant taking care of his aim, he could finally do both at once.
Neuralink is also working on Blindsight, an implant designed to give blind people a degree of vision by stimulating the brain's visual cortex. It received the FDA's breakthrough device designation in September 2024. At the time, Elon Musk compared the level of detail he expected from early versions to the graphics on an Atari.
Take-Two recently confirmed that day-one retail sales of Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI reached an estimated $3.79 billion, making it the most successful launch in any entertainment medium.

articles.title: SAP NetWeaver, Cisco Expressway Flaws Exploited in Attacks
articles.text:
Threat actors have been exploiting SAP NetWeaver and Cisco Expressway vulnerabilities in the wild, the US cybersecurity agency CISA warned on Friday.
The NetWeaver flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-42884 (CVSS score of 6.5), is a medium-severity issue that could allow unauthenticated attackers to leak or modify server information.
Successful exploitation could allow attackers to “inject JNDI environment properties or pass a URL used during JNDI lookup operations, enabling access to an unintended JNDI provider,” reads a NIST advisory.
SAP patched the bug with its November 2025 security updates. There appear to have been no reports of the security hole being exploited in the wild before CISA’s Friday alert.
Tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), the Expressway defect is a critical hardcoded credentials weakness that could allow attackers to execute system commands with root privileges.
The use of persistent cookies, combined with insufficient validation of client certificates in certain conditions, could allow attackers who possess the cookies to connect to the database service and invoke specific RPC commands.
It impacts Expressway Core (Expressway-C) and Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) devices running vulnerable software versions and configured in a cluster, and was patched on October 21 in Expressway Series release X15.5.20.
On November 20, CISA added the Expressway security defect to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to patch it within three days.
CISA’s alert came two days after Russian cybercrime prevention firm F6 warned that threat actors started exploiting the vulnerability in attacks shortly after proof-of-concept (PoC) code was released publicly.
On Friday, CISA also expanded the KEV list with CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter bug exploited by China-linked espionage group Armory Castle (Warp Panda) as a zero-day, and CVE-2026-129448, a critical Apache Roller flaw patched on November 17 as a zero-day.

articles.title: A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
articles.text:
A hidden limit of space and time could unlock electronics 100,000 times faster
- Date:
  November 7, 2026
- Source:
  University of Regensburg
- Summary:
  Scientists have discovered a surprising quantum limit that prevents electrons from being tracked with unlimited precision in both space and time. The breakthrough could pave the way for manipulating chemical reactions and developing electronics hundreds of thousands of times faster than today's technology.
- Share:
Quantum physics places fundamental limits on what scientists can know about the behavior of particles. Werner Heisenberg's famous uncertainty principle states that certain properties, such as a particle's position and momentum, cannot both be measured with unlimited precision. This restriction is not caused by flaws in scientific instruments. It is built into the laws of nature.
But position and time are different. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle does not impose the same restriction on these quantities. Now, researchers have experimentally demonstrated another fundamental limitation: an electron's location and its behavior over time cannot both be determined with arbitrary precision. Known as the "space-time limit," this newly observed relationship could have major implications for the future of quantum technology and ultrafast electronics.
The discovery comes from an international collaboration involving research groups at the Regensburg Center for Ultrafast Nanoscopy (RUN), led by Profs. Jascha Repp, Rupert Huber, Franz Giessibl, and Klaus Richter, along with a team at the Max Planck Institute in Hamburg led by Angel Rubio.
Watching Electrons Move at Incredible Speeds
Understanding how matter behaves at the smallest scales is essential for developing the next generation of technology. Advances in clean energy, quantum computing, and powerful electronics for artificial intelligence all depend on knowing how chemical reactions unfold, how light interacts with materials, and how electrons travel through electronic devices.
However, even the sharpest microscopic photographs cannot reveal the full picture. Scientists also need to observe how these processes change over time, effectively creating slow-motion movies of events occurring at the atomic scale.
At RUN, researchers are developing ultrafast microscopes capable of recording the movements of electrons, atoms, and molecules with extraordinary precision in both space and time. About ten years ago, scientists in Regensburg used ultrafast scanning tunneling microscopy to resolve the movement of a single molecule across space and time for the first time.
Tracking individual electrons presents an even greater challenge. At these microscopic distances, electrons can move roughly a thousand times faster than atoms and molecules, with important changes taking place over just attoseconds.
To appreciate how extreme these scales are, consider that an atom is approximately ten million times smaller than a millimeter. An attosecond is one-billionth of a billionth of a second. The difference between an attosecond and a second is comparable to the difference between one second and the entire age of the universe.
Making these measurements is especially difficult because electrons do not behave like ordinary objects. Their motion follows the unusual laws of quantum mechanics rather than the familiar rules of classical physics.
Ultrafast Lasers Reveal Quantum Tunneling
To observe electron behavior at these extraordinary speeds, the researchers built a new laser system that provides much finer time resolution than earlier experiments. The system allows them to control and study the quantum motion of individual electrons directly.
In the experiments, carefully timed laser pulses drive electrons from an extremely sharp metal tip toward a silver surface. The distance they travel is only a few atomic diameters.
The researchers detect this movement by measuring the resulting electrical current. To determine exactly when the electrons move, they use two pulses of light separated by a precisely controlled interval.
Simon Maier, the lead author of the paper, explains: "By varying the time interval between the two laser pulses, we can directly observe how the electrons respond."
This approach revealed clear evidence of electron motion occurring on attosecond timescales. It showed that the laser pulses could transfer electrons within these incredibly brief intervals while allowing scientists to observe the process as it happened.
What makes the result particularly remarkable is how the electrons travel. Instead of moving like conventional particles, they behave as quantum waves. This allows them to pass through an energy barrier separating the metal tip from the silver surface, even though classical physics predicts they should not have enough energy to cross it.
This phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling, is somewhat like an object passing through a solid wall without breaking or damaging it.
"Our measurement can be understood as a high-speed camera for the electron wave packets, since you can see at what point in time the tunneling process takes place," explains Katharina Glöckl, a doctoral student and co-author of the publication.
A Surprising 500-Attosecond Delay
To understand the measurements more deeply, researchers working with Prof. Angel Rubio performed sophisticated quantum simulations of the electrons' behavior near the "space-time limit."
Their calculations closely reproduced the experimental findings and uncovered another remarkable detail. The electrons did not respond to the light field instantaneously. Instead, their motion lagged behind it by approximately 500 attoseconds.
At such extreme scales, several fundamental features of quantum physics become important simultaneously.
For example, the researchers found that the laser pulses could not be described entirely by treating light as a wave or entirely by treating it as individual particles called photons. Their effects displayed characteristics of both descriptions. This combination was essential for exploring electron behavior so close to the "space-time limit."
The team also discovered that controlling electron motion over extremely short intervals changes how the electrons are distributed in space. Quantum mechanics describes these electrons using wave packets, which represent how their wave properties extend across different locations.
The relationship between the timing of electron motion and the spatial extent of these wave packets revealed the central limitation behind the discovery.
A Hidden Tradeoff Between Space and Time
Raffael Spachtholz, another co-author of the study, explains: "The more precisely we want to pin down the electron's position in time, the more energy we need to provide. And as a result, the electron wave packet spreads out more spatially."
In other words, improving the precision of an electron's timing comes with a cost. The more tightly researchers define when its motion occurs, the more broadly its quantum wave packet spreads through space.
To examine this relationship experimentally, the team placed a single atom on the surface to confine the electron wave packets to an extremely small region immediately before the laser pulses arrived.
This setup allowed the scientists to directly measure the connection between the electrons' spatial distribution and the timing of their motion.
Importantly, even when the electrons received substantial energy from the laser pulses, their wave packets remained sufficiently localized for microscopy with atomic spatial resolution and attosecond time resolution.
The findings provide experimental insight into a fundamental space-time constraint that scientists had previously only suspected. They also make it possible to systematically investigate how changes in electron motion over time affect the spatial structure of quantum wave functions.
Could Quantum Electronics Become Hundreds of Thousands of Times Faster?
Beyond revealing a new aspect of quantum behavior, the discovery could open the door to technologies that operate on timescales far beyond the capabilities of today's electronics.
One especially promising possibility involves using precisely controlled electron wave packets to influence chemical reactions.
Transferring a single electron to a molecule represents the smallest possible transfer of electric charge. But when that electron is concentrated within an exceptionally small region of space and time, the resulting local peak current density can reach as much as 1 trillion amperes per square centimeter.
Such extreme conditions could give scientists new ways to control chemical bonds and observe how molecules change during reactions.
"In the future, we want to use such wave packets to specifically trigger chemical reactions and observe, on the relevant length and time scales, how chemical bonds can be broken or altered," explains Prof. Jascha Repp enthusiastically.
The implications could extend well beyond chemistry. Greater control over electron motion may eventually help engineers develop electronic devices and quantum information systems that operate at speeds approaching the fundamental limits of electron dynamics.
"In the long term, the insights gained could also contribute to operating electronics and quantum information processing at the intrinsic speed limit of electron motion itself -- hundreds of thousands of times faster than the currently dominant CMOS technology," adds Prof. Rupert Huber.
That possibility remains a long term technological goal rather than an achievement demonstrated in the current experiments. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new foundation for exploring how electrons can be manipulated at the smallest distances and shortest timescales.
For Repp and Huber, the results suggest that the range of potential applications is extraordinarily broad. They believe that future advances in controlling electrons at the space-time limit may ultimately depend more on human creativity than on the constraints imposed by nature.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Regensburg. Original written by Karoline Stürmer. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- S. Maier, R. Spachtholz, K. Glöckl, C. M. Bustamante, S. Lingl, M. Maczejka, J. Schön, A. Riedel, K. Richter, F. J. Giessibl, F. P. Bonafé, M. A. Huber, A. Rubio, J. Repp, R. Huber. Tracking electrons at the space-time limit. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (8): 961 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01932-0

articles.title: “Serei um CEO melhor”, promete Jensen Huang em discurso a funcionários da Nvidia
articles.text:
Jensen Huang voltou ao escritório da Nvidia nesta segunda-feira (23) como presidente-executivo da companhia, após deixar o cargo em meio a denúncias sobre relacionamentos extraconjugais. Recebido com aplausos pelos funcionários, o cofundador da fabricante de chips agradeceu pela nova oportunidade e prometeu melhorar sua atuação à frente da empresa.
“Obrigado a todos pela segunda chance. Vou ser um CEO melhor desta vez”, declarou Huang em vídeo de seu retorno, divulgado nas redes sociais.
O executivo também pediu desculpas aos funcionários pelo período de turbulência. “Este é meu primeiro dia de trabalho. Sinto muito por ter feito todos vocês passarem por tudo isso”, afirmou, segundo um vídeo divulgado pelo Business Insider.
Por que Jensen Huang deixou o comando da Nvidia?
Huang renunciou ao cargo em 12 de novembro, depois de reportagens sobre supostos relacionamentos extraconjugais, incluindo um alegado envolvimento com uma suposta espiã chinesa e outro com uma funcionária subordinada diretamente a ele na Nvidia.
Dois dias antes de deixar a posição, o executivo admitiu ter sido infiel à esposa.
A saída provocou movimentação nos bastidores da empresa e também envolveu integrantes do governo estadunidense. O presidente Donald Trump defendeu publicamente a volta de Huang antes de sua reintegração.
Na segunda-feira, a Casa Branca afirmou que Trump esteve “totalmente envolvido” no processo de retorno do executivo.
Leia mais:
- Amante de ex-CEO da Nvidia mantinha contato com espião chinês, diz jornal
- Trump temia que China contratasse Jensen Huang após saída da Nvidia
- Alta da Nvidia impulsiona Nasdaq e ações de rivais de chips
Governo dos EUA participou da decisão
O conselho de administração da Nvidia também confirmou que recebeu informações de representantes do governo americano durante o processo de avaliação da volta de Huang.
Em comunicado sobre a reintegração, a companhia afirmou que recebeu contribuições de autoridades de alto escalão dos Estados Unidos e que essas informações deram ao conselho confiança de que o retorno do executivo não representa risco à segurança nacional.
Segundo o The New York Times, Trump pediu ao vice-presidente JD Vance que ajudasse a viabilizar a reintegração durante o fim de semana, inclusive auxiliando o conselho a obter as garantias necessárias para tomar a decisão.
Com a volta de Huang, a Nvidia encerra período de incerteza na liderança. O executivo, que cofundou a companhia, reassume o comando e promete conduzir sua gestão de maneira diferente depois da crise.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Opinion: Jensen Huang didn’t believe in succession plans. Your startup shouldn’t make the same mistake
articles.text:
Erin Bury is the co-founder and CEO of online estate planning company Willful.
In a March 2026 podcast interview, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that he doesn’t believe in succession planning and that he could be CEO “until the last day of my life.” Seven months later, he resigned amid a scandal over his multiple alleged affairs, and his multi-billion-dollar company was left without a clear successor. 
Beyond the affair, this was Huang’s biggest mistake: believing that because he didn’t plan to exit the business, he didn’t need to plan for a successor or set the business up to run smoothly without him. Now, he’s been reinstated, perhaps further highlighting the company’s lack of a plan to move forward successfully without him at the helm.
“Think of your succession plan as a playbook for an absence.”
Every founder needs a succession plan, both for themselves and their key people, regardless of whether they plan to sell the business or not. Despite the importance, the CFIB reported in October that only six percent of Canadian small business owners have a formal written succession plan. We can’t predict the future; succession planning covers both planned absences, including parental leaves and sabbaticals, and unplanned absences due to illness, death, family caregiving requirements, or, like Huang, a public scandal.
If you’re a founder who falls into the 94 percent of business owners who don’t have a formal succession plan, here are the key steps to put in place.
Create a written succession plan for key leaders
Many business owners have playbooks for what to do if a crisis happens. Think of your succession plan as a playbook for an absence. At Willful, we work with the value creation firm Horizon; they had us go through the exercise of creating a formal succession plan for my husband and me, as well as our key leaders. It asked questions I hadn’t thought about, like:
- Who would take over this person’s responsibilities if they were unexpectedly out of the business?
- Would you need to engage a recruiter to replace the role externally, or is there a natural successor?
- What processes, relationships, and knowledge does this person own that aren’t documented anywhere?
- How and when would you communicate about this person’s absence?
- Who would need to be informed, and in what order?
- Do key stakeholders know about this plan, and have you discussed this with them to ensure alignment?
- What are your wishes in the event you pass away or leave the business? Would you want it to keep going, be sold, or wind down?
This written plan came in handy when a leader left the business months later. Instead of scrambling, I simply referred to the plan and ended up promoting a team member who was identified as a clear successor.
This also helped me imagine my own exit, whether because of an accident or leaving voluntarily. We need to ask ourselves hard questions as founders, one of which is “how would my business carry on without me, and what would my team need to succeed?”
Document key processes, people, and passwords
Knowing who would step in once you’re gone isn’t the same as ensuring everything in your head, and those of your leaders, is documented for that person. When I took parental leave, I created a Notion CEO playbook that outlined all key processes and functions that I owned and that no one else had insight into, including tutorial videos, contact information, written explanations, and links (there’s a full breakdown of prepping for parental leave in this article I wrote for BetaKit). It was a brain dump of everything I owned, and I felt so much peace of mind after I shared it with our COO, who acted as CEO while I was on leave.
You should document:
- Key logins and passwords (I use 1Password and have a shared vault for many key accounts).
- Key contacts for lawyers, board members, or other stakeholders that leaders don’t interface with as often.
- Key accountabilities and priorities, with deadlines and/or cadence if applicable (for example, “send investor update every quarter” with instructions on how to do that).
- Clear access to key documents and artifacts.
This can feel overwhelming to build, so you can work with an ops team, executive assistant, or virtual assistant to compile everything. And unlike when I created mine in 2021, AI tools can support it as well, if you’re comfortable using them. I asked Claude how it could help me with my succession plan, and it suggested drafting the plan outline, prompting the questions that should be considered, and helping to fill in gaps from scanning my ongoing communications and documents. It then recommended setting up a scheduled task that would audit my email, Slack, and Notion on a regular basis to both identify key stakeholder relationships and how they’ve changed over time, and keep information up to date.
Consider key person insurance
When we raised our first round of institutional funding, one of the stipulations was that we take out a key person life insurance policy and critical illness insurance on me. This means that if I have to step away from the business due to an illness, or if I pass away, the business will receive a payout in order to help with continuity (paying a recruiter, supporting bereavement resources for the team, hiring external resources to support during a transition, or any other costs).
While this is usually required by investors, it’s important to consider for any founder and for any of your key executives. It’s inexpensive and ensures that your business will have the buffer to figure out what’s next.
Ensure your plans are in order
As a founder, your business is one of your key assets, and if you are ill, injured, incapacitated, or pass away, you want to ensure you have proper estate plans in place that allow the people you choose to manage your business.
For example, power of attorney documents name someone to manage your finances if you’re incapacitated, and this person can do anything related to your business that you can do, except for acting as the director of a corporation. This is especially important if you’re a consultant or sole proprietor and you don’t have staff who can step in to support.
When you pass away, a carry-on business clause in your will means the executor can act on your behalf related to the business: keeping it active, winding it down, selling it, or taking other actions. Your will also instructs how your business assets should pass on (unless you have shareholder documents that outline this already), and a dual will can also separate your business assets from your personal assets to reduce probate fees owing.
And, as a business owner, term life insurance can be an inexpensive way to ensure your family would have the funds they need to carry on in your absence.
Keep it current
Your succession plan needs to be reviewed regularly, not just after a key person exits or is promoted. This can be an annual to-do you complete around tax time or in the New Year. Remember, this plan only works if it’s current.
For me, succession planning hits close to home. At Willful, I see daily the impact of people who don’t put plans in place. And as someone who has also been on parental leave twice, I’ve seen firsthand the need to create structures that allow us to step away. As a former business coach said to me, it’s about being needed but not necessary to run your business. Ensure that playbook is in place for your business, so it doesn’t end up in the lurch like Nvidia.
The opinions and analysis expressed in the above article are those of its author, and do not necessarily reflect the position of BetaKit or its editorial staff. It has been edited for clarity, length, and style.

articles.title: The catch in IBM’s offer to relocate its U.S.-based immigrant workers
articles.text:
For some IBM employees, keeping their jobs could mean moving to another country — and taking a steep pay cut in the process.
Earlier this month, IBM said it would no longer support the U.S. immigration status of workers in its consulting division, offering them the option to take a role with the company in another country or exit, according to a Bloomberg report citing a company document.
“IBM Consulting participates in U.S. high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages,” an IBM spokesperson told Rest of World. “That participation has been declining for a number of years, and as skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting.”
IBM Consulting employs more than 150,000 people globally. The company does not disclose the geographical split for its workforce, making it hard to ascertain the exact number of workers impacted by this decision. On November 19, the company’s career portal listed 1,278 open roles for the consulting division outside the U.S., including 1,125 in India, 23 in Singapore, and 18 in the U.K. In the U.S., it listed 89 roles.
For employees, relocation does not automatically ensure continued engagement, effective collaboration, or equal access to professional opportunities, Zakaria Laaraj, founder of consultancy Global New Ventures, told Rest of World. It may affect their access to decision-makers, established networks, and career opportunities. “The credibility of such an offer depends on employee tenure, available positions, immigration requirements, and compensation,” Laaraj said.
Discussions on Blind, an anonymous employee forum used by 14 million professionals, suggest relocating may not be realistic for many.
Moving to India, for instance, could mean an approximately 80% pay cut, one IBM employee wrote on Blind.
“Employees get three weeks to decide,” Blind’s CEO Sunguk Moon told Rest of World. “The alternative is three months of severance and a last day of December 31. And the news came in a surprise one-on-one ‘career sync’ with a manager.”
For any relocation option to be viable, companies must go beyond just assigning a new job to their employee, George Carrillo, CEO of career development and staffing company HireMe, told Rest of World.
“Moving a position can mean uprooting a family. It affects a spouse’s employment, children’s schooling, healthcare, and years of planning. HR should provide clear options, deadlines, and coordinated support. Leaders must own the follow-through,” Carrillo said.
Most U.S. tech giants are navigating the challenges arising from changing visa norms under Donald Trump’s leadership.
“IBM has an advantage because it already operates international offices with the infrastructure and staff to absorb those workers,” Lacey Kaelani, CEO of job search engine Metaintro, told Rest of World. “Rather than abandoning the talent, companies like IBM can move the work to where the talent is.”
Earlier this year, Amazon allowed stranded H-1B workers to work from India amid consular delays but only temporarily. Microsoft defended its international talent hiring strategy in an October blog post pushing back against the U.S. administration’s allegations that it replaces American workers with foreign visa holders. The statement followed its suspension from the Department of Labor’s PERM green card program alongside Adobe and six other IT outsourcing firms, including TCS and Infosys.
“Companies are looking for solutions, but they’re also making business decisions,” Cassandra Fultz, co-founder of Doherty Fultz Immigration, told Rest of World. “Sponsoring an employee indefinitely, particularly when the outcome is uncertain, can be expensive and disruptive. Moving that employee to an existing operation abroad may be an option with more stability for the business. That doesn’t mean every employee will be offered the opportunity for placement abroad. Each country has its own eligibility requirements and work authorization rules. Companies will inevitably prioritize the people and positions they consider most valuable or difficult to replace.”
Even employees are reevaluating the lure of the American Dream as the uncertainty tax of constant visa changes weighs heavily on them. The wait for green cards for Indian nationals — who typically receive three-quarters of the H-1B visas and comprise the majority of the green card queue — can take several decades, according to the National Foundation for American Policy. Even with Democrats winning control of both the House and the Senate, immigration issues will stay with the White House and executive agencies.
“Mid-career professionals in the queue for green cards are most impacted,” Abhijit Bhaduri, former general manager for global learning and development at Microsoft and author of the upcoming book AIdentity: How to Become Irreplaceable in the New World of Work, told Rest of World. “They built a life in a country that still lists them as temporary. A visa is a document. But the vanishing green card queue feels like a broken promise. They followed every rule for years, and the finish line moved. You can relocate a job overnight. Rebuilding and redesigning a new identity takes years. That is the invisible price that gets missed.”

articles.title: AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks
articles.text:
The clean energy revolution hinges on electrifying the entire global economy just as power-hungry data centers are surging. It’s a challenge delegates from all over the world had to grapple with during the United Nations climate conference, called COP31, that came to a chaotic and unsatisfying close in Antalya, Turkey, on Sunday.
AI data centers throw another wrench into chaotic UN climate talks
Global climate negotiations fell apart as delegates tried to tackle AI’s growing carbon footprint.
Each year, attendees try to make good on the commitment to stop climate change as part of the 2015 Paris climate accord. Preventing extreme weather from growing more terrifying, coastal communities from flooding, and droughts from wrecking food and water systems requires slashing greenhouse gas emissions. But in order to power homes or cars with solar and wind instead of oil and gas, they need to go electric.
“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this”
To that end, one of the most anticipated outcomes of this year’s negotiations was a deal to raise electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035, compared to about 20 percent today. That becomes harder to do, however, when data centers are causing electricity demand to skyrocket. That made the rush of new AI data centers a climate issue alongside talks on how to transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy.
“Every climate minister in the world is thinking about this, and it will inevitably come up in the discussions. It’s part of the broader energy transformation,” Chris Bowen, Australia’s minister for climate change and energy and the president of COP31 climate negotiations, told Politico in an interview at the start of the COP31 summit.
Despite becoming the longest COP yet, with debates lasting two days longer than scheduled, official negotiations fell apart spectacularly. Delegates ultimately failed to garner enough support to pass the “pact” they’d been bargaining on for two weeks. The EU, UK, and several smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change rejected the deal that they saw as too weak. The pact omitted the term “fossil fuels” despite many nations calling for stronger commitments to phase out oil, coal, and gas. And the US, the epicenter of the data center buildout and the biggest climate polluter historically, was a no-show after the pro-fossil-fuel Trump administration pulled the country out of the Paris accord (twice).
With official negotiations falling apart, and countries only making voluntary commitments on AI and electrification, some environmental and humanitarian groups called this year “the worst COP” ever.
To meet the Paris goals, nations will need to cut their greenhouse gas emissions roughly in half by 2030 before reaching net zero by the middle of the century. Many tech companies made similar commitments in recent years, including Google, Microsoft, and Meta. But thanks to the AI boom, those goals have fallen by the wayside.
Meta is “re-evaluating” its timeline to reach net zero emissions as it focuses on AI, the company said in its annual sustainability report on Thursday. Meta reported a 45 percent year-over-year increase in climate pollution. Google’s and Microsoft’s carbon footprints are also growing despite climate commitments the companies have made. Data centers’ electricity consumption is forecast to double by 2030, according to a forecast by the International Energy Agency.
“That is a huge climate risk: rising power demand from data centres is not yet sustainable, and an AI boom cannot be allowed to become a fossil fuel boom,” Bruce Douglas, CEO of the Global Renewables Alliance, tells The Verge in an email. Data centers were “a key topic” at COP31, according to Douglas, whose organization cohosted a panel on the challenges during the event.
In the US, the country with the most data centers, power sector emissions could increase 42 percent by 2030 as energy companies build more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a recent analysis by the Sierra Club. Already, hyperscale data centers in the US create more climate pollution than the country of Denmark, a separate study by Harvard researchers recently found.
To stop data centers from creating more pollution, they would need to be powered by additional new sources of renewable energy, Douglas says. He adds that data centers are currently competing with everyone else for grid connections, finance, and electricity generation capacity — and against arguably more essential tasks like heating and air conditioning, as well as electrifying transportation.
Many tech companies match their electricity use with renewable energy purchases. But unless they’re helping to build new sources of green energy to meet their added electricity demand, they might just end up hogging limited renewable energy capacity. And if more fossil fuels make up the difference, then greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise overall.
“Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?”
“In many cases, datacentres are outbidding other consumers to get speed to power,” Douglas says. “Should new green electrons be used for air-conditioning, electrification or data centres?”
There was some progress. Around 80 nations signed onto a voluntary pledge to increase electricity’s share of energy consumption to 35 percent over the next decade, according to COP31 president Murat Kurum. The list of countries that includes, however, hasn’t been published yet, Carbon Brief reports.
Another voluntary pledge to keep AI from derailing climate action by calling on data centers to run on less polluting energy also failed to garner much support. Douglas notes that by using the term “low-emission energy,” the pledge still leaves the door open for natural gas (which produces less carbon pollution than coal when burned but is a significant source of methane pollution) to keep powering data centers.
“The Antalya A.I. pledge is a step in the right direction to address an important piece of the impacts, but needs teeth in order to translate into stronger protections for people and the planet,” the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council said in a statement when the pledge was first announced. “The speed, scale and scope of this challenge is bigger than perhaps anything before it, and the guardrails must be commensurate.”

articles.title: Tesla annonce enfin un nouveau modèle grand public, mais attendez vous à une douche froide
articles.text:
Le Tesla Roadster est une révolution ! Non parce qu’il est capable des pirouettes les plus improbables. Juste parce qu’il s’agit d’un véhicule remplaçant un modèle existant. C’est peu, mais chez Tesla, c’est tout simplement historique ! Sauf que dans les faits, une telle folie sur roues a peu de chances de débarquer chez nous telle quelle. Tesla explique même qu’il est possible que le véhicule ne soit pas du tout livré !
Avouez que ça jette un froid… C’est peut-être la raison pour laquelle le constructeur vient d’annoncer un autre modèle plus raisonnable. Sauf qu’encore une fois, il y a un hic qui pourrait gâcher la surprise… Lors du sommet Dealbook du New York Times consacré à l’économie et à la politique, Elon Musk a confirmé l’arrivée d’un Model Y sans volant ni pédales « adapté pour transporter 6 ou 7 personnes ».
Un Model Y avec 7 places… mais sans volant ni pédales
Le soufflé retombe aussi sec, nous qui attendions avec impatience un nouveau modèle d’entrée de gamme. Inutile de dire qu’un Model Y sans aucune commande ne fait pas sauter au plafond… Pourtant, l’engin est censé combler l’attente avant l’arrivée du Roadster. Un peu maigre comme lot de consolation, vous l’accorderez. Pourtant, il s’agit bien d’un véhicule complémentaire au Cybercab, qui ne peut trimbaler que 2 occupants.
Musk l’a bien confirmé en expliquant que Tesla a « toujours besoin de véhicules autonomes si ses clients voyagent en famille ». C’est la raison pour laquelle la marque prévoit « une version autonome du Model Y qui n’aura pas de volant ou de pédales ». En y réfléchissant plus profondément, on se dit que le constructeur avait possiblement prévu le coup depuis 2016 avec la Model 3. Le tableau de bord ultra dépouillé n’était peut-être pas là par hasard.
Vers l’arrivée d’un Model Y L autonome en Europe ?
En retirant volant et pédales, vous vous retrouvez avec un intérieur parfaitement symétrique, comme sur le Cybercab ! Aucune information supplémentaire n’a cependant été livrée. Cela dit, le fait d’évoquer le transport de 7 personnes est un indice révélateur convergeant les hypothèses vers le Model Y L. Cette version rallongée du SUV offrant une meilleure praticité est néanmoins indisponible chez nous.
Elle pourrait bientôt l’être si ce futur véhicule est confirmé en Europe. On bénéficierait alors d’une version améliorée des Robotaxis circulant outre-Atlantique. Pour rappel, ces engins autonomes ne sont ni plus ni moins des Model Y pouvant être utilisés à la demande. Mais ils conservent leurs volants et pédales, par sécurité. Et ils ne sont pas à vendre, contrairement au Cybercab. Le futur Model Y L autonome devrait donc suivre la même recette.
